en: [That which is] devoid of the operations of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśa*), both, the self (*ātman*), and so forth; [that which is] mobile;
the support for the determination of action (*karman*), its fruit, their connection, and so on;

[that which is] empty of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), actions (*kriyā*), universals (*jāti*), and inherence (*samavāya*); and [that which is] the object of words and cognitions whose forms are superimposed [upon it].
[That which is] ascertained by the two means of valid cognition (*pramā*) endowed with clear characteristics, even by the slightest part, is not mixed with anything else in nature;
it is non-transmigrating, without beginning or end, resembling a reflection and the like, free from the entire mass of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and unattainable by others.

Having bowed down to that Omniscient One—the best among speakers—who, out of a desire to bring about the welfare of the world, spoke of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through countless incalculable eons, he who is free from attachment to independent scripture (*svatantra-śruti*), whose great compassion has become his very self; this *Tattvasaṃgraha* (Compendium of Reality) is now being composed.
From the primary cause alone—specifically from that which is accumulated and possesses all powers without exception—the various effects proceed forth, having the very same nature as it.
If an effect were to exist as a non-existent thing by virtue of its potentiality within the cause, it could not indeed be produced, because of its lack of form, just like a sky-lotus.
Why do they grasp only specific appropriated aggregates (*upādāna*)— such as rice seeds and the like— by way of distinction, yet not another [aggregate],

even though non-existence (*asattva*) is equal [in all cases] and everything that possesses the nature of arising (*dharmaka*) would arise from everything, because there is no distinction in the absence (*vigama*) of their identity (*tādātmya*) with respect to all things?
[If it is argued that] "it is not thus because of the restriction of these powers," this is no answer; for causes are capable only of producing an effect that is possible [for them].

And how indeed could that which is devoid of excellence (*atiśaya*), formless (*nīrūpa*), and unchanging (*avikāri*) be produced by them? For if there were modification (*vikṛti*), there would follow the loss of its own nature (*ātman*).

Since an effect is thus impossible [without a cause], what could be acting so as to be a cause? Therefore, even the state of being a cause for the first [moment] of a seed and so forth is clearly observed to be accompanied by pleasure and so forth, because of the perception here of the effect's serenity, heat, dejection, and so on; hence, the followers of Kapila [conclude] thus from the observation of that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with that genus.

That [pleasure and so forth] which is produced from that [primordial matter] and consists of that, and its differentiation—starting with the "whence" (*kutaḥ*) and so on—the wise have declared that the *pradhāna* is the cause here. Furthermore, the objection (*codanā*) is equal in regard to the existence [of the effect]; as for the answer to that [objection], it is the same for the wise as it is for you.

If curds and so forth exist in every way within the substances such as milk—which already possess their own nature—then what is there for them to produce? That effect is not something to be generated from the existence of its cause, just like the cause itself or its cognition;
therefore, it is like that which is not yet to be accomplished, such as another's self.

If there exists some [entity] that is distinct [from its causes] and so forth, and it goes toward the state of being expressible, then if it existed previously, an answer has already been given; if it did not exist, how can it obtain manifestation from them?

21. Therefore, there is no object to be established [by the argument] that "there is no grasping of material causes, nor birth even from a specific cause, nor power, nor activity, because [the effect] is produced in its entirety [already]; hence, even the designation of 'cause' is not tenable."
Every means [of knowledge], being [already] established, would not be a remover of error nor a producer of certainty; thus it is not consistent with reason.
Furthermore, since doubt and error would never cease to exist, there would be no arising of certainty at all; therefore, everything would be in vain.

Now, if it is argued that even an unreal certainty might arise from a means of proof (*sādhana*), then surely all these [means of proof] would be fallacious (*vyabhicārin*). If you say this, [we reply]: What manifestation (*vyakti*) could there be for this [certainty], which is unmanifest (*avyakta*) prior to its figurative expressions (*bhākta*)? There is no production [of it], because there is no differentiation of excellence (*atiśaya*) and because there is no connection (*asaṅgati*).
There is no destruction of that object-domain because of the perception of an obscuration; even if [the cause] were eternal, it is impossible for a second perception [to arise].

Likewise, since there is no differentiation in the three qualities (*triguṇa*), everything is not a causal agent of everything. Similarly, since there is no existence [of distinct entities], everything is not a causal agent of everything.
Because [they] are produced, those powers do not have limits; they are not restricted to existence. Is it not indeed logical that their restriction has a limit?
It is not so; let there be no such thing through their production. Furthermore, there is no harm to the nature of the entity as distinct from all adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).

The form (*rūpa*) of things (*vastūnām*), which is that wherein conceptual constructions (*vikalpāḥ*) and denoters (*vācakāḥ*)—all manner of conceptualizations (*viśva-kalpāḥ*)—proceed (*pravarttante*) according to habituation (*yathābhyāsam*) toward that which is non-differentiated (*abhedini*), is indeed the arising (*utpādaḥ*) of the thing (*vastu*). That [arising] is not connected (*sambadhyate*) with an existent (*satā*) in that way, but rather it is connected only with a non-existent (*asatā*) through a conceptualizing cognition (*kalpikayā dhiyā*).

The form of the substance (*vastu*) is perceived immediately; it did not exist priorly as a single [entity], nor was there its seed. However, that which is considered to be curd and so forth exists within milk and so forth in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*). What kind of potentiality for curd and so forth would be seen, like that of milk?

If [something] else [is meant], how can the existence of *sattva* be said [to exist] without figurative usage (*abhaktyā*)? The existence of *sattva* is clearly established for us in some way as being inherent in pleasure (*sukha*), delusion (*moha*), and so forth, because they are internal to one's own consciousness (*svasaṃvid*).

Due to [their] distinction (*bhedataḥ*), [qualities such as] cultivation (*bhāvanā*), genus (*jāti*), attachment (*saṅga*), and so forth, are perceived (*lakṣyante*) as being restricted (*niyatāḥ*) to a single [object], such as a word (*śabda*) and the like. If [the object] were not included [within that single entity], then a single cognition (*saṃvit*) of one thing would result in being variegated (*citrā*).
And if [it were so], it would not follow (*anuyāyinī*) from the object by virtue of [factors such as] the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so on.

How can those [cognitions], which possess a single form, be appropriate as being of three forms with respect to an object? How could they, being of a different character from that [object], be joined to it?
Furthermore, how is it that for yogins, pleasure, agitation, and obscurations arise toward a single man who is desired by them, yet is not of that same nature for others?

Even if the Manifested (vyakta) is established as consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), the Primal Nature (pradhāna) is not proven to be a single, eternal cause of that [Manifested]; for it is not endowed with a single genus (ekajāti).

All individual instances (*vyaktayaḥ*) are seen as if they were iron rods (*ayaḥ-śalākā-kalpāḥ*), consisting of a sequence of conjunctions (*saṅgata-krama-ātmikāḥ*) mixed with conceptual constructions (*miśrita-kalpanā*).

Likewise, the various modifications (*vikāra-bhedāḥ*) such as clay (*mṛd-ādayaḥ*) are not seen as being endowed with a single genus (*eka-jāti-anvitam*) or having a single cause (*eka-nimittāḥ*), due to their distinctness (*vibhedataḥ*) from the lump of clay (*mṛt-piṇḍāt*).

Even if [the souls] possess the quality of being endowed with [qualities such as] consciousness (*cintya*) and so forth, if that were [only] prior [to creation], then why is it not equally [secondary] here as well?
Furthermore, even in the absence of a primary cause (*pradhāna*), all the diversity of effects and instruments, and so forth, would exist through the differentiation of power (*śakti*).
Others say that the Lord is the cause of all opinions; indeed, it is said that the insentient [matter], by itself, initiates its own cause for the sake of production.

Whatever possesses a specific arrangement (*viśeṣa-sanniveśa*) of its own constituent parts (*sva-ārambhaka-avayava*), such as a jar (*kalaśa-ādikam*) and the like, is understood through the reason (*hetu*) of being "possessed of intelligence" (*buddhimat*). Such [an object] is perceivable by two sense organs (*dvīndriya-grāhya*); however, that which is not so perceivable (*a-grāhya*) must have as its antecedent (*pūrvakam*) something "possessed of intelligence" (*buddhimat*). Therefore, by means of this [reason], atoms (*aṇavaḥ*) are considered [to be non-intelligent] by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

[The atoms] possess a substrate (*upādāna*) [of sentient beings], because they are endowed with consciousness (*cetanatva*), like [the threads and so forth] which possess form (*rūpādimat*) and are seen to be the makers (*kṛt*) of their own effects (*svakārya*).

All dharmas and adharma-s, as well as the atoms (*aṇavaḥ*), are initiators (*ārambhakāḥ*) of their own effects, being presided over (*adhiṣṭhitāḥ*) by a conscious agent (*cetanavat*), because they proceed from that [consciousness], like a shuttle (*turi*) or a thread (*tantu*).
At the beginning of creation, the linguistic usage of men arises from [the teachings of] elders, because it is regulated by instruction, just like the linguistic usage of children.

The manifest, beginning with the great elements (*mahābhūta*), becomes the cause (*nimitta*) of pleasure and pain for the entire world; this is clearly perceived as being presided over by Him (*tasya*), because it possesses the qualities of having an intelligent cause (*buddhimaddhetumat*), being insentient (*acetanatva*), being an effect (*kāryatva*), being perishable (*vināśitva*), and so forth—just like an axe (*vāsī*) and other such tools. All of this is clearly understood.

When the agency of all [things] is established, omniscience is established without effort; because the agent who experiences the effects of form and so forth is clearly a perceptible entity for someone, by virtue of reasons such as the existence of the entity,
just like the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth.

In this first proof, there is the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason (*hetu*), because the "arrangement" (*saṃniveśa*) designated as "conjunction" (*yoga*) is not established, nor is the "whole" (*avayavin*) established in that way, due to the non-perception (*anupalambhana*) of both [the arrangement and the whole] which were accepted as being perceptible (*dṛśyatva*); furthermore, this example (*udāharaṇa*) is also irrelevant (*ananvita*) to the proof (*sādhana*).

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises (*upajan*) through the eye (*cakṣus*) and the tactile organ (*sparśana*) when there is the presence (*ābhā*) of those two as its single objective support (*ekālambanatā*). It does not exist [in that way] like the cognition (*vitti*) of odor (*gandha*) and so forth.

Consciousness determines (*vyavasyati*) the aggregate (*samudāya*)—which consists of that [capacity] and is produced by following after conceptual construction (*anugatikalpanā*)—by means of its own capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Therefore, this [entity] such as water, fire, and so forth, is certainly not to be apprehended by two sense-faculties (*dvīndriya-grāhya*), just as there is a lack of establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) when the subject (*dharmin*) has been stated to be unestablished; for even though the specific configuration (*saṃniveśaviśiṣṭatva*) found in things such as temples (*devakulādi*) is perceived when an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*) is observed as the maker (*kartṛ*).
In subjects such as the body, mountains, and so forth, something similar might be observed; therefore, it is logical that [the probandum] follows from this means of proof (*sādhana*).

For the rule is established thus: whatever is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the effect of something, the determination of that [cause] is seen in that [effect]. Thus is the principle settled.

However, such a specific configuration (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*) does not exist at all in these various instances of bodies, trees, and so forth; for the word alone, when stated in that manner, incurs the fallacy of a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekatā*) in cases such as anthills made by potters.

[Objection: Is this not a futile rejoinder (*jāti-uttara*), because it establishes the proof (*sādhana*) through the conceptual differentiation (*vikalpanāt*) of properties (*dharma-bheda*)? [Response: It is indeed the demonstration (*pratipādana*) that the universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth are merely the exclusion (*parāvṛtta*) of other things (*vastu-mātra*) from what does not possess that nature (*a-tad-rūpa*). Since there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the probandum and the proof (*sādhane*), this [rejoinder] does not exist here.
The self (*ātman*), seen as smoke, possesses non-deviation from fire; yet from the mere fact of being denotable by the word "white," there is no comprehension of that [fire], even from snow.

However, when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) regarding a universal (*sāmānya*), and a specific instance (*viśeṣa*) is resorted to as the basis for the injunction (*codanā*), it is in such a case that this is cited as a "refutation based on a genus" (*jātyuttara*).

The expressibility by words of "motherhood," "cowness," and "hornedness" would be established otherwise [than through inference], if this same logic applied to the directions and so forth; for this [logic] does not apply to the diamond.
If it were applicable in this case of valid cognition, then once it is established here through reasoning, there could be no dispute regarding anything whatsoever.
However, [the concept of] a single, eternal, and omniscient substratum possessing eternal consciousness does not attain proof, due to the deficiency of pervasion regarding the probandum.
Likewise, palaces, staircases, gate-towers, watchtowers, and so forth, are ascertained to be preceded by multiple, non-eternal cognitions.

For this very reason, even this [argument] is accepted as being a destroyer of what is desired, because it establishes [the existence of a creator] preceded by many non-eternal cognitions; yet the connection [between these] was stated by you merely as a logical reason (*hetu*). This is clearly expressed by us in the second [case].

[If they were] eternal, [they would be] non-performers of effects, because of the contradiction between an effect and [the notions of] succession and simultaneity; and because of their being successive, succession would [belong] even to the cognitions of that [Ishvara].

Furthermore, the cognition of Ishvara would be successive, due to its connection with successive objects of knowledge, just as the cognition of Devadatta and others has as its object a flame and so forth.

A jar and so forth are asserted by us to be merely an aggregation of atoms, the potter and other such factors being their very causes; therefore, the property [of being produced] desired as the probandum is not excluded from this example of an atom that has been illustrated by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

As for that which is intended [by you] as being preceded by an intelligent agent (*pūrvaka-buddhimat*) in a general sense, we have no dispute regarding that; for, in the proof that the manifold variety of the world (*vaiśvarūpya*) is born of karma, there is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the probandum (*sādhya*), because [the world] is empty of a prior, eternal, and single intelligence, since [buildings such as] palaces and the like are seen to be constructed by many [agents].

This alone is appropriate; just as another refutation might be applied, [it is shown that] having briefly explained [the point], [the existence of] atoms and so forth is not established through their momentary destruction. Therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule] regarding its occurrence in succession.
At the time of dissolution, [if] we humans lack consciousness and memory due to the destruction of the manifestation [of the faculties], then, since [the state of being] here arises from that,

if [there is] the status of being a teacher for one who is turned away [from the world], it must be accepted as such through faith, because [he possesses] the qualities of non-materiality and discernment regarding dharma and adharma.

In every case, there is a contradiction regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the proof by inference (*anumāna-sādhana*). A pervasion of the reason (*hetu*) with a contradictory property (*viruddha-dharma*) is not possible.

God (*īśvara*) is not the cause (*hetu*) of produced things (*janmin*), because he is devoid of the capacity for production (*utpatti-vikalatva*), like a sky-lotus (*gagana-ambhoja*). Otherwise, everything would come into existence simultaneously (*yugapat*).

Those [things] which arise sequentially, having God as their cause—just like the notions that have arisen among the dull-witted regarding the aforementioned proof—regarding the arising of those [notions], the designation "God" as a means of proof is fruitless because of his eternality; thus, he cannot be an auxiliary cause at all.

For one by whom [the cause] has never been seen among non-existent things when existent things are present, how can there be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) for him in the state of being a cause? By the refutation of [his] agency, his omniscience is also to be understood as rejected through the very same force (*balena*).

Even if the means of proof (*sādhana*) were not defective (*duṣṭa*) as previously stated, nevertheless, because the oneness of the agent (*kartṛ*) has been shown to be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), and because a single agent is unestablished (*asiddhi*), the proof (*sādhana*) that was proclaimed as the basis for [the agent's] omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) shines forth only among the followers of Jaimini (*jaiminīya*).
Because [they] have been refuted individually— both the causality of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and that of the Lord (*īśvara*),
as well as both together— they are not the creator of living beings.

The conjunction (*sāhitya*) of these two [causes], when imagined (*kalpite*) due to their being co-operative (*sahakāritvāt*), would either exist by virtue of [the first cause] imparting (*ādhānāt*) an excellence (*atiśaya*) [to the second], or it would be the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of a single effect (*ekārtha*) for the first [cause]. [However,] such a conceptualization is not tenable (*na yuktā*) for those two [causes]; nor is it [tenable] for the second [cause] alone, because that would entail the simultaneous occurrence (*yaugapadya*) of all effects.

It is said: "Established as the cause of creation, Maheśvara is then joined with *rajas*. But when he again resorts to *sattva*, whose function has become manifest, he becomes the instrumental cause of the stability of the entire world. When he is joined with *tamas*..."

At that time, by means of its manifested power (*udbhūta-śakti-rūpeṇa*), this [Pradhāna] effects the dissolution (*pralaya*) of the entire world (*sarva-jagataḥ*). Since *sattva*, *rajas*, and so forth are its auxiliary factors (*sahakāriṇaḥ*), there is no lack of sequence (*akrama*) among the effects (*kāryāṇām*) here;
rather, it is said that at the time of those two [dissolution and creation], there exists the capacity (*sāmarthyam*) for that [Pradhāna] to bring about other effects in succession.

If that [duality] does not exist, or even if it exists at the time of creation, then another duality would also come to be; thus, if there is the existence of one thing, another duality follows as a consequence.

Furthermore, that [cause] which is a factor of action (*kāraka*) is not [existent] in another form; its own nature (*svarūpa*) is precisely that [same thing]. From where, then, could there be a cessation of its activity?

However, in the absence of its causal capacity (*sāmarthya*), it could never be a producer of that [effect], because it would be devoid of power (*śaktiśūnya*), just like a lotus and so forth at other times.

If the intense form were the sole cause of the capacity, then that [capacity] would exist at all times because of the constant presence of the cause—the eternal form. Furthermore, nothing else is accepted by the opponents; therefore, this [capacity] does not arise from anything other than itself, as it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatva*). Thus, it is indeed independent.
[In the case] of an entity, [there is] indeed no self-causation because it is contradictory for an entity to act upon itself; for the occurrence of entities is occasional.
For indeed, the activity of a non-entity toward its own self is not admitted, since that which is already established is well-known to be so in this state.
The self-nature (*ātmatattva*), being unproduced, is not active anywhere, because it is devoid of all powers, like a sky-lotus and so forth.

The arising of entities is described by those who propound the doctrine of "independence from all causes" (*nirāśaṃsa-sarvahetuvādibhiḥ*) as being without dependence [on causes]. For they do not even state their own cause.
For who indeed creates the diversity of lotuses, their filaments, and so forth? Or by whom was the variegated plumage of peacocks and such fashioned?
Just as the sharpness and other qualities of thorns and the like are without cause—occurring only occasionally—in the same way, suffering and the rest are without cause.

When the cause—consisting of the seed, mud, water, and so forth—is ascertained through perception and non-perception to be present in the filaments and other parts of the lotus, and is pervaded by the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with its specific states (*atiśayāvasthā*), then why is another cause for these [parts] being asked?

If place and time were restricted (*niyatau*), how could they belong to all things? If they did not exist [as such], these things would lack causality; yet you [maintain that] they exist everywhere, at all times, and furthermore, that they are restricted to a particular place, a particular time, and a particular thing.

They are dependent on that; therefore, the occurrence of something other than that [which is to be excluded] is likewise called "dependence" (*apekṣā*) and "being an effect" (*kāryatā*). Thus, the occurrence is directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*); by that, the reasons (*hetavaḥ*) are established (*siddhāḥ*).

That [theory]—the claim that [the reason] possesses an intrinsic nature—is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the form of the reason is ascertained through both perception and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

Alternatively, even if the existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were not established for the sake of proving the reality of the reason, nevertheless, due to the absence of such a means of cognition, there can certainly be no ascertainment of the non-existence of the object.

Since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of existence (*sattā*), because of the presence of distinctions (*bheda*) in the object (*artha*) and because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) arising from that [existence],

that which is not of such a nature— due to its exclusion (*nivṛtti*) from that— is understood as being non-connected (*asambandha*) [to it] and thus inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to anything else.

Non-perception (*adṛṣṭi*) of everything is doubtful; non-perception of one's own [absence] is deviant (*vyabhicāriṇī*), as in the case of *dūrvā* grass and the like, even when there is non-perception in the crevices of the Vindhya mountains.

If the reason (*hetu*) is not employed (*prayujyate*) for the sake of establishing [the probandum], then there is no establishment (*siddhi*) that is devoid of a cause (*ahetukatva*). Furthermore, an unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇikī*) establishment does not exist; therefore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not established (*sidhyati*).
Even if a reason (*hetu*) is employed for the sake of establishing that [object], nevertheless, because it is not the production (*janya*) of the reason, it is not [the cause of] its establishment.

For in that way, a reason is called "indicative" (*jñāpaka*), or a statement (*vacas*) is said to be "indicative" of the probandum (*sādhya*), by virtue of its being the means of establishment (*siddhi*).

Therefore, it is the *kāraka* (the producer) alone that is called [a cause], whereas the *jñāpaka* (the indicator), because it does not produce the object to be established (*sādhya*), is not designated as a *kāraka*.

Consequently, even those other things which possess causes for their arising are restricted by that [nature]; thus, they possess a cognition of the object to be established that arises subsequent to the means of proof (*sādhana*).

This collection of entities (*bhāva-grāma*) is perceived as a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of that Brahman, which consists of sound (*śabda-maya*), is supreme, and is untouched by destruction or origination. As for those who also declare [it] thus, they must be asked: having abandoned its form as sound, does it enter into the state of being blue and so forth, or not? If the first position is maintained...

[Pass. (Then) there would be a separation from the nature of the syllable due to its prior destruction; or else, on the other hand, the cognition of blue and so forth would clearly be a cognition whose nature is sound, even though [the sound] has not been heard.

By which [it], everything is established in its primary sense as consisting of sound (*śabdamaya*) by way of its basis (*nidhānataḥ*; i.e., by way of its designation), without abandoning its nature as a transformation of sound;
and thus, when blue and so forth are one in a non-figurative sense, how could there not be the cognition of this [blue] at the time of the cognition of that?
If this [cognition] were not perceived, there would be no awareness even of blue and so forth, because of their identity; for even if they possess distinct properties, an absolute difference follows.
Indeed, the association with contradictory properties is the definition of the difference among many things; otherwise, even that [difference] among individuals would not be imagined.

If a single word-nature (*śabdātmā*) is asserted to be distinct for each individual object (*prati bhāvam*), then it would follow that all [words] possess the quality of occupying the same location (*ekadeśatva*). However, if there is a difference with respect to each individual manifestation (*vyakti*), then Brahman would result in being manifold (*aneka*), because its own form (*ātmarūpa*) is divided, just like the diversity of individual manifestations (*vyaktibheda*).
Even if the word "eternal" has the suffix "-maya-", the eternality of entities cannot be established on the basis of their simultaneity; therefore, transformation is not tenable.

For transformation could only be established if there were the disappearance of one form and the simultaneous emergence of another form—as in the case of clay and so forth—but this is not possible in the absence of succession.

Even if the world consists of the Word-Brahman (*śabda-brahma*) in the form of its effects, nevertheless, because it is changeless, there can be no sequential emergence from it. Since they arise mutually from that single essential nature, how indeed could it be said that [the world] has ceased in the form of objects?

In the case of various [products] such as jars and boxes, because they are perceived [as having] the nature of clay, that which is excluded from that form [of clay]—being of a different nature—is postulated here as a single essence of clay;
however, blue, yellow, and so forth are not perceived in this way. Furthermore, even the conceptual construction of their exclusion from the word "self" (*ātman*) lacks a seed.
Now, this reality of Brahman, which is eternally undifferentiated, is perceived by the world as manifold due to the affliction of ignorance.

Even there, form exists in a manner characterized by blue and so forth; yet, for people overwhelmed by ignorance, how could that form—which is the basis for rejection and acceptance—be perceived as the uncharacterized form of Brahman by minds that have emerged from meditative absorption, were it not through its existence?

That [entity], being undivided, is not established through perception because it does not appear; nor is there a mark consisting of an effect [produced] from a permanent [cause] due to the impossibility of its arising;

and since the existence of a property-possessor (*dharmin*) is unestablished, an essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be a prover; furthermore, apart from these, there is no mark that can establish [the existence of] being (*sattā*).

Cognition is established as arising sequentially from the object of knowledge; otherwise, its effect, which is consciousness, would follow simultaneously. Furthermore, even in the case of a mere [object], cognition cannot have a form that is distinct from it; therefore, there is an identity between the son and the barren woman.

Therefore, even yogis whose mental continuums are purified by knowledge do not perceive the form of that which arises from conjunction when their cognition is occupied; furthermore, the vision of Brahman must be understood here as being equal to the transformation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), for that [view] is subject to refutation.
But others, whose intellects follow poorly expounded doctrines, imagine a Person who is the Lord of Dharma and the Creator of the World;
he is said to be possessed of power and unimpaired knowledge even during the dissolution of all things, being indeed the cause of all living beings, just as a spider is the cause of its threads.
The refutation of this [position] is as follows: Even if [the world] were like Īśvara, for what purpose would he perform such an activity as this?
If his independence (*svatantratā*) is due to being employed by another, then [on the other hand], he might create the world as exclusively happy out of compassion.
Compassion is perceived toward that person who is afflicted by mental anguish, poverty, grief, and so forth;
even though compassion did not exist prior to creation, the Creator is nevertheless postulated as the possessor of compassion, yet this is not logically tenable.
And he would not always bring about the dissolution of yogins [possessing] spiritual prosperity; for, in dependence upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), his sovereignty is forfeited.
For what purpose does he look toward an unseen cause of suffering? Furthermore, when compassion is present, indifference toward him alone is appropriate.
If his activity were for the sake of play, he would not be the master of play, because of his dependence on various means of sporting, just like a child.

Whatever means of accomplishment there may be for that pleasure which is to be achieved through play—if one who is capable of its production were to perform all of it simultaneously—[then that would be possible].
If [it] were not [existent] at the beginning, it would not be capable [of acting] sequentially; for capacity and incapacity are both applicable to an undivided entity.

Now, if its activity at the beginning of creation is described as being due to its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), just as [the nature] of fire and the like [is established] in relation to actions such as burning, so too [is this] by its very essence (*prakṛtyā*).

Therefore, if all entities were to exist simultaneously due to the proximity of a cause endowed with the capacity for production, then the powers existing within things such as fire would be restricted solely by the force of their own causes and would not exist at all times.
Otherwise, every effect would arise simultaneously; if [this were so], even for those [causes], this restriction is not admitted.
Even the spider (*ūrṇanābha*) is not admitted to possess causality with respect to its threads; for by its very nature it produces a web of saliva out of a craving for devouring living beings.
What kind of intelligence is this [person's], whose activity is such that he proceeds even slowly without having examined what ought to be done?
Those who are conceived as the sustainers, beginning with the Self-born (Brahmā) and others—by this very method, they are in reality refuted.

Furthermore, others here maintain that there exists a self (*ātman*), which is the substratum of desire and the other [mental states], which is by its own nature non-conscious, eternal, and likewise all-pervading.

The agent (*karttāram*, masculine ṛ-stem, nominative singular); the enjoyer (*bhoktāram*, masculine ṛ-stem, nominative singular) of the fruits of good and evil deeds (*śubha-aśubhānām*, neuter, genitive plural); that consciousness (*cetanam*, neuter, nominative singular) is not [an agent] by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Rather, its status as an agent (*kartṛtvam*, neuter, nominative singular) is said to arise from its connection (*yogāt*, masculine, ablative singular) with consciousness (*cetanā-*) and its relation (*sambandhaḥ*) to knowledge (*jñāna-*) and effort (*yatna-*) and so forth. Its state as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*, feminine), however, consists in its inherence (*samavāyaḥ*) in cognition (*saṃvitti-*) and pleasure (*sukha-*) and pain (*duḥkha-*) and so forth.
[Its] birth is designated by means of a specific collection of unprecedented cognitions, feelings, and so forth;
[its] death is the separation from them prior to [the present] existence; and its "rebirth" is the conjunction with the mind, accompanied by merit and demerit, while still possessing a body.

Violence (*hiṃsā*, feminine, nominative singular) is attributed (*kalpyate*, passive of *kḷp*) to this [person] (*asya*, neuter, genitive singular) on account of the destruction (*vadhāt*, masculine, ablative singular) of the body, eyes, and so forth (*śarīra-cakṣur-ādīnām*, masculine, genitive plural). Even so (*ittham api*), this process (*eṣā prakriyā*, feminine, nominative singular) is observed (*īkṣyate*, passive of *īkṣ*) to be pure (*vimalā*, feminine, nominative singular) even with respect to an eternal person (*puṃsi nitye*, masculine, locative singular).

My cognitions (*jñānāni*) are to be known (*vedyāni*) by a perceiver (*saṃvedakena*) distinct (*vyatirekiṇā*) from them, because they possess the nature of being cognitions of reality and so forth (*tattvādipratyayatvāt*), like that which is other than them (*tadanyavat*).

All these [qualities], beginning with desire (*icchādayaḥ*), are dependent upon something (*kvacitsamāśritāḥ*), provided that there exists a substantial entity (*vastutve sati*), because they are effects (*kāryatvāt*), like color-form (*rūpavat*); and that [entity] is our Self (*sa naḥ pumān*).

Because [it] is apprehended, [the property of] being a real entity (*vastutva*) is not subject to deviation in regard to destruction; for even though destruction possesses a cause, it nonetheless possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastutā*).

All cognitions (*pratyaya*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth have a single or multiple cause (*nimitta*) by way of their actual existence (*bhāvataḥ*). Because of the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of these [cognitions], I, as it were, am a cognition; otherwise, the synthesis of many [cognitions] regarding the movement of a dancer’s brow-creeper would arise without a basis (*anibandhana*).

The word (*vacana*), which is considered to be a single term (*eka-pada*) distinct from the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and so forth—since it is held to be so—is the designator (*abhidhāyaka*) of the self (*ātman*).
That which is thus determined, being established as synonymous (*paryāya*) [with "self"], is stated by the property (*dharma*) as exemplified by the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) as previously indicated.
This living body might be devoid of breath and so forth, because of its selflessness, like a jar; therefore, it does not indeed possess selflessness.

Every subsequent consciousness (*uttara-vijñāna*) is indeed perceived (*vedyate*) by the perceiver (*vedakena*) who has arisen from the initial consciousness (*ādya-vijñāna*), because it possesses the nature of being produced immediately (*sadyas-tvāt*), just like the initial cognition (*ādya-jñāna-vat*).

Furthermore, that [subsequent consciousness] is also logically consistent (*yukta*) even with respect to a distant location (*dūra-deśa*), because it is possessed of a material form (*mūrttimattvāt*), like my own body (*asmadīya-śarīra-vat*).

When there is a definitive determination (*viniścaya*) of the self (*ātman*) as being thus characterized by sentience (*sattva*), permanence (*nityatva*), and omnipresence (*vibhutva*), [the opponent might argue] that "all phenomena (*sarva-dharmāḥ*) are not without a self (*na nirātmānaḥ*).

In this regard, at the first [point], the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is established (*siddha-tā*), because the state of being known (*pravedyatva*) by your omniscient knowledge (*sarvajña-jñāna*) and so forth is accepted (*iṣyate*).

Consciousness (*cit*) arises (*prajāyate*) as its own conscious form (*sva-cit-rūpa*), independent (*an-apekṣam*) [of external objects] and illuminating (*prakāśaka*). In this way, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also an example (*nidarśana*) for the [proposition that it is] empty (*śūnya*) of [external objects], which is the point to be proven (*sādhya*).

Even so, if that [consciousness] is taken as the illustrative instance (*udāharaṇatve*), then since it is perceived (*pravedyate*) by means of a colored mental aspect (*ākāra-uparaktena*), there would arise a doubt (*saṃśaya*) regarding it [as being empty] by another [cognition].

If it is established that desire and so forth are dependent upon something, and if in that case a mere cause is postulated as their substratum, then what you desire is proven. However, if you maintain that the substratum is the support [of desire and so forth], then that conception of a substratum is devoid of any logical movement and is fruitless.

A locus such as a pit is established (*upapadyate*) as the support (*āśraya*) of jujube fruits and the like, either by way of obstructing their movement (*vibandha-gateḥ*) or by producing a specific quality (*viśeṣa-utpādanena*).

However, it is not at all logical (*naiva yuktimat*) for that which is formless (*nīrūpa*), namely destruction (*nāśa*), to possess the status of an effect (*kāryatva*). Therefore, the qualification stated by others regarding the reason (*hetau*) here is redundant (*vyartham*).
This [notion of] "reconnection" (*pratisandhāna*) appears to me, due to the affliction of ignorance and so forth, as a unity [of the perceiver] or an agent across all momentary [states].

However, because of this false conceptualization (*mithyā-vikalpa*), the persistence of reality (*tattva-saṃsthiti*) is not tenable; nevertheless, even though they are distinct, there exists a basis for unity due to their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

If mental states (*cittānām*) were the effects (*kāryatve*) of [the sense objects] such as form (*rūpa-*) and sound (*śabda-*) and so forth, then their single, continuous sequence (*eka-anugāmika-paurvāparyam*) would be contradicted (*viruddhyate*). Since they arise from the presence (*sannidheḥ*) of the causal capacities (*kāraṇa-śakta*), the manifestation (*samudbhavaḥ*) of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-*) is clearly perceived (*vedyate*) as occurring simultaneously (*yugapat*) from a single immediately preceding consciousness (*eka-anantara-vijñānāt*); therefore, the proof (*prasādhanam*) is established as desired (*iṣṭa-*).

It is not logical for those occurring in succession to have a single cause immediately following [the first]; therefore, because of this pervasion, a clear contradiction of inference is observed here, like the knitting of the eyebrows of a dancing girl. Indeed, it is not a single entity, because it is a collection of many atoms; its unity is merely conceptualized.

If [the word] "one" is intended to be the object (*gocara*) of the word "single effect" because of its utility, then even if it is thus desired as the probandum (*sādhya*), the proof (*sādhana*) is established;
for even in the case of words such as "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "mind" (*citta*), there is the denotation of a single term (*eka-pada-abhidhāyitā*) despite their distinctness.

Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). [Objection: But has that qualification not been stated? [Reply: It is said: "It is certainly not established," because of the persistence of synonymy (*paryāyatā-sthiteḥ*).

The mind (*citta*), as the substratum (*āśrayatvena*), is called the "I-maker" (*ahaṅkāra*)—thus it is designated as the "self" (*ātman*); however, its object (*viṣaya*) is not perceived through conventional reality (*saṃvṛttyā*) by means of the mental function (*vṛttyā*) directed toward an entity (*vastu*).

Therefore, even that which is the single word "beginning" (*ādi*) as the active agent is seen to be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāraḥ*), since it is applied at the outset to such things as the surface of the sky (*nabhas-tala*) or a lotus (*aravinda*).
Words, which are merely conventional designations, are not connected with anything; nor indeed is there any manifestation of meaning by words through their own nature (*prakṛti*).

If a connection between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth were established as being together with the Self (*ātman*), then this consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be logical; otherwise, it is inconsistent.

If [the self] were empty, it would not follow that the living body is the son of a barren woman, provided there is no separation from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. For this same consequence applies to you as well here;
for we do not admit their identity due to their difference, nor is there a relation of cause and effect, because of their simultaneity.
For if that [self] were to cease, then why would these [functions], such as prāṇa and apāna—which are devoid of any connection with it—cease from the body?

Furthermore, since the existence of a self is not established by any means of proof, the example cited for [proving] its eternity and omnipresence is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya-hīna*).

The establishment of the self (*ātman*) as being established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is imagined by others [as] self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*)— since the self is held to be the object of this [notion of] "I-consciousness" (*ahaṅkāra*)—

is untenable, because its form (*rūpa*), such as eternality (*nityatva*) and omnipresence (*vibhutva*), does not appear within that [consciousness], for no manifestation (*nirbhāsa*) of such qualities is perceived therein.
The manifestation therein is clearly [of the form of] white color and so forth; however, its own nature as the self is not admitted. Therefore, this [self] is not the object of that [cognition].
If the person were truly apprehended by direct perception, then for what reason would this dispute proceed regarding his existence and so forth?

This ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) arises from the self (*ātman*), which is established as the basis for the determination and superimposition of the two cognitions (*buddhi*). Since it possesses the nature of being both the sublater (*bādhaka*) and the sublated (*bādhya*), therefore, desire (*icchā*) and all such [qualities] are certainly not inherent (*samavāyin*) in the self, because they arise sequentially, like the seed, sprout, and creeper.
Alternatively, all internal forms are pervaded by the reasons consisting of existence (*sattva*), [momentariness], and so forth, just like external objects such as jars;

for if those reasons possessed a self-nature (*sātmakatva*), it would follow that the self is eternal, and being eternal, it would be incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, [the reasons] do not lack existence and the other [properties].
That selflessness which is denied by others as existing in things such as jars is established by us as being the same in this living body.
Thus, since the self is not established, that entire framework which has been constructed remains, as it were, without foundation—like the son of a barren woman.

Others, however, maintain that the self is of the nature of consciousness, characterized by the exclusion [of others] and persistence; they hold the self to be defined by consciousness (*caitanya*) and intellect (*buddhi*).

Just as the state of being a coil (*kuṇḍalāvasthā*) of a snake (*ahi*) departs (*vyapaiti*), immediately thereafter the state of straightness (*ārjavāvasthā*) arises (*sambhavati*), yet its nature as a serpent (*sarpatva*) persists (*anuvarttate*);

even so, there is neither the complete disappearance of the form of the self (*ātman*)—which is of the nature of eternal consciousness (*nityacaitanya*)—nor is there the persistence of everything [else].
However, the states characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, undergo transformation (*vinivartante*); yet, consciousness (*caitanya*) persists (*anuvartate*).

For if there were absolute destruction (*atyantanāśa*), there would result both the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtāgama*) for one who is of a single nature; thus, there could be no experience (*bhoga*) of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

When the state of being an agent (*kartṛ-tva*) and an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-tva*) is not relied upon by the person (*puṃsaḥ*), then, because of that very nature, the person experiences the fruit (*phala*) in those various states (*avasthāsu*).

Such a person (*pumān*) is established (*pramīyate*) through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) as existing in reality (*bhāvataḥ*); for indeed, by this very [recognition], the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is refuted (*prabādhā*).

If the notion of "I" (the first-person singular) knows (*vedmi*), understands (*pratipadyate*), or [perceives] the knower (masculine, second person singular)—and if that [notion] were either the self (neuter, nominative singular) or knowledge (neuter, nominative singular) that is absolutely perishable—then [it would follow].

If the self were the object of that [cognition], then everything would be perfectly consistent; however, in the case of the doctrine of momentary cognition, everything is indeed extremely difficult to establish.

"For indeed, I knew [it] previously, and I know it now"—such is the cognition that arises; which moment of knowledge, then, is conceived as its object: is it the past, or the present, or is it that continuum?

(First section, verse 7) Having understood that "it is appropriate" (*yujyate*) in that case, [one realizes] that when the object is known, it is not appropriate to think, "I know this," because he does not know it now.

(Regarding the object, locative singular) (while it was present, locative singular), it is logically consistent (*upapadyate*) that I knew (*pravedmi*) it to be "unreal" (*asatya*), since this [object] did not exist at all previously (*prāk*).
Therefore, neither of these two is at all conceived as the apprehended object of that [cognition]; for neither of the two has known it previously, nor do they know it even now.

Furthermore, an external continuum of that [object] is impossible because a second [moment] does not exist; for that [continuum], having not been known previously, does not exist even now due to its lack of substantial reality.

Therefore, that in whose sphere of activity the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) operates is established as the Self (*ātman*), which is eternal by nature, distinct from what has been mentioned, and transcendent; furthermore, it is the knower (*jñātṛ*) who persists even today, because it is the object of the notion of "I" (*aham-pratyaya*), just like the present cognizer.

Or, this [person] is the knower of yesterday because he possesses the nature of a knower; for that very reason, by virtue of being a knower, he is like the knower of yesterday. Furthermore, all those cognitions—both those of yesterday and those of today—have as their object the same thing, because they are connected to a single continuum of a knower through the nature of the "I-cognition," just as [they are connected] to a single cognition.

In this regard, it is considered: if consciousness (*caitanya*) is held to be eternal, one, and thus, then even the intellect (*buddhi*) would necessarily be of that very same nature. Furthermore, the activities of the person (*puruṣa*), as well as the intellects themselves, would possess eternality and oneness due to their inherent nature of consciousness. If, however, there were a distinction based on its substratum (*āśraya*)—namely, the objects (*viṣaya*)—then [the objection does not hold].
Likewise, fire, by its own nature, is eternally characterized by the property of burning; it burns only the combustible object brought near to it, and not anything else, nor at any other time.
Or, just as a clear mirror, or as a crystal stone, receives the reflection of whatever is placed upon it.

In the same way, men, who are eternally conscious, perceive forms and other objects brought to them by the functions of the body and the instruments; and this intellect of ours is not eternal because of its susceptibility to agitation by the bringer, just as the fire is not eternally a burner due to the absence of combustible material.

In that case, cognition (*mati*) is recognized as being of the nature of awareness (*bodha*), which is accepted by the world as being identical to the intellect (*buddhi*), the pot, the elephant, and so forth.

However, because of their difference from that [intellect], the intellect itself is not called [the object] by those who follow the distinctions of objects; nor is there a lack of recognition when one relies upon the distinction of objects.

[Objection: But surely, those cognitions which, superimposing elephants and so forth, arise with respect to a ground that is empty—what is their basis? If [you say] it is the particulars (*vyakti*), [we reply] no, because they are dependent on other places and so forth; for otherwise, the object of cognition (*ālambana*) would exist everywhere, regardless of place and time.

[Objection: But surely there exists such a connection between those [elephants] and that location; why then do they appear in that form? For in your view, an external aspect (*ākāra*) is not attributed to the cognition, nor are the elephant, the staff, and so forth situated in the intended location.
If cognition is always of the nature of the apprehension of all objects, then for what reason is the consciousness of all [objects] not found at all times?
[If you say] "cognition has sound as its adjunct" or "has taste, form, and so forth as its domain," [we reply:
no, for those distinctions have not been established by you; thus, it is that very [consciousness].

Furthermore, fire would not be eternally of the nature of burning all combustible forms; otherwise, it would reduce them entirely to ashes even in the mere presence of a single combustible object. For indeed, the burning of all objects simultaneously is not observed.
Mirrors, crystals, and the like, being momentary, are the causes of the arising of an illusion [of] that reflection due to their connection with the blue lotus and so forth;
[they appear] either always in a state other than that [reflection], accompanied by an external substrate (*upadhāna*), or else they would be seen as separated from that [reflection] otherwise.
The surface of a mirror never at all bears a reflection, because of its stability, its indivisibility, and because material objects cannot coexist [within it].

When two sides are observed to be perfectly white like a crystal stone, even this [crystal] does not perceive its own shadow; yet it follows that there would be a distinction in the crystal and other such objects according to the substrate (*upadhāna*). If, however, there were a real perception of that shadow, it would have to exist as something ontologically real.

Therefore, this error [resides] in those [entities] possessing diverse and inconceivable powers; even in the case of cognition (*buddhi*), the existence of error is not tenable because of the absence of difference.
However, by superimposing a single identity upon all cognitions despite their multiplicity, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) proceeds based on the non-perception of their distinction.

Even though it is devoid of distinctions based on differences in state (*avasthā-bheda*), while a single, eternal Self (*ātman*) remains absolutely constant, these states such as pleasure, pain, and so forth are conceptually constructed (*parikalpyate*) within that Self; and even as a person undergoes change, he certainly does not relinquish his nature consisting of consciousness, substantiality, existence, and the like.
At the time of arising, the preceding state does not perish; rather, it merges into the universal self.
For there is mutual contradiction among the states by way of their own specific forms, whereas the universal self is perceived in all of them.
In that case, if the states were not absolutely distinct from the person, then those two—destruction and origination—would belong to him as well;
however, due to association with contradictory properties, there would necessarily be a difference [between them], just as you maintain for men through their own fixed individual natures.
And if your states dissolve into the Self by their very nature at the time of the emergence of nectar, suffering, and so forth, then [that emergence] would indeed be experienced;
furthermore, if there were a transition into another form, there would be no transition into something else, and the Self would be subject to arising through its identity with that transition.

If agency and enjoyership are dependent upon states, then there is no possibility of agency and so forth belonging to that which possesses the states, because of its being the substrate of those states.
Therefore, the expressibility of this [self] by the word "eternal" is not refuted, since it undergoes modification in its own nature; thus, its cessation exists.
Even a serpent undergoes crookedness and so forth because of its momentary nature; however, in that which possesses a stable form, there can be no connection with other states.
This ego-consciousness does not indeed proceed without a basis, owing to the power of beginningless seeds, perception, and existence—for this is certainly the case somewhere.

Certain conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) attain sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over that which is characterized by attachment to such-and-such a form; for that [sovereignty] does not exist everywhere [in all things].
Otherwise, this objection would be equal for you regarding the Person (*puruṣa*) as well, since everything would be free from confusion due to the existence of its specific capacity (*śakti*).

In that case, all ego-constructions (*ahaṃkṛti*) having a permanent object would arise simultaneously, because the cause—their capacity—is fixed. On the other hand, if the object were impermanent, they would appear clearly; therefore, others [the opponents] pointlessly interrogate the existence of an object as a basis.

The latent impression (*vāsanā*) is capable of producing recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the knower (*jñātṛ*). That [impression] is not the cause of error (*bhrānti*) with respect to what is not that [object]. Furthermore, this notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) is not accepted as being an error, because it is not sublated (*bādha-varjanāt*). If it is argued that it is not so, [we reply] no, because sublation of that [notion] has been demonstrated by the reasoning (*yukti*) stated immediately above.
How is it that from the mere existence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) various delusions (*vibhrama*) arise for devotees regarding Īśvara and others as being the cause, and so forth?
And thus, since objectlessness (*nirālambanatā*) resides in the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), there exists no knower (*jñātṛ*) with respect to the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*).

Therefore, in all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there exists no example that possesses established proof; furthermore, the reasons (*hetu*) cited according to their respective applications are themselves unestablished with respect to their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Others think that consciousness is distinct from the nature of the intellect; we, however, conceive of consciousness as being one's own inherent form, the very essence of the self.
He enjoys only the fruit presented by Pradhāna; he has no agency at all in that matter, for it is held to belong to Prakṛti alone.

Even in that case, if consciousness (*cetanā*) is held to be a single entity, how could the clearly distinct forms of mental states (*cetas*)—such as those of color (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth—be perceived (*vedyate*) within a consciousness (*caitanya*) that is of a single nature (*eka-rūpa*) and remains constant at all times? Indeed, how could the status of being an experiencer (*bhoktṛ-tva*) of various objects (*artha-nānāvidha*) be logically established?

The [desiderative nouns] beginning with *didṛkṣā* (the desire to see), being distinct [from the self], do not constitute the basis for its experience; for in that case, the person would be subject to origination.

Desire to see and so forth exist [in it], yet they are not distinct from consciousness. This [consciousness] exists during the occurrence of arising and passing away; this [arising and passing away] is unavoidable even for the Puruṣa.
If, moreover, pure and impure karma has not been performed by the Self itself, then how could its experience arise?
Nature bestows [the fruit] in accordance with desire; this connection between the two is established. For it is like the case of the lame man and the blind man.
If that is so, why is it that even when there is a longing for the desired object, nature does not bring it about? Nature certainly does not depend upon anything else.

Now, if at the time of enjoyment there were no modification whatsoever in this [self], it would possess the status of being an enjoyer; yet, if Prakṛti is its benefactor, then upon the existence of that modification, its eternity is lost—for modification is indeed a state of change. How could this occur while it remains in the same condition?

It is held that, at the outset, the intellect (*buddhi*), which possesses the form of the object (*viṣayākārā*), undergoes a transformation (*vivarttate*); the person (*puruṣa*) then perceives (*pratipadyate*) the object as determined by that [intellect].

Thus, by way of its being the enjoyer (*upabhoktṛtā*) of the arising of a reflection, this Puruṣa never abandons its own nature (*svarūpa*); it is said that when a reflection arises through identity (*tādātmyena*), there is no state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) in the case of a distinction (*vibhede*).

How indeed could the *pradhāna*, which is insentient by nature, know how to act—whether for the sake of diverse arrangements or in accordance with the desire to see and so forth—and yet not know how to enjoy? Therefore, what else could be more illogical?

Because the primary cause possesses intellect (*buddhimat*), everything is non-contradictory for it; however, by virtue of possessing intellect, consciousness (*caitanya*) is as if attained [by it], just as consciousness exists in the *puruṣas*.

(Buddhiḥ, f. nom. sg.)—intellect; (adhyavasāyaḥ)—determination; (saṃvit, f. nom. sg.)—consciousness; (saṃvedanam, n. nom. sg.)—experience; (saṃvittiḥ, f. nom. sg.)—awareness; and (cetanā, f. nom. sg.)—sentience—all these are synonyms (vācakam, n. nom. sg. for consciousness (caitanya-). If it is argued (matam, n. nom. sg. that "Buddhi is insentient (acetanā-) by nature (ātmikā, f. nom. sg.), like sound, smell, taste, and so forth (śabda-gandha-rasa-ādi-vat), because of its having an origin (utpattimattva-) and its being perishable (nāśitva-)," [then we reply:]

These two reasons, in their own right, are not established for both [parties] in the view of the proof; nor is there the undesirable consequence of a contradiction with the opposite [of what is intended], even though one wishes to state it.

There is no harm for us even in the application of the word "self" to consciousness; however, its eternality is difficult to establish because of [the existence of] the eyes and so forth which possess their respective fruits.
If consciousness were eternal, then objects, the eyes, and so forth would be fruitless; there would be no purpose for fuel if fire were eternal.

Furthermore, by that reason—namely, by virtue of being a composite (*saṃghātatva*)—the fact that the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) is established, just as in the case of beds, seats, and the like.

It is established that for these [entities], their status as having a preeminent nature (*atiśaya*) consists in being something to be produced (*ādheya*); thus, the proof of what is desired (*iṣṭasiddhi*) is achieved for you. Since we accept those who assist in the production of cognition (*jñānasādhana*) as being benefactors (*upakārin*), they are logically consistent with the example of a benefactor that is subject to change (*cala*). However, [if you maintain] that they are immutable (*avikārin*), then they are devoid of the quality of being a probandum (*sādhyasūnyatā*). Therefore, they are not suitable as examples of a benefactor.

However, even if their being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) is established in a general sense, the proof is nevertheless redundant, because [the objects] are already established as being useful to the mind.

The Jains, like the followers of Jaimini, say: "A person is characterized by the nature of persistence (*anugama*) through the form of substance (*dravya-paryāya*), and by the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) through the form of modification (*paryāya*)."

In that case as well, if the substance remains unmodified even when conjoined with its various states (*paryāya*), then there would be no distinction; thus it could not be said to be "subject to transformation" (*pariṇāmin*). However, there is indeed a distinction based on the difference in place, time, intrinsic nature, number, characteristic, name, and purpose.
Thus, a jar, color, and so forth, possess differentiation by number, differentiation by name, and differentiation by characteristic; they also possess continuity, function, purpose, and exclusion.
In this way, between substance and mode, the substance does not, in an absolute sense, remain without distinction; rather, it itself attains distinction through the form of the mode.

When there is oneness in the absence of difference of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), distinctness is difficult to establish in any way whatsoever, just as [it is impossible] for the self-nature of color and its modifications (*rūpaparyāya*).

Furthermore, if there were such oneness of substance and modification (*dravyaparyāya*) in a non-figurative sense, then the substance would exist as possessing the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the intrinsic natures of the modifications.
If your modes (*paryāyāḥ*) were also of the nature of following [the substance]—just as [the substance is]—then they would attain oneness of essence with that substance (*dravyeṇa*).

Therefore, substance (*dravya*), such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, exists (*vidyate*) as something established (*avasthita*), because it is not distinct from its modifications (*paryāya*), just like its own nature (*svarūpa*).
Furthermore, no modifications whatsoever are subject to arising (*udaya*) and passing away (*vyaya*), because they are not distinct from the substance, just like the fixed substance itself.

Therefore, either destruction or [the destruction of] everything that is stable must occur; however, these two—exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*)—do not exist at all within a single essence (*ekātman*).
There is no manifestation of a substance (*dravya*) whose nature (*rūpa*) is perceived as being inclusive of its modes (*paryāya*); thus, it does not exist, like a sky-lotus.

Those things which are capable of performing various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), which are the causes of cognitions having similar objects and so forth, and which are the referents of conventions, words, and concepts—these very phenomena, being mere synonyms, are perceived solely as arising and passing away; from that, selflessness (*nairātmya*) becomes clearly and most purely manifest.

Now, the unified form (*mūrchita-rūpa*) of substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) is indeed held to be dual-natured (*dvi-rūpa*), partless (*nirbhāga*), like Narasiṃha. [Objection: Is it not the case that this very dual-naturedness is the basis for the various designations (*nānārtha-nirdeśa*) by means of words (*śabdena*) denoting its essential nature (*rūpa-svabhāvasya*)?

(Narasiṃha): "Even so, he is not indeed one, nor is he dual-natured; for he is perceived as such. Likewise, the Self is a collection of many atoms. Others, however, say: "The earth, fire, water, and so forth are the illusory transformations (*vivarta*) of the eternal consciousness-Self; that [Self] is their essence."

Nothing here is conjoined with the characteristic of the apprehended; therefore, this entire transformation of consciousness is observed. However, their view contains little fault from the perspective of verbal expression, because the permanence [of the object] is indicated by way of its differentiation from the forms of color, sound, and so forth within consciousness.

If [the self] were of a single nature consisting of cognition, then form, sound, taste, and so forth would follow as being cognized simultaneously; moreover, in that which is eternal, there can be no succession of states.
Cognition is not perceived as distinct from the consciousness of form and so forth; since there is no difference [between them], what remains established as non-different at every moment?
There is no distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognition in a person who possesses a single cognition. How, then, could there be bondage and liberation?
Or how could a yogi turn back or accomplish [this] through practice? It is not possible to abandon it, for it consists of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*).
Furthermore, that knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) cannot be produced at all; therefore, even this practice of yoga is entirely fruitless.

Some among the Vātsīputrīyas, however, proclaim the Buddhist doctrine [to be] a "self" (ātman) that is devoid of the designation "person" (pudgala) and is free from the [duality of] identity and difference (tattvānyatva).

The person (*pudgala*), by logical consequence (*prasaṅgataḥ*), is not non-different (*ananya*) from the aggregates (*skandhebhyaḥ*), because it would follow that there is no unity (*anaikatā*) with respect to the first [alternative]. Therefore, its ineffability (*avācyatā*) is correct.

Those [persons] are to be designated as "person" (pudgala), yet an ultimately real person does not exist at all, because of being inexpressible in terms of identity or difference, just like the sky, a lotus, and so forth.

Neither non-difference nor even difference from the entity (vastu) transcends that which, in reality, is conceived as formless and inexpressible in its true nature (*bhāvataḥ*). However, with respect to the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of difference and non-difference, it is logical that there be an indefinable [status] regarding otherness and identity among those things that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
That which is the negation of an entity is not, indeed, that very entity—as if it were something else; therefore, its distinctness is clearly stated.
The negation of its non-existence is itself said to be the reality (*tattva*); that entity does not transcend its own particularity (*bheda*), nor does it [transcend] the reality of the entity.

"This person" [is] not other than the aggregates; this [statement] "not non-other" is an indication [that they are identical]. "This aggregate" is not the person; thus, its distinctness is made manifest.
A connection with contradictory properties is said to be the difference between things; and why is distinctness not found between the person and the aggregates themselves?

For indeed, the person (*pudgala*) is said to be "inexpressible" (*avācya*) as being other than reality (*tattva*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth; whereas form (*rūpa*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and the rest are considered to be expressible as impermanent (*anityatva*). But the person is not so; therefore, its distinctness (*anyatā*) is perfectly clear.
The capacity, which is the defining characteristic of existence, is restricted solely to momentary things; likewise, in that which is inexpressible, there is no substantiality.

However, regarding the contradiction between scripture and its meaning, this has been thoroughly investigated by the great-souled ones; for the compassionate one’s words are manifold, intended for the refutation of nihilism.

The negation of [theories] such as "teaching" (*deśanā*), "vehicle" (*hāra*), "burden" (*bhāra*), and so forth, as well as the [negation of] "collection" (*samudāya*) and so forth by means of the mind (*cittena*), shines forth (*rājate*) as a specific refutation (*viśeṣa-pratiṣedhaḥ*) against those views (*dṛṣṭīn*).

Alternatively, this exertion (*āyāsaḥ*) is made (*kriyate*) quite pointlessly (*evāsthānaḥ*), since [theories] such as "primordial matter" (*prakṛti*) have already been refuted (*nirākṛtam*) by the established proof (*prasiddhyā*) of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Then, momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is clearly established (*prasādhyate*) for the purpose of negating (*niṣedhāya*) that which has been mentioned (*uktasya*), such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth (*ādeḥ*), which will be discussed later (*vakṣyamāṇasya*), without distinction (*aviśeṣataḥ*).

Some (*kaiścit*) maintain (*iṣyate*) a twofold division (*dvairāśyam*) based on being produced (*kṛtaka*) or unproduced (*akṛtakatvena*); others (*paraiḥ*) consider (*matam*) all entities (*bhāvānām*) to be divided by their being momentary (*kṣaṇika*) or non-momentary (*akṣaṇikatvena*).
In that regard, all those very entities which are produced and subject to momentary destruction [are so] because they do not depend on anything else for their destruction.

That which does not depend on another cause (*hetvantara*), but rather arises from its own causes (*svahetubhyaḥ*) in such a manner, should be understood as being restricted (*niyata*) in that regard.
Just as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is independent in the production of its own effect, so too all things that are born are independent with respect to their destruction.
If this [destruction] were independent [of causes], yet it were to occur at another place or time, then by virtue of such dependence, it would follow that it is not independent.

All living beings are entirely indifferent to destruction; otherwise, causes would be utterly incapable of effecting destruction, because [destruction] is not distinct from the entity itself, which arises from its own cause.
For it is not logical for a cause to be the producer of a destruction that is non-different from the entity, since the entity arises from its own cause.

And when an entity has arisen from its own cause as a partless unity within its own self, it is not possible for that self to be affected by destruction through other factors at that time. Indeed, the self remains exactly as it was.
When destruction exists as something distinct from the entity, nothing whatsoever is produced by its causes.

Therefore, [the faults] such as the perception of an effect (*kāryopalambhādi*) necessarily follow (*anuṣajyate*), just as before, because of its remaining in that same state (*tādavasthyāt*). Furthermore, it is not at all logical (*naiva yuktam*) [to say] "this [effect], though non-existent (*asat*), is produced" (*ācaraṇāt*), because even in that case, the entity (*bhāvaḥ*) is destroyed (*nāśyate*) by the thing called "destruction" (*nāman*). This is because [the term "destruction"] applies (*anuvṛttitas*) to the conceptual constructions (*vikalpānām*) regarding the difference from the object (*arthānyatvādi*) and so forth, even in that instance.

If destruction is produced—which is of the nature of non-existence and designated as "other than existence," namely, annihilation—that production is not logically consistent; for even in the case of that non-existence, if it were an effect, it would follow that it possesses substantial reality (*vastutā*), just like a sprout and so forth, because [an effect] arises from a potency residing in its cause.

In this way, non-existence is produced by means of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) based on an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Furthermore, in that case, there occurs a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "prior" or "distinct.

Now, if it is a negation (*niṣedha*) of action (*kriyā*), then indeed this [negation] does not produce existence (*bhāva*); nevertheless, the lack of causality (*ahetutā*) of the agent (*kartṛ*) is established through the abandonment of its status as a cause (*hetutva*).
[Objection: This destruction of an entity exists at the very time of its existence, not before the entity, nor long after; rather, it occurs immediately [after].

And thus, for this reason, it is necessarily restricted by time and must possess a cause; for the occurrence of occasionality (*kādācitkatva*) in that which is independent [of causes] has been refuted.

Because of the existence of the immediately preceding entity, it is indeed logically consistent that [the subsequent entity] possesses a cause; moreover, it is considered to exist by way of having not previously existed, just like another moment.
Furthermore, because it lacks a cause, it would be non-existent—like the son of a barren woman and so forth—or else it would be eternal—like space—since there is no distinction in its mode of being.

If all things were non-existent, there would be permanence; and the cause for the perishability of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would be without a basis. Furthermore, since permanence would coexist with destruction without contradiction, the statement that "destruction occurs" regarding that which has not yet arisen would certainly not be consistent with reason.

What kind of destruction do others question you about—whether it be the existence of phenomena that endure for a moment as they arise, or rather the cessation of their own nature designated as "destruction"? For in questioning the former, nothing at all is contradicted.

That entity (*bhāvaḥ*) which, possessing the suffix *-in*, is said to endure for a moment (*kṣaṇasthāyī*)—we maintain that its destruction (*vināśaḥ*) is caused (*hetumantam*), whereas [the destruction] of another [entity] is causeless (*a-hetukam*), because of its non-existence (*abhāvāt*).
That which is to arise immediately after [the cause] does not exist there; for in such a case, because of the emergence of the nature of change, it exists simultaneously with that very state.

Therefore, because destruction is present, all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are not eternal. Furthermore, the notion that "it is perishable" would not follow as being without a basis (*nirnimittā*).
Because destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is devoid of self-nature (*nairātmya*), it does not possess the state of being immediately subsequent to a connection (*yoga*). It is like a sky-lotus and so forth;

thus, this [destruction] is simply a non-entity (*abhāva*). Therefore, no entity (*bhāva*) comes into being, and no object is communicated here. However, there is no affirmation (*vidhi*) of anything whatsoever.

When a name has been given in this way [e.g., "Bāleya"], the donkey indeed does not acquire the status of being a "donkey" with respect to this man; for when the destruction of the name of an object is effected, nothing further arises from that thing. Thus, what is it that ceases?

In this way, the non-existence of the self’s destruction—that is, its annihilation—is maintained as being devoid of any substantial entity (*vastu*) by its very nature; nor is it described as having the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*).
In this regard, neither the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of its form is asserted through affirmation, nor is the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) of its substantial form denied after the first moment (*kṣaṇa*).

Therefore, it is not established that form is so ordained; thus, this conceptualization regarding [eternal things] such as space (*vyoma*) and the like—which are accepted as being uncreated—is groundless. By their very nature, they do not exist as real entities, because they are devoid of causal efficacy (*śakti*).

Then, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "momentariness" or "non-momentariness" would have no basis (*an-āspada*) among those [entities], by which it might be said that a thing (*vastu*) is indeed momentary or otherwise. For a thing is called "momentary" when its form (*rūpa*) is unstable from moment to moment; conversely, a thing is "non-momentary" when it is pervaded by a stable form.
The nature of an entity (*vastu*) which is non-abiding immediately prior to its arising—that which is called a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)—is held by us to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Even when there is no difference in the object, that [word] is not sublated; for it exists as a denoter produced by a convention according to one's will. However, the intended thing is unstable; thus, let the word be employed either with a causal basis (*sapratyaya*) or without a causal basis (*apratyaya*).
If space, time, and so forth were existent, even they would not transcend this momentary destruction, just like produced things.
