For indeed, those who exist are all momentary; just as conditioned phenomena are established as such immediately [after arising], so it is with them.
(And) these—the sky, time, the Lord (Īśvara), and so forth—are asserted by you to exist; however, their existence does not logically follow in the absence of momentariness.
Since stable entities do not perform purposeful action either successively or simultaneously, they are therefore considered to be devoid of reality.
Effects are delayed due to the absence of the presence of a cause that is capable [of producing them]; for when such a cause exists, what delay could there be for them?
Now, even though [the cause] is eternal, there exist successive auxiliary factors which it depends upon, by means of which it produces this village as an effect that relies on a sequence.
This [is] good; however, they become its auxiliaries (*sahakārin*) either because of their being the cause of its suitable form, or by means of producing a single effect.

If it is the case that [the entity] is the cause of the suitable form, then that state would have been produced by them; yet that [state] is incapable of being produced, since it was already established at that time.

If an excellence (*atiśaya*) distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*) is produced (*kṛti*), then its permanence (*nityatā*) is lost (*avahīyate*). If that [excellence] were separate from it, how could it be the agent (*kāraka*)?

For the production (*utpāda*) of effects (*kārya*) occurs when that [excellence] exists; since there is no production [of effects] in the absence of that [excellence], it is precisely that [excellence] which is established as the cause (*hetu*).

Even if causality exists due to a relation, what relation between those two is intended? Is it identity (*tādātmya*), since they are distinct? It cannot be identity, because that would entail their being simultaneous; and from that, the arising of effects would occur all at once.
In that case, even if there were mutual dependence (*vyapekṣā*), another [infinite regress] would result; consequently, because there is no connection, the effect is not produced at any time.

If this relation is considered to be inherence (*samavāya*), then in that case, is it held to be an inherent entity by becoming a benefactor (*upakārībhavan*) or not? If the first alternative is accepted, then that very same "origination" (*utpatti*) of that [inherence] would result; and that too has just been refuted immediately above.
If this [entity] is considered not to be a benefactor for that [other], then all other entities would be its inherent constituents (*samavāyin*), because there is no distinction;
for each alternative—whether it be difference or non-difference—there arises a dual-natured excellence (*atiśaya*) of that thing when analyzed.
Because [the categories of] "beginning," "two groups" (*dvairāśya*), and so forth have been refuted in the examinations, there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) that is dual-natured, non-dual, or both;

nor is it eternal, for if it were, it would not depend upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) or conditions (*pratyaya*). Even so, being devoid of that [excellence], it is not a causal agent, just like the final cause (*antya-hetu*).
Its own nature, which is considered to be its agency, exists only in the presence of those [auxiliaries]; for even when they are present, it does not [exist] at all times.
Let it be so; however, if its nature is held to be complete in every respect, then those very things which would be desired as its auxiliaries when there is incompleteness must be eternal.
If [it is argued that] even when their existence persists, because of the nature of their connection with that [cause], something else is deficient [and thus] oneness is lost;
likewise, there would be no sequential arising of effects even through dependence, nor is simultaneity desired, precisely because of the observation of sequence.
If this [entity]—the self possessing causal capacity—ceases after having performed all its effects simultaneously, then its momentary destruction is established.
But if that form persists, how could it produce an effect again? How can the causal capacity of a form that does nothing at all be admitted?

All [things], being non-existent, are non-momentary, like the sky-lotus, because they are devoid of all causal efficiency (*sarvasāmarthya*). If that which is characterized by causal capacity (*śakti*) is accepted as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of a real entity (*vastu*), then what is pointed out by others as another definition of entities must be something distinct.

If existence (*sattā*) is intended as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of things (*vastūnām*), that [definition] is not [established], because [existence] is unproven (*asiddheḥ*) in relation to [the relation of] inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth. Or how else could another [property] be the definition of another?

Furthermore, every operation (*vyāpāra*) beginning with the investigation of the object is appropriate only for a person who desires an object free from confusion; it is certainly not [appropriate] by way of madness.

In that very context, the established existence (*sattā*) is what is employed by some, somewhere, at some time, and in some manner; and it is precisely that form of the object which is proven to be momentary (*kṣaṇikatva*). Furthermore, it is in that [context] alone that the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*), through its synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) with all [instances], is stated.
That which is empty of all residual capacity, like the son of a barren woman, never attains the status of being a cause, even for the mind of an omniscient one.
Therefore, since no effect—such as form and so forth—is observed therein, the wise do not at all establish this groundless existence [of such a cause].
No purpose whatsoever is accomplished by proving momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) with respect to that [subject]; and even if an inquiry (*paryanuyoga*) were made regarding it, it would be fruitless.

Now, [one might object]: "Are not the sky-lotuses (*nabhas-tāmarasa*) capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by virtue of being the cause of their own cognition? And yet, these do not exist as real entities (*bhāvika*)."

In cases such as these—namely, [the cognition of] space (*ambara*) or a lotus in the sky (*ambhoruha*)—cognition (*jñāna*) proceeds without an objective support (*nirālambana*). This [cognition] arises from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of mere verbal proliferation (*mātra-vāsanā-jalpa*).

However, if non-existence (*abhāva*) were the cause, then non-existence, being continuous (*nairantaryeṇa*), would necessarily arise; it does not depend on anything else, because it is always devoid of differentiation (*nirviśeṣatayā*).

How can there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in entities that are momentary? [If it is argued that] the primary auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) produce a particularity (*viśeṣa*) in one another—[we reply: this is not possible, because such a production would have to occur either through their entire nature (*sarvātmanā*) or not at all; and if it does not occur, then since no particularity exists, how could an effect not arise from an entity that is devoid of distinction (*nirviśeṣa*)? It must indeed arise.

Nor are we distinguished from others because the same objection applies equally; for if there were [such a distinction], it would lead to an infinite regress regarding the collections of auxiliary causes.
Furthermore, since those [causes] do not produce causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously, their dependence upon momentariness is therefore useless.

And thus, when no excellence (*atiśaya*) has been produced by the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then the continuum (*santati*) is held to be always without distinction (*nirviśeṣā*). If destruction were causeless, it would exist even at the beginning; if its occurrence were at the beginning, how could it also occur at the end?

If no other cause is admitted for the destruction of entities than their own [causes], how can their contrariety (*viruddhatā*) to destruction ever be asserted? Furthermore, it is not the case that they are mutually assisting one another in their initial state; rather, these [factors] become cooperative causes (*sahakāriṇaḥ*) through a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyayā*).

Since we are all alike in being mutually unhelpful, we are each produced by the power of our own respective causal complexes (*upādāna-kalāpa*). From that point onward, those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) which have arisen or been produced through the efficacy of those [complexes] possess the nature (*prakṛti*) of that very form.
In this world, things (*vastu*) exist at every moment with fixed and inconceivable powers (*śakti*); they are not to be questioned, just as the power of burning exists in the act of burning.

However, that destruction which consists of the annihilation of the continuum (*santāna*) is not something caused; it is not an entity (*bhāva*), nor does it exist even at the end [of the continuum]. Yet, its arising (*janma*) is likewise prevented.

The arising of things such as a potsherd that possess distinct characteristics is indeed not produced at the very beginning even when accompanied by a cause, because at that time the cause is non-existent. Entities are of two kinds: some momentary things, such as fire, cold, and so forth, are causes of diminution; others are not of such a nature.
The world, not having perceived the true nature [of things], conceives of contradiction in many ways even regarding the existence of cause and effect;
however, no real state of being characterized by the subverter and the subverted exists at all. Therefore, this is the conclusion concerning contradiction, as it has been stated.

But surely recognition arises; thus, its existence when the operation of the sense organs is present is unshakable and uncontradicted. Therefore, this [recognition] results in an unavoidable contradiction of perception regarding all reasons adduced for the purpose of establishing momentary destruction.
Recognition is not tenable as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that form of the object is inexpressible;

furthermore, recognition is erroneous, since it is distinct from direct perception by virtue of its mode of operation through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of identity, even with respect to a form that is actually different.
If this [cognition] were to arise having as its object a previously established form, it would indeed [arise] from that [form] because it has that as its purpose, just like a prior cognition;
and yet, this is not at all accepted as the grasper of that [object], because it arises at the same time as that knowledge, just like [a cognition] of another object.

Even if there is non-difference through its mode of operation (*vṛtti*) and through determination (*adhyavasāna*), even though it has a distinct form, this [cognition] remains like an erroneous cognition of a magical sphere (*māyā-golaka*).

Furthermore, it is not logical that this [cognition] be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks the capacity for purposeful action (*artha-kriyā*)—such as the accomplishment of an object—just like memory and the like.

The existence [of an object] at the present moment has not been apprehended by the previous cognition; therefore, that which does not exist in recollection is the distinction of this [present existence].
Recollection arises merely from what was previously cognized. However, this recognition—that "this is that very same thing"—is something additional.

Because doubt and error do not exist [in that case], recognition alone would obtain the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatām*), having set aside those two; even an object cognized by other [means] would be [otherwise]. However, when [the object] is already encompassed by perception, there is no possibility for the arising of another [means of knowledge].
When the object has been determined with firmness by the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), who would subsequently determine its contrary through other weaker [means]?
Indeed, if you maintain that present existence is distinct from the prior state of being, then the distinction has already been established by you yourself.

Even if [the object] were not different from the sentient being, how could that which was previously unapprehended by cognition be apprehended? For if it were not apprehended, it would follow that what is perceived as a real entity would be subject to sublation by perception and inference, etc.; thus, like [objects such as] those seen by one with cataracts, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of such sublation.
But that state of being an object of aversion would not exist in the absence of inference and so forth; [therefore] it would certainly not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Is it not the case that by this inference, the universal pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which is the inclusion of all [instances] in all reasons—is sublated, or else there is a contradiction of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*)?

The cognition whose object is the sun and so forth (*sūryādiviṣaya*)—that which arises having as its object the time connected with the sun and so forth (*sūryādisambaddhakāla*)—is indeed [a cognition] because it lacks the sun, moon, and so forth as its objects (*aviṣayatve*), due to the designation of "earthen" (*pārthivābhidhānataḥ*) and because it is a cognition (*jñānatvāt*). Just like the first cognition whose object is the beginning of the time of the sun and so forth (*arkādikatatkāla*).
All those things which are the objects of that [cognition], which serve as the basis for its nature as form and so forth, and whatever conditions arise for them—

these do not at all become subject to destruction immediately after their production, like a sky-lotus, on account of [their] being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and being denotable (*abhidheyatva*).

(Proclamation, nominative singular feminine): "Those [cognitions] which are the objects of dispute, all of which are about to arise in succession—they are all objects of a single referent (*ekārtha*), because they are established in a single substratum (*āśrayatva*) that is uncontradicted, due to their being expressed by a common term (*samānokti*); just as [multiple] cognitions [do not conflict] when directed toward a single present moment. (Not in a manifold way.)

In the first reason (*hetu*), the example (*nidarśana*) is deficient with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*), because [the reason] is a cause (*hetutvāt*). For indeed, no object (*viṣaya*) is simultaneous with its own cognition (*svajñāna*);

when words (*śabda*) such as "sun" and so forth—which arise merely from the intention to speak (*vivakṣāmātra*)—are applied (*viniveśayante*) to a lamp or similar object, there is deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) with respect to those cognitions (*jñānaiḥ*).
Because the genus (*jāti*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), those [words] are certainly not accepted as the proof (*sādhana*) for that purpose which was indicated [by you].

To speak of "denotability" (*vācyatva*) by a common word (*sama-śabda*) with respect to cognitions (*pratyaya*) such as "lamp" and so forth is futile; therefore, this reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*).

Is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) not seen to be sublated? This sublation is quite clear even with respect to those cognitions (*dhiyaḥ*) that have ascended to the position of dispute; they are not objects of a single referent (*ekārtha*), because they arise successively, like the cognitions of lightning, lamps, and so forth.

In the case of cognitions that arise from a single object, there is a contradiction with others regarding their sequential existence; this is because [the cognition] lacks non-difference from its effect, due to the dependence on that [cause].
In all these reasons, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, because no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) is shown for those [reasons] that would exist in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Examination of the Relationship Between Actions and Their Results:

Action and Reaction Since every entity (*vastu*) is consumed by impermanence and is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), how can there be a relationship (*sambandha*) between an action (*karman*) and its fruit (*tat-phala*), such as the [categories of] cause (*kāraṇa*) and effect (*kārya*), and so forth?
That moment of the wholesome and so forth which is conceived as the agent does not at all persist until the time of the production of the fruit.
The action was certainly not performed by that very moment which is described as the enjoyer of the fruit, because such an enjoyer is impossible prior to the production of that fruit.
Thus, because there is no single agent who appropriates [the self], there would be the destruction of the action and its fruit; and the attainment of what was not done would be a great contradiction.

However, in the position of the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya-vāda*), this is understood: prior to destruction, the fruit would either not exist at all, or it would belong to someone other than myself.

Thus, a discerning person would certainly not engage in the undertaking of either auspicious or inauspicious action out of a desire for its fruit; for a future entity, being distant, is incapable of performing an action that produces an effect, nor is a past entity capable of it, and even a present entity does not remain for such a duration of time.

An entity that has not attained its own nature (*an-ātmaka*) is postulated as having the status of being a subordinate factor (*aṅgatva*) for another; yet it is neither destroyed nor does it persist. Furthermore, if its destruction is postulated as being without any continuity (*niranvaya*) following the preceding moment, then its subsequent arising is not possible, because it would lack a cause (*animittatvāt*).

In the case of the equality of destruction and arising, there is indeed no mutual dependence; nor do [these two] exist in the state of cause and effect, because that [cause] does not provide assistance. Just as a fragrance and so forth, while being produced, perishes within the form of a jar and is accepted as its effect, so too are the other [sensory qualities] like form.

Therefore, that alone is the cause whose activity is observed prior to the production of the effect; however, mere immediate succession is not [the cause]. If this occurrence of the effect were from a destroyed cause, then it would be causeless, because that which has perished is beyond description.

If [it is argued that] because [the jar] arises from that which has not perished at the moment of its birth, it persists through multiple moments, then how would the momentariness of entities (*bhāva*) not be contradicted?
For if a jar or similar object were stable for a moment, it would not be perceived by the eye, just as objects that have long since passed away are not cognized.

Furthermore, because of the non-perception of cause and effect, and because of the non-perception of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities (*bhāva*), the agent (*kartṛ*) is established [as non-existent]. He connects the course [of events]—just as when this [effect] is seen, it is seen as belonging to him; but when he is not seen, nothing is perceived.

Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is difficult to establish (*durghaṭā*) with respect to entities (*bhāveṣu*) that are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgiṣu*); for an object seen by one person (*anya-nara*) is not recognized (*pratyabhijñāyate*) by others (*paraiḥ*).

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) might occur due to similarity (*sādṛśya*) when [the hair] and so forth are divided, provided there exists a single cognizer (*jñātṛ*); however, if there were a duality [of cognizers], it would be without foundation.
If no single entity exists that performs the function of synthesis (*pratisandhāna*), then how could there be an initial desire for taste and so forth upon seeing a form?
Furthermore, it is not understood how one moment, bound by the fetters of passion and the like, could be the one that enters existence, while another, unbound, is the one that is liberated.
Liberation for one who is bound is never possible, because of absolute destruction; therefore, it is useless for those seeking liberation. [Objection:
One who is seen to be bound by shackles and the like attains such liberation; thus, the bound one goes to liberation—[this is] contradicted by what is observed.

Bondage and liberation (are) in the same substratum; these two exist thus, like those [concepts] found in common worldly usage. Therefore, everything is established most beautifully by this very method: that in objects which perish moment by moment, memory and so forth are impossible due to the absence of a single substratum.
In this regard, it is said: When the causal relationship exists, all these [principles] are established without contradiction even in things that are devoid of self (*nirātman*).
Just as the capacity of the seed and so forth is restricted to the sprout and so forth even in the absence of a persisting self, so too is the case for the internal [reality].
Whether indirectly or directly, whatever is capable [to produce an effect] in some respect, from that [arises] the connection; thus, the relationship between action and its fruit is established.

However, the determination of agency and so forth, intended through the unity of the continuum (*santāna*), is merely an imputed conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); it is not a factor for the establishment of reality (*tattva*).

In the absence [of a persisting entity], a specific causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*) might exist; that alone is logical, just as the causal relation of seeds, sprouts, and so forth with respect to subsequent continua is observed to be restricted, even though there is not the slightest part consisting of a continuous persistence.

Since there is no distinction between earth and the other [elements] with respect to seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so forth—due to their being of a single nature (*aikātmyāt*)—any differentiation is untenable. Consequently, the effort made for the sake of establishing the existence of entities, non-existents, actions, fruits, and the like, is rendered superfluous by those who seek to establish the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*). Thus, [the doctrine of] total annihilation (*niranvayā*) is established. Therefore, the exertion of others is quite enough.

It is said: "For here, the effect (*kārya*) is produced (*prajāyate*) in the second moment (*kṣaṇe*), while the cause (*kāraṇa*) has already arisen (*jāta*) in the first moment (*prathame*). And at that time, it [the cause] has not perished.

However, because of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatvāt*), at the time of the moment of the effect (*kṣaṇakārya-kāle*), or during its activity (*vṛtau*), it is fruitless (*viphalam*); for by then, that effect (*kārya*) has already been accomplished (*nirvṛtta*)."
That which has already been produced cannot be produced again because the entity is non-existent; otherwise, there would be no stability.
Therefore, that effect arises in the second moment from a potent cause that was present in the first moment but has not perished.

If the effect were to arise in the third moment from a cause that has already perished—that is, from one that has been utterly destroyed—then it would follow that [the effect] arises simultaneously [with its cause], just as [one might argue] that an effect arises from a cause that has vanished. Furthermore, if that [simultaneity] were to occur in the first moment, then again, that [simultaneity] is not tenable according to reason, just like the case of a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Because of the incapacity of that which is non-existent (*asataḥ*), and because of the possibility of an effect (*kārya*) when there is capacity (*sāmārthye*), simultaneity (*yaugapadyam*) of cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇayoḥ*) is clearly contradicted.

For a cause (*kāraṇam*) produces (*janayati*) its own effect (*ātmīyam kāryam*); it does not do so by first grasping (*gṛhītvā*) it—as one would with a pair of tongs (*saṃdaṃśena*)—whereby simultaneity might occur.
Nor, having embraced them firmly as if he were a lover embracing his beloved, would there be for those two a state [of pleasure] occurring even once.

Since [the object] is inactive with respect to the entity, by necessity, that which arises immediately after the first moment—which is produced from its own causes—is said to "generate" that [second moment] due to the proximity of the second moment; [this is asserted] by those who follow mere convention arising from the intention to speak.
In this case, what is the use of an operation (*vyāpāra*) that is distinct from time? Existence (*sattā*) itself is the operation, since when that [existence] is present, the effect arises.

That [existence] is designated as the "immediate succession" (*ānantarya-niyama*). Furthermore, the dependence (*apekṣā*) of the cause upon the operation for the arising of the effect is the constant presence [of the cause].

Even if an operation (*vyāpāra*) is postulated, it becomes a cause merely by virtue of being produced from that [entity] (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*). Therefore, it is better, or rather, let that [entity] itself, as possessing that [operation], be the cause.

When the seed exists, the sprouts are indeed seen to arise from it; however, when its causal activity is postulated as its causal power (*śakti*), nothing at all is observed to exist. Why, then, is this not accepted as the cause of something else? Or rather, what distinction is there between this [seed] and that [other thing] such that it alone possesses causality?
If a cause of an effect is held to exist without another [cause], why then would other things not likewise be causes?
526. [The verse is missing from the printed text, though its commentary is extant.]
We perceive that which is accepted as "perceptibility" (*dṛśyatva*). How then can we accept its connection and its basis?
Just as the very arising of cognition is considered its validity (*prāmāṇya*), why is its causality with respect to all entities not likewise accepted?
Just as cognition is momentary, so too have we established that other produced things [are likewise]. Therefore, this world is likewise devoid of activity;

the causality of odor and the rest is accepted as existing solely through a continuous series (*prabandha*) of mutual functioning. Thus, this [objection] regarding the fallacy of being a non-reason (*ahetutva-prasañjana*) does not undermine our position.
Even if there were some other cause immediately preceding [the effect], it would be accepted as such by virtue of its restrictive nature; and this [principle] is equally applicable to stable things.
Wherever something is engaged in an effect, if it is not considered the cause, let that [thing] in which its presence is restricted be accepted as the cause.

If it is your view that an object is cognizable by a cognition possessing a form (*sākāra-vijñāna*) on the basis of the non-perception of existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva-pratyakṣānupalambha*), then [you must admit that] an object is also experienced by a cognition devoid of a form (*anākāra-dhī*). This is because [the object] is perceived equally in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇatva*) and its opposites (*tadādi*).

Every single consciousness arises from its own preceding causes, such as form, cognition, and the like, which are of a similar nature and belong to the same time. If consciousness were endowed with an image (*sākāra*), there would be a diversity of the mind; however, if it were not marked by an image, there would be no basis for proximity.
If you [plural] must say something by way of reply, and if there is a resolution for you regarding this matter, let that be ours as well;
likewise, let there be the destruction of what has been done, provided that the cause does not produce the effect, and provided that it is not accepted that there is causality within the continuum.

(Origination) (even) (without being produced) (might exist) (if) (any) (effect) (were to arise) (without) (a cause). This [consequence] is not (incurred) (by force of logic), because it is (already) (objected to) (through the conceptual distinction of) (momentary destruction, momentariness, etc.), which has been (established) (by the opponents themselves); for there is (not at all) (anything) (undesired) (for them).
Conceptualization regarding the distinction between moments does not proceed for those who possess views that are not devoid of the conceit of a "being" or of a "single continuum.
However, we who have fully awakened to reality, having understood the restriction of causes that perish at every moment, undertake virtuous actions.
The specific nature of the relation between cause and effect is restricted to certain minds alone; therefore, memory and the other [mental states] are unimpeded everywhere.
Ignorance and the rest, being established as causes and effects, are considered bondage; through their cessation, purity is held to be liberation.
Moreover, these two—bondage and liberation—are established in common worldly experience as having a single substratum; for indeed, everything is well-known to be momentary.
However, because such a state of being an agent, an enjoyer, bondage, and so forth is entirely non-existent in a self, it is contradicted; otherwise, there would be impermanence.

The Mātrikas say: "It was previously stated that the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) regarding birth (*jāti*) and so forth has been demonstrated; [therefore,] it is incorrect [to claim that] the six categories (*ṣaḍ-artha*), beginning with substance (*dravya*), exist as ultimate realities (*pāramārthika*). This negation is now being stated in brief."

Substance is held to be ninefold, divided according to its distinctions as earth and so forth; it consists of four categories beginning with earth, and is twofold by way of being eternal and non-eternal.

Those ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) which are accepted as being composed of earth and so forth are eternal; however, those which are produced by them and others are perishable. In that regard, the non-existence of the forms of eternal atoms has been established through the proof of the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of all things without exception.

If [atoms] were eternal, all gross objects would arise simultaneously, because there is no distinction among them; nor is there any requirement for conjunction and so forth [to act as causes], if it is not admitted that atoms are the producers [of gross objects], since they are accepted as being objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend existing things (*vidyamāna-artha*).

[It is] because [the atom] is unestablished—that by which the atom is seen as the cause, just as a weaver and others [are seen as the causes] of cloth and so forth; or [because] the existence of all things consisting of ultimate atoms is not established due to the absence of a grasper of the existent. For when there is an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no certainty regarding non-existence.

The whole (*avayavin*), which is composed of those [parts] and possesses their distinctions of qualities and parts, is simply not perceived; therefore, it is established as lacking any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). [Objection:
But surely a crystal stone is seen even when in contact with an underlying substrate (*upadhāna*), despite there being no apprehension of its own color; likewise, a crane and so forth are also seen.
Even when a man is hidden by a cloak (*kañcuka*), although his form and other qualities are not perceived, the cognition of "man" is observed.

When a cloth is red, the notion of "cloth" is distinguished from its color and other attributes, just as [the notion of] a lotus is distinguished from [other things] such as the *indīvara* flower; this occurs because of the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of those [attributes], and thus the horse is distinguished from Caitra and others.
Earth and the other elements are absolutely distinct from form, odor, and so forth, due to the difference between their being designated as one or many—just like the moon and the stars;
likewise, the threads and the cloth are distinct, because they possess different capacities and so on, just like a pillar and a jar, by virtue of their association with contradictory properties.

In the absence of a gross object, there could be no perception of trees and so forth; for atoms, being beyond the reach of the senses, do not exist [as such], nor can there be a designation of "atoms," since a very subtle object is designated as such only in relation to a gross entity. But in the absence of a single gross entity, what is the subtlety of this [atom] in relation to?

[Objection: But surely crystals and the like are perceived in a form that is initially red and so forth; yet they do not possess the nature of that [form], because it would entail the destruction of their own position.

Furthermore, no essence distinct from that form is apprehended. Moreover, it is not logical for them to be cognizable through the form of another cognition, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

(And) even if it were possible that "it is so," [then] for us who perceive white [objects], this cognition—just like the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and so forth—is inferential with respect to the Person who is within the coverings; it is not [directly perceived] in the Person, because there is no perception of the covering, its configuration, or its cause.
In the destruction of the prior form and so forth, such as saffron, there is the arising of another form on the cloth due to its momentariness;
therefore, from that very form, another form—white—arises in dependence upon water and so forth, just as [the color] of iron and the like [changes].
If the form remains in that same state (*tādavasthya*), there can be no overcoming by another, because the previously overcome intrinsic nature continues to persist.

Therefore, the establishment of the intrinsic nature of things based merely on the use of the genitive case, the word "difference" (*bheda*), and so forth—which arise from a mere intention to speak (*vivakṣā-mātra*)—is not tenable.
For indeed, it is not at all accepted by others that there exists a distinct [entity] for the six; nor is any single category admitted by them as being common to them.

If it is held that the existence of the six [categories] is accepted as their reality with respect to the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes them known, then for you, they would follow as being something other than those six.

If it is argued that these six, which possess the property (*dharmin*), are intended as properties (*dharma*) that are distinct from them, then what kind of relationship is considered to exist between that [subject] and those [properties]?

A conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not logical [as their relation], because it is restricted to substances (*dravya*). Nor does another [relation], namely inherence (*samavāya*), exist; and no other [relation] is accepted by others (*paraiḥ*). Since a relation is untenable, how could there be a property (*dharma*) belonging to them? If [it is argued that they are properties] merely by virtue of being produced from that [cause], then others would likewise be [properties].

Thus, even for that [entity], the separate case-ending (*vibhakti*) denoting existence (*astitva*) occurs; furthermore, in the case of another [property], the undesired consequence (*aniṣṭā*) of being a substratum (*dharmi-tā*) follows when there is a co-inherence (*samāveśa*) therein of other properties (*dharma*), substances (*dravya*), and so forth. Therefore, it is accepted that [the entity] itself is the substratum (*dharmi*).
If the difference of the cloth from the initial threads is being established [by the causal argument], then there would be an unavoidable futility of the proof;

for we [others] maintain that those other threads which have arisen without distinction, having reached that state, are attached to specific causal efficiency and are non-different from the initial ones.

In order to make this known, those who— considering that [the individual denotations] possess utility for a single purpose (*ekakārya*) upon hearing [the word], and who, desiring to avoid separately the faults of prolixity (*tyāgadoṣa*), complexity (*gaurava*), incapacity (*aśakti*), and fruitlessness (*vaiphalya*),
perceive a brevity (*lāghava*) through a complete expression (*sākalyenābhidhāna*)— have employed a single speech (*ekā vāk*) toward those [objects].

A cloth (*paṭa*) is certainly not established as being simultaneous with those [atoms], since it possesses the properties of the agent’s capacity, dimension, and so forth, which are distinct [from them].
And likewise, those atoms which have arisen in mutual association—their [existence] is not at all within the range of others due to their being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatayā*).

The imagined form of blue and so forth belonging to the ultimate atoms is its own manifestation; although it is perceived by the cognition of the eye and other senses, even though their sequence is unobservable due to the lack of distinction [between them], nevertheless, direct perceptibility remains uncontradicted, as in the case of a beverage and the like.

In that way, when there is the perception of all material things as being excluded from everything else, there is no certainty regarding the universal aspect; nevertheless, even though the object has a partless characteristic as its cognizable form, it is perceived through the cause of non-conceptual sensory cognition.

Just as there is an illusion regarding a single flame arising from its production, so too, when many subtle [atoms] exist in immediate proximity (*nairantarya*), if their perceptibility is not admitted because they lack the characteristic of being distinguished [from one another], how can that [perceptibility] be seen in the case of a lamp and so forth? Or rather, is a composite whole (*avayavin*) accepted in that way?

But even if this much is certain regarding them, why is it not understood that the form of blue and so forth belongs to the atoms? That too is not a valid reason, because cognition is certainly not without an object (*agocara*), nor does it have as its object a single gross entity, due to the contradiction between grossness and oneness.

If the gross [object] were of a single nature, then by the covering of even a single spot the size of a fly, everything would be covered; [this] would follow because of its lack of differentiation (*avibhāgataḥ*).
If one part were colored, everything would be colored, just like that [colored] part; or else, in the case of a single entity, a plurality resulting from contradictory properties would follow.
Surely, because it has a single nature, what is the basis for the word "all" here? For that [word] has multiple objects, and moreover, the whole does not possess a manifold nature.
We, who are established in the world as the cloth, the body, the mountain, and so forth, which have been described by you as being wholes (*avayavin*), all employ [the following reasoning]:
"The entire cloth—everything, without exception, in its totality—is produced merely from desire."
If [it is argued that] even by us such [a thing] is described as "beginning with" (*ādi*), then everything would be red; for words would be without restriction.
If [it is claimed that] the designation is figurative (*bhākta*), then a distinction of speech follows, but there is no distinction of cognition regarding the two intended objects.
Because conjunction does not exist by pervading [its substratum], redness is not attached to everything, nor indeed is everything seen as covered.
Now, in a partless substance, what nature could be established that is non-pervasive? For if it were so situated, difference would necessarily be established.

Stability (*sthitiḥ*), having no foothold at all in many locations (*bahu-deśa-*), is therefore established (*siddhā*) as the manifold nature (*aneka-rūpatā*) of cloth (*paṭa*) and so forth, [arising] from atoms (*aṇubhyaḥ*).

However, the world (*lokaḥ*), whose true nature regarding objects (*avijñāta-tattva-artha-*) is not understood, considers (*manyate*) a single mass (*ekam piṇḍam*) with reference to those imagined ultimate atoms (*tat-kalpita-parama-aṇu-apekṣaḥ*); thus it is spoken of here (*ucyate iha*).

This notion (saṃjñā), established in such a manner, is independent of [external] signs (nimitta) and follows from convention (saṅketa), just as the word "Lord" (īśvara) [is applied] even to those who possess no [such qualities].

Furthermore, [terms such as] "thread," "weaver," and so forth, do not at all follow a single composite whole (ekāvayavin), because [the objects denoted by] "mat," "wall," "pot," and so forth, are manifold.
The substance [which is] intended [by you] is not dependent [on parts], because it is a unity like an atom; this is illogical, as the [perceptual] cognition [of its] existence is subverting.

If that [entity] were to exist either by way of its own form alone, as possessing a single occurrence within another part, or else by means of something other [than itself], because there would be no difference in mode.
Therefore, it is not logically tenable that its operation occurs only there and not elsewhere, because by being embraced by that [operation], it would otherwise not possess an operation there.
The child does not at all harbor anger within his heart toward the female student; likewise, he would not resort to another object once one has been embraced.

Even though [the entity] is connected with its own nature (*svabhāva*), because it exists [only] there, it would follow that it has the property of being in a single location (*ekadeśatva*) and that it possesses a single essence (*aikātmya*) due to its lack of division (*avibhāgataḥ*).

Furthermore, if it were established by means of another nature (*ātmanā*) while existing [in one place], it would not be a single thing, because it would consist of multiple distinct entities (*vastubhedātmakatvataḥ*). Thus, the distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) could not be established.
If it is argued: "The inherence (*samavāya*) residing in them is the [nature] of those [universals]," this analysis falls upon that very [inherence] with great force.

Or else, if [the universal] exists in its entirety within each individual instance, it follows that there would be multiplicity; or if it exists by way of a single part, then [the universal] would not be unitary, nor would it exist anywhere at all.

That means of proof (*sādhana*) which operates independently or by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is consistent with reality; however, its own apprehension is not characterized anywhere as occurring either in its entirety or in part, because that [means of proof] from which substance (*dravya*) might arise is non-existent, and yet another [substance] also [does not exist].

If there is no non-prevention [of perception] when that [substance] is seen somewhere in respect of a substance and so forth, then, on the other hand, when it is not seen, an inquiry regarding its difference is not appropriate.

"This much" (first person singular nominative) "might be" (*bhavet*, third person singular optative) "to be stated" (*vācyam*, first person singular nominative)—such is the [opponent's] position (*vṛttiḥ*, feminine first person singular). But that is not tenable (*na... yuktam*, first person singular nominative), because it is established (*siddheḥ*, fifth person singular ablative) through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*, with suffix *-tas*) by means of cognition (*buddhitaḥ*, with suffix *-tas*). Thus it is here.

Let it not be said that there is any subverting [evidence] whatsoever; for even otherwise, the state of being direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) would certainly not belong to the mental states whose forms are color and so forth.
It has already been established previously through non-difference that such an occurrence does not exist here; moreover, there is no cognition of that [object] because its form does not appear.
This meaning is being elucidated by these two words (*śabda*): either its occurrence (*vṛtti*) is in its entirety or in part; or rather, how is it that this [occurrence] of his is otherwise?
Is it like that which is indicated at the beginning of a vessel's arrangement, or like that which is indicated at the beginning of a multi-seated arrangement?

Words are in some cases dependent upon causes such as perishability and so forth, like a jar, a lamp, and the like; and indeed, space will become the basis for cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior," through its distinction from action, substance, and so forth, just as the cognition of a jar and the like [is based on its distinction from others].

Since [time] is characterized by the onset of wrinkles, grey hair, coarseness, and so forth—which are distinct from the conditions [of youth], etc.—it is indeed accepted as the cause [of these changes].
In this same way, space is inferred from cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior. Furthermore, the inference of the mind is held to occur through the sequence of successive cognitions.

[The opponent] regards the cause as distinct from the eye and so forth; [but] the cognition of color and so forth occurs sequentially, just like [the cognition of] a chariot and so forth, because the sound is admitted to have the great elements (*mahābhūta*)—whether appropriated (*upātta*) or otherwise—as its cause. Thus, the words [used in the argument] are established as residing in those [elements]; therefore, the first [reason] is not a valid proof (*asādhana*).

Inherence in space is not established as being unitary, all-pervading, and eternal, because it lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and because it would entail [the absurdity of] simultaneity and so forth.

Furthermore, cognition and the like, which are based on the prior and subsequent [moments] and arise from a specific mental attention (*manaskāra*) conditioned by convention (*samaya*), do not [originate] from time, nor from space.

If it is argued that because [the mind] is partless (*niraṃśa*) and of a single nature (*eka-svabhāva*), there is no possibility of priority (*paurva*), posteriority (*aparya*), or sequence (*ādi*), then—due to the difference (*bhedāt*) between those two related things (*sambandhi*)—surely those two are fruitless (*niṣphalau*). Furthermore, we maintain that the mind (*manaḥ*) is distinct (*atirikta*) from the eye (*cakṣus*) and other [senses]; for indeed, the mind is that cognition (*pratyaya*) which arises immediately after (*anantaro-udbhūta*) the six [sensory cognitions].
Since [we] have obtained [the cognition of] cognitions as being simultaneous within the eternal mind, that reason stated here becomes an obstacle to what is desired;
I consider this sūtra to have been composed for the sake of establishing the non-existence of the mind as taught by the other Sugata, though it has been turned around with the letter "sa" [added].

By this negation, qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth are likewise considered to be dependent (*āśrita*) upon substances (*dravya*); [but since substances] are thus cast aside (*apāsta*), whose inherence (*samavāya*) could there be, and where? Nevertheless, the specific negation is stated once again.

If the beginning of blue is held to exist in a large substance as a single entity, why is it not [visible] as a manifestation? Furthermore, its perception would occur in that manifestation through light entering through a hole;
yet the beginning of blue is not held to exist in a location that is spatially divided, which is what is manifested by that [light]. Therefore, there is a distinction [in the blue] atom by atom.

Number (*saṅkhyā*), which is desired (*iṣṭā*) and visible (*dṛśyā*), does not appear (*na bhāsate*) in cognition (*jñāne*) as something distinct (*vyatirekiṇī*) from elephants (*gaja-*) and so forth, because it is excluded from them (*parāvṛtta*) and lacks their nature (*atad-rūpa*). That [number] certainly does not exist (*na eva asti*) in the initial stage (*ādau*) of cognitions of jars (*ghaṭeṣu*). This consciousness (*vijñānam*)—such as "one" (*eka-*) and so forth—is a mental construction (*anvayam*) produced by attention (*manaskāra-*) and linguistic convention (*saṅketa-*) fashioned by desire (*icchā-*).

There exists no distinct number among them, because they lack substantiality (*adravyatva*). However, it is not logical that this cognition should be merely figurative (*bhākta*), because it is unerring (*askhalitatva*).

If [it is argued that] the cognition of oneness is conceptually constructed (*parikalpyate*) with respect to qualities such as singleness and so forth, due to their being one, because of their inherence (*samavāya*) in that substance which is inherent in them; and if [it is argued that] there is a single object—then [the following applies].

Let it be [so]. In a single cognition, what cause does the notion (*mati*) depend upon—be it the "name" (*nāman*), or the six categories (*ṣaṭ-padārtha*) and so forth? This notion of "inherence" (*samavāya*) is secondary (*gauṇa*) with respect to a single object, and likewise it is erroneous (*skhalita*), because it is like the cognition of "fire" applied to a boy (*māṇava*).

Number (*saṅkhyā*, feminine, nominative singular) is established (*prasādhyate*, present passive third person singular) by virtue of its distinctness (*vailakṣaṇyāt*, fifth case singular) from cognitions (*pratyayebhyaḥ*, fifth case plural) arising from elephants (*gaja-*) and so forth, just like [the distinctness] of cognitions (*buddhi-*) and so forth from blue cloth (*nīla-vastra*).

This is the proof of what is desired (*iṣṭa-siddhiḥ*, nominative singular). Or rather, number (*saṅkhyā*, nominative singular) may exist (*bhavet*, optative third person singular) within cognitions (*buddhi-*) and so forth, which are fashioned (*racita-*) by mental attention (*manaskāra-*), linguistic convention (*saṅketa-*), desire (*icchā-*) and so forth; it is precisely by this (*etena*, third case singular) that [the point is made].

If the accomplishment (*niṣpatti*) of number (*saṅkhyā*) is described as being dependent upon cognition (*buddhi*), why is that cognition not accepted as being [established] merely by the application (*ābhoga*) of convention (*saṅketa*)?
Why is magnitude (*parimāṇa*)—such as "large," "long," and so forth—not likewise considered to exist through its distinction from color (*rūpa*) even in the case of an object (*artha*)?

A long garland (dīrghā mālā) on a palace (prāsāda-) is perceived as great (mahatī). For indeed, there is no dimension (parimāṇa) therein corresponding to the form (yathārūpa) as it is conceptually constructed (prakalpita). If [it] is designated (vyapadiśyate) in that way by means of inherence (samavāyena) with a single object (ekārtha), then neither greatness (mahattva) nor length (dairghya) exists as intended (vivakṣita) in the constituent parts (dhāmasu).

The palace is intended [by the root] *iṣ*; that conjunction (*yoga*) is a quality (*guṇa*) and is possessed of immeasurable magnitude (*aparimāṇavat*). There is no other "garland" (*mālā*) belonging to it, nor is there any basis (*āśraya*) for metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).

Is that linguistic convention (*vyavahṛti*), which is postulated (*kalpyate*) on the grounds of its distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) from the [constituent] parts, not considered to be the ultimate reality (*niṣṭhā*) of the entity (*bhāva*) as a distinct self?

Just as cognitions, pleasure, and so forth—which are distinct from one another—are designated separately even without anything else [as their cause], so too conjunction and disjunction, which are restricted to substances, are merely imagined by others as the causes of cognitions such as "conjoined" and so on; those two are therefore purposeless.

[If it were] by way of non-existence, then the conjunction of the seed, water, earth, and so forth would follow as being always the cause of the effect, because there is no distinction [in their state of non-existence].
However, the field, seed, water, and so forth are understood to be dependent [on other factors], because they produce their own effects, just like a staff, a wheel, water, and so on.
That entity which is perceived by them as conjunction is understood to be distinct precisely because it possesses qualifiers; thus it is said:
"Bring these two conjoined things," for one brings only those two in relation to which one perceives the conjunction, excluding anything else.

"This" (this), "that object" (that thing) is "with an interval," and "this" is "without an interval. And if, in this case, those two do not exist, by what means is this distinction of cognition found?

This [cognition] which rests upon that which is separated by an interval, and that other [cognition] which [rests] even upon that which is without an interval—this twofold false cognition is as follows.
And false cognition is entirely imitative of the primary object; therefore, the primary [object] must be stated here, for when that is stated, those two are established.

For what reason does this cognition, "he is wearing earrings," arise? It cannot [arise] from the existence of the man and the earring, because that would entail [the absurdity of it arising] at all times. Furthermore, since the presence [of the earring] is observed elsewhere, its negation [in one place] and its conjunction [with another] would have to be observed; how then could it be denied?
Thus, Caitra is without earrings; likewise, therefore, there exists a real distinction such that the application of affirmation and so forth proceeds through differentiation.

It is said that water and other things, although they are not without distinction due to their momentariness even while existing, depend upon another state characterized by non-interruption and so forth.

If water and the like were dependent solely upon conjunction (*saṃyoga-mātra*), then the effect would necessarily arise immediately after that conjunction; or else, these [elements] would not exist at all.
For one perceives two objects of such a kind when they have reached a state of contiguity (*nairantarya*) by virtue of their birth, and one brings them together.

[That which is] born, [and] severed, goes to the state of being a cause for cognition, along with its interval; otherwise, it would be like [the cases of] the house, the Vindhya mountains, and the Himalayas.

A false cognition (*mithyābuddhiḥ*) is not at all necessarily concomitant with a primary object (*pradhānārtha-anusāriṇī*), just as the initial perception of two moons (*dvicandrādimatiḥ*) is independent [of such an object]. Some [cognitions] arise from an internal disturbance (*antar-upaplavāt*) of the mind (*cittasya*), or else, in this case, there exists no primary object (*pradhānam*) that has arisen as something delimited (*avacchinnādijātam*).
The notion that "this is a person with earrings" arises as if it were a conjunction between the two distinct states—the state of being Caitra and the state of possessing earrings.

Such an excellence produced by the state is observed [in the case of Caitra] and is denied in other cases; for instance, at the beginning, when Caitra is without earrings, no such conjunction exists because it has not been perceived.

A cognition (*dhī*) associated with a single object (*vastu-yukta*) does not arise (*na jāyate*) from a desired [cause] other than that [object], because it is associated with the nature of being a cognition (*buddhitayā*), just like a cognition associated with a palace (*prāsāda-yukta-dhī*) and so forth.

Alternatively, by virtue of its being produced (*jāyamānatayā*) when there is a plurality of objects (*aneka-vastu-sadbhāve*), cognitions are like the objects of multiple distinct threads (*aneka-vibhakta-tantu-ādi-viṣayāḥ*).

The two [terms] are to be designated as valid cognitions according to their respective divisions; moreover, they are not sublated. Thus, it is not logical for a single [entity] to have a dual function.

Furthermore, "priority" (*paratva*) and "posteriority" (*aparatva*) are postulated as the causes for [the notions of] "far" (*para*) and "near" (*apara*); that [cause] is not limited by space or time.

Just as forms such as blue and so forth are said [to be distinct], so too, even when there is a distinction from other adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), others [maintain] that this is likewise [the case]. If it is thought that all the followers of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and other schools are not non-distinct from substance (*dravya*) by virtue of their being its delimiters—just as a staff and so forth [are delimiters of a person]—then [this is not so].

Because it is described as having the desired color by virtue of its conventional existence (*saṃvṛti-sattva*), it is therefore not at all expressible (*anirvācya*) as being either of the nature of reality (*tattva*) or of something else that exists (*anya-sat*).

Furthermore, the state of being indefinable (*anirvacanīyatva*) regarding the collection (*samūha*) and so forth is denied, because it possesses the property (*dharmatva*) of being restricted, just like [the properties of] form, sound, taste, and so on.

In reality, because that [entity] lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), just like a sky-lotus, we maintain that those phenomena (*dharmāḥ*) are established as being merely superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā-āropita*).

Thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) in what has been stated; for, through examples such as the sky-lotus, both non-difference (*abheda*) and difference (*vyatireka*) are indeed established with respect to a real entity (*vastu*).

If it is thus argued that number and so forth are distinct from substance by way of their ontological status (*dravyataḥ*), then because number and the rest are unestablished, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). However, if substance itself is distinct from the collection and so forth, then even as it is stated to be a distinction, it would be contradicted [by its own nature] once it has been established.

The threefold [disposition] (*saṃskāra*) has been described as consisting of that which is termed velocity (*vega*), characterized by mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*). All of this is not tenable, because all entities (*padārtha*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*); for no action (*kriyā*) exists within a continuum (*prabandha*) such that it could serve as the cause for that which is designated as velocity-disposition (*vega-saṃskāra*).

The [postulated] *saṃskāra* (impression) is untenable; whether it consists of *bhāvanā* (mental cultivation) or *vāsanā* (latent impression) of the mind, this is not logical, because a quality (*guṇa*) belonging to a self (*ātman*) is excluded by the refutation of that [self].

Furthermore, the form of *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity) is not tenable due to the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) [of all things], since the existence of a persisting object is impossible; for stability can only exist through the very nature of such [an enduring] entity.

[The moment] abides for a single instant due to its own cause, and there is no persistence in a continuum because of the power of each preceding [moment]; otherwise, of what would this [continuum] be the producer? Furthermore, neither the conditioned factor (*saṃskāra*) nor anything else could be seen to possess the status of a cause.

An agent who establishes the name of a garment that has already arisen—[namely] its quality and refinement—is not possible, because [such an agent] has been refuted at length previously regarding the mind, the connection [with objects], and the selves. Furthermore, the "unseen force" (*adṛṣṭa*) does not occur as something endowed with the characteristics described above.

Lifting up and so forth are impossible in entities that perish moment by moment, because of their falling away from the very place where they were born, due to the impossibility of reaching another location. For others have declared that time is the agent; yet even in things such as lamps, which are desired to perish most rapidly, [action] occurs at a time distinct from birth.

(Conjunction) is the manifestation of the cause of the universal. From that, action arises in its own constituent part; immediately thereafter, there is disjunction and the destruction of the conjunction. Following that, the destruction of the substance occurs—even in the case of an object such as a lamp—wherein a duration of exactly six moments is accepted.

Every other goer, who is postulated as being either characterized by a separation from one location or by a subsequent contact with another, and who is mobile by nature—that person never remains even for the duration of a single atom; thus, a transition to another location is impossible for him.
If going and the other [motions] were by their very nature inherent in this [entity], which is stable and lacks distinction across all its states, then all of them would be impossible for it;
for if going and the others were its nature, it would always be of the form of a goer and thus could not remain motionless for even a single moment.

Since [they]—being devoid of motion (*gati*) and so forth (*ādi*)—would necessarily (*dhruvam*) attain those [states], because they have not abandoned their prior nature (*atyakta-pūrva-rūpatvāt*), just like time (*kāla-vat*), which possesses arising, motion, and so forth;

or else, if by its very nature it were a non-mover (*agantṛ*), then non-going (*agamanādayaḥ*) and the rest would always exist, and it could never even for a single moment (*ekam kṣaṇam*) be anything other than that.

Since [it exists] even when there is the state of motion and so forth, that [entity] is of that nature—immovable and not having abandoned its prior form—because it possesses the nature of time and is immovable.
However, if this [entity] were at one time a non-goer and again otherwise, then due to the mutual connection of distinct natures, there would be a state of difference.

(They) are determined (*vyavasīyate*; *vi-ava-so*, present passive third person singular); (thus), those two are absolutely distinct (*atyanta-bhinnau*, nominative dual) because of their possession of contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharma-vṛttitvāt*, ablative singular), such as mobility (*cala*) and immobility (*niścala*).

Furthermore, action (*karma*, nominative singular) is considered to be visible (*dṛśyatva-abhimatam*, nominative singular); it is not non-distinct (*avyatireki*, nominative singular) from the substance (*vastu*), nor does its existence (*sattā*, nominative singular) follow logically (*anupātinī*, nominative singular) from that [action]. Indeed, [action] is never perceived (*naiva dṛśyate*; *dṛś/paś*, present passive).

Thus, there is the impossibility of motion and so forth, whether [the object] be stable or unstable, because of the lack of connection with two locations— the preceding and the succeeding— [motion being] an illusion, like [the appearance of movement] from the arising of a lamp in successive similar objects due to their uninterrupted succession in different locations.

When substances and the other categories have been refuted, the universals (*jātayaḥ*) are also thereby rejected; for all of them are postulated as subsisting within the three categories [of substance, quality, and action]. Among these, the universal is accepted by our opponents as being of only two kinds: that which is called "Being" (*sattā*), because it persists through all things collectively.

However, "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth are designated as "universals" (*sāmānya*). They exist as "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) with respect to their own substrates (*sva-āśraya*) by virtue of being the cause of a recurring cognition (*anuvṛtta-buddhi*), and because they differentiate their own substrate from all things of a different class (*vijātiya*). Therefore, it is established that these [universals] alone possess the status of being the cause of the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-buddhi*).

Certain particularities (*viśeṣas*), which have been described as the ultimate particulars (*antya-viśeṣas*) residing in eternal substances (*nitya-dravya*), are themselves the causes of differentiation; by their power, cognitions arise for yogins regarding atoms and so forth—this is the unique [reason] that rests upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The universals, such as "existence" (*sattva*) and "cowness" (*gotva*), are well-established through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*), because they arise from the cognition of "being" (*sat*) and so forth when the sense organs (*akṣa*) are functioning. Their existence is cognized by the force of inference (*anumāna-bala*). Furthermore, the cognition of their specificities (*viśeṣa-pratyayaḥ*) is based on other causes (*antara-nimitta*).

The specific qualities (*viśeṣāḥ*) in cows, elephants, and so forth, which are the causes for the cognition (*prajñāna*) of the words "cow" and so on, are indeed distinct from the object (*artha*), the convention (*samaya*), the form (*ākṛti*), the individual body (*piṇḍa*), and so forth.

For, when these [specific qualities] are the objects of the word "cow" and so on, they are different from the word and the cognition; just as in the case of those two sounds (*dhvanī*) that produce the cognitions of "with calf" and "with goad" regarding these very same [animals].

Because of deviation (*vyabhicārāt*), the designation of things such as a "hare's horn" by means of cognitions (*vijñānaiḥ*) serves as an illustration (*nidarśanam*) by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

On the other hand, a cognition (*vijñānam*) that occurs (*anuvṛttam*) with respect to cows (*go-*) and so forth arises (*jāyate*) from something else—namely, from the individual bodies (*piṇḍataḥ*)—because they possess the quality of being qualifiers (*viśeṣakatvāt*), just like the cognition of "blue" (*nīla-*) and so forth.

"Cowness" (nominative singular) is a distinct entity from "cow" (ablative singular), because it is the object of a cognition different [from that of the cow], like color, touch, and so forth; and because of the statement regarding it [as such], like Caitra.

Thus, this description consisting merely of a formal procedure is unsubstantial; furthermore, no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is found here that serves as a prover (*jñāpaka*) for that.

The conditions, such as "being" (*sat*) and so forth, do not exist immediately following [the object] due to the operation of the senses; rather, they [are known] through the application of convention (*saṅketa*).
Just as in the case of nurses, fearlessness, and the like, each one is perceived individually, or even when combined, they possess the power to ward off various diseases.

There exists no commonality whatsoever among them [the medicinal plants] possessing the power [to cure], because of the perception of a difference in the pacification of diseases—whether rapid or slow—for indeed, there is no excellence in the universal (sāmānya) due to the distinction of field and so forth, since it is eternally of a single nature; that [excellence] is found in the specific plant (dhātrī) and the like.

Even so, although there is absolute difference, some things, by virtue of their fixed capacity, become causes for a single reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa*) and the like; others do not, because of the mere utility of the convention (*samaya*) established when there is a desire to speak of existence. Or rather, [the convention] is made among them according to one's own preference for another [word].

A convention (*saṅketa*) is established by users (*vyavahartṛbhiḥ*) for that which is useful (*upayogini*) in the form of a particular effect (*bheda-kārya-rūpeṇa*), such as carrying (*vāha*) or milking (*doha*).

These cognitions (*pratyayāḥ*) of "existent" (*sat*) and so forth are observed (*lakṣyante*) as they arise (*jāyamānāḥ*) from mental attention (*manaskārāt*) toward the convention (*saṅketa*); they do not [arise] immediately after the activity of the senses (*akṣa-vyāpṛti-anantaram*).

At first, consciousness alone arises in the form of that which is devoid of verbal expression; from that comes the mental application (*ābhoga*) regarding conventional designations (*samaya*). Therefore, for you, that [consciousness] is merely mnemonic (*smārtta*).

Furthermore, from that very [application], there occurs in the mind—having moved elsewhere—an apprehension (*upalambhana*) consisting of the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*), through the exclusion (*viveka*) of all adventitious attributes (*upādhi*).

In the first case, their fruitlessness is established at the very moment of the occurrence of [mental] application (*ābhoga*); that [application] is associated with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Since it is not external to the subject (*pakṣa*), the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhya*). Cows, calves, goads, and so forth are not direct causes of that [cognition].

There is no operation of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the denotable object, by which [conceptual construction] the particular characteristic would become the form (*mūrti*) that is the domain of past speech.
Rather, those [constructions] proceed by taking hold of—having determined as external—the conventional form that is mounted upon the "hook" of the internal measure (*antara-mātrā*).
Non-existence (*abhāva*) is described as the cause (*hetuḥ*) of the cognition (*pratyayasya*) [of it]; thus, the qualification (*viśeṣaṇam*) "non-existence" (*abhāva-*) is redundant (*anarthakam*).

That too is illogical (*ayuktam*) if it is a cause, because it would possess substantiality (*vastutā*) by virtue of its causal capacity (*śakti-tas*). Furthermore, the cognition of non-existence would result in being indistinguishable (*aviśeṣa-tas*) from the cognition of existence (*sattā*) and so forth.

The distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) of those cognitions from the intellect (*buddhi*), the lump (*piṇḍa*), the shape (*ākṛti*), and so forth, is unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), even though the cognition (*pratyaya*) is accompanied by a manifestation (*avabhāsavat*) of the word (*śabda*) and the individual (*vyakti*). However, the universal (*jāti*) is described as being devoid of form (*ākāra*), color (*varṇa*), shape (*ākṛti*), and syllables (*akṣara*).
If [the universal] were of the nature of blue and so forth, what distinction would there be for it by way of its qualities? A single, recurring blue and so forth is perceived.

Even if this [blue] appears, it is not characterized as distinct [from the particular]; how then could those two—the cognition and the verbal expression—operate upon the individual by the power of that [universal]?

This cognition, which is accepted by others as having the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) alone, is a conceptual determination (*niścaya*); and since it would follow that [the universal] is not apprehended, its non-perception is not tenable.
Furthermore, even if another cause were established, that which conforms [to the object] would not be proven to be distinct and non-eternal, because it arises sequentially (*krama*).

The word "existent" (*sat*) depends upon a cause (*hetum*), namely the meaning of the word (*padārtha*). Furthermore, there exists a cognition (*pratyayaḥ*) [of the form] "it is. If it is argued that this [cognition] which persists (*anuvarttate*) with respect to existence (*sattā*) and so forth [is the cause], then in that case, the notion of existence (*astitā-matiḥ*) would have another property (*anya-dharma*) as its cause. Consequently, since the status of being a subject (*dharmitā*) would entail the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa-āsakteḥ*) of having another property as its cause, [the opponent's position is untenable].
Therefore, this reason (*hetu*) is asserted by these [opponents] to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*); nor has its universal pervasion (*sarvopasaṃhāra-vyāpti*) been established.

Furthermore, the proof (*sādhana*) of the universal (*sāmānya*) that was mentioned immediately after that has been refuted by this very [argument]; thus, "the establishment of what is desired" (*iṣṭasiddhi*) and the other [objections] are equal in relation to it.

A distinguished cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) arises even without a single following [entity], such as the notion of a "cook" (*pācakabuddhi*). Furthermore, because it occurs in the absence of [entities]—such as in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), or regarding forms (*rūpa*) that have been fashioned by desire, or those that are destroyed or not yet born—it follows, for all these aforementioned reasons, that [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*).

There is no basis for the cognitions of "cook" and so forth, if [it is argued that] the action exists; surely that [action] differs with respect to each individual, and thus a universal possessing the recurrence across all individuals is not admitted. Therefore, in the absence of a recurring [entity], a recurring cognition is not logical with respect to distinct things.
If the universal (*anvaya-jāti*) is postulated as the cause of the cognition [of "cook"], then why are the individuals themselves not the causes of this [cognition]?
Furthermore, the cognition of a "cook" would not exist in that case when the action has ceased; for others do not accept that the action is always present, just like the universal.

If the word "cook" (*pācaka*) and others are applied to those [past and future agents] by taking as their cause (*nimittī-kṛtya*) a past or future action, that [action] is not the cause because of its non-existence (*asattvataḥ*).

If it is thought that [the application occurs] through connection with the action, through the relation with the universal (*jāti*) "action-ness," and through the indication (*upalakṣaṇāt*) by way of being the constant cause (*dhruvahetutayā*), then even when the action has perished, [the designation would still apply].

In that case, however, there is no genus (*jāti*) that is perceived as permanent when it is apprehended; nor does it exist even when characterized by its own substratum, because of the cessation [of that substratum]. When the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the staff, the armlet, and so forth cease at one time, the cognition (*mati*) of "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth does not arise upon their separation.

Now, if another cognition such as "cook-ness" and so forth were to arise immediately even when [the object] has just been born, due to its connection with that [universal], then— just like the cognition of "existence" and so forth— it would not be inherent (*samavāyinī*) in it even later, because there is no difference [in the circumstances].
Because of the deficiency of their own nature in relation to those two [the universal and the individual], how could that inherence (*samavāya*) come into being later through identity (*tādātmya*)?
If the manifestation (*vyakti*) were unstable, then it would acquire a deficient form distinct from the genus (*jāti*), which would never cease to exist.

And [terms] such as "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth are the primary means (*pradhāna-sādhana*) for the action of cooking and the like; moreover, this primacy exists within the "cook" itself. This primacy is not a capacity (*śakti*), because there is no concomitance (*asamanvaya*); therefore, it is conceived as the self-nature (*ātman*) of substance (*dravya*), action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth.

That cognition (*śemuṣī*) regarding cooks and the like is dependent upon distinctions of convention (*saṅketa-bheda*), and it consists merely in the exclusion (*viśleṣi*) of heterogeneous (*vijātīya*) forms.

For this very reason, words (*śabda*) and cognitions (*buddhi*) operate only with respect to differentiation (*vibhāga*) according to convention (*yathā-saṅketam*), and not without a single recurring [universal] (*anugāmin*).

Cognition (*vijñāna*) is not contradicted (*na virudhyate*) by non-existents (*abhāveṣu*), nor is the term (*dhvaniḥ*) that follows them; because it conforms (*anugamāt*) to those two through convention (*saṅketa*), this cognition (*dhīḥ*)—such as "the prior non-existence of the jar" (*prāk-abhāvo ghaṭasya*) or "the destruction of the jar" (*pradhvaṃso ghaṭaḥ*)—is understood (*prapadyate*) as being based on non-existents (*abhāvān*) that have [particular] entities (*vastu*) as their limiting adjuncts (*upādhikān*).

If [it is argued that] because of the power of its universal (*sāmānya*) and its inherent attributes (*upādhi*), there is continuity (*anuvṛttatā*) everywhere, [we reply: it is not so, because of the lack of such distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) in those [entities]. Therefore, a non-concomitant cognition (*anugāminī buddhiḥ*) such as "this is a jar" is not logically possible from those [individuals]; nor is this [cognition] a non-entity (*abhāva*). Rather, the cognition is indeed distinct (*vilakṣaṇā matiḥ*) from them.

For the cognition "cow" or "horse" is not admitted [to arise] by virtue of existence (*sattā*) alone; otherwise, a single universal would have to be postulated as the means for all [such cognitions]. If that were so, the cognition [of "cow," etc.
would not correspond to its cause, since it is accepted that the basis for cognitions such as "army" and the like is number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth.

If this [cognition] is thus, why is it not accepted that the cognition regarding these various particulars follows from the desire to compose conventions based on the distinction between the manifestation and the particular?

Since there is knowledge of the distinction, then there is the desire, the application of the convention, the production thereof, the hearing thereof, and the manifestation of it; from that, the cognition [arises].

This alone is determined to be the capable cause in that [cognition] by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). There is no infinite regress (*anavasthiti*) regarding other things;

thus, the conceptualization of another object would be a related entity (*saṃsargī*), but it would be more appropriate to rely on this much alone, given the distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) of cognitions.

In this case, a restriction must indeed be postulated based on capacity; and it is better that this [restriction] be postulated with respect to the potencies, which are known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, there is no conformity to positive concomitance (*anvayānuvidhāna*) among universals (*sāmānya*), because they are eternally non-existent [in relation to the effect]; however, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not possible for eternal entities.
