The property of being a cause (*hetutva*) for cognition (*dhiyaḥ*) regarding non-substances (*adravya*) and the like is not logical; nor, consequently, does inherence (*samavāya*) exist in multiple [non-substances].

Even if [inherence] were to exist in number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth, just as it does in universals (*sāmānyeṣu*), then cognitions would have to be universals (*sāmānyam*) with respect to those [number and so forth].

The universal (*sāmānya*), such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, exists only in things like pots; however, its occurrence (*vṛtti*) in absences (*abhāva*) does not. Therefore, how could there be a cognition (*dhī*) or even two words (*dhvani*) regarding them? For [cognition and word] are not applicable when they have occurred elsewhere, in a different substratum (*āśraya*), such as a white horse (*karka*). Furthermore, "elephant-ness" (*hastitva*) and so forth do not exist here, even though it is a single substratum for multiple objects (*ekārtha*).

Intellect (*matiḥ*, feminine nominative singular), taste (*rasaḥ*), and that which is cold (*śītaḥ*) and heavy (*guruḥ*, masculine nominative singular) may (*syāt*) be the substratum (*āśrayaḥ*) of a single object (*eka-artha-*) here (*iha*). Yet, this [substratum] is certainly not a non-entity (*a-bhāvaḥ*); nor does it exist anywhere (*kvacit*) as something separate.

If there exists here a relation (*sambandhaḥ*) between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya-*), then surely (*nanu*) that [relation] is conceived (*prakalpyate*) through another relation (*sambandha-antara-*) existing (*sad-bhāve*).

The qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṇya*) are conceived (*kalpyate*) by relying (*āśritya*) upon their proximity (*āsatti*); however, in the absence of that [proximity], it [the relation] is not established, being without a cause (*animittā*).
This expression, "prior non-existence of the jar" (*prāg-abhāvo ghaṭasya*), and so forth, is like [the term] "heroism" (*śūratā*) and the like when applied to what is merely imagined (*kalpite*).

Wherever there is a thing (*vastu*) that serves as the basis for both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), the existence of another [thing]—namely, a relation (*sambandha*)—is necessarily postulated (*prakalpyate*). Likewise, it is stated here that the cognition "this is non-existence" (*abhāva*) is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*) residing in a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), which exists only within its own substrata (*sva-āśrayeṣu*).

Nor is it accepted that there exists a persisting entity (*sattva*) among those [objects], for cognitions (*buddhi*) do not arise with respect to non-existent things (*abhāva*), except insofar as they are constructed by desire (*icchā-racita*) regarding objects such as color-form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, a universal (*jāti*) does not exist at all because of the impossibility of its manifestation (*vyakti*); thus, its [the universal's] deviation from the object remains established.
If there were knowledge [of universals] regarding past and future [particulars], then this [universal] would have the eternal universal as its object; however, this universal alone is not perceived.

Or, if there were the apprehension of the universal alone, this [universal] would not exist as a universal of particulars, nor would it be manifested by them—just as the Himalaya is not manifested by the Vindhya.

For this [cognition] is not dependent for its arising upon those [objects] by way of dependence on them; rather, the dependence of cognition [is due to] its permanence, because it is apprehended as being solitary, and because there is no possibility of its requiring [anything else], such as a connection with its own basis, the sense organ, or the like. Or else, it would be perceived at all times, or else never at all.

Whether it be capable (*yogya*) with respect to the production of cognition (*jñāna-janana*), or whether it be itself (*ātmani*) incapable (*ayogya*), at one time or another, it would indeed [remain so] always (*sarvadā*).

For its nature (*rūpa*)—whether capable or incapable—is established by its own intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-sthita*); because of that permanence (*dhaivryāt*), who indeed could move that which is unshakable (*aprakampya*)?

The universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is distinct from the object "cow" (*go*) because it is the object of a different cognition, just as color, touch, and so forth are; this statement [of yours] is subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as in the case of "horse" and "Caitra.
Furthermore, by this same line of reasoning, all other fallacious arguments (*kuhetu*) are likewise to be refuted.

Moreover, regarding that which is said—that the universal has the property of subsisting in many—what kind of subsistence (*vṛtti*) is considered there? Is it persistence (*sthiti*), or indeed manifestation (*vyakti*)?

Stability is the non-falling away of this [entity] from its own nature by virtue of its inherent essence; it is the substratum capable of performing that [act], by which there would be the state of being a stabilizer.
Furthermore, since there is no obstruction to its movement—just as in the case of a jujube fruit—it possesses no activity (*niṣkriyatva*); therefore, a substratum is not postulated.

If inherence (*samavāya*) is that [connection] which is the subsistence (*sthiti*) of those [things], then that very [inherence] is being examined: is it of the nature of the relation between the locus (*āśraya*) and the located (*āśrayin*) among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*)?

That [inherence] is accepted as the support (*ādhāra*) for water and so forth, and as the preventer (*pratibandhaka*) of motion; but what is the use of postulating supports for universals (*sāmānya*), which are themselves devoid of motion (*agati*)?

If [the entity] is already capable of producing its own cognition, what is the use of causes for its manifestation? If it is incapable of producing its own cognition, what is the use of causes for its manifestation? If that which is already capable is produced by manifesting agents (*vyañjakaiḥ*), then the entity would be non-stable, like a jar or other objects [manifested] by a lamp.

Or rather, the particulars (*bhedāḥ*) that subsist in universals such as "jar" (*jāti-ghaṭādi-vṛtti-bhājaḥ*) might exist only in their own respective substrata (*sva-eva-āśrayeṣu*) everywhere (*sarvatra*), just as other universals do (*para-jāti-vat*), at the time of the manifestation of a substance (*vastu-prādurbhāve*) in another location (*antara-deśe*). If this is so, how is it not understood (*na gamyate*) why those particulars (*te nu*) are seen (*dṛśyante*) as subsisting (*vṛtti-bhājaḥ*) in that [specific] location? (*tasmin*)?
They are not produced together with that [cause], because of its permanence; nor do they abide there, because they lack prior pervasiveness; and being inactive, they do not come from elsewhere.

If [it is argued that] when there is the apprehension of one [object] by the sense-faculties and so forth, which have their own substrates as their basis, all [objects] would indeed be perceived because of the non-distinction of its own nature;

[then] if it were not distinct from the knower, there would be the apprehension of that [knower] as well, or else there would be no apprehension of that [object] either, or likewise, there would be [only] difference.

These [words] such as *vṛka* and so forth are not [denotative] of universals (*jāti*) other than those [universals] such as *āditva* (the state of being first) and *kramitva* (the state of being in sequence), just as the cognitions of "cook" and so forth [are not denotative of universals].

Furthermore, the fact that an eternal entity is not a producer [of cognition] is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), and everything that was stated regarding the refutation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) serves as a subverting argument against [the opponent's position].
Thus, this category (*jāti*) has been utterly refuted; however, that which was accepted by the followers of Jaimini will be refuted in the *syādvāda*.

Furthermore, these particularities (*viśeṣas*) which were postulated as being ultimate (*antya*), even though they are impossible through exclusion (*vyapoha*), those moments (*kṣaṇās*) [are likewise untenable].

When the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of atoms, space, direction, and so forth is unmixed (*asaṅkīrṇa*), then [that] is the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of their distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) from this [other].

However, if they were to become mixed with another essence (*miśrībhūtāparātmānaḥ*), even in the presence of something else, there would be no unmistakable (*avibhrānta*) indicator of their distinctness.

If it is argued that the distinctive characteristic (*vailakṣaṇya*) among those various things is merely an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), then why is it not likewise accepted that even in the case of atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth, impurity (*aśucitva*) exists intrinsically (*svataḥ*), just as it is established in the case of dog-flesh and the like? However, if it is maintained here as well that for others it exists through connection (*yoga*) with that [impurity], [then the same applies].

Just as a lamp, existing by itself, is the illuminator of a jar and so forth, and this [lamp] is restricted to its nature of illumination—just as that is so, is it not the case that this impure state is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) and not real (*tāttvika*)? Therefore, how indeed could it come to be either by itself or from another?

Alternatively, even if these entities (*bhāvāḥ*) were real (*bhāvikatve*), they would arise (*jāyante*) as impure things (*aśucayaḥ*) by virtue of [being made from] dog-flesh and so forth; they could never be eternal (*nityāḥ*) because they are not unproduced (*ajanyataḥ*).

Furthermore, by the power of lamps and the like, jars, ornaments, and other such things (*kalaśa-ābharaṇa-ādayaḥ*) obtain their own nature (*svarūpatām*) through production and cognition (*utpāda-jñāna-*).

"Cognition (*matiḥ*) characterized by distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya-*) cannot exist (*na bhāvinī*) based on a specific force (*bala-viśeṣa-*) that has become the locus (*āspadībhūta-*) for the arising of dispute (*vivāda-utpatteḥ*), just as in the case of pleasure (*sukha-ādi-vat*).

Inherence (*samavāyaḥ*) is understood (*avagamyate*) from the existence (*bhāvāt*) of cognition (*mateḥ*), and so forth. Here, "this cloth" (*paṭaḥ*) [subsists] in these threads (*tantuṣu*), whereas again, "the mat" (*kaṭaḥ*) [subsists] in the *vīraṇa* grasses (*vīraṇeṣu*).

If that [non-existence] were the basis (*nibandhana*) for this cognition (*mati*), then no cognition of distinction would be observed as being devoid of another cause; and because there is no distinction in the intellect (*buddhi*), it does not differ here, just like [the cognition of] conjunction (*yoga*). However, it is perceived as one and the same in all cases, just like [the cognition of] existence (*bhāva*).
Because no cause is perceived, that [consciousness] is indeed eternal, just like [the nature of] existence; for no cause of it is apprehended by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This notion exists here among others solely out of attachment to their own tenets, but it is not observed in common worldly experience.

Since there would be a difference in characteristics between the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) would [not] exist here in cases such as the *śrīphala* fruit and so forth, or the cloth and its threads; for there exists no characteristic of difference by which cognitions (*buddhi*) could arise with respect to them. Thus it is here.

In this [work], composed at will as if it were a mere fabrication regarding objects, no further causal necessity is applicable. This worldly understanding arises from the perception of branches on a tree and stones on a mountain, due to their uninterrupted connection with the remaining parts.

[The cognition] "this" [refers to] those two [the jar and the cloth] in relation to those [other objects]; furthermore, [the cognition] "transcending the world" [refers to] the form of the action in the jar.
Indeed, words such as "form" and "jar" are expressive of all states for the purpose of denoting that specific [object], and thus they are applied accordingly.
Depending on those [threads], consciousness arises by means of that form; it does not [arise] through inherence (*samavāya*), because no distinction is perceived among all of them.
Furthermore, if there were only one single inherence in all things, then the cognition "it is a cloth" and so forth would necessarily follow even with respect to potsherds and the like.

(The term) "is attached" (*anuṣajyate*) is used in the passive sense. Thus, "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth exist (*samasti*) even in elephants (*gaja*) and the like. Therefore, their being the form of "cow" (*go*) and so forth is perceived (*pratīyate*), just as in the case of *śābaleya*.
Just as a cloth exists in threads due to inherence (*samavāya*), and that same [cloth] exists in potsherds—why then is it not likewise [the case] for that [universal]?
If it is not dependent upon the potsherd, then surely it is dependent upon those threads by way of inherence (*samavāya*). But does that [inherence] not exist in the potsherd?
For it is said: "Inherence of the cloth is in the thread; inherence of the jar is in the potsherds. Therefore, there would be a cognition that is without a limit.

In this way, inherence (*samavāya*) [exists] in the elephant and so forth with respect to elephant-ness (*gajatva*) and so forth; that very same [inherence], moreover, exists as the restriction of the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*) even among the various universals (*jāti*) such as cow-ness (*gotva*) and so forth within their own respective substrata (*sva-āśraya*), despite their being one. For indeed, the state of being an object (*karmatā*) exists only in relation to the objects that are universals.
Because it is perceived everywhere through the cognition of the positive concomitance (*anvaya-vijñāna*) arising here [in this world], inherence (*samavāya*) is understood as being indeed one.

Because it is perceived, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the causes such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth is determined by cognitions; thus, there is a restriction regarding the universals (*jāti*) of substance and so forth.

Just as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), even when there is identity (*aikya*), is observed to have a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the relationship between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*), such as that between a bowl (*kuṇḍa*) and curds (*dadhi*); likewise, a restriction is held to exist here in the case of inherence (*samavāya*) despite its oneness, due to the distinction (*bheda*) between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) among universals (*jāti*) and so forth, beginning with substances (*dravya*). If this is so, then it is not at all contradicted.

If [the relation] is one, then surely the restriction of the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*) is difficult to establish. Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is held to exist only in substance (*dravye*); how then does it [exist there] through inherence (*samavāyataḥ*)?
And that inherence exists in it [substance] as well as in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, because of the connection; yet this [inherence] is indeed one for both of them.

Otherwise, this [cognition] would indeed be distinct from genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, just as the connection (*yoga*) varies with each individual (*prativyakti*) according to its specific relation (*bheda-yogin*). Furthermore, it is not logical that there be a distinction (*vyatireka*) among cognitions, because the causes (*nimitta*), such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like, are present; therefore, even in that case, there is no restriction (*niyama*) regarding them.

[The term] "is denoted" (*abhidhīyate*) [is used in the sense of] being dependent (*āśritatva*), abiding (*sthāna*), and so forth; therefore, it is precisely because of inherence (*samavāya*) that this is not logical as a restrictive factor (*niyāmakam*).

Even though there is a distinction between the capacity of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), that [distinction] does not arise from anything else, because for eternal things (*nityānām*), such a distinction is untenable (*an-upapatti*).
Just as these [entities] do not arise due to the presence of lamps and the like, so too the primary classes [of objects], such as jars, are incapable of producing consciousness;

furthermore, the single conjunction of the bowl and the curd was previously refuted, and therefore that [conjunction] is not tenable as a fixed cause, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

[If it is argued that] all [entities], beginning with jars, would necessarily be eternal because they always possess an inherence (*samavāya*) in their substrates due to their [eternal] configuration (*saṃsthiti*), [we reply:

they do not perish either through the disjunction (*vibhāga*) from their own constituent parts (*sva-ārambhaka*), or through the destruction (*vināśa*) of those [parts], just as [the destruction of] action (*kriyā*) and so forth results from the cessation of conjunction (*yoga*) and so forth; if this is [your] view, that is not so.
Inherence is held to be eternal even for those [qualities] with respect to their own substrata; however, upon the existence of their destruction, perishability is necessarily established.
For when a related entity ceases, it is difficult to maintain that the relation persists; indeed, when a conjoined object is destroyed, the conjunction does not remain.
Just as there is a state of conjunction for those things that are conjoined when conjunction exists, so too would it be for those things that are inherent when inherence exists.

Even upon the destruction of one related member, inherence remains because of the existence of the other related member—if you say this, [we reply] no, because conjunction does not [persist] due to its distinctness.
If those things such as the jar, which are inherent [in it], perish,

would that [substratum] itself remain— possessing the nature of their subsistence— due to its connection with another [entity], or would it be something entirely different, like [the substratum of] conjunction?

The first [alternative] is not [tenable], because if that which is characterized as inherence were established, then those things such as jars would follow as being already established—just like [the inherence itself]—since there would be no further basis for their existence; and thus inherence, being their very nature, would not subsist anywhere at all, even by means of a mere designation.
Therefore, they would not exist after [the cause] as they did before, because they have ceased to abide in their substratum; likewise, this functioning of theirs is unreal (*avastutaḥ*).
Now, if it is argued that inherence (*samavāya*) persists even when its other related entity is absent—just as in the case of conjunction, disjunction, plurality, and so forth.
In this way, there would be a multiplicity of this [inherence]—just as in the case of conjunction and so forth; thus, if it were to exist, there would be many such [instances], which is inconsistent.

If no limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), what two objects could there be for cognition and verbal expression—such as "the man with a staff," "white," "moving," "there is a cow," and so forth?
Those two [cognition and expression] would not be considered to be without a cause; for their occurrence (*vṛtti*) through non-distinction (*avibhāga*) is possible in relation to everything.
It is said: "There is no object whatsoever for these cognitions and verbal expressions; rather, their basis is the seed established within [the mind].
Whatever is expressed as the object of whichever word, that very thing does not exist at all. For such is the nature of things."

Since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*jāti*), the connection (*yoga*) with that [universal], the possessor of that [universal] (*tan-mat*), the universal itself, and likewise the form (*ākāra*) of cognition do not, in reality, apply to the object of a word, then first of all, the particular characteristic is not expressed by words, because it lacks the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of time, place, and conventional linguistic usage (*saṅketa-vyavahāra*).
Individual selves are not [distinguished] by differences in place, time, action, capacity, intuition, and so forth;
therefore, an object perceived through convention is seen in linguistic usage, and that convention, if not grasped, would not be understood from a sound, just as something else [would not].

Even those atoms of the Himalayas and so forth, which are non-different with respect to place and time and are established as momentary—since they are observed to be distinct [from one another], a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) regarding this convention (*samaya*) is not tenable, whether [the object] has arisen or has not arisen; for a real convention is not possible with respect to what has not arisen, just like [the convention for] a horse's horn.

Even when [the object] has arisen, a convention (*samaya*) is not formed through recollection (*anusmṛti*) of things previously apprehended; how indeed could that [recollection] occur with respect to something past and long gone?

Furthermore, there is no other similar [object] by whose power there might be an application (*ābhoga*) of the convention; nor even in that case is there any similarity (*sādṛśya*), which is merely conceptualized (*vikalpita*).
That [cognition] which is to arise from heat and so forth, appearing as sound, name, and so on, does not appear clearly like the cognition of sense objects;
such a connection of that [sound] with the word is not logical, since the object does not manifest when that [word] has been produced, just as taste does not manifest in the cognition of form.

By this very same method, the refutation of both the individual (*vyakti*) and the form (*ākṛti*) is established; for since their identity with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is accepted by others, yet [their identity with] substance (*dravya*) and so forth, as well as [their identity with] connection (*yoga*), has not been previously stated, it is not tenable that there is a real establishment of those two as being the referents of words.

The three kinds of word-meanings (*śabdārtha*)—namely, the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the universal (*jāti*)—are not conceived as being immediate [to one another]. Therefore, that which is said regarding the individual, the configuration, and the universals is impossible, because all of them are devoid of intrinsic nature (*nīrūpatā*).
The mental aspect (*ākāra*) residing in cognition does not follow the object; furthermore, it produces the intended effect. Therefore, it cannot be said to be [the object] in reality.
Even those who otherwise explain the meaning of words—such as [those who claim] that the object exists and so forth—are likewise refuted by these [arguments]. Nevertheless, it is stated once more:
[They] say: "The meaning exists as the common characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of all words—such as 'cow' and others—with respect to [objects like] apūrva, deities, and heaven.

By some it is said that the meaning of a word is either the denotable object (*abhidheya*), or the collection (*samudāya*) free from conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*), or even a non-real relation (*asa-tya-saṃsarga*).

That [object] is real which is the basis for the word; or else, even though the word has arrived at the state of being a mental construct (*abhijalpa*), it goes toward the state of being denotable (*vācyatā*).

When a form (*rūpa*) is unified with a word (*śabda*) by means of its connection with an object (*artha*), that very word is declared to be "inner discourse" (*abhijalpa*). The object (*artha*) is the domain (*viṣaya*) of cognition (*buddhi*), which is based upon an external thing (*bāhyavastu*); when it is known as such, it is regarded by some as the external thing itself, namely, the object of the word.
In brief, every word is the cause of intuition (*pratibhā*) through practice (*abhyāsāt*), just as it is for children and animals in the communication of meaning (*artha-pratipādane*).

In that regard, there exists an intended denotable object (*abhidheya*). Is this [object] the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the universal (*jāti*), or the relation (*yoga*), or something else—an image (*pratibimbaka*) which is the cognition (*buddhi*) itself?

Our own faults have already been stated; furthermore, it is possible for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) to occur through differentiation (*bheda*) when the object (*artha*) alone is to be communicated. This would be the case because [the cognition] arises from the mere existence (*sattā-mātra*) of the object qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*), the word (*śabda*), and so forth. However, that [differentiation] is held to arise from the mention (*ākhyāti*) of distinctions such as "horns," "shape" (*ākṛti*), "blue," and the like.

[Objection: In that case, there would be a denotation of the object (*artha*) and of that which possesses it (*tadvat*), as well as of the particulars (*bheda*). Furthermore, since those do not exist therein, there would be a fault; moreover, no other object exists that could be perceived.
Even when there is the denotation of a collection (*samudāya*), the clear expression (*abhidhā*) of the genus (*jāti*) occurs through the denotation of its distinctions (*bheda*).

However, the connection (*sambandha*) of substance (*dravya*) and so forth with their own forms (*svarūpa*) is determined through their association (*yoga*). Furthermore, that universal (*sāmānya*) which was previously established as real (*satya*) has been refuted.

A distinction between meaning and word does not occur in the form of a genus (*jāti*), because it is logically untenable. The form of the word, when made identical with the object, is not established as distinct;

this mental discourse (*jalpa*) resides only within cognition (*buddhi*). Since there is no external connection (*yoga*), what distinction could there be for this [word] from the aforementioned position (*pakṣa*) regarding cognition?

Furthermore, the view that the form (*ākāra*) is the object of cognition has already been refuted; for a word [denoting] an object that is not distinct from cognition would be devoid of its pervading nature (*vyāpakatva*).
Moreover, if the mental image (*pratibhā*) were the external object, then since the referent of the word would be restricted to a single external essence, how could there be diverse mental images?

Now, if these [cognitions] are, in reality, devoid of objects—being merely the impressions (*vāsanā*)—how could there be either a comprehension (*pratipatti*) or an engagement (*pravṛtti*) with external objects?

If it is held that the object of the word is attained through a mental resolve (*adhimokṣa*) toward the form of the external [object] within its own [mental] aspect, then that object is not real, because it proceeds in such a way through delusion (*bhrānti*).

That [cognition] would be seedless, which is untenable because it would lead to an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*). If, on the other hand, its seed were everywhere [the same], then this would be our position:
that all this is momentary. Or else, if it were not so—[that is,] if there were no momentariness—then there could be no sequential cognition.

By this [same argument], even that which is to be understood from words is refuted; for when the meaning of a word is impossible, where could there be an intention to speak, or where could there be the hearing [of the word]?

And how could there be the application of the hearing [of the word] through similarity (*sārūpya*)? [The case of] what is not enjoined by a word through similarity, such as the names "Yamalaka" and so forth, has been refuted by this very [argument].

If the activity of those two who determine [the object] is based on the form being conjoined with the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) by virtue of the existence of an inference regarding the external [object], then that very thing is our own position.
But how is it said by you: "The word here consists merely of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); negation alone is not at all apprehended in the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*)"?
However, the verbal cognition (śābdī matiḥ) in the form of "cow," "gavaya," "elephant," "tree," and so forth, proceeds by way of a positive determination (vidhirūpāvasāyena).

If this word "cow" has as its meaning the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), let another sound be observed which produces the cognition of a cow with respect to a cow. Are not words the fruit of cognition? And how can there be two fruits for one [word]—namely, the fruits of affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*apavāda*)? Or how could these be the fruits of a single [word]?

It might be argued: "The cognition [arising] from the word 'cow' would be of a non-cow, by which the sound 'cow' is employed for the purpose of negating the non-cow. By those who have accepted that the universal (*sāmānya*)—the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*)—is the denotable object, it is indeed stated by this very expression that "cowness" (*gotva*) is a real entity (*vastu*).

Since every non-entity (*abhāva*) is established as having the nature of the absence of another entity (*antarbhāva*), let it be stated what that non-entity is whose nature consists of the exclusion of horses and so forth (*nivṛttāśvādi*).

For you do not accept a specific nature (*viśeṣa*) that is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), because [such a thing] would be beyond conceptual construction (*nirvikalpanāt*). Furthermore, by such a consequence, the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others would follow as being non-universals (*asāmānya*).

Therefore, if the object of a word is conceived as that form which is fully established in each individual cow-cognition, then there would be a mere negation of other modes; thus, the emptiness of the word's denotation would be [the meaning], namely, non-existence.

In that case, [the property of] being denotable (*vācyatva*) by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) would belong to horses and the like; for indeed, the meaning of a word would then be merely a conceptualized form of a mental cognition (*buddhyākāra*), which is a real universal (*sāmānya*). This [position] is accepted [by you] as such, but it is entirely in vain.

If that cognition (*buddhi*) arises with respect to objects (*artheṣu*) in the form of words (*śabda-rūpā*), then the object itself would have to be conceived as the denotable (*vācya*) [meaning] that which is devoid of the exclusion of other cognitions (*an-apoha-buddhi*).
Just as the meaning of a sentence (*vākya-artha*) appears even when an external object (*bāhya-artha*) does not exist, so too might the meaning of a word (*pada-artha*) be;
why then is *apoha* postulated?

In cognition (*buddhau*), no exclusion (*vyavacchedaḥ*) from another cognition (*antarāt buddheḥ*) is perceived; rather, it perceives [it] only through its own nature of arising (*utpādasvarūpamātrāt*). That [cognition] does not bear any other part (*anyaṃ aṃśam*).

If exclusion (*apoha*) were the denotable object, then all words would be synonyms; for there exists no distinction whatsoever among exclusions, because they are non-entities (*avastutva*), being devoid of conceptual construction and lacking both unity and plurality.

If [it is argued that the universal is] not a real entity because it is being differentiated—just like the unique portion (*asādhāraṇāṃśa*) of a thing—then it is not released from [the charge of being a non-entity], because of its synonymy with [the universal] and because there is no difference [between them].

Furthermore, will the differentiation of the exclusion (*apoha*) not indeed be established by means of the differentiation of horses and so forth? No distinction whatsoever arises either intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*).

Even though we, who are the substrates possessing [the property of] association, do not divide that which is [identical] in its essential form, it would be divided by the excluded parts as external factors; this is an excessive conceptualization.

In that case, a distinction [between the universal and the particular] is not tenable for this [universal], by means of a distinction from its substratum; for even a distinction in a real entity (*vastu*) is held to exist by means of a distinction from its correlate (*saṃbandhin*).

How much more so, then, would it be excluded [from the universal]—that which is a non-entity (*avastu*), unconnected (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*), undifferentiated (*avyāvṛtta*), a part (*aṃśa*) that is not pervaded (*avyāpta*) by any specific property (*viśeṣa*), and entirely indefinable (*anirūpita*)?
Furthermore, no one is able to know the similarity of cows and so forth [to others] when the exclusion (*apoha*) of an unestablished object is not yet known;

moreover, without a single common property (*anvaya-eka-dharma*), there is no capacity to determine the things to be excluded (*apohya*), such as horses and so forth. Therefore, that exclusion (*apoha*) is established.

The operation of words and logical marks is not devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*); nor is there exclusion (*apoha*) without those two, nor is there positive concomitance in the case of that which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).

Since exclusion is unestablished [in such a case], where could there be co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*)? Tell me! And when that [co-occurrence] is not perceived, how could those two possess the status of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇatā*)?
There would be no cognition [of exclusion] by means of mere non-perception; for, because it is not seen, the cognition is not distinguished in every case.

Now, if there were no similarity (*sārūpya*), there might be the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of an exclusion (*apoha*); why then is this exclusion of the "non-cow" not conceived in relation to both the cow and the horse?

If [the] distinctness from a brindled cow is equal [to that] from a black cow and from two horses, and if no other universal is admitted, then where could the exclusion of the non-cow (*agopoha*) operate?

Furthermore, the exclusion (*apoha*) of the non-cow is not first apprehended by the sense organs; nor does the application of the word occur elsewhere [than in the object]. Having seen what, then, should it be employed?
As has been stated previously, there is no inference here either, and for that reason, there is certainly no experience of its relationship [to the word].

But how can it be understood [thus]? "The word 'cow' (*go-śabdaḥ*), which does not have 'cow' (*go*) as its denotable object (*an-abhidheya-śabda*), is not observed at that moment when there is the experience of the relation [of the word] with 'cow. Therefore, everything that might arise from the individual cow (*go-piṇḍāt*) would be the object of exclusion (*apohyam*). Consequently, by this [reasoning], there is no denotability (*vācyatā*) for a universal (*sāmānyasya*)."

If the non-cow (*agauḥ*) were established (*siddhaḥ*), it would have to be excluded (*apohyeta*). And that [non-cow] consists of the negation (*niṣedha*) of the cow; therefore, only the cow itself (*gauḥ eva*) must be stated—that which is being negated (*pratiṣidhyate*) by the negative particle (*nañ*). If that [cow] were to be the very nature (*ātmā*) of the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of the non-cow, based on mutual dependence (*anyonya-saṃśraya*), then since the cow is already established, the conceptualization (*prakalpanam*) of exclusion for the sake of exclusion is redundant (*vṛthā*).

If the non-cow is not established, then there is no "non-cow. But if that [non-cow] does not exist, how can there be a cow? Furthermore, between two absences, there can be no relationship such as that of the contained and the container. Moreover, a thing that is unique [to itself] cannot be understood by way of exclusion (*apoha*). Or else, how could a relationship be postulated between a real entity and a non-entity?

No qualifier whatsoever [exists] by virtue of its mere existence as its own nature—that by which the qualificand might be colored by its own cognition through a word such as "horse" and so forth; nor is there produced a cognition of exclusion (*apoha*), nor is the cognition of the qualificand accepted here [as being produced], since a qualifier that is unknown [cannot function as such].
One would not make a qualification [of] a cognition that is of a different nature; and how could that be called a qualification with respect to a cognition of a different kind?

Even if there were a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it would still be otherwise with respect to the qualified (*viśeṣya*). For whatever slight qualifier might be apprehended in a qualified entity that lacks the nature of being cognized, it possesses no substantiality (*vastutā*); therefore, for you, there is no real entity (*vastu*) that can be expressed as qualified by an exclusion (*apoha*).

Even though the operation (*vṛtti*) of word and logical mark (*liṅga*) does not occur in that which is devoid of exclusion (*apoha*), nevertheless, cognition (*bodha*) takes hold of the object (*vastu*) to be known;

and the unique (*asādhāraṇa*) object does not appear (*viparivarttate*) in the intellect (*buddhi*). Furthermore, its being apprehended (*adhigamyatā*) is not tenable, because it is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatvāt*).
And [if it were argued that] "that which is not being cognized by the word" is the object of the intellect and the word, then that particular (viśeṣya) must be accepted as the universal (sāmānya).

When individuals (vyakti) are what are excluded (apohyatā), because they cannot be expressed by the word, then the universal would itself be excluded; and from its exclusion, its status as a real entity (vastutā) would follow.

956. "Non-existents (*abhāvānām*) cannot be the objects of exclusion (*apohyatvam*), because they are themselves excluded from non-existence. Therefore, the exclusion of one thing from another is clearly established as a positive entity (*vastu*). If [it is argued that] non-existence is distinct from [other] non-existences, then it would follow that it is indeed a positive entity (*bhāvaḥ*). If it were not so, then for you, the 'cow' would result in being a 'non-cow'."

In other words (*anyeṣu śabdeṣu*), there could be the state of being excluded (*apohyatā*) for a real entity (*vastunaḥ*). However, that which is distinct (*bhinnaṃ na*) from existence (*sat*) cannot be accepted (*iṣyate*) as the object to be excluded (*apohyaṃ*), since it is described (*ākhyāta*) as non-existence (*a-bhāva*).
In that case as well, if non-existent things were to possess existence, there would be a great difficulty; for if that [existence] is not established, neither existence nor non-existence is proven.

Furthermore, neither a distinction nor a positive nature (*sadrūpatā*) could be conceived for exclusions (*apoha*), because of the distinction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*). For that [nature] is not admitted by you to exist in a non-entity (*avastu*).
Nor can a distinction caused by words be obtained, for a word is not expressive of what is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), since it has not been perceived previously.

In that case, since the imagined universal (*sāmānya*)—which is an exclusion (*apoha*) of other words—is by its very nature not a real entity (*avastu-rūpatva*), no distinction between words is postulated in that way;

nor is there any distinction between the denotator and the denoted, either mutually or otherwise. Thus, it has been demonstrated that there is no distinction [between them] by means of an exclusion (*apohya*).

It may be that there is no relationship of signifier and signified (*gamya-gamakabhāva*) between two exclusions (*apoha*), because they are non-entities (*avastutva*) according to your own position, just as in the world there is none between a sky-flower and a hare’s horn.

If you say that [the relationship] is seen despite the absence of rain and clouds, we reply that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to our own position; let it simply be a real entity (*vastu*)—for how could that [non-entity] exist even here?

If that object which is not accepted as being of the nature of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) expressed by a word were not to exist, then even its exclusion (*vyatireka*) would be preceded by that [positive form].

It is admitted that [the word] "go" or "gaccha" has the status of being denotative merely through exclusion (*apoha*). However, in this case, there is no establishment of the properties of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), qualified (*viśeṣya*), and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in words such as "blue-lotus" (*nīlotpala*) which denote their objects.
For when the variegated object is excluded, there is the loss of non-blueness from the non-lotus, and not from anything else;
therefore, in that case, there can be no relationship between the qualified and the qualifier, nor can those two [terms] exist as the denotations of two words that are independent of one another.

If it is argued that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because the two exclusions (*apoha*) are not distinct, then if that were accepted, by what kind of "locatedness" (*ādheyatā*) would those two [be related] in terms of their actual meaning? Neither the unique [particular] is perceived, nor does anything else exist for you; where, then, could the single referent (*ekārthya*) of the two words—which is not being perceived—be of use?

Now, it might be argued: "The object [denoted] is that which possesses exclusion (*apoha*). Even in that case, the pervasion by the word is difficult to obtain, because [exclusion] is dependent on another.
Furthermore, there is no connection between exclusion and gender, number, and so forth, because exclusion is inexpressible; therefore, it does not exist even by way of those [categories].

In verbal forms (ākhyāteṣu), the exclusion (nivṛttiḥ) of another (anyasya) is not perceived (na sampratīyate); for in that case (tatra), there exists no (na) thing to be negated (niṣedhyam) in the form of a paryudāsa.

Indeed, even when it is stated (ucyamāne) "not not" (na na), there is a negation (niṣedhanam) of the negation (niṣedhasya); thus, [the action] such as "he cooks" (pacati) or "he stands" (tiṣṭhati) remains unprohibited (a-niṣiddham) in its own essential nature (svarūpeṇa).

In that case, it follows that there would be a cognition of the state of being the object to be proven (*sādhyatva*), as well as the determination (*rūpaṇa*) of the exclusion (*apoha*) of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth, because [that exclusion] is already established (*niṣpannatvāt*). Furthermore, in the case of a collection (*rāśi*) of positive objects (*arthavidhi*) and the like, what kind of exclusion (*apoha*) of the other could possibly exist (*bhavet*) when joined with the negative particle (*nañ*)? It would be a groundless (*nirnimitta*) determination.

Since there is no connection at all with the negative particle (*nañ*) for words such as "beginning" (*ādi*), there is no exclusion (*an-apohana*) in the meaning of the sentence; the cessation of others cannot be designated when [a word] like "beginning" is used, because it is not the exclusion of non-others (*ananya-apoha*). Nor is that which is to be expressed (*vācya*) determined; for how indeed could that which is to be excluded (*apohya*)—namely, the beginning of words, objects of cognition (*prameya*), or things to be known (*jñeya*)—be established?

In the case of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), it is better to posit (*kalpita*) a real entity (*vastu*) itself as the object (*artha*) denoted (*abhidhīyate*) by the word, because of the exclusion (*niṣedha*) of the form (*ākāra*) of cognition; [it is] not [an external thing], nor is there the state of being excluded (*apohyatā*) from that [entity].

Therefore, among those words beginning with "beginning" (*ādi-śabda*), that which is to be excluded (*apohya*) is not established (*na sidhyati*). Thus, in this way, that which is to be excluded (*apohya*) is not determined (*na nirūpyate*).

What meaning (*arthaḥ*) of the word "all" (*sarva-*) is conceived (*prakalpyate*) as that which is to be excluded (*vyavacchedyaḥ*)? For there would be nothing that is "non-all" (*a-sarva-*) whose exclusion could take place.

If it is argued that "one" (*eka-*) and so forth constitute the "non-all," then [the term] "exclusion of objects" (*arthāpohaḥ*) would follow as applying to the parts (*aṅgānām*), because [the exclusion of the whole] has been refuted, and furthermore, it is not desired that the whole (*aṅginaḥ*) be separate from its parts.

"In this way, by excluding [the meaning] from a collection of words (*śabda-samūha-vyapohataḥ*), all constituent members (*samudāyin*) would follow as being devoid of meaning (*nirarthaka*), because nothing else is desired.
Furthermore, those words such as 'two' and so forth, which have as their object a collection (*samuccaya*), would not exist as such if there were a negation of 'one' and so forth."

The meaning of the word "cow" is said [to be] "not a non-cow. Is that [meaning] a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative non-entity (*abhāva*)? Or is it a positive entity that is a cow, or even a positive entity that is a non-cow?

If it is a cow, there is no dispute; let it be so. But if the meaning is a positive entity characterized by affirmation (*vidhi-lakṣaṇa*), then if a non-cow were the denotation of the word "cow," what skill would there be in understanding the meaning beyond the word itself?
Furthermore, this non-existence is not logical, because of the impossibility of [verbs such as] *pra-iṣ* and so forth; for no one at all understands non-existence from the word "cow."

Why is it maintained that the meaning of a word is *apoha*? [For instance,] "cow" is not "non-cow. Indeed, by whom has "non-cowness" been attached to the cow, such that this [non-cowness] is excluded (*apohyate*) from it?
It is said: the *apoha* of the non-cow [is the meaning] in the cow. Is that [meaning] accepted as distinct from the cow, or as non-distinct?

It might be either distinct [from the substance] or dependent; or else, because it is not dependent, it would be non-dependent. If it were dependent, then the quality would be obtained [as the primary referent], and consequently, there would be no mention of the "substance.

Therefore, by the word "cow," there would be a mere denotation of the quality, and there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [the expressions] "the cow moves" or "the cow stands."
Now, if it is indeed non-dependent, what object could there be for it by which it might be designated for the sake of negation as "non-cow"?
Furthermore, if this exclusion of the other (*anyāpoha*) is held by you to be non-different [from the cow], then the cow itself is obtained; what more is there to be said than that?

This exclusion (*apoha*) would be either one with respect to each individual entity, or it might be many. If it were one, it would not be the "non-one" [of various cows]; it would be "cowness" itself.

Furthermore, if there were multiplicity, there would be an infinity, like [the number of] individual bodies; therefore, by that very fact, like [the case of] distinctions, its status as the denotable object (*vācyatā*) is not applicable.
Is this exclusion (*apoha*) intended to be denoted by another [term] (*anya*), or is it not denotable? If it is denotable, is it so through affirmation (*vidhi*) or through negation (*niṣedha*)?

If it is denotable by its own nature as an affirmation, then the view previously described—that there is an absolute [denotation] everywhere consisting of the exclusion of other things (*anya-artha-nirāsa*)—must be abandoned.

If, moreover, exclusion (*apoha*) is expressed by means of another exclusion (*vyudāsena*), then there would be an infinite regress (*an-avasthā*) if such a desire were entertained. If, on the other hand, you maintain that this very exclusion is itself inexpressible, then by that statement of yours, the word "exclusion" would be contradicted by something else.

Furthermore, if those things that possess unity, permanence, and inherence were to produce [their effects] individually in each of the exclusions (*apoha*s)—which are themselves devoid of any defining characteristic—then the cloth would be without threads.
Therefore, in those words where there is only the connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), the exclusion of others would result; whereas in other cases, only its own nature is understood.
These people of evil views, who are wicked-souled regarding [the doctrine of] apoha, have themselves perished and likewise cause others to perish as well;
for indeed, apoha is of two kinds—by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and by way of negation (*niṣedha*)—and even exclusion is of two kinds, distinguished by its nature and by its cognition.
The objects previously mentioned—such as "fearlessness" and so forth—which are distinct from one another, serve as the causes for a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).

Relying upon them, a reflection (*pratibimbaka*) appears within the conceptualizing cognition (*kalpaka-jñāna*); that which is thus determined is the state of being the object itself (*arthātmatā*), even in the absence of an external object.

Because it is the cause of the appearance of another [exclusion] due to its differentiation, there is the attainment of the real entity through the exclusion of others. Even though the real entity is not actually connected [to the conceptual image], because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*), the result resides in that [exclusion]. The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is excluded from what is of a different class, is [superimposed] upon this [conceptual image] by those who are deluded; thus, this designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to it.

The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) has been stated to have a basis even in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which serves as the reason (*hetu*) because of its nature (*bhāvataḥ*) as the dissociation from others;
and this non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—namely, that "it is a cow" and "it is not a non-cow"—is understood as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) itself, most clearly.

This first type of exclusion (*apoha*) is established (*pratipādyate*) by words (*śabdaiḥ*), because it arises from the intellect (*buddheḥ samudbhavāt*). This occurs when there is the production (*janmani*) of a cognition (*dhiyaḥ*) that is determinative (*adhyavasāyinyāḥ*) regarding an external object (*bāhyārtha-*)—a cognition produced from a word (*śabdāt*) whose form is that [external object]—and which consists of the nature of the signified (*vācya-vācaka-ātmakaḥ*) as cause and effect (*hetu-phala*).

When this positive form (*ākāra*) has been directly established, even a non-affirming negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is understood by implication (*sāmarthyena*). Thus, [it is understood that] "the self is not the self of another. When there is a connection with real entities (*vastu*), there occurs—by the force of the meaning—an apprehension (*adhigama*) of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*) of those entities as well.

By that [word], this [exclusion] is also figuratively designated (*upacaryate*) as the "own-meaning" (*svārthaḥ*) of the word; however, this twofold verbal exclusion (*śābdo 'pohaḥ*) is not expressed directly (*na sākṣāt*).

Since the hearing (*śrutiḥ*) brings about the exclusion of other objects (*vyavacchedam antarārtham*), it is said to "denote its own object" (*abhidhatte svārtham*); thus, this [figurative usage] is not contradictory to that [direct expression].

This [cognition] produces a reflected image (*pratibimbaka*) that has proceeded through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external object; however, it does not touch its own distinct nature (*ātman*), which is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), except for a mere portion (*aṃśa-mātra*) of that [nature]. There is no such activity (*kriyā*) belonging to it.

When that reflection moves, its separation [from its original] is perceived through the power of another; for it does not possess the nature of another, just as in the case of a sentence and so forth, where the two results—abstinence from food and the day—are [obtained] directly or through implication (*sāmarthyataḥ*). This is because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that is devoid of negative concomitance (*avyatireka*).
Since a word does not directly produce this pair— (1) the denotation of its own object and (2) the exclusion of other things—
it is therefore accepted that the universal "cowness" appears in such a manner through determination (*avasāyataḥ*) as a commonality in all cases, beginning with the *śābaleya* cow.

Because of [this] determination (*adhyavasāya*), the thing (*vastu*) is said to be "the thing" (*vastu iti*). For that is indeed an erroneous cognition (*bhrānta-jñāna*) produced instantaneously from its own seed (*sva-bīja*).

That very [cognition] is called the "exclusion" (*apoha*), the "object" (*artha*) of the word, and the "universal" (*sāmānya*). It is the form of the thing (*vastu-rūpa*) by virtue of being determined (*avasāyataḥ*) as such through error (*bhrāntyā*).

It is not logical for this [cognition] to possess a real generic form as its object-entity; for how could that which is non-different in form from the cognition itself reach another state, namely the object?
Even though this mental image is non-distinct in nature from the cognition, nevertheless, its external form is determined by those who are deluded.

Its independence from an external object is established because it arises from that [word] through a traditional lineage (*pāramparyāt*), and because it exists in that very form as a real entity (*vastutva*).

Thus, it has been demonstrated that even for us, this very thing called the "reflection" (*pratibimba*)—which is the nature of the exclusion (*apoha*)—is produced by the word; indeed, this alone is the meaning of the word.

She does not bear any other portion than that which consists of the nature of the arising [of cognition]; therefore, the exclusion of one cognition from another cognition is perceived by means of that [portion]. It is perceived by means of that.
Just as the distinction of that which does not exist is not ultimately real, so too is the distinction [of words]; thus, by that [reasoning], synonymy would follow.

For non-distinction is the state of having a single form; how could that [non-distinction] exist in things that are formless? Moreover, [if there were no distinction between word and object], the denoters [of objects] would become synonyms when the object is a single entity.

Just as even in the absence of form there is the unity [of it] produced by conceptual construction alone, so too, from where could differentiation arise? Therefore, [in that sense] they are synonyms; however, in terms of their actual existence (*bhāva*), these words are neither synonyms nor non-synonyms. For it has been described thus: "The external object is neither one nor many for them."

But if [the agent] is seen to be manifold, [he is so] by means of the superimposition (*āropa*) of a single effect or a single property; in that case, a single term (*śruti*) is applied (*niveśyate*).

For example, if someone were to employ a term without a single recurring factor (*anugāmin*), such as the eye and so forth, with respect to the result, which is cognition (*vijñāna*) of form (*rūpa*).

Even though that effect—the first [function] of jars and so forth, such as the holding of water and the like—and the cognition which has that as its object are two distinct things, nevertheless, because they are the cause of a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*), the cognition is said to be "one," while the objects are many.

Because they do not differ from that cause, words such as "jar" are said there to be denoters of a universal (*sāmānyavacana*), having a single cause consisting of reflections delimited by what is heterogeneous.

Likewise, because it performs many functions, a single thing—as if it were [many]—is expressed through the multiplicity of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) from those things which do not perform those functions; it is not, however, a single [real entity].

Just as form (*rūpa*) is known to be resistant (*sapratigha*), so too it is known to be demonstrable (*sanidarśana*); or just as sound (*dhvani*) is known to arise immediately after effort (*anantara-prayatna*), or just as [sound] is audible (*śrāvaṇa*);

in some cases, a word (*śabda*) is applied (*niveśyate*) with a distinction (*bheda*) based on what is not its cause (*atat-kāraṇa*), such as "sound produced by effort" (*prayatnottha*) or "honey from bees" (*bhrāmara madhu*).
In some cases, due to the exclusion of the effect of that cause, a form is here said to be "inaudible," or "lightning," or "unborn" [due to] effort, and so forth;
by such distinctions, exclusions are postulated based on different objects, and likewise, the verbal expressions are grounded in them.
Therefore, words denote only unmixed objects, functioning according to their respective conventions through [their] distinction; they are not synonyms for us.
Nor is there any contradiction in their being denotations of both the universal and the particular, due to their having many or few objects, as established by inference from those conventions.

Those exclusions (*vyāvṛttayaḥ*) of objects (*arthānām*), which are constructed merely through conceptualization (*kalpanā-mātra*), do not differ in an ultimate sense (*na paramārthataḥ*) by way of a distinction between the excluded (*apohya*) and the substratum (*ādhāra*).

Their external form (*bāhyarūpatvam*) is imagined (*kalpitam*); it is not real (*na vāstavam*). The two distinctions (*bhedau*) are established (*vyavasthitau*) only as such within a single entity (*vastuni*) according to its true nature (*tattvena*).

Conceptual constructions (*vikalpāḥ*), which are determinative (*adhyavasāyinaḥ*) regarding form and that [object], are differentiated according to their own seeds (*sva-bīja-śaktitaḥ*). Having as their objects (*artha*) various conventions (*an-eka-saṅketa*) dissociated from the real thing (*vastu-viśliṣṭa*), they—though having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their essence (*ātmaka*)—attain a single nature (*ekātmatām*) and are split into fragments; such is this conceptual construction (*vikalpaḥ*) that it floats away.

Even though they are non-existent, those [cognitions] whose objects are the exclusion (*apoha*) of a single common property (*ekānvayadharma*) are understood to be distinct from one another by virtue of their difference in reflective awareness (*bhinnapratyavamarśataḥ*).
Furthermore, it has been established that even while possessing differentiation, certain [cognitions] are by nature conducive to a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśe*).

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*) itself, is excluded from what does not possess that nature; this positive concomitance (*anvaya*), when formulated with effort, is not contradicted.
For, in whatever [locus] the particular characteristic exists as distinct from non-smoke, in that very [locus] there also exists the particular characteristic excluded from non-fire.
Just as in a kitchen, here [in this world] there exists a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is distinct from non-smoke; therefore, it is differentiated from non-fire.

And here there exists a particular characteristic which is distinct even from non-existent things such as a human horn, and which is excluded from the permanent—just like cognition, a lamp, and so forth.

Furthermore, this specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound and so forth does not exist as a non-existent form (*asadrūpa*) in this way; rather, it is precisely through this aforementioned distinction (*bheda*) that [the universal] is designated.

Moreover, that very distinction, when not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), is proclaimed as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of the universal (*sāmānya*); there is no other [definition], because [such another] is not accepted.

In the case of a brindled [cow] and a bāhuleya [horse], which are equal [in respect to their offspring], why does "cowness" (*gotva*) exist in the brindled one—excluding the horse—and not in the other? That [cowness] alone is capable [of producing the cognition] in the individual [cow]; it is also capable in the conceptual recognition (*pratyavamarśa*) of that [brindled cow], whereas the horse is not.

In whatever object such a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) exists, there the exclusion (*apoha*) of the non-cow (*ago*) operates— even in the case of a non-entity (*abhāva*)— since that which is distinct from the non-cow is determined by the senses as a reflected image (*pratibimba*) superimposed [upon it], and is cognized through one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).
Having seen that this word "experience" (*anubhava*) is employed by people (*loka*), its connection (*sambandha*) [with the object] is also clearly established (*upapadyate*).
Wherever there is no such reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) regarding an entity, there the state of being denotable by a word (*śabdābhidheyatva*) is clearly understood to be absent.

Both "cows" and "non-cows" are established through distinct conceptual synthesis (*pratyavamarśa*). However, the word alone is not established [independently] and is applied according to one's desire. For a distinct object does not depend upon the apprehension of another for its cognition; therefore, this fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) is groundless in this case.

Even though the cognition produced by a word (*śabda-dhī*) has as its reality (*tattva*) that which is not an external object (*a-bāhya*), it nevertheless determines (*adhyavasyati*) its own internal representation (*sva-ullekha*) under the form (*rūpeṇa*) of an external object due to a powerful delusion (*upaplava*).
This much alone is accomplished by words; for words do not touch the actual object, nor is any object denoted as being qualified by an exclusion (*apoha*).
Furthermore, it has been stated by the Proponent of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇavādī*): "They say that [the word] is distinguished by the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of other objects;

those entities which are intended [to be expressed] are distinguished from others either by their very nature or by some cause, and are thus determined to be unmixed with things of different classes."

The Resonance (*dhvāna*) says: "I [address] those [who say] 'we'—those who, by producing [the notion of] trees, are resolutely determined (*adhyavasāyin*) regarding knowledge; [it is] the negation of the existence of that [tree], or rather, of genus (*jāti*) and so forth.
And I address those internal ones who revolve within the intellect (*buddhi*); and their distinctness has been stated immediately following [their] exclusion."

It has been stated: "A certain portion (*bhāga*) of an object (*vastu*) is understood (*gamyate*) through the exclusion (*parāvṛtti*) of other things (*antara-artha*); that very [portion] is taught (*upadiśyate*) as a reflection (*pratibimbaka*), because of its arrival (*āgati*) from the perception (*darśana*) of the object as excluded from other things, and because of superimposition (*āropa*)."

The meaning [of the word] "cause" (*hetu*) is as before; and the meaning [of the word] "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is likewise. Therefore, if an entity were not distinct from that which is of a different class, then there would be no exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of the non-cow (*ago*). That exclusion resides in the very nature (*ātmagatā*) of that [entity]; even if its difference [from others] is stated, mere non-existence (*abhāva*) does not itself cease.

Even though [the object] exists as a single entity (*bhāva*), the cognition of its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa-dhī*) regarding the real thing (*vastu*) is not lost, even in the absence of actual difference. This qualifier is constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*); having been drawn out from that [entity], it is established as if possessing difference. By means of this, [the cognition] arises; therefore, that qualifier is like a staff (*daṇḍa*) and so forth.

Those who contemplate reality have said: "The appearance of a word is the meaning. However, the world, ignorant of the distinction between the perceived object and conceptual construction, imagines it to be external.

Therefore, its status as the denotable object belongs only to the individuals through mental determination (*adhyavasāya*), and in reality, there is no denotable object for words; thus it has been established.

And thus, there is the state of being excluded (*apohyatā*) for individual instances (*vyakti*), because they are the denotable objects (*vācya*) of words; however, there is no exclusion (*apoha*) of the universal (*sāmānya*), nor does it possess the nature of a real entity (*vastutā*).

Furthermore, even in the case of exclusion (*apohe*), a non-entity (*abhāva*) is not itself excluded, for a non-entity cannot be excluded. A non-entity is not the state of being excluded (*apohyatā*); this is what is intended by the statement that its nature is not that [of an exclusion].

That which is called "self" (*ātman*) is said to be the exclusion (*apoha*) of that [which it is not]; and its nature is not the absence (*abhāva*) in the exclusion of that [non-self]. Therefore, there is no substantiality (*vastutā*) in things (*vastu*) when they are thus urged; for the state of being produced from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśa*), and so forth, is not established as a real entity.

Therefore, even from that which is non-existent, no affliction whatsoever arises; and when that [non-existence] is established, its existence is not present, and thus that non-existence is itself established.
Furthermore, the cow is accepted as the exclusion of the non-cow, and is indeed an entity; consequently, for me, the cow does not follow as a consequence of the non-cow.

Even though there is no real entity (*avastu*), there exists a latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced solely by the mind, as if it were a distinction among things fashioned by various conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*).

And from that, there arises the exclusion (*apoha*) of others; furthermore, the nature of existence (*sadrūpatā*) is indeed postulated through the differentiation of latent impressions, just as in the case of things fashioned by conceptual construction.

Just as this exclusion (*apoha*) of other objects has been explained as being the very thing expressed by words, so too should the exclusion of other words be understood; for, due to the nature of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), these two exclusions are not established as non-entities (*avastutva*) on the conventional path, even though they are real in the ultimate sense (*tāttvika*). This is the intended proof.
If it is argued that there is neither a signifier nor a signified due to the absence of pervasion among entities that are momentary, [we reply:
if this conventional relationship of the signified and the signifier is being negated by relying upon the ultimate unreality of the two exclusions (*vinivṛtti*).
Even so, the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāritva*) from objects is difficult to avoid, even with words that express them, which are constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

For there exists no universal (*sāmānya*) among those [objects] that is either the denoted (*vācya*) or the denoter (*vācaka*) of it; nor does the word possess the nature of a denoter, since its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is momentary (*kṣaṇabhaṅgin*).

Therefore, that pair [of object and word] must be accepted as conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), such as a reflection (*pratibimba*) and so forth; for in those cases, the presence of deviation (*vyabhicāritva*) is firmly established and difficult to avoid.
Indeed, for one who does not admit that the referent of a word is a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) apprehended by the mind, a cognition arises from the word that bears the appearance of that [referent].

In the denotation of words (*śabdānām*), by the very fact of [denoting] their own referents (*svārtha-arthāt*), there is an exclusion (*nivarttanam*) of others; this too is my "negative concomitance" (*vyatirekaḥ*). For this [exclusion] is preceded by that [positive concomitance].

Indeed, the impossibility (*asambhavaḥ*) of a positive injunction (*vidheḥ*) has been stated, because [the universal] is impossible as a real entity (*vastutaḥ*), since words (*śabdānām*) and conceptual constructions (*vikalpānām*) have that [universal] as their object (*viṣayatvataḥ*).

From words such as "blue lotus," only a single reflection (*pratibimbaka*) is apprehended as excluded from non-blue, non-lotus, and so forth. However, we do not maintain that there is a real entity (*vastu*) possessing exclusion (*apohavat*) other than [the reflection]. There is no exclusion of one thing from another, nor is there exclusion from what is already excluded.

This fault of dependence (*pāratantrya*) is not applicable to the meaning of a word, because [the word] is non-different [from it]; thus it is as clear as day. Therefore, the established rule regarding the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—which exists in the case of a universal (*jāti*)—is contradicted if the referent of a word is an exclusion (*apoha*).
From the initial word "blue" alone, a distinct reflection arises, floating over [the domain of] words such as "lotus," "bee," and so forth;

by means of the word "indīvara," it is established through the exclusion (*apoha*) of "cuckoo," "collyrium," and the like; that [reflection], moreover, becomes definitively determined as a distinct object.

Thus, the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [of these] is certainly not sublated; however, the systematic establishment (*vyavasthā*) of that [coreferentiality] for all [entities] is extremely difficult to maintain under the opponent’s position.

In that same way, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been stated in every respect by means of a word; and when it has been thus expressed, why is there no cognition of the difference (*bheda*) within it? For what purpose would another word be employed here? If that [particular characteristic] were not expressed in every respect, then it would follow that it is manifold.
If the universal (*jāti*) "blue" or the quality (*guṇa*) is denoted by the word "blue," then another universal, that of the *indīvara*, must be determined from the hearing of the word "lotus.

This being the case, because of the difference between those two—just as in the case of the words "blue" and "lotus"—grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are all the more impossible.

If a substance connected with both quality (*guṇa*) and genus (*jāti*) is expressed by the word "blue" (*nīla*), it would be redundant (*vyarthā*) that [the substance] possesses the genus *utpala* when it is already connected with those two; for in that case, the expression of the genus *utpala* is already stated by the hearing of the word "blue," and thus the hearing of the word "blue-lotus" (*nīlopala*) would be redundant.

If the word for the genus (*jāti*) "lotus" were different from [the word] connected with the quality (*guṇa*), then the two words for the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) would have distinct substrata. Alternatively, if the sound "blue" itself were not a substance (*dravya*) connected with that genus by way of its form as a relatum of "lotusness" (*utpalatva*).

The nature of form (*rūpatva*) might be the lotus-ness (*utpalatā*) of the yogi; however, that which is not of that nature is nevertheless connected with lotus-ness, and it is precisely that which is connected with these two.

That which was declared [by the word] in its entirety (*sarvātmanā*) is not [grasped] by its parts (*aṃśaiḥ*). It is made an object (*viṣayīkṛta*) by the auditory sense (*śrutyā*), but it is not made an object by the conceptual cognition (*buddhyā*) arising from words (*śābdyā*). Therefore, the word "lotus" (*utpala*) would be meaningless (*anarthā*).

If it is argued that there is a conceptual construction (*vikalpana*) regarding the exclusion of difference (*bheda-vinirmukte*) in its totality (*kārtsnyena*), [we reply: no such thing exists here. This is not what is intended to be expressed (*na vivakṣita*), for there is a lack of understanding of the meaning of the sentence (*aparijñānād artha-vākyasya*).
That which is manifested is indeed expressed by the first word; in every respect, that [object] remains exactly as it is, and no essence whatsoever is abandoned by this very mode of utterance.
Therefore, the utterance of other words in that context is certainly not fruitful, even when they are spoken.

An external object (*bāhyārtha*) is not established (*pratipādyate*) by us (*asmākam*) through a word (*śabdena*); nor is cognition (*vijñānam*) held (*matam*) to have an external object as its domain (*viṣayam*) on account of the word (*śabdāt*).
Since [the word] itself (*ātmanā*) is distinct (*antara*) from both of those—namely, the cognition and the word—it will [therefore] fall into synonymy (*paryāyatvam*) with respect to them (*tatra*).

By means of the word, through sequence, and due to delusion, that reflection appears as if it were identical with and external to [the object], in accordance with [notions such as] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthena*), these words are considered to be without an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*).

This application [of grammatical] gender, number, and so forth does not exist for individual instances (*vyakti*), because it is caused by a convention established by desire and is not real; thus, there is no lack of form (*nairūpya*) in the single object, since it is apprehended as variegated in the appearances of all cognitions.

If [the universals] were to follow [the particulars] by virtue of our desire to speak [of them], they would not be objects [of cognition] due to that [desire]; nor would those [particulars] possess a single form.

If that entity were not of a single form, then its existence as a sign (*liṅga*)—based on its stability, production, and configuration—would result in a state of having diverse signs (*viliṅgatva*), unless it were [conceived] without distinction.

Regarding that which is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*), "the indefinable" (*nirupākhya*), or "insubstantiality" (*tucchhatā*): what connection could there be for [terms such as] "endurance" (*sthiti*) and so forth to be conceptually constructed (*parikalpyate*) in relation to non-existent things?

Furthermore, their "arising" (*utpāda*), "origination" (*prasava*), and "destruction" (*nāśa*) are asserted; however, "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) is designated as "endurance" (*sthiti*), and it is said to be the very nature of the self (*ātmarūpa*).

If there is no destruction in [the case of] arising, why is it said that "arising" is its nature? And if there is no persistence characterized by its own form, how is it proclaimed that "birth" occurs in the state of stability?
Furthermore, since these two are not distinct, why is it said that "disappearance" is "destruction," and that "concealment" is also [destruction]?

By what is "abiding" (*sthiti*) said to be expressed? Is it the state of abiding (*sthiti*), or rather the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or perhaps the form (*rūpa*) of these [factors]? If they were indeed indivisible, there would be a single gender (*ekaliṅgatā*).
If these—such as femininity (*strītva*) and so forth—were considered to be like "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like, then they too are discarded by the refutation of the universal (*sāmānya*).
[This is] agreed upon. Among those [categories], "universal" (*jāti*), "existence" (*bhāva*), and "generality" (*sāmānya*)—for other generalities are not applicable to generalities.

Or how could [terms such as] "non-existence" (*abhāva*), "the state of being indefinable" (*nirupākhyatva*), and "insubstantiality" (*tucchatā*) apply? Therefore, this threefold classification of genders is merely conventional (*sāmāyikī*).

Number, indeed, is merely conventional (*sāmayikī*), for it is postulated (*kalpyate*) by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣayā*). This is just as [the term] *dārā* and so forth [is used] for a distinction (*bheda*) or a non-distinction (*abheda*), or as [the term] *vipina* and so forth [is used].

[Objection: But surely, when the word *dārā* is employed, it applies to an individual (*vyakti*), and it also exists in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), having taken on either the number of the individual or the number of its parts (*avayava*).

Furthermore, the word "forest" denotes a single [entity] (*ah*); or rather, it denotes many individual instances (*vyakti*) qualified by number and genus (*jāti*), which are dependent upon a genus that itself depends upon many individuals.

Surely, by this method, every [instance of] speech (*vacas*) denoting a single [thing] is destroyed. If you say that there is no intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) in other cases, let that alone be the basis (*nibandhana*) for this [distinction].

Nor can number [belong] even to a genus; or, if it were present in the entity itself, how could [individuals] be qualified by it? [They would be so] either through a relation with that which is related, or even through the relation itself.
If this were so, then even a single tree would be designated as "a forest," and many [trees] would likewise be called [a forest] simply due to that relation; yet such is not the case.

That [cognition] which is based on many individuals remains present even when only one [individual] is there, because the cause for that [cognition] is the same; thus, the cognition of a "forest" would also arise there.

Therefore, this restriction of speech—such as "one" and so forth—arises from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not from the object itself, because of its deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The [concepts of] connection (*yoga*), action (*kriyā*), time (*kāla*), and so forth have already been refuted. Therefore, these [notions] are merely conventional (*sāṃketika*); they do not [inherently] exist in individual instances (*vyakti*). Or, even if "exclusion" (*apoha*) is said to be expressed by a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) having the form of an individual instance, it possesses a connection with gender (*liṅga*) and so forth through the medium of the individual instance.
