A word (*śabdaḥ*) is employed (*prayujyate*) for the sake of a meaning (*artham*) intended (*abhiprete*) to be established (*niveśa-*) in the cognition (*buddheḥ*). Therefore, by its very capacity (*sāmarthyena*), the exclusion (*vyudāsaḥ*) of what is not desired (*an-abhīṣṭa-*) is accomplished (*siddhyati*).

Furthermore, everything that is not desired is [excluded] through the attainment (*āptitaḥ*) of non-restriction (*a-niyama-*) regarding all objects (*sarva-artha-*); thus, for words such as "cooks" (*pacati*), the object to be excluded (*vinivarttyam*) is perfectly clear (*parisphuṭam*).

For instance, when it is said "he cooks" (*pacati*), [the agent] does not remain indifferent (*udāsīnaḥ*), nor does he eat (*bhuṅkte*) or play (*dīvyati*). Thus, the cessation of activity (*nivarttanam*) is understood through the method [of exclusion].

In this way, whatever is intended as something that exists as a fixed object of exclusion (*apohyam*), it is considered to be of the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa-ātman-*) and distinct from indifference (*audāsīnya-*) and [other] actions (*kriyā-antar-*).
This statement of yours—"He cooks" (*pacati*) and "he stands" (*tiṣṭhati*)—is not prohibited; yet it is mutually contradictory in its own nature.
This [act of] standing remains in its own nature as a negation of another form; otherwise, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) employed would be purposeless.

What kind [is it]? (1st singular) The state of being established (niṣpannatva, neuter, 1st singular) of the exclusion (apoha, masculine, 6th singular) called "ascertainment" (ākhyā, feminine, 6th singular)—for indeed, there is no establishment whatsoever of things such as a sky-lotus (gaganendīvara, masculine, 6th plural).
Because of the determination that "it is [so]," this entity appears as possessing a designation; therefore, what is understood from it—that it shares the same nature as real entities?

Therefore, the state of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*), as well as its conceptualization (*rūpaṇa*) as "existent" (*bhūta*) and so forth, follows [as a consequence] because of its having a form identical to [the forms of] real entities (*vastu*).

Furthermore, in the context of a collection (*rāśi*) such as "positive instances" (*arthavidhi*) and so on, its existence (*astitā*) and other such properties are negated; however, that which is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*) is not [negated] by the word through its own inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Such would be the *apoha* of the negative particle (*nañ*) when joined with a negative particle—just as it is perceived when the fourfold [negation] exists; for when there is a connection with a negative particle, the meaning is understood through the first [negative particle], while its absence is conveyed by the third negative particle.

The fourth [alternative] is employed for the purpose of negation (*niṣedhāya*). When that [negation] is intended (*vivakṣite*), it is made known (*jñāpyate*) in that [context] by means of it (*tena*). [Thus,] the exclusion of others (*nivarttanam anya-*) is understood (*gamyate*) from what has been stated (*ukte*). For example, when it is said "he does not cook" (*na pacati*), it is understood that he is cooking; however, by the third [alternative], there is a connection with indifference (*audāsīnya*) and so forth.

In the fourth [instance], that which is isolated from that [object] is determined as such; therefore, it is cooked by that [means]. Herein, the exclusion of others is equivalent to an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*), and through the particle *ca* and so forth, some intended meaning—such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the like—may arise; by that [particle], there occurs the exclusion of another, such as an alternative (*vikalpa*) and so forth.

The exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of others is indeed well-known as the meaning of a sentence. Certain word-meanings, when combined, are said to be the meaning of a sentence—those which are clearly distinguished from those of a different class (*vijātīya*) and are to be excluded (*apohya*). And it is precisely these [exclusions] that constitute the meaning of the sentence;
for there is no other [meaning] apart from them.
When the meaning [of the sentence] "Caitra, bring the cow" has been understood, it is recognized that the exclusion (*apoha*) of other agents, objects, and so forth constitutes the meaning.

At first, the word is determined (*vyavasīyate*) as being nothing other than the exclusion of others (*an-anyāpoha*); a positive injunction (*vidhiḥ*) is not intended by others because it has already been refuted previously [in the section on] the universal (*jāti*) and so forth. Rather, from this sound (*dhvani*), a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises that is determinative of a positive injunction; subsequently, a cognition (*matiḥ*) regarding the negation of the object, the word, and the exclusion (*apoha*) arises.

However, because it lacks correspondence with such a real entity due to the loss of its connection, all verbal cognitions (*śābdāḥ pratyayāḥ*) are not determinative (*adhyavasāyinaḥ*) regarding the actual object at the outset—namely, that which is denoted by words (*śabdaprameya*), that which is to be known (*jñeya*), or anything else. For what [object] could there be that is not to be excluded (*apohyam*)? Indeed, nothing exists that is employed (*prayujyate*) by discerning people (*prekṣāvadbhiḥ*) in isolation (*kevalaḥ*) and out of context (*akāṇḍe*).
However, when there is the possibility of doubt or error regarding something, that [negation] is employed by the wise for the purpose of its cessation in certain instances;
therefore, by that very [negation] being employed by them, its fruitfulness is experienced through the production of a conviction free from doubt and error.

It is accepted (*iṣyate*) by those with dull minds (*jaḍa-cetobhiḥ*) that there is a basis (*āspadam*) for suspicion (*āśaṅka*). In that case, that very [basis] is rejected (*kṣipyate*) by him (*tena*), because otherwise (*anyathā*) the utterance (*uccāraṇā*) would be fruitless (*viphalā*).

For how could he, not suspecting anything (*a-śaṅkamānaḥ*), ask (*paripṛcchati*) for some purpose (*kim artham*), or how could one who is sound-minded (*svastha-dhīḥ*) speak (*bruvat*) a word (*śabdam*) devoid of refinement (*a-saṃskārakam*)?
Thus, form and so forth are to be known by means of visual cognition and the like; for it is this [notion] that is refuted when something superimposed by someone is denied.
Form and so forth, such as blue, are not indeed cognized by one who relies on the eye alone, but rather by a single, permanent consciousness that relies on the ear as well.

The term "to be known" (*vijñeya*) is said (*ucyate*) in reference to the arising (*udbhūtau*) of initial delusion (*ādi-vibhrama*). Thus, these phenomena (*dharmāḥ*) exist within that delusion (*vibhrame*) by way of their momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva-rūpeṇa*), and they are to be known (*vijñeyāḥ*) by the knowledge of the Omniscient One (*jñāna-sarvajña*). What indeed are those non-existent things (*abhāvāḥ*) which do not produce (*na janayanti*) knowledge (*jñānam*)? They are the objects to be known (*vijñeyāḥ*).
These [things] possess such knowability because of the proof of momentariness and so forth; moreover, non-existence is also knowable conventionally, since it is established by this very nature.

Having observed that sound and so forth are the causes for the cognition of what is to be known through inference (*prameya-jñeya*), even when a sentence remains present, that cognition—which occurs upon the perception of [the word] alone even at other times—is [the one in question].

In the case of particulars (*bheda*), [cognition] arises (*upajāyate*) following the drift (*plavamāna-anusārataḥ*) of sentences (*vākya*) concerning objects (*artha*); and that [cognition] exists (*asti*) in exactly the same way (*tathāvidhā*) from words (*śabda*) such as "jar" (*ghaṭa-ādi*). Therefore, sounds (*dhvani*) regarding [objects] such as "knowable" (*jñeya-ādi*) are equal (*samāḥ*) to the word "jar" (*ghaṭa-ādi-śabdena*).

This [which has been] stated is [done] in the context of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); having excluded [the literal], it is better to assume a [specific] entity (*vastu*) alone. [Otherwise,] there would be a contradiction because of the exclusion of others by way of restriction.
Only that entity which is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*) is assumed; therefore, there is no rejection of what is intended to be expressed. However, not everything is intended to be expressed.

But the negation of the cognition of the form [of the object] cannot be established, because it is self-cognizable (*svavedyatvāt*). For one must necessarily admit that the superimposing [cognition], though without an external support (*nirālambam*), possesses some inherent nature (*gatātmaka*) of its own that is restricted to each respective object; and that very nature is what constitutes its essence.

We have stated that "form" (*ākāra*), "reflection" (*pratibimba*), "appearance as that" (*tad-ābhatā*), "mental impression" (*ullekha*), and "manifestation" (*pratibhāsa*)—these are synonyms (*bheda-saṃjñā*). However, [the word] "but" (*tu*) indicates that [the term "exclusion"] is not the cause (*akāraṇam*) for words such as "beginning" (*ādi*) and so forth. [The opponent says: "It exists in this way" (*evam vidyate ādiḥ*) and "it does not exist in this way" (*na evam iti*); these are clearly the things to be excluded (*apohyam*), which is the definition (*lakṣaṇam*) of another type [of exclusion].

Even when every word is brought forward in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), there exists something to be excluded (*vyudāsya*) for it; its intended meaning (*abhidhitsita-artha*) is this "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).

Alternatively, all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of self (*nirātman*), or all persons (*puruṣa*) have reached that state; thus, totality (*sāmastyam*) is understood, while some particular portion (*aṃśa*) is excluded (*apohyate*).

Some outsiders (bāhyāḥ) mistakenly maintain that jars and the like (ghaṭādayaḥ) are desired to be devoid of self-nature (nirātmānaḥ), and that the very movement (gamanam) of anything whatsoever is excluded (vinivarttate).

Since this negation (pratiṣedhaḥ) of all parts (sarva-aṅga) is not at all intended (na vivakṣitaḥ) in that context, this [objection] regarding the consequence (prasaṅgaḥ) of apoha having its own meaning (svārtha-) is stated out of ignorance (ajñatayā).
Apoha is neither an entity nor a non-entity; it is without characteristics, neither distinct nor identical; it is neither dependent nor independent in reality; it is neither one nor many.
Thus, it does not exist in its true nature, yet it is determined as such. Therefore, from the standpoint of determination, it is neither an entity nor a non-entity in terms of being a real thing.

Differences and non-differences established in relation to an existent entity (*sat-vastu*), as well as the referent (*artha*) of a word, are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Therefore, these [concepts] are without foundation for us.
A word does not directly effect the exclusion (*vinivṛtti*) of other referents; rather, when its own referent is expressed, that [exclusion] is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*).
Thus, that which has its self [in that] is not the self of another; this has been established in detail. Therefore, it is said here: ...

By what means has the non-cowness of the cow been attached [to it], such that this [non-cowness] is excluded by [the word]? This [objection] is not at all excluded by the word addressed directly by one who is ignorant of the opponent's position.
Is expressibility being questioned by which word? What is the point of this [question] regarding exclusion (*apoha*)? Or rather, what is the point of defining it as "pot" and so forth?
Is the meaning of a word exclusion (*apoha*), or is it a positive injunction (*vidhi*)? In that case, that which appears and is perceived as exclusion—[what is its nature]?

The meaning is that [the word] "cognition" (*mati*) is the direct reflection (*pratibimba*). However, the exclusion (*hāni*) of [terms such as] "positive injunction" (*vidhi*), "genus" (*jāti*), and so forth is understood through implication (*sāmarthyāt*).
Furthermore, words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) express that very same reflection; by implication, they produce it directly, whereas other [words] exclude it.

Therefore, there is no fault [in our position] regarding the injunction, nor does an undesirable consequence follow; for that fault regarding the "inexpressible" alternative does not apply to us, since oneness, permanence, and so forth are merely conceptual constructs and not real. Thus, this laughter here is indicative of great learning.

Therefore, for whomsoever no external object (*bāhyo ’rthaḥ*) existing otherwise is admitted, where is "exclusion" (*apoha*) said to exist by him? Since there is an absence of [external] entities, words are not even to be suspected of being denoters of universals (*jāti*) and so forth; rather, they are established as indicators of mental appearances.
That reflection which is produced solely from the arising of mental discourse (*abhijalpa*) devoid of external objects, and which appears as if constructed, is what is being explained by words.
These words are direct indicators of that [reflection] alone; however, they are accompanied by doubt because they depend upon conventional designations (*saṅketa*) for imagined objects.
These sounds are not conveyors of the establishment of difference and so forth as they are apprehended by others; therefore, let it be understood that [the reason] is like that.

For here, the impossibility of convention regarding difference and so forth has already been established previously, and thus there is no fruitlessness of the two reasons, nor is there any doubtful exclusion (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*).

(On the other hand,) even in the case of *apoha*, how could there be the possibility of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), and how could it be effective? For that [convention] is not established for both the speaker and the listener; their cognition is not mutually experienced, and what was perceived during the establishment of the convention is not observed during actual usage.

Even though the manifestation within one's own cognition occurs with respect to the determination of an external object, it is nevertheless the same for both [parties]. For just as a person whose eye is afflicted by cataracts perceives two moons to himself, so too all verbal usage is considered [to be of that nature].
This pervasiveness of that [conceptualization] is accepted as being determinative; for these cognitions are produced by words and appear falsely.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), which were stated by others for the sake of establishing [the definition of] a limiting condition (*upādhi*), are not established; for such a definition—namely, that perception is "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*)—is not tenable. Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition (*pratīti*) associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpinī*); however, it does not have as its nature the postulation (*kḷpti*) of causality (*hetutva*) and so forth.

That connection (*ghaṭanā*) between meaning and word which arises (*jāyate*) as something accompanied by verbal expression (*sābhilāpaḥ*), even though it is [in reality] the form of speech (*vācām rūpataḥ*), occurs—such as "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*) and so forth—even in the absence of [actual] usage, due to the continuity (*anvayāt*) of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from past lives (*atītabhava*). Furthermore, even one born this very day (*sadyojātaḥ*) becomes proficient (*paṭuḥ*) through the application (*yogāt*) of that [cultivation], which consists of the knowledge of what is to be done (*itikartavyatā*).

That [which] is clearly perceived (*pravedyate*) at the time of reflection (*cintā*) and imagination (*utprekṣā*), as if interwoven (*anuviddhā*), cannot be denied (*apahnotum*) by means of words (*śabdaiḥ*).

The persistence of word and meaning through conceptual determination is erroneous with respect to non-existence; even such [persistence] as this would not be possible for it, because of its lack of connection with anything else.

Others know that the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) which is appropriate for the connection of genus (*jāti*) and so forth—that [construction] is not applicable, because genus and so forth have been refuted and because they are not perceived.

Since [universals] such as *jāti* are not perceived (*adṛṣṭatvāt*) and their connection (*tadyogāpratibhāsanāt*) does not appear, how can a synthesis (*ghaṭanā*) with an object (*arthe*) be possible? It is like [the mixing of] milk, water, and so forth.

This conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) has been stated in two ways—as supreme (*parā*) and non-supreme (*aparā*)—for the purpose of explaining the objects (*viṣaya*) of what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is to be adopted (*upādeya*).
This interpretation, namely [the one beginning with] "ādi," occurs by implying its own immediate cause; therefore, the designation is not irrelevant.

All [terms] beginning with "name" (*nāman*) and "universal" (*jāti*) are joined by this [definition] that has been stated; likewise, that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is declared to be a cognition (*pratīti*) associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpinī*).

Or rather, since the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that has arisen as purely [conceptual] is established precisely through its own connection with the [speaker's] intention (*sva-mata-yojanāt*), the meaning (*artha*) is everywhere said (*ucyate*) by them to be the object of the name (*nāmnaḥ*) by means of the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇa-vibhaktyā*). Thus, this [conceptual construction] establishes itself (*adhyavatiṣṭhate*) as having the name’s universal (*jāti*) and so forth as its object.

Since the universal (*jāti*) that is to be denoted exists, there should not be considered a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) for this [definition] regarding arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*). However, the term "word" (*śruti*) is mentioned separately because it is well-known as such. But surely, is the word [denotative] of the universal alone, because its denotable object is exclusion (*apoha*) of others, or because it is dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*)? [The answer is: the word is indeed [dependent on] the speaker's intention.

It is true that this [word] has been stated in such a manner by the knower of logic (*nyāyavid*) through conformity with worldly usage; for indeed, this much of a word has reached its destination in the sphere of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).

However, those [categories] beginning with "universal" (*jāti*) are not distinct from the world-knowing [linguistic usage] here—this is for the sake of understanding this [point]; but others [beginning with "quality"] have already been described.

Even if they were to resort to a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—namely, a connection (*yojanā*) with universals (*jāti*) and so forth—they would have to admit that cognition (*pratīti*) is necessarily expressive (*abhilāpinī*).

Otherwise, because there would be no connection between two entities (*bhāva*) that are distinct, and because [the object] is determined independently, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) could not be postulated at all.
Thus it might be [said]: "This entire universe is inexpressible; therefore, this is considered expressible when it is conjoined with form, genus, and so forth.
And the application of genus and so forth is non-deviant; furthermore, this statement is thus spoken, and so it becomes fruitful."

Therefore, this conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is considered to be established without effort, because there is no dispute among the proponents who stand upon their respective complete systems of tenets (*siddhānta*).
Having disregarded all this description of names, universals (*jāti*), and so forth, he has here undertaken the presentation of these two views—his own and that of others.
"Not saying 'so'—this is the difference between us and them; immediately thereafter, he sang this very first verse, while we others [sang] thus."

Thus, it should be explained in the *Nyāyamukha* by means of this same direction (*diśā*): the cognition (*pratīti*) prompted therein is due to the connection (*abhisambandhāt*), such that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) by which the word (*śruti*)—which has performed the exclusion of others (*kṛt-apohānya*)—effects (*karoti*) the differentiation (*vyavacchedam*) of universals (*jāti*) and so forth.

Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), which is considered to be of the nature of cognition (*pratīti-rūpā*), is thus described as the negation of perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of its identity with it; yet it is not sublated (*bādhyate*) by verbal testimony (*śabda*) or other means of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). For in perception (*adhyakṣe*), there is an absence (*viraha*) of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), since that [perception] is not denotable by words (*śabda-vācyatā*).
Otherwise, form, smell, and so forth would possess conceptualization (*savikalpatā*). Therefore, this [position] is not at all a basis for what those of poor intellect say:
"If the perceptible is denoted by the word 'perceptible,' how, how can that which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) be understood? It is illogical."

Perception, which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), is experienced with extreme clarity even by the mind (*manas*) when it is occupied elsewhere; yet, because of the cognition of blue, that very conceptualization does not apprehend that object, due to the exclusion of [words] such as "denomination" (*abhidhā*) and "past," and because of the connection with its name.

At that time, there exists no other conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) associated with that [name], because the visible object is not cognized simultaneously with the two [the name and the object], since such a simultaneous occurrence is not accepted.

Therefore, that which arises subsequently as a conceptual construction is experienced together with the cognition; for this reason, this sensory consciousness is clearly free from conceptualization (*akalpaka*).

If it is thought that cognitions arise only in succession, yet there is the conceit [of simultaneity] due to the rapid occurrence [of their arising], like [the perception of] a fire-brand circle—then there exists no conceptual construction accompanied by a connection with objects that have become present, such that it could be said, "This is what is seen. This is indeed what was stated.

Note: In the final quarter there are two indistinct syllables preceding the final *-nā*. The Baudhabhāratī edition reads the final quarter as: *... ityatroktaṃ na kiṃcana* // (And) that [cognition] is continuous; [therefore] error is clearly evident. And thus, that very simultaneity of object and cognition is manifest.

If [it is argued that] even when there is an interval of many [moments], the entire [performance] of the dancing girl is perceived all at once due to the rapid succession of cognitions, then why does the notion of simultaneity not arise here as well,
given that the occurrence of cognitions is extremely swift?
In a pure mental [cognition], no sequence could be determined; furthermore, because all cognitions do not persist for long, their activity is rapid and brief.
Therefore, in every case, there would be a perception of sequence; however, there would be [a perception] like that of the cognition of sound and so forth, which occurs simultaneously.

Even in the case of a firebrand, the illusion of a wheel arises all at once as a single appearance; it does not result from the synthesis of individual visual perceptions, because [the wheel] appears quite clearly.
For indeed, synthesis is performed by memory alone, and not by the act of seeing, since the object has already passed away and is no longer present.
That object of this [consciousness] is not clearly manifest because it has perished; consequently, the appearance of a wheel would follow as a logical consequence, yet it is not clearly manifest.
Furthermore, if the cause for the presence of an entity—which possesses a certain form—is not found, that entity is not established by the Buddhas as being real in its true nature.

Just as a white horse (*karka*), which lacks [the dewlap] and so forth (*avidyamānasāsnādi*), is not apprehended as being qualified by the qualifier "cow" (*goātmanā viśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭārtham grahaṇam na*),

and since conceptual cognition (*savikalpakabhāvasya*) does not exist at the moment of sensory perception (*sthiter akṣe*), there is no basis for it; otherwise, the spotted cow (*śābaleya*) and other such animals would absurdly follow as its counter-examples (*vipakṣa*).

Nor is there non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*), because [we] negate birth (*jāti*) and so forth; and because [birth and so forth] are not determined as distinct [from their substrates], [the reason] exists. Furthermore, that which is called a "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*) does not exist even for a word’s own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), for the own-characteristic is certainly not denotative (*vācaka*), since the state of being denoted (*vācyatva*) and the state of being denotative (*vācakatva*) have already been refuted.

Therefore, that which is superimposed is held to be the denotator (*vācaka*) of the denoted (*vācya*), while direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) apprehends the object (*artha*) as it is, un-superimposed, because of the existence of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and even when that [particular] exists, [perception remains distinct] due to its difference from the state of being mediated by [conceptualization] and so forth.

The self is the partaker of blue and other [objects], which are non-different from it and incapable of being conventionally designated; moreover, the consciousness of them is therefore not accompanied by verbal expression (*abhijalpa*).

Granted that [universals] such as "name" might not be the apprehended qualifiers of that [object], nevertheless, for this reason, the charge of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) does not at all cease to apply. Why? Because...
If there were non-apprehension by way of a form excluded from another object, or if there were apprehension of the object itself, or rather non-apprehension [of it], just as in the case of a jar;
that is, if there were non-apprehension by way of a form excluded from another jar, or apprehension of the jar alone, or indeed non-apprehension of the jar.

If it is held that consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which is the grasper (*grāhin*) by its very nature (*bhāvena*) and is distinguished (*vyavacchinna*) from other objects of cognition (*grāhya*)—would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*), like the cognition of a tree and so forth; and if there exists no distinction [between them] such that [the latter] is untouched by the universal (*sāmānya*); then, because of its non-manifestation (*avibhāvatvāt*) when that [universal] is not clearly apprehended (*aspaṣṭagrahaṇe*), it would not be grasped (*na gṛhyate*).

To say that "cognition has a qualified object" is not a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); such a claim is reckless. For the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is impossible without a relation (*sambandha*) [to a qualifier]. Cognition is considered to have a qualified object because it apprehends an object as excluded from its own class and from other classes; it is not so because of a connection with a qualifier.

Distinctness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is difference (*bheda*); it is not a connection (*saṅgati*) with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Even that [difference], being distinct (*bhinnam*), is not perceived as permeated (*anuviddha*) by speech (*vācā*).
However, when that [distinctness] is grasped as something excluded (*vyatirekin*) from all other things (*niḥśeṣa-padārtha-apara-svabhāva*), a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises accordingly.

The universal (*sāmānya*), as it is accepted by others (*paraiḥ*), is unqualified (*an-avacchinna*) by any particular (*viśeṣaṇa*); it is the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) for non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-vijñāna*). Therefore, even in that case, the universal is understood (*avagamyate*) as being qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) by the particular; consequently, the cognition that apprehends (*grāhaka*) it is established as being conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

If it is said that [the particular] is apprehended without distinction (*nirviśeṣam*), then it is called a "universal" (*sāmānyam*); consequently, it is not logical for it to possess the quality of being qualified by a particular (*viśeṣa-viśiṣṭatvam*) on account of a particular.
Indeed, these [particulars], while being known through their state of similarity and difference, bring about the establishment of the universal and the particular within themselves.

If existence (*bhava*) is held to be divided into similarity (*samatva*) and dissimilarity (*vaiṣamyatva*), then that [division] is the state of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). [But] how indeed can this state (*sthiti*) be unmixed (*asaṅkīrṇā*) if it is undivided (*avibhakta*)? Without the exclusion of one another, there is no distinction (*antara*) between movement (*gati*) and stability (*sthiti*).

There is no other characteristic [of difference] apart from the specific nature (*ātma-viśeṣa*) [of the objects themselves]. How, then, can their apprehension be said to occur without contact with that form, or even when there is contact with that form? For if they were apprehended as distinct from one another, it would follow that the cognition regarding them is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
The universal is perceived as distinct from the indefinable particular; therefore, it would be the object of conceptual cognition.
If that [distinction] is not distinct from the non-existent, what is its nature? If it is not [distinct], why is distinction not considered to belong to it?

For even in the case of a real entity, this distinction has precisely that [non-existent] as its nature; and since the universal does not have the nature of the non-existent, how is it not distinct from that [non-existent]?

Therefore, whatever cognition arises with respect to a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), having as its object that which has passed beyond the path of speech—that is entirely non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

For there exists an initial non-conceptual cognition of mere observation (*ālocana-jñāna*), which is similar to the consciousness of infants, the mute, and so forth, and is born from the pure object itself.

At that time, neither the universal (*sāmānya*) nor the particular (*viśeṣa*) is perceived (*anubhūyate*); rather, only the individual (*vyakti*), which serves as the substratum (*ādhārabhūtā*) for those two, is determined (*avasīyate*).

Thereafter, the entity (*vastu*) is again determined by the intellect (*buddhyā*) through properties such as the genus (*jāti*) and so forth; yet that very [intellect] is also regarded as being of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣatvena*).

Even in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whatever degree of realization (*adhigama*) there may be in accordance with that connection (*sambandha*), all of that is accepted as being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Just as objects that have entered into warm inner chambers and the like do not appear [directly] to mothers, nor are they again perceived by their senses as they were previously known through mere appearance, but are subsequently awakened to there in their own nature and according to their characteristics such as genus and so forth; so it is in this case.

If, however, someone, having perceived [an object] and then closing their eyes, were to construct [a mental image] (*kalpayet*), that [image] would not possess the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) because it does not follow from the [perceived] connection.

That is incorrect; for even when cognition is directed toward a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), although there is the grasping of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, that [cognition] remains unassociated with verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).

And thus, it was established previously that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is indeed inexpressible; and when cognition (*vijñāna*) occurs with respect to that [characteristic], it is necessarily non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

If there were apprehension of the mere genus (*jāti-mātra*), then the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) would necessarily (*ekāntena*) be distinct (*vibhinnatā*); however, this is not accepted (*iṣṭam*) by the opponents (*paraiḥ*), as it has been stated (*uditam*).
If [the qualifier] were absolutely distinct from the qualified, then how could it produce in the qualified a cognition corresponding to itself?

It is not logical that a single cognition should be the knower of both its own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) and its universal nature (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); for if it possesses conceptualization (*savikalpa*), it is not the cognizer of the former, and if it is otherwise [devoid of conceptualization], it is not the cognizer of the latter.

If [it is argued that] there is a difference [between them] because [the first cognition] does not exist [at the time of the second], then [the subsequent cognitions of] birth and so forth would be the same as the first [cognition], because they are apprehenders of an object already known, like a memory-cognition. If [it is argued that] there is an apprehension [of the object] in a form that is indistinct due to various commonalities, yet the object is not at all determined, then the determination is merely successive.

Just as the object of inference is the determination (*niścaya*) of the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and the removal of superimposition (*samāropa*), so too is the validity (*mānatā*) of inference [established] through that [determination], and not by virtue of being the object of the exclusion and removal of superimposition belonging to memory (*smṛti*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [memory] also being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*).
Inferential knowledge is accepted as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it arises immediately after the removal of superimposition; therefore, that [inference] does not exist for you.
First, [the thought] "this white cow moves" arises; immediately thereafter, no superimposition (*samāropa*) is perceived within this cognition (*vijñāna*), which is what is being negated here.

Birth and the other [characteristics] do not exist as entities characterized by identity or difference; for that conceptualizing cognition which would attain the status of direct perception does not exist, because [identity and difference] do not appear through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), nor do they appear as distinct, since identity and difference remain mutually exclusive.

Non-conceptual cognition possesses the capacity for the arising of conceptualization; therefore, by means of that [capacity], it becomes an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) for all worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*).

Furthermore, non-conceptual [cognition] is not capable of [producing] conceptualization, because there is no difference between the form of the object and the form of the cognition, and because it is devoid of construction, just like the eye and other [senses].

In this case, there is no contradiction between these two [cognitions] and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Nor is there a difference in their object (*viṣaya*), because [the object] is determined (*adhyavasāyataḥ*) as the thing itself.
However, in reality, conceptual construction proceeds without a basis (*nirālamba*); therefore, that which might be differentiated in any way whatsoever is not its object at all.

The mutual causality of cognitions (*buddhi*)—such as those of form, sound, and so forth—indeed exists; therefore, this example cited [by you] is unestablished with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*). Furthermore, because the relationship of cause and effect between fire and smoke and so forth is clearly evident, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is perceived even in this case.

The apprehension that has been made non-erroneous for the purpose of the cessation of consciousnesses such as [the perception of] floating hairs and the like is not accepted as a valid cognition (*pramā*), because it is erroneous; so say some. However, even this is mental, because [it occurs] when the sense faculty is present, and because it is perceived when there is a change in that [faculty], and when [the object] is changed.
This [cognition] would cease from the delusion of the mind—just like the delusion of a snake and so forth—even when the sensory organ has not perished, because it appears clearly.

That [cognition], being cultivated through the presence of that [object], is not established as direct [perception]; rather, it is erroneous by way of a traditional succession, because it is associated with that cognition which is a memory.

The state of being subject to transformation (*vikāritva*)—that [transformation] itself—is clearly perceived (*dṛśyate*) in the world (*loke*), even in the case of effects (*kāryeṣu*) that arise (*udbhaveṣu*) through a succession of momentum, flow, and so forth (*pāramparyavegasarādīṣu*).
Thus, all mental errors cease through investigation; in this [investigation], the variability [of objects] is [perceived] by cognitions as the generality of existence.

If it is argued that there is a cessation of these [cognitions] with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity (*vastu*), and thus they do not arise—just as in the case of the two moons—and if it is further argued that there is no cessation of existence (*sattā*) because it is common to all cognitions, including those erroneous cognitions of those who are dogmatically attached to [theories such as] *Īśvara* and so forth; [then we reply: that is not so.

On the contrary, there is no cessation [of the objection] even upon hearing the reasoning regarding the alternatives; thus, you dull-witted ones speak again yourselves, saying, "These are not logical arguments."

The [cognition] cultivated [as the nature of that object] is not established as being that very state; for indeed, no intervention is established. Since that [intervention] is not perceived even by a mind that is unattached to other objects, it perceives [the object] without interruption, such as the double moon and so forth; therefore, there is no indirect origination.

When the existence of a commonality (*bhāvasāmānya*) among cognitions is possible, the withdrawal [of that cognition] occurs by one's own will alone; this is what others maintain. Furthermore, they declare that even in the case of an error—such as the cognition of a yellow conch—the validity (*pramāṇatā*) of cognitions is established because of their non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
That [cognition] does not possess an effective action (*arthakriyā*) corresponding to the form as it is determined; otherwise, there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

Since [the cognition] is non-concordant with reality (*bhāvataḥ saṃvādi*), even when there is an appearance of hair and so forth in the case of light and the like, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) is difficult to avoid.
Nor does a configuration exist as something distinct from color; nor is it admitted that there is a correspondence with the color as it appears.

Validity is established through non-contradiction with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), disregarding the [perceived] form; for how could everything that has been stated not be contradicted? Such is the certainty regarding the object and its nature; therefore, the occurrence of correspondence arises from the causal impression (*vāsanā*) of cooking.
The principle is this: that which is the non-conceptual nature of mental and sensory cognition is the means of establishing the non-conceptuality of pleasure and so forth.

Yet, if these [pleasures] do not themselves cognize another, how indeed could they be possessors of their own cognition? For if they were, they would be objects of cognition dependent upon a single [cognizing] consciousness.

Pleasure and so forth are experienced continuously during the perception of external objects; why, then, at that time, is it maintained that the object of cognition itself is cognized by the mental consciousness alone, and yet its existence at that time is not admitted, given the description of the sequence of their arising?

If it is argued that simultaneous birth is not admitted, nor is there stability, nor even the establishment of stability due to the momentary destruction [of things], and if this is considered an illusion arising from rapid succession, then that too has been refuted; for indeed, a vivid appearance would occur within the range of memory.

If that error is conceived as having the nature of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and so forth, then the existence of pleasure and the other [feelings] is established as being characterized by that alone.
When yogins perceive pleasure and so forth through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that [perception] is equal to [ordinary] experience, they too would become afflicted (*ātura*).
Your power is indeed the very existence of suffering; however, the knowledge of it has that [suffering] as its object, and that [knowledge] exists in another's continuum.
And this [inference] is equal in the case of inferring another's suffering; for that inference is described as having an object, but not as being beyond the range [of perception].

Pleasure, pain, and so forth are indeed perceived (*gamyante*); thus, pleasure and so forth are perceived. That [perception] is indeed knowledge (*jñāna*). It is not [knowledge] like a jar and so forth.

If this is so, then when there is a difference in convention (*samaya*), that knowledge would reside only in the mind (*cetas*) and not elsewhere; consequently, in that case, the state of being non-knowledge (*ajñānatā*) would follow.
Because of its being manifest through the illumination of form, that [manifestation] does not follow as a consequence; for why is all this not equal to the case of pleasure, pain, and so forth?

We shall explain the cognition of the yogin (*yogivijñāna*): it is produced by the cultivation of real objects (*bhāvanābhūtārtha*), is free from conceptual construction and error, and is sufficient [as a means of knowledge].

Here, either the apprehension of the object is accepted as the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), or the similarity of form (*sārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition, or else the self-awareness (*svavitti*) is [the fruit], while the capacity (*yogyatā*) is also [the means of valid cognition].
Just as when cutting is applied to a *khadira* tree, the act of cutting does not occur in a *palāśa* tree, so too in the world there is no identity between the axe and the cutting;

nor is there a relationship of means (*sādhana*) and end (*sādhya*) established by way of a substratum (*āśrayatva*), for such a designation is not tenable in the case of a formless consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Therefore, while a distinction [between them] is imagined—as, for example, [the distinction between] a bow and its parts—this established rule (*vyavasthā*) is not accepted on the basis of [the axe being] the producer (*utpādakatva*) of that which is produced (*utpādya*).
When a piece of wood is being split, it is said that the axe, as it enters therein, is being cut; by that [fact], their identity (*ekatva*) remains established.

In this established system (*vyavasthā*), once [the distinction] has arisen (*jātāyām*), let it be conceived (*kalpyatām*) even otherwise: that the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is called the "means" (*vidhi*) by virtue of being the producer (*utpādakatva*) of the object to be produced (*utpādya*), while the causehood (*kāraṇatva*) of the immediately preceding [cognition] (*vṛttasya anantarasya*) is held to be the "result" (*phala*) with respect to the cognition (*jñāne*) when it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇe*); however, the subsequent [cognition] is the result.

The state of being a fruit of self-cognition is not at all tenable, because it is negated by [the fact that] there would follow the consequence of having distinct objects when there is a form of the object within the means of cognition. That [self-cognition] cannot be negated by the consequence of the non-cognition of everything; nor does the state of being an object exist as something distinct here in self-cognition, even though it is considered to be a cognition of an object.

If [it is argued that] the instrument (*pramāṇa*) is distinct from the action (*kriyā*) because it possesses its own causal agency (*kārakatva*), then [we reply]: if [you claim] there is another result (*phala*) [besides the cognition], that would indeed be fruitless;
for by the logic already stated, no other result exists, and moreover, its status as a causal agent is not established merely by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) to produce [the cognition].

In the case of the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*), there is no contradiction whatsoever (*na ... asti kaścana virodhaḥ*) with its status as a stabilizer (*sthāpakatva*). Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because of the demonstration (*pratipādanāt*) of contradiction.

If it is argued that cognition (*jñāna*) does not indeed possess a common form (*naiva sādhāraṇākāra*) of the object to be grasped (*grāhyajāti*), due to its being of a different nature (*antaratvataḥ*), then [it is] like taste, color, and so forth (*rasarūpādivat*).
In the *Nyāyānusāra*, all this has been described by us; and this other matter has also been clearly distinguished in the analysis of the grasped and the grasper.

Cognition would fall into the state of non-cognition through some part [of itself] if there were similarity [only with respect to that]. There would be similarity [only] in every respect if everything were a knower [of everything].
However, in the doctrine of the existence of external objects, the possibility of similarity must certainly be accepted; for this purpose, it has been explained.

Even though there is a difference between the cognition and the mind that appears as the object, there would still be an experience [of it], albeit figuratively, due to the reflection possessing that same form.
For one by whom consciousness is not held to be the receptacle of the conformity to the object, even this mode [of explanation] does not exist at all regarding the cognition of external [objects].

Inference (*anumāna*) is held to be twofold by way of division: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). For oneself, it is the perception of the object to be inferred (*anumeya-artha*) from a mark (*liṅga*) that possesses the three characteristics (*tri-rūpataḥ*).

Furthermore, for others, it is said to be the statement (*vacana*) of the meaning of the three-characterized mark; its forms are considered to be the fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*) of each individual or two of those characteristics.

Indeed, the state of being a good reason (*suhetutā*) is observed [to consist] in the impossibility of [the probandum's existence] otherwise (*anyathānupapannatva*); it does not exist even when the three members [of the syllogism] are absent. Therefore, those [reasons] possessing the three characteristics are impotent.
That which is accepted as having the impossibility of [the probandum's existence] otherwise is the reason; that object has only one characteristic, or rather, it does not have four characteristics.

Just as in the world a man with three sons is called "one who has an only son" because that one son is excellent, so too let it be seen here that the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is never found at all among reasons (*hetu*) possessing the three forms, except for the single factor of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathā-asambhava*).
The state of being a cause belongs to that [thing] for which there is the impossibility of existing otherwise; let the two examples be [present], or rather not, for they are not the cause.
Where there is no impossibility otherwise, what is the use of the triad? Where there is impossibility otherwise, what is the use of the triad there?

"The reason (*hetuḥ*) [is as follows]: He is dark-skinned (*śyāmaḥ*) because he is his son (*putratvāt*), just as the others (*itare*) are seen to be dark-skinned (*śyāmāḥ*). [However,] the three-fold characteristic (*tri-lakṣaṇaḥ*) does not function (*na pravarttate*) for the sake of certainty (*niścayai*).

In that case, a reason (*hetuḥ*) possessing only one characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇaḥ*)—being devoid of the two [other characteristics], namely the example (*dṛṣṭānta-*) and the presence (*bhāva-*) and absence (*abhāvau*) which constitute its nature (*ātmakau*)—[is established] by some means (*kathaṃcit*) through the fact of being perceived (*upalabhyatvāt*)."

"The hare-marked one is not the moon, because it has been pointed out as such [as having a hare], by way of being the moon"—this is called a "two-characterized" reason (*dvilakṣaṇahetu*). Furthermore, another [type] is understood as follows: "This sensation of mine was produced by the contact of a falling insect, because of the arising of the contact with a falling insect."

[The eye], possessing an excellence of power (*atiśaya-śakti*), is always operative with respect to the object, namely form (*rūpa-graha*), because it is being employed; or else, because of the perception of that [form].
Alternatively, the self, the jar, and so forth, are in no way non-existent, because they are somehow perceived, just like [the horn] belonging to a donkey.

Moreover, [you might argue that] rabbit-horns and the like are always existent because they are somehow apprehensible, just like the self, pots, and so forth; [and] it is understood from your own statement, "There is one in your house," due to hearing the word "father" used by you here in this dwelling.

Precisely by way of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), even in the case of things such as words, lamps, and so forth, although they do not possess the property of being a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), their status as indicators (*jñāpakatā*) is observed. Therefore, let our reason (*hetu*)—which possesses only a single characteristic—be the means of comprehension (*gamaka*), primarily on account of its predominance; what is the use of these imagined, useless [distinctions] such as "property," "subject," and so forth?

Is this characteristic (lakṣaṇa) understood (gamyate) in a general sense (sāmānyena), or in a specific [sense] (viśeṣe) regarding that which is desired to be known (jijñāsita), or rather in the illustration (nidarśane) of the subject (dharmiṇi)?
When that [subject] has been understood through its general existence in the reason within the locus of the probandum, it would not be manifested as possessing the intended proof.
Just as the non-deviation of visibility from destruction by means of the universal [of destruction] is not a proof for that [impermanence] in the case of sound.
If its existence is declared in the subject (*dharmī*), then even according to your view, that very three-fold nature (*tri-rūpatā*) of it is established.

Because the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatirekau*) of that [reason] are understood through the impossibility of its being otherwise (*anyathānupapattyā*), and because it exists in the subject (*dharmiṇi*) as a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma-saṃśrayaḥ*), such a concise definition was taught by the Teachers (*ācāryaiḥ*). Thus, the reason (*hetuḥ*) is a property (*dharmaḥ*) to be grasped as pervaded (*vyāptaḥ*) by a portion (*aṃśena*) of that [probandum].

Now, this characteristic of the reason is understood (*avagamyate*) in the subject (*dharmiṇi*) itself; however, since there is no non-establishment (*asiddhiḥ*) by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāt*), for that reason, it does not belong to that [subject] either.

If there is no comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), there can be no certainty regarding the reason (*hetu*) either; therefore, the reason is useless for establishing the probandum through anything other [than itself].
Furthermore, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): since both the probandum and the reason are unestablished, if one is not ascertained, the other cannot be established either.

Even if that [reason] were established, there would be no cognition of the probandum in the subject (*dharmin*), for its pervasion (*vyāpti*) has not been ascertained through universal application (*sarvopasaṃhārāt*).
This reason which has been stated here—that [the object] exists in some way through apprehension—does not have a doubtful object at all; therefore, it is fruitless.
For when a thing is ascertained by everyone, why is it described in this way as being "to be proven" in some manner?

Even in the doctrine [of yours] that all things are identical, by virtue of their difference from the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*), the state of being [identical to] those is clearly manifested by someone through a distinct nature.
You, who have resorted to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of all things, yet have also resorted to the qualification "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) as "primordial matter" (*ādi*).

Otherwise, indeed, the apprehensibility of conventional discourse could not be established in any way; for if it were something to be proven (*sādhyatve*), there would be no well-known example (*prasiddhaṃ nidarśanam*).

The state of being pointed out (*apadiṣṭatva*)—even by way of "moonness" (*candratva*)—persists (*anuvarttate*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Or else, in some case, such as a young brahmin (*māṇavaka*) [who is actually] camphor, silver, or the like, there would be the state of being an uncommon (*asādhāraṇatā*) reason (*hetu*) for the proof (*sādhana*) of moonness; and furthermore, in the absence (*vyatireka*) of the well-known basis (*prasiddhi-samāśraya*) consisting of the nature of a real entity (*rūpa-vastu*).

No distinction is observed between the state of being produced (*kṛtatva*) and the arising (*udaya*) of a falling insect that has acquired contact with a falling insect; for if [the former] were the effect [of the latter], then this qualification of "falling" would be superfluous, and otherwise, an unavoidable deviation (*vyabhicāritva*) of the reason (*hetu*) would result.

If the conventional practice of [proving] the effect-status [of the eye] were to depend on its being forgotten, then [the reason] would possess the three forms by virtue of the example; however, the existence of the subject-form—the eye—having been previously established remains as yet unascertained, and thus it is not logical for that [reason] to be a means of proof, because of the consequence of non-establishment and other such faults.
But when form and so forth exist, visual cognition does not arise; therefore, it is understood that this [cognition] alone is not the cause.

The sprout and so forth exist as an emergence determined by its own specific cause; thus, in that example, there is a very clear dissimilarity with the probans (*sādhana*) in the case of the jar and so forth, because it possesses in some way a nature that lacks the cause [of the sprout], and [furthermore, the reason] is seen to be either futile or unestablished.

Even here, there is a very clear example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*); for that very same nature of theirs attains the state of being a counter-example (*vipakṣatā*). Thus, the establishment of [the reason] in things that are existent but devoid of self (*nirātmasu*), as well as its non-establishment and the attainment of dissimilarity, occurs in exactly that manner.

The relationship with the father’s house is established by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*); the reason (*hetu*) for this, consisting of three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*), is clearly manifest therein. However, since the accent (*svara*) was previously perceived only in some instances, its non-perception at other times renders the reason unestablished (*asiddhatā*), which is difficult to refute.

In that [place] where it was previously perceived, and in that [place] where it was not perceived—where positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is clearly seen—the word (*śabda*) does not at all indicate an external object in any way; for otherwise, [such indication] would be impossible. Rather, this [word] is the indicator of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*).

In that case [the lamp], which is the object to be established, the distinction is extremely clear; for when there is no intention to speak of [the presence of] an entity, the word "lamp" is not employed [in the passive sense].

However, the lamp is not at all an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of blue and so forth by its very nature (*bhāvataḥ*), because it produces a suitable capacity for the generation of cognition; rather, it is described as such.

When the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the form of a property (*dharma*), subject (*pakṣa*), and so forth (*ādi*) is considered as the means of cognition (*jñāpaka*), why is it [the eye, etc. questioned otherwise? Otherwise, the non-occurrence (*an-upapatti*) of the state of not being visible (*acākṣuṣatva*) would establish [the existence of the invisible] even for the eyes and so forth (*cakṣur-ādīnām*). Therefore, those [reasons] possessing only one characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇāḥ*) are impotent (*klībāḥ*).

The dual nature (*dvairūpya*) of the aforementioned [reasons] is characterized by their being of a single form; and the triple nature (*trairūpya*) of the aforementioned [reasons] is characterized by their having two forms, by virtue of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

If [it is argued that] this [is established] solely through implication (*ākṣepāt*)—that is, by the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapattyā*)—then that [implication] does not exist at the outset even with respect to the visibility of sound (*śabdacakṣuṣatve*), since it is otherwise accepted [that sound is not visible].

Furthermore, if [the reason] does not exist, then because of the absence of the [logical] grounds such as "being a son" (*putratva*) and so forth, and because its three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) are doubtful due to the lack of exclusion from heterogeneous instances (*vijātīyavyatirekataḥ*), there is no non-contradiction (*avirodhataḥ*) regarding its existence.
Even if that [non-perception] were the sonship of that [object], its alteration is indeed possible (*saṃbhāvyate*), especially due to causes such as karma, food, and so forth.

This [non-perception] is neither the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor the effect (*kārya*) [of the object]; furthermore, since it is merely the non-perception of a perceptible thing (*dṛśya*) that is distinct from it, it does not possess infallibility (*avyabhicāritā*).

Infallibility is observed even in other cases; for example, the rising of the moon is seen as the sign (*liṅga*) of the blooming of night-lotuses, and the swelling of the ocean is recognized through the presence of sunlight on the opposite shores.
In darkness, when a firebrand is seen nearby, smoke is perceived; and from the rising of the Kṛttikās, there arises the conceptualization of the proximity of Rohiṇī.

All those others, such as the Buddhas and so forth, are considered to have arisen at one and the same time because of such reasons for their qualities that are inferred; this is the establishment of the cause from the effect.
(5th s. Thus, by such a rule, if there were no [logical] establishment of a connection, there would be the comprehension of everything;
furthermore, the specific wind would be the cause of the rising of Kṛttikā, for it is precisely that which, through its continuity, is the cause of proximity to Rohiṇī.
Therefore, that cognition is considered to be the cognition of the property (*dharma*) and the reason (*hetu*); here, there is no such independent cognition whatsoever.

That inference which proceeds toward an object that is a reflection, arising from a mark (*liṅga*) designated as a "counter-reflection" (*pratibimba*), is rightly [considered] distinct from the effect produced by that [original] mark.
[The reflection] does not exist as two real entities because they do not both exist together in one place; therefore, how could its causal efficiency be ultimate? [Objection:
Even if this reflection lacks the nature of a real entity, by what means will consciousness arise having that [reflection] as its appearance, since it is a non-entity?

For its status as a sign (*liṅgatva*) is indeed accepted here as that very effect (*kārya*); this [cognition] proceeds without a [real external] support (*nirālambana*), by virtue of the predominance (*ādhipatya*) of the reflected image (*bimba*).

[The thesis] is described by others for the sake of another [purpose] through words beginning with the "proposition" (*pratijñā*), because it is a constituent part (*aṅga*) that is not a means of proof (*asādhana*). Therefore, the proposition is useless; due to a lack of connection, it is not appropriate as a demonstrator of the meaning, nor is it even fitting [to do so] indirectly, since it does not indicate what is relevant.
If, however, this [word] is accepted as a member (*aṅga*) [of the proof] because it demonstrates the object of the means and the goal— just like the word "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*)—

then surely there is deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) here due to the admission [of other members] such as the statement (*vākya*), and furthermore, the demonstration of the object would be useless in cases where [the object is already known].

If it is asked how there can be a formal determination (*vyavasthā*) regarding the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and so forth, since there is no application (*aprayoga*) of the thesis (*pakṣa*), then even the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) would have no basis (*nibandhana*) for depending upon that [thesis]. If this is your objection:

In the [treatise on] expression (*abhidhāna*), there exists the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and so forth; however, in the *śāstra*, those [categories] are analyzed in that manner for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

Or rather, that [reason] which is the basis for the subject matter under discussion is not contradicted; for the proponent does not state a proof even for the opponent at an inappropriate time, because the nature of the thesis persists due to the equality of those respective absences with respect to the particularity sought to be known.

If the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not stated, then because of its non-statement, the statement of the application (*upanaya*) should not be made for the sake of establishing [the presence] of the reason (*kāraṇa*). Furthermore, once the mere existence of the entity has been stated both before and after [the reason], the reflection [of the application] is fruitless, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has already been manifested through the establishment of the intended meaning.

Since it is established by the very force of the statement of the three-fold reason (*trirūpahetu*), there is no possibility of error (*viparyaya*). Therefore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is indeed redundant.
A single meaning is established by means of interconnected statements; thus, for the sake of establishing that connection, the conclusion need not be stated separately.

Some explain that inference is of two kinds based on the distinction between the perceived (*paridṛṣṭatva*) and the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). (A) [Inference] is the cognition produced regarding a specific location (*viśeṣa-tad-deśa-mati*) based on a connection (*sambandha*) that has been directly perceived (*dṛṣṭa-pratyakṣa*) between two particulars (*viśeṣa*), such as firewood (*indhana*) and cow-dung (*gomaya*).
By that very person, having gone even to that place again and again, when he perceives that fire at another time through his prior cognition;
The validity (*pramāṇatā*) of that [cognition] is doubted because of the existence of a real object (*vastu-sadbhāva*) that is being perceived; this was written by Vindhyavāsin.

However, when a specific [object] is seen, it is expressed in a general way within the means of valid cognition (*mitau*), such as "the sun is a mover" due to the internal relationship between fire and smoke; thus, the generality (*sāmānya*) is what is seen with absolute certainty.

In this case, because there is a counter-proof against momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), which is all-pervasive, there is no possibility of inference (*anumāna*) based on that very same prior [perception]. If, however, through the intention (*vivakṣā*) of [identifying] a continuity (*prabandha*), a unity (*ekatva*) is conceptually constructed (*kalpita*) regarding it, then that [unity] has no real persistence whatsoever; moreover, such a thing is not a real entity (*vastutva*).
Knowledge, being devoid of an object, is not admitted by you when it has a conceptualized object; indeed, it would clearly be devoid of an object.

Even if the individual form (*vyakti-rūpa*) of those two were to perish, their generic form (*ākṛti*) would surely remain; for even in its existence, the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇa-bhaṅga*) is certain.
For what reason have you stated this restriction—that inference is [the means of knowledge] only for those two particulars whose connection has been perceived through direct perception at some time?
Having seen it once, why is that very same [inference] not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by means of inference? For what distinction is there from the former case?

If this [cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it apprehends an object already known—just like a memory—why is this [subsequent cognition] not seen to be the same as the previous one?
If you say there is a distinction there due to the removal of doubt that had arisen in the interim, why is it not similar in this case as well?
Therefore, for one whose doubt has been dispelled, is it that [the object] exists, or is it that it does not exist? This perception of a generality (*sāmānyadarśana*) is free from further expectancy.
Yet some of evil vision (*kudṛṣṭi*) have declared: "Inference (*anumāna*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," even while they themselves communicate their intention through words.

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not logically tenable as having its own object (*svārtha*), because it [precedes it] like false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), which is produced by a potter who desires [to create] it.

Furthermore, the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) does not exist as the cause of inference (*anumiti*), because even in the absence of inference, there is a two-fold character (*dvairūpya*). Therefore, there is a contradiction with [the definition of] inference, since contradictory reasons (*viruddha*) are possible in every case of a probans (*sādhana*). Moreover, [there is no reason] that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) regarding the contradictory.
Due to the differences in state, place, and time, when potencies are diverse, the establishment of entities through inference is extremely difficult to achieve.
In relation to this [object], the capacity of that particular substance is known; yet that capacity is obstructed with respect to that specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Even when an object has been inferred through great effort, it is only established as such by those who are more diligent and skilled among the inferents; otherwise, it is not.

Inference for the sake of others (*parārtham*), however, is not a means of valid cognition (*mānam*) because it is a restatement (*anuvādāt*), depending (*apekṣayā*) upon the speaker (*vaktṛ*). This [inference] does not itself (*svayam*) establish (*prapadyate*) the object (*artham*); therefore, even depending on the hearer (*śrotṛ*), this [inference] is established (*upapadyate*) as being for one's own sake (*svārtham*) alone. For what difference (*viśeṣaḥ*) is there between the cognitions (*saṃvidaḥ*) that are the source (*mūlāyāḥ*) of both the hearer and the seer?

With respect to the listener, the speech [of the speaker] does not possess the nature of an inference (*anumānatva*) with regard to the object, because it functions as a cause for the consciousness of the listener’s mental continuum by way of making [the object] known—just as a sense faculty [is a cause for cognition].

Nor is there a direct manifestation of the inferable [object]; therefore, since this [speech] lacks an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with knowledge, it does not possess that [nature of inference].

Now, it might be argued: "Exclusion [of others] depends upon something else for its meaning; therefore, even that [exclusion] is untenable in its own sense, because it would follow that it serves the purpose of another.

But surely, the possession of the three characteristics of the mark (*liṅga*) is the definition of [valid] correspondence, and that is what constitutes being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*). Why, then, is that [exclusion] denied?

False cognition is said to be similar [to valid cognition] with respect to the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*), because it is produced by the destruction of what is desired; however, this is not so in reality (*vastutas*).

For, according to the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), that cognition is non-contradictory (*avisamvādin*) and certain (*niścita*) regarding the opposite of what the proponent desires; therefore, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, there is contradiction (*viruddhatā*) of the reason (*hetu*) with respect to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); and by this very same method, there is also the unestablished nature (*asādhyatā*) [of the probandum] and the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the second reason (*hetu*).

The proponents of logic declare that to be a means of proof for the sake of establishing [a conclusion] which possesses a relationship that is thoroughly ascertained through identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*utpatti*).
There is no such contradiction through inference and so forth; for that [contradiction] cannot possibly occur anywhere without [the presence of] an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or a cause (*hetu*).

Furthermore, two mutually contradictory properties (*dharma*) are not logically possible within a single entity (*vastu*); therefore, there is no possibility of a non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) contradiction.
The operation of the definitions of inference, however, is said to be one [type] when there is a correct ascertainment of a familiar sign (*liṅga*), while another is designated [as the second type].
Thus, because the capacities [of things] are diverse due to the difference in their states, times, and locations, the establishment of entities through inference is not at all difficult to obtain.
Even an object that has been inferred with effort by skilled inferents is not established as such by others who are even more proficient.

There is no intrinsic nature apart from intrinsic nature, nor is there an effect apart from a cause; because of the attainment of difference, [intrinsic nature] would lack a causal basis, and without those two, inference does not exist.

That which was stated as being inference (*anumānatva*)—namely, the word (*vacas*), which possesses the three-fold mark (*tri-rūpa-liṅga*)—is so designated because it indicates a meaning beyond itself (*artha-parasūcakatvāt*). This [designation] is applied (*sakta*) in dependence upon the listener (*śrotṛ-apekṣayā*).

Thus, this status of being inference is based on a figurative (*gauṇa*) and conventional (*sāṅketika*) sense; therefore, by virtue of its being indicative (*saṃsūcakatvena*), no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occurs.
If inference is not a valid means of knowledge for you, then your objection is fruitless; for no argument whatsoever can establish the speaker's intention.

The worldly mark (*laukika-liṅga*) is indeed accepted [as a means of proof], but it is not imagined by others; for surely even the world understands [the relationship between] the causes and so forth (*hetv-ādi*) and their effects (*kārya*).

In reality, that very thing which has been stated by the proponents of logic (*nyāyavādibhiḥ*) is indeed worldly; even when that is admitted, why should it be abandoned by you yourself? It does not become [abandoned].

What other [person] (paraḥ) understands (pratipadyate) by means of this (etena) invalid cognition (apramāṇena)? And how could that (asau) cognition (pratyayaḥ), being produced (kṛtaḥ) by an invalid cognition (apramāṇena), be [considered valid]? (kīdṛśaḥ)

If inference were not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the speaker’s own words—just as this [inference] reveals [the object] by that [means]—then it would be accepted as non-authoritative because it does not reveal an object that has not been known. Is it not the case that your [position] is likewise [invalid], since it is not capable [of proving anything] by way of being indicative?

[Objection: Why is it that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of the intermediate means of knowledge (*antara-pramāṇa*), such as verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) and so forth, is specified only for the two [other] means of knowledge? [Reply: It is said:

"Another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) distinct from the two does not hold, because of the lack of a definition of a [separate] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and because it is included herein."

Others say: "Verbal knowledge [is valid] because it is a cognition of an object beyond the senses derived from a word, and because that [word] is a sentence that lacks an author, as well as because it is uttered by a trustworthy person."
This [object], it is said, is not perceptible because it is an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). Nor is inference applicable, due to the absence of its defining characteristic;
for as long as the subject (*dharmin*)—the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) qualified by the property—is not well-ascertained, there can be no inference having that as its object.

Furthermore, that which is postulated (*kalpyate*) here as the subject (*dharmin*)—the object of cognition (*prameya*) itself—and while that [subject] has not yet been determined, there can be no determination of its being a property (*dharmatva*).

If it were already grasped prior to this because of its being a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharmitvāt*), then what would be the use of the [logical] reasons (*hetu*) and so forth, by means of which the status of inference (*anumānatā*) would arise?

Nor is the concomitance (*anvaya*) of the word with the object of cognition (*prameya*) established; for the capacity to follow (*anvetṛtva*) is perceived in all [words] through their function (*vyāpāra*).

In that case, where there is smoke, there is clearly a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by virtue of the existence of fire; however, it is not certain in this way that "there is sound" where there is [smoke]. This is the meaning. Where there is sound, there it exists.

It is not understood that [the word-sound] is being perceived (*gamyate*) in that place (*tatra deśe*) and at that time (*tasmin kāle*); for if it were eternal (*nitya*), it would exist equally (*sama*) in all sounds (*sarvaśabdeṣu*) due to its omnipresence (*vibhutvāt*).
Because it is not perceived anywhere due to the absence of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it follows that there would be a comprehension of all objects by means of all words.
Therefore, verbal cognition (*śābda*)—being devoid of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*)—would not be inference, because it lacks such an object as perception does.

Because of the statement [of the Veda], which is unshakable due to its origin in the Agnihotra and other rites, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) cannot be refuted. Since it is impossible for a sentence that lacks an author to have two meanings that are mutually inconsistent, the first definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*) stated [by the Naiyāyika] is untenable.
Since a nature that is either capable or incapable always persists, consciousness would either always exist or never exist at any time;
just as hatred, delusion, and so forth are the causes of falsity, so too are compassion, wisdom, and so forth the causes of truth.

In the absence of a person (*nara*), there is no possibility even for those two [truth and falsity] which have him as their basis (*āśraya*); therefore, it follows that speech not based on a person (*apuruṣāśraye vacasi*) is devoid of purpose (*ānarthakyam*).

If our comprehension of the meaning were to arise from the explanation [itself], then this [comprehension] would exist by virtue of the explanation; for a person is seen to be independent when explaining according to his own will.

If its power alone were established by nature for the illumination of the actual object, then the comprehension of that object would occur even for one who does not know the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).

A lamp (*dīpaḥ*) or illuminator (*dīpakaḥ*), by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), does not depend (*apekṣate*) upon a convention (*samayam*). Therefore, when there is another convention (*antara-samaye*), there is no comprehension (*agatiḥ*) of the other meaning (*antare arthe*). For even if a convention (*saṅketa-bhāve*) were to exist, a lamp does not illuminate (*na prakāśayati*), nor can that capacity (*sā śaktiḥ*) be cognized (*vijñātum śakyate*).

Therefore, since there is no connection with the meaning of a cognition, how could there be unshakeability for him? Rather, that [cognition] is conventional (*sāmayika*) and is not contradicted by the person who consists of speech.

No distinction whatsoever is perceived by those learned in logic (*nyāya*) between these two; however, this unshakable conviction of the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) regarding the path of logic (*nyāya*)—due to their non-acceptance of an authoritative person (*āpta*)—is such that the second definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*) is not even capable of being established, nor is it desired. Thus, this [definition] remains undetermined.
That conviction which is observed from a statement is generally accepted for the sake of understanding what is beyond the senses;
for even if there was no prior conviction, due to the absence of contradiction elsewhere, there is a restriction that what holds true in one instance applies everywhere.
What obstruction could there be even for words that set forth external objects, by which [obstruction] they would lack the status of being a means of valid cognition?
