There is no apprehension of a single identity [of the object] due to the senses and so forth being distinct; nor does its arising from them occur, because of their deviation; and it is not logical for anything else to possess non-deviation.
The intention (*vivakṣā*) is inferred from all words; moreover, that [intention] is ascertained as the cause by means of both perception and non-perception.

The speech of one who is deluded is perceived as something else when there is a desire to express something different; likewise, even when the speaker intends [something else], it proceeds by way of a generality. Therefore, this [speech] does not indeed proceed [as intended] if [it is otherwise].
The wise clearly determine the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous [cognitions] applied to the subject at hand and so forth; [this is] sufficient for words.

Those who, through a lack of discernment (*availakṣaṇyena*), do not perceive the distinction (*viśeṣam*) among the reasons (*hetūnām*), for them there is indeed a fault (*doṣaḥ*); however, there is no [fault] regarding the logical mark (*liṅgasya*).
Otherwise, because smoke might at some time have a doubtful nature, it would not possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to fire at the time of [its] ascertainment;

for even in the case of inference based solely on the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), there is no contradiction, since there is the certain existence of [the mark] for the sake of establishing [the object], such as being alive and so forth.

When the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is what is to be understood, the three-fold nature (*tri-rūpatā*) is indeed clearly evident in the person (*pums*) who is the subject (*dharmin*); that [three-fold nature] is what is to be proven (*sādhyā*), since it is by means of the effect, namely speech (*vacas*).

This person, who possesses the intention [to speak], is recognized as being the speaker of the word "tree" with respect to the object "tree," because he is an agent of the word "tree," just as I was in previous states.
Therefore, where the three-fold nature [of the reason] has been refuted by others regarding external objects, we certainly do not admit the validity of words.

In that case, however, where the possession of the three forms is intended for these [reasons], this [threefold nature] is clearly revealed when the intention to express the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) regarding the probandum (*sādhyā*) is present.

This being the case, [the cognition] would be inferential with respect to the word, just like smoke and so forth, by virtue of its possessing the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) through its existence within the object-domain.
When asked in this way, "What is a *gavaya* like? by city-dwellers, the forest-dweller speaks the sentence: "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*."

In this regard, its status as a well-known standard of comparison (*upamāna*) has been described in the *Śābara* [Bhāṣya] precisely in another way, because it does not originate from anything external.
Having seen a cow, this [person], when he beholds another [animal] in the forest—a gavaya—which possesses many common parts such as a rounded neck, [perceives it].

At that time, even that cognition of this gavaya which consists merely of the apprehension of its form is indeed perception; specifically, the [cognition] "this animal is similar to a cow"—in the presence of a universal (*jāti*)—is accepted as perception when the operation of the sense organs (*akṣa-vyāpāra*) is present.
Even though that cognition arises after having remembered the cow in the proximity of a gavaya, it would still have the sense-faculty as its object.

Similarity, like a universal (*sāmānya*), is also fully established in each individual instance even when the counter-correlative is not perceived; furthermore, the reality (*vastutva*) of similarity cannot be refuted, for it consists in the connection with many constituent parts (*avayava-yoga*) that are common to another [object] belonging to the same class (*jāti*).
In that very state (*vyavasthā*), the consciousness (*vijñāna*) which proceeds (*pravartate*) is similar (*tulya*) to this animal (*paśu*); thus it is a simile (*sa-upamā*).

Therefore, that which is remembered as qualified by similarity would be the object of cognition (*prameya*) for the object of comparison (*upameya*), or rather, it would be the similarity itself residing therein.

When similarity has been perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the cow is remembered, since the qualified [object] is not established through any other means, comparison (*upamāna*) possesses the status of a valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*).
Just as, even when the place is perceived and the fire is being remembered, it does not follow that inference lacks the status of a valid cognition because the object is qualified.
[The direct perception] of consciousness is unestablished because of the absence of the operation of the connection with the sense-faculties at that time;

nor indeed is its nature as inference possible, because the three characteristics [of a logical reason] are not applicable, and a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) cannot be conceived in this case in any way whatsoever.
For similarity belonging to the cow is not apprehended beforehand as a property (*dharma*); and even when it is being apprehended in the gavaya, it does not serve as a means of comparison for cows.

The cow, having gone [to the forest], does not possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅgatā*) because it is only a single part of the object of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*). Furthermore, the gavaya does not even attain the status of a logical mark for the cow, due to the lack of a [necessary] connection.
Nor is that cognition invalid, because it reveals an object not previously known; for prior to this, there was no apprehension of its similarity [to the cow].

If it is held that the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) for this [cognition]—which has as its object of knowledge (*prameya*) an entity (*vastu*) consisting in non-existence—is not intended, provided that there exists a similarity (*sādṛśya*) through a connection (*yoga*) with many common parts (*sāmānyāvayava*).

The universals [are] discarded. Whence [could there be] that plurality in them, and their connection with those [particulars]? If there were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing the reality (*vastutva*) of the universal and its perceptibility (*grāhyatā*), even so, it would be like other non-existent things, because of its being an object of knowledge (*prameyatvāt*), like a unique entity (*asādhāraṇa-vastuvat*).

There is no proof for the proponents regarding the non-existence of the subject (*pakṣa*) as it is set forth in the meaning of the general property (*sāmānyārtha*). Furthermore, in the first case of the probandum (*sādhya*), there is the status of being a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). In that regard, certain parts (*avayava*) of the *gavaya* are the causes of the cognition of similarity together with the parts of the cow’s form.

And thus, when a gavaya is seen, there arises this recollection (*smṛti*) regarding the parts of the cow that were previously seen many times. Therefore, because of that similarity, the cognition [of similarity] does not occur in the case of a horse and so forth when a gavaya is seen; otherwise, what would be the distinction?

This [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because the object has already been cognized; however, how could there then be the existence of another means of knowledge? Or let there be similarity, which—like that [similarity] in a cow—is seen as a universal (*sāmānya*), even though its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is unperceived.

Furthermore, the nature of memory does not cease to be [memory] in any way; and while similarity within the essence of the cow is known merely by its existence, it is not definitively ascertained in this manner.
However, when one cognizes the similarity with the gavaya through the means of valid cognition called analogy (*upamāna*), that constitutes a distinction from memory.
If that [object] was previously grasped by him through that very name, but was grasped in its own essential form—that which is designated as "it is" (asti)—that is its self (ātman).

The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of things is that which [constitutes] their very name; if that [nature] were not apprehended even when [the things] exist, there would be a state of non-cognition (*avijñātatā*) of the self, even for those who have fully understood reality.

By this much [causal] factor (*leśa*), when validity (*pramāṇatva*) is established, there is no fixed limit (*iyattā*) to the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even otherwise, because of their being means of valid cognition.

For instance, upon seeing a row of trees (*paṅkti-taru-ādi*) and having the cognition of a single tree, there arises the ascertainment (*niścaya*) that "this is a second tree" from the sight of the first; thus it begins.

[If it is argued that] the object (*antara*) is apprehended independently of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of its similarity (*sādṛśya*) and so forth, [we reply: no, for what is already grasped is grasped again as something identical even in the case of analogies (*upamā*). Furthermore, when a gavaya is perceived, the cognition of its dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*) to a horse (*turaṅga*) and so forth arises; why then is this not another [distinct] means of valid cognition (*pramā*)?
If, because of not apprehending [it] in this way, existence were not included within non-existence— [which is] equal to cognitions [regarding] similarity or mutual non-existence—
for in that case, just as the distinction of similarity is cognized (*pramīyate*), so too would the distinction from all commonalities and parts be understood (*gamyate*).

When a connection (*yoga*) characterized by a general property (*sāmānya*) and a specific part (*avayava*) is apprehended (*adhigamyate*), then, in the case of every such connection, the consequence follows that the reality (*tattva*) of all general properties and parts would be established. Some maintain that when there is the perception of a sentence expressing a transfer (*atideśa-vākya*) whose meaning is similar, the resulting cognition of the relationship between the name and its object is analogy (*upamā*).

If the cognition of the connection with the name is indeed unconfused, then, upon hearing that analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), because it apprehends an object already grasped, it possesses no status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*), just like memory; for it is likewise devoid of the production of a new object.
(Then) she was not yet born; nevertheless, how does she understand at that time, thinking, "This is the name which has been heard by me"?
For indeed, the lord, having that [cow] as his mental representation, does not know anything at all upon perceiving a gavaya, thinking, "This is its name," as it was heard by me.
When there is the apprehension of similarity, one who has employed the means of comparison understands the relationship by way of its having a qualified object.
He knows the relationship, which has the universal as its object, from scripture; however, through the basis of analogy, he cognizes that particularized object.

Indeed, in the case of the cognition of a relation or a name, its comprehension occurs elsewhere; for its comprehension within the object itself is not tenable, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Even while [the sound] is being perceived, no one indeed perceives that beautiful word within the interval of time between the two variegated armlets on the wearer of the diadem.
Therefore, that which is known by that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as "this name" within the mental reflection (*pratibimba*) designated as external, is called the universal (*sāmānya*).
Even there, upon the perception of a gavaya, one who does not discern the distinction between the perceived and the conceptualized understands it; he conceives that "this is an external object.

And thus, whatever is to be understood—that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and verbal expressions (*dhvani*) have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objective domain—has been refuted at length.

Even when these [cognitions] have that [similarity] as their objective domain (*gocaratva*), it is precisely inference (*anumā*) that arises; and indeed, its being produced from a three-featured logical mark (*tri-rūpa-liṅga*) is thus recognized.

For that which resembles a cow is the object of the verbal expression "gavaya," just as the word "gavaya" resides in the cognition established by the apprehension of the convention (*saṅketagrahaṇa*).

In that state, he would not exist even as one situated in cognition; at what time could this [convention] be established? And this similarity to a cow—this relation has not been established as something distinct from the related entities themselves. Indeed, prior to the convention, the word was apprehended by the auditory consciousness.
That animal, standing before one, is seen with the eye; this connection [between the two] is not tenable as a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) for two things that have been cognized separately.
Just as in the case of what has been grasped, the cognition of that fragrance and sweetness does not transcend the status of being a memory (*smārtatām*) through its connection with a name;
and likewise, cognitions produced by an infinite number of means through their connection with designations arise among kings and others, even without regard for any commonality (*sādharmyam*).

In their midst, the lord of men, whose white parasol was held over him, was addressed as follows: "After some time, when that specific instruction was seen, the thought arose in him: 'This is his name. Then, that other [name] was obtained."

Because it does not depend on similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth, another [means of knowledge] establishes the existence of perception (*pratyakṣa*) by the force of another means of knowledge, namely inference (*anumāna*).
This is consistent, because [perception] is a means of knowledge, just like inference; and inference also is likewise [established].

In this way, this reason is not uncontradictory because it does not establish [the point]; and in this way, your own [position] would be contradicted. That which is your rebuttal regarding the fourfold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) will apply here as well.

When the meaning of a group of six [statements] has been cognized through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they do not postulate anything else that is unobserved (*adṛṣṭa*). That is what is called *arthāpatti* (presumption).

In this regard, the power of burning in fire is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because of its act of burning; whereas the possession of power in the sun is established through inference (*anumāna*) because of its movement.

The capacities (*śaktayaḥ*) of all entities (*sarva-bhāvānām*) are the means of proof (*sādhanāḥ*) for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on an effect (*kārya*); and those [capacities] are understood (*gamyante*) as being unprecedented (*apūrvāḥ*), except through the apprehension (*grahaṇāt*) of a relation (*sambandha*).

Nor is their relation—neither a prior one nor another—perceived at present, since there would be two positive concomitances (*anvaya*) here together with the effects, [namely] the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and [the other].

(In the alternative,) the reason (*hetu*) consisting of the capacity of the ear and so forth would follow as being unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Furthermore, that [reason] would follow as being unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because it is unestablished in the hearing (*śruti*). Thus, the cognition (*vijñāna*) that "he is fat and does not eat during the day" is called *arthāpatti* based on what is heard (*śruta*).

The word-meaning (*padārtha*) [of the term] "night" and so forth is understood (*gamyate*) from the sentence (*vākye*) [containing the term] "day. Since there is a connection (*saṃsargaḥ*) of the word-meanings (*padārthānām*) beginning with "day" with the act of eating (*bhojane*) at night, that sentence (*tat vākyam*) would be the means of conveying (*pratipādakam*) that [fact]. Furthermore, there is no assumption of a second meaning (*dvitīya-artha-kalpanā*), because [the words] are already occupied (*vyāpṛtatvāt*) with another meaning.
Therefore, this [sentence] is understood even without that sentence which exists within the mind and is understood as being non-scriptural.
That which might be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) among perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others must be stated; however, when the sentence has not been uttered, there is no perception.
For this inference is not [valid] anywhere without an example; however, if it is accepted that the state of being a logical mark (*liṅgatā*) occurs even when the relationship is unperceived.

The capacity of all speech (*sarva-vākya*) would exist merely by virtue of being devoid of [actual] utterance (*uccāraṇa-rahitatvena*), and it is not distinguished from that [capacity] by anything else (*na viśiṣyate tad-anyataḥ*).
That cow which has been compared (*upamitā gauḥ*) is understood (*pratīyate*) through the power (*sāmarthyena*) produced by the force of the comparison (*sambhūta-bala-upamā*).

Thus, [the word's] denotative capacity would not be established otherwise than by understanding its expressive power through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since there is no other way to ascertain it. Indeed, without the permanence of the word, that which is impermanent cannot possess the continuity required for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra-saṅketa*).
The establishment of the absence of Caitra by means of the valid cognition of his determined absence outside the house—qualified [as being] from the house—is that which has been described here.

One might state that other [form of] presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from non-existence (*abhāva*) is also distinct from inference (*anumāna*), because it lacks the members [of an inference] such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

For how could non-existence in the house—which is the object of cognition (*prameya*) and the property of the subject—be [present] in a specific object, either in an external location or in a location qualified by that [non-existence]?

The property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is postulated here as the absence [of Devadatta] in the house while he is alive; yet, no cognition of that [absence] arises for one who has not perceived his existence outside. That pure absence in the house which is devoid of [perceived] existence outside is not a prover, even in the case of those who are dead, because it occurs [there too].
There is no power whatsoever that could be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), for [the object] is indeed perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*).
Fire and so forth are observed to be the cause of burning and other such effects; therefore, what power could there be that is distinct [from them], which is non-erroneous and free from doubt?

If [the capacity] were distinct [from the entity], then its existence in effects would result from utility alone; thus it would be a non-agent even when there is utility, and it would not be differentiated.

The essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), namely, the capacity (*śakti*) for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); and thus this entity (*bhāva*) is determined (*vyavasīyate*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for the establishment of another characteristic; even if it were known, there would be no purpose served by it, because its effect is established through its own nature.

If there were another characteristic, accessible through the power of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the effect, [it would not be necessary], because the effect exists even otherwise; for this [fire] exists in its actual state as fire, distinct from water and so forth, since it is capable of burning from the very beginning. What, then, would be the purpose of another capacity?

If power (*śakti*) is not absolutely distinct [from the entity], then it would be identical with both; yet even that [identity] could not exist because of contradiction, since there is also non-difference from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Permanence being established as a matter of direct perception, the denial of its status as an object of inference does not cause any harm; for it is precisely because [permanence] is not accepted as being inferred in this regard that [the objection] is not desired.

Those [entities] beginning with *tu* which are the states (*bhāva*) of the hearer and which are not within the range (*agocara*) of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), their very existence (*sattā*) is understood through an inferential mark (*liṅga*) characterized by capacity (*śakti*).

That perception of sound is dependent upon other causes; for even when that [sound] exists, there is an absence [of the perception] due to the absence of something else, just as in the case of a sprout and so forth.

Due to the pervasion of the sun across different locations, the universal (*jāti*) is perceived as if it were continuous, even though it resides in dissimilar substrata (*asamānopādāna*), just like a flame or similar phenomena.

Because of its specific nature (*viśeṣatvāt*), this attainment of a different location (*antaradeśaprāptiḥ*) by the self (*ātmanaḥ*)—which is stable (*sthira*)—does not follow as a logical consequence (*na prasajyate*). However, otherwise (*anyathā*), [the self's] capacity (*śaktiḥ*) is refuted (*nirākṛtā*).

There is no certainty (*na niścayaḥ*): "The fat man (*pīnaḥ*) does not eat during the day (*divā na bhuṅkte*)," even though a person (*pumān*) might say so (*vadet*) due to [the influence of] hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and so forth (*ādibhiḥ*), in another way (*api anyathā*).

If, however, a meaningful intermediate [phrase] within the sentence is implied by that which is independent of the comprehension of the meaning, then there would be an implication [of it] by that intermediate word.

Now, the comprehension of the object is accepted there in the form of an admission (*upagama*), or rather, the comprehension of the object occurs through the internal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Let it be so; from that, the person is understood as one who possesses the connection with eating at night by virtue of his corpulence, just like another [person] who lacks eating during the day.
Fatness, when food exists, is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance; therefore, there is the cognition of the object from that which is essentially related to it.
For how could a sentence be understood as being devoid of all connection? Otherwise, everything would be understood from a single word alone.

If there were no such connection (*asati sambandhe*) and [that connection] were not ascertained (*an-avadhārite*), then this sentence (*idaṃ vākyam*), even while being understood (*gamyamānam*), would result in being without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇakam*).

If [you argue that it is so] by the king’s command (*nṛpājñayā*), how could that which is connected (*sambaddhasya*) possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatvam*), or how could perception (*pratyakṣasya*) possess the status of a means of valid cognition without a coherent connection (*vinā saṅgatim*)?

[Objection: If [an object] were cognizable despite being unconnected, what would be our understanding of another [object] as well? For even in the case of emptiness, no distinction whatsoever is observed in direct perception (*adhyakṣa*).

Furthermore, validity (*mānatva*) is established solely through connection; for validity consists in correspondence (*saṃvāda*), and that [correspondence] arises from the attainment of the object itself.
That [conformity] is not logically tenable by necessity, because it lacks that cause and because it is without a cause; otherwise, there would be conformity for all [cognitions].

Or rather, the intention (*vivakṣā*) appearing in the second sentence is inferred; and by this, the understanding of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is considered to be derived from the positive sentence (*anvaya-vākya*).
When the validity of analogy has been refuted at length, the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from that [analogy] is likewise precluded.

However, the cow is accepted as the objective support (*ālambana*) of the means of knowledge that is analogy; and it is held that it is both the object to be apprehended and the producer of its own cognition by its very existence.

In this case, what need is there for another capacity for the sake of comprehension, such that one must resort to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as the basis for the validity of analogy (*upamāna*)?

Even in the absence of non-difference [from other means of knowledge], the communication of the meaning of words is not contradicted, just as the cause of trembling in the hand and so forth [is not contradicted by its non-difference from other causes].

Because they are the cause [of it], the capacity of words to convey [an object] is not at all contradicted, just as the uniform reflective awareness [of them] is. Just as trembling [is the effect of a wind], so too [the capacity to convey] is not obstructed.

Now, as for those actions which are seen (*dṛśyante*) occurring in perceptible substances (*pratyakṣa-dravya-vartinīḥ*), their eternality (*nityatvam*) is indeed desired (*iṣṭam*), just as [the eternality] of phonemes (*varṇa-vat*) is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñayā*).
Since these [sounds] are not perceived due to the absence of a continuous stream [of them], that which would be the producer for you must itself be considered the manifestor.
If that capacity were unimpeded, then that cognition would exist continuously; however, in its absence, it would never occur at all.

Furthermore, the manifestors of those [sounds] are logically consistent; however, recognition regarding their permanence has already been refuted previously. Furthermore, the manifestors of those [sounds] are logically consistent; however, the reasons for their permanence have already been refuted previously.

The existence of Caitra outside [the house] is not logically tenable, because of his absence from the house; for it is only through the suspicion of death that [his existence] elsewhere is established.
Even if there were an absence of the living man from the house, this would not lead to the establishment of his existence outside, because even in that case, there is no certainty.
For one who perceives only what is near (*arvāk-darśin*), not seeing Caitra in his house, there exists no valid cognition whatsoever, even regarding the connection with his being alive.

Now, when there is certainty regarding his being alive through sound and so forth, and when his absence from the house is ascertained, this [inference] possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) because of that absence.

Even then, the fact of being unconnected with the house is ascertained through the non-perception of what is perceptible; therefore, in that case, its existence outside is determined solely by means of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
That man, unmingled with his dwelling, exists certainly as if outside; he is seen by those standing at the door, like a person situated in the courtyard of a house.

A person who has entered the house exists; even though he is an absent one (*vipakṣa*) here, nevertheless, therefore, this presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not distinct from inference (*anumāna*). Regarding the nature of the real entity (*vastu-rūpa*), the pentad of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-pañcaka*) does not arise for the purpose of cognizing the existence of the entity; in that case, there is the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*abhāva-pramāṇatā*).

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is accepted as the non-arising (*anutpatti*) of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This [non-arising] is either the non-modification (*apariṇāma*) of the self (*ātman*) or the cognition (*vijñāna*) of another object (*vastu*). Furthermore, the non-existence of objects (*vastu*) is cognized through the absence (*abhāva*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramā*). And this [non-existence] is divided into four types according to its distinctions, beginning with prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*).

That which exists as curds and so forth is not milk; that is designated as prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*). There is no existence of milk in the curd; this is the definition of destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
The non-existence of horses and so forth that is said to exist in a cow—that non-existence does not possess another form; therefore, its non-existence exists by way of its own nature.
The parts [of the head], being devoid of hardness, are like the horns of a hare in their form; that [non-existence] is held to be absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

And if non-existence were not found through the distinction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding causes and the like would not exist in its various divisions.
And these distinctions could not belong to a non-entity; therefore, its substantiality is that which is the existence of effects and so forth through causes and so forth.

Or rather, let the object itself be understood as being like a cow or similar things, because it is apprehended through both the cognitions of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anuvṛtti*), and because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatvāt*).

If [it is argued that] non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a means of valid cognition (*māna*), then what kind of object of cognition (*prameya*) would it be? In this regard, just as non-existence is the object of cognition (*meya*), let it also be accepted that non-existence is a means of valid cognition (*māna*).

For non-existence (*abhāva*) is not differentiated from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is expressible by words such as "non-perception" (*apratyakṣa*) and so forth, just like [the term] "non-existence.

Or else, non-existence is measured (*mīyate*) by a means of valid cognition through its own form, because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), just like existence (*bhāva*). Therefore, it is not distinct in nature from existence.

In this regard, the transformation of an eternally existent entity has been refuted; its existence as the opposite [of that] cannot be logically justified as being occasional. If, however, the intended self is what is meant here, then, given its existence, its substantiality would have to be perceived at all times, because it is never subject to cessation.

Let it be that there is no transformation of this [consciousness]; nevertheless, there is deviation from the object because [the consciousness] exists even during states such as sleep and fainting, provided that [the object] is absent.
If this [consciousness] of his is held to exist when other objects such as a jar are present, because [it is observed to be] distinct from them.
Then, what distinction is stated for this [subject] from the second position—that pair of positions which was indicated by you through an alternative?
If there were doubt regarding the non-existence of another object when consciousness is occurring toward it, then the non-existence of everything—even that which is invisible—would be understood.
The non-existence (*nāstitā*) of that other thing, which is distinct from consciousness, occurs when there is the presence of suitable and equivalent causes for it;

if it were perceived in such a state, then this very non-existence would be a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), appearing as the observation of the object to be grasped, and would not be fallible with respect to other things.

How, moreover, is it known that consciousness (*vijñāna*) has arisen with respect to another object (*vastu*), by which [fact] cognition (*buddhi*) is considered to be non-perceptual (*apratyakṣa*)? If [it is known] through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), then since that [presumptive testimony] is likewise of the nature of cognition (*jñānātmikā*), from what [source] is its own apprehension obtained? [If it were] through another presumptive testimony, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.

If non-existence (*abhāva*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramā*), and non-existence is the object of cognition (*meyavastu*), then that being so, how is it that for you non-existence is not included within perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
For that which is the existence of effects (*kārya*) and so forth, by way of the cause (*kāraṇa*) and so forth—that very self, being distinct from others, is apprehended by perception alone.
In an entity that is eternal, consisting of both its own nature and the absence of other natures, some form is known by some at some time;

and when a portion of existence is grasped through perception and so forth, there is an entry into the portion of non-existence, which is the function of the non-arising [of that form], and thus it is desired to be grasped.
Such is the nature of things that is accepted as being excluded [from others]; by that very essence it is existent, and by this same essence it is perceived directly.

That which is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is called "existent" (*sat*), while the other is "non-existent" (*asat*); moreover, the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of these two in a single locus is not tenable, due to their mutual contradiction (*virodha*).

[Objection: If that which is capable with respect to its own [corresponding] probandum is incapable with respect to this [other one], then indeed this dual nature does not exist at all in a single entity.

But if it is maintained that [the thing] is indeed other [than the cognition], and thus incapable [of being known] by another [cognition], then two entities would be obtained; therefore, that double nature does not belong to a single [thing].
If non-existence is accepted as a real entity (*vastutva*) existing previously, for what purpose is its formlessness (*nīrūpatā*) described?

For if there is the loss of the form of the object of cognition (*prameya*), which is itself formless, it is not tenable that it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*); for that [status] is defined by the awareness (*saṃvitti*) [of an object].

If it is said that [non-existence] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it possesses the nature of being a cause (*hetutva*), like the eye and so forth—[we reply: for that which is formless (*nīrūpa*), there is never any possibility of being a cause. Moreover, since [non-existence] is devoid of both form and cognition, how can that non-existence be apprehended? Thus, because there is no object of cognition (*pramā-gocara*), there would consequently be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*).

If it were understood that [non-existence] arises from the absence of a thing (*vastv-abhāvāt*), then non-existence (*nāstitā*) would arise from the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-abhāvāt*), resulting in mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśraya*).
Therefore, that very vision which belongs to one [person] is said to be non-vision for another; moreover, it is established as independent by virtue of its own nature, because it is not insentient.

The establishment [of the object] does not occur in any way from something other than cognition, either because there is no mark (*aliṅga*), or because it is impossible for anything else, or else, if such an establishment were possible, there would be many endless and spreading chains of questions regarding each of the three. Thus it stands here.
Therefore, because the self is perceived through a cognition that is equally capable [of perceiving it], the non-existence of others is ascertained with respect to one [individual].
In the cognition of what single [object] is the sky understood as being without the moon? And how is the distinction from all sounds ever determined anywhere?
One considers that very thing to be the light and the darkness of the aggregate; for there is no existence nor even perception of the sky as something distinct from it.

Even when all sounds are absent, [non-existence] is perceived because of the non-perception of its effect; and that [non-existence] is established ultimately through self-awareness (*svavedana*) distinct from other cognitions.

Thus, since the non-existence of the self as a means of valid cognition (*pramā*) is established, the denotability of the word "non-existence" remains uncontradicted even when it is included within [the category of] internal [cognition].

(Regarding Text 1659) (non-existence) is cognized (*mīyate*) by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇena*) that conforms to itself (*sva-anurūpeṇa*); thus, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhyatvam*) here, because of such conformity (*anurūpatā*).

"When this exists" (*asmin sati*), "this does not exist" (*na bhavati*); and when "this does not exist" (*asati*), "this does not exist"—therefore, for this very reason, this is called the "logical principle" (*yukti*).
The sage Caraka said: "This very thing is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is not inference (*anumāna*), because no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) can be found."
When an object is known through its apprehension, the non-existence of that [object] is understood from the absence [of such apprehension]; this is considered to be its non-apprehension.

This [feminine nominative singular] also, because it does not depend on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and so forth, establishes non-existence (*nāstitva*) even in the case of an example by this very [means].
The practice [of the means] is not restricted by the state of being the cause or the effect, because in this case there exists no distinction between the two means and the goal to be accomplished.

Apart from the cultivated state of cause and effect (*hetu-phalatā*), no other non-existence (*nāstitā*) is perceived, once that very state has been abandoned, except for the non-perception of the visible.

In the case of the application of the fitness for proof, there exists an illustration (*nidarśana*) in common usage: when an object has been cognized at the time of its convention (*saṃketa-kāle*), the constituent parts (*samudāyinaḥ*) are the causes for establishing the cognition of the whole (*samudāya-vyavasthāyāḥ*), which arises from hundreds and thousands [of such instances] and is produced from a mark that is an effect (*liṅga-kārya-jam*).

The fallibility of tradition, intuition, and the like is for the most part established; their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is not tenable due to such over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, this effort is made quite out of place, since [valid cognition] is strictly established as being of two kinds: direct (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect (*parokṣa*).
That other [cause] is certainly not tenable as the self of both [action and non-action], for action and non-action are mutually contradictory in a single entity.

For an object is said to be directly perceived when it is the producer of cognition; however, that which is the opposite of what has been thus described is considered by the wise to be imperceptible (*parokṣa*).

Now, this [cognition] consisting of verbal testimony, analogy, and so forth, does not have the initial object as its domain because it occurs after [the object] has been apprehended by perception; or else, it would be as futile as memory.
Even if it were to have the imperceptible as its domain, how could it be the object of all [people], if this [object] were not directly perceived as being like an imperceptible thing?

By means of reliance on another (*paravyapāśrayeṇa*), what is that [cognition] connected to this [object] (*asya*), or otherwise (*itarataḥ*)? Is it not so that there is no appearance of difference (*bhedābhāsā*)?

If [the universal] were to arise from that which is unconnected [to it], then a lack of systematic determination would follow; moreover, if the appearance of differentiation were to exist, pervasion would not be logically consistent.
[That] cognition which has as its basis objects that are beyond the senses, which is connected with an object, which does not grasp [the object's] particularity, and which is clear—that is inference.

Now, if an entity possesses a manifold nature, just like a *mecaka* gem, then what contradiction is there in the fact that existence (*sat*) and so forth are [inherently] present by their very nature?

If an entity that is not equal [to others] is not distinguished from the absence of another entity by means of a sky-flower, then it cannot be established as distinct from them, being devoid of the state of inequality.

For if there is absolute dissimilarity with that which is intended, then, in the absence of a real entity (*vastu*), the status of being a real entity (*vastutva*) is necessarily lost; for when a real entity has ceased to exist, what other possible state (*gati*) can be observed for it, apart from non-existence (*nāstitā*)?

Therefore, by one who desires [to establish] that object, its non-equivalence to a sky-flower must be accepted; for "being an entity" (vastutva) is the commonality (sāmānya), that is, the similarity (samānatā) with it.
"What has been done?"—this cognition does not occur with respect to the teeth of the crow and so forth; rather, it is restricted solely to [real] entities.
If this restriction [is based] on similarity, then that alone is our "universal" (*sāmānya*); by this very [restriction], the capacity (*śakti*) of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been described.
Therefore, absolute difference is not at all tenable for anything; for everything is not divided from one another by way of the nature of a real entity.
If that entity were devoid of dissimilarity from the things delimited [as its limit], it would not be distinct from them, just like their own nature.

It is stated that dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of things], which is distinct from those [individuals]. This is not so; for dissimilarity and mutual difference are mutually contradictory.

Therefore, by one who accepts [the existence of objects], some degree of difference among objects must be accepted; for this very reason, even their nature as particulars (*viśeṣa*) is desired to be the very essence of this entity, which is admitted to possess multiple forms. And you maintain that these [objects] exist as the apprehended (*grāhya*) by cognitions of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
These [entities] are called "universals" because they are inclusive; however, others are designated as "particulars" because they are exclusive.

If the universal and the particular were of the same nature (*svabhāvatva*), there would be a mutual confusion (*paraspara-sāṅkarya*). This [confusion] is not logically tenable (*na... upapadyate*) from the standpoint of reality (*vastutas*), for even if they possess two forms (*dvairūpya*), it is not established.
Furthermore, if these two were of different natures (*asvabhāvatva*), their distinctness (*nānātva*) would also exist; yet even in that case, such a dual form is not logically tenable.

Even if there were a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāvatva*) here, a distinction of properties (*dharmabheda*) would be established, as would the non-contradiction of that distinction with the configuration (*saṃsthāna*). This is just as [there is no contradiction] among the potencies (*śakti*) of causal factors (*kāraka*). Furthermore, nothing that is logically untenable is observed even when the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) possess a single essence (*aikātmya*), provided that the maintenance of worldly affairs (*lokayātrā*) proceeds through their distinction.

[Objection: If there is a single form (*ekarūpatva*), difference (*bheda*) is not established; for it is the non-conceptualized distinction (*vibheda*) that is designated as "manifoldness" (*nānātva*). Furthermore, the manifold nature of the powers (*śakti*) is merely constructed (*nirmita*) by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). Indeed, even in this case, if there is a single essence (*ekatattva*), difference is not logically tenable.

That which is called "one" is that which is sung as being "thus"; however, that which is called "name" is manifold in nature. Furthermore, that [oneness] becomes neither its own state nor the state of another, because of mutual contradiction; indeed, it cannot be conceived within a single entity.
Affirmation and negation, which are mutually contradictory, cannot be performed by anyone with a healthy mind in a single place.

From that [entity], which is manifold in its similar and dissimilar [aspects], there is described a distinction of properties; thus, even for a single entity, an imagined state of having innumerable forms is logical. However, a real duality of form in a single thing is not tenable.
Even for those such as Narasiṃha and others who have been described as having a dual nature, that real dual form does not exist at all;
for that nature consists of a combination of many atoms, and whatever is variegated cannot be one, just like a collection of various kinds of jewels.

If [the atoms] were identical, there would be no manifestation of various forms, because they would possess a dual nature; and furthermore, when a fly’s eye is covered, there would be no non-obstruction [of other light rays], since those atoms are by their very nature the causes for the recognition of a continuous whole, as arises from the cognition of a "Man-Lion" (nṛsiṃha) [which is a unified complex].
By this very same method, variegated jewels and the like—which possess manifold diversity through their various natures—are indeed contradicted by [the doctrine of] oneness.
If its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—which is designated as its "reality"—is pervasive throughout it, then everything would be produced by that single entity.
Since it is capable of producing all effects by virtue of its connection with that capacity, and since that capacity is no different in other [entities], how could it not be a producer?

If only blue and so forth are accepted as the persisting entity (*anugāmi-vastutva*), then even white and yellow would necessarily be established as effects produced by blue; consequently, the entire universe would become a single reality devoid of a second nature. Therefore, for us, there exists no single entity that possesses multiple forms.

That very thing would not possess substantiality, just like the existence (*sattva*) as conceived by the followers of Kaṇāda (*Kaṇāśin*). Furthermore, for you, there could not be a multiplicity of forms in a single entity due to its distinct divisions;

moreover, the characteristic of the difference between things is the association with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṅga*), and otherwise, a distinction between blue and yellow could not be established in any way whatsoever.
That [universal] exists because of the presence of both the universal and the particulars; otherwise, how could it exist? For it is not clearly manifest in those two particulars.
Just as there is a restriction of a variegated color (*kalmāṣavarṇa*) to its specific color, and just as [a thing] is perceived according to one's desire due to its manifold nature (*citratva*),

so too, when a thing (*vastu*) that is variegated (*śabala*) is apprehended simultaneously (*yugapat*), then all distinctions (*bheda*)— whether of difference (*anya*) or non-difference (*ananya*), and so forth— are dissolved (*pralīyate*).

Of an object (*vastu*) that possesses multiple forms (*aneka-rūpa*), it is intended (*iṣṭa*) by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) through two modes of operation (*vṛtti*), either sequentially (*krama*) or simultaneously (*yugapad*). There is no other way for words (*vacas*) [to function].

For in this manner, multiplicity (*citratva*) is not precluded; indeed, unity (*ekatva*) has just been refuted. Thus, manifoldness (*vaicitrya*) consists of multiple forms (*aneka-rūpa*) that cannot coexist with unity (*ekatva*).
Whatever future forms there are that have arisen in relation to that object, there are just as many objects; thus, there is no identity.
If there were otherness [from] a single entity, it would be deficient in identity; it would not resemble a sky-flower, for even that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
A single form that is capable [of producing effects] does not exist in other things, because of the difference in their effects, appearances, perceptions, and so forth; thus it has been described.

The state of being that [nature] (ātmatva) is not logically joined with the thing (vastu) through non-adherence (aśleṣa). Therefore, it is not a real thing (bhāva) by its own nature (*bhāvataḥ*). In the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the non-substantiality (*avastutva*) of the thing characterized by its specific definition (*lakṣaṇa-vastu*) is indistinguishable [from the absence of causal efficiency].

Thus, even that [conceptual object] is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-yogya*); therefore, it is a real thing (*vastu*). Its similarity consists in the exclusion (*parāvṛtti*) of what is incapable [of such action].

Moreover, even if there is absolute difference, conceptual similarity exists; therefore, that entity is distinguished from other entities as being equal [to them], yet it is distinguished from a sky-flower.
[Objection: If a thing is excluded from another similar thing by a certain nature, then it must be similar to its own kind by that very same [nature].
Then it would be cognized as being indistinguishable even from heterogeneous things due to the identity of that self; yet it is not cognized in that way.
Therefore, that by which it becomes dissimilar to its own kind and similar to itself—that is the difference between the two natures.
By that [reason], this very thing is understood as being the same by virtue of its causality for a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*), despite the difference from others;

for indeed, certain causes, due to the restriction of their form and capacity, produce a single unifying cognition even when there is a difference—just like the sense organs (*akṣa*) or *amṛtā* and so forth.
[Objection: How can it be maintained that the eye is the producer of a cognition of blue and so forth, if it is held to be characterized solely by its exclusion from blue and the like?

Just as the ear, though possessing distinctions such as [the cognition of] blue and so forth, is not the producer of that [cognition], because it is distinct from the producer of the cognition of blue and so forth; in the same way, let the eye also be accepted [as not being the producer].
For what other entity could there be that is excluded from the producer [of the cognition]? Therefore, there is the certainty that there is also a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among things.
Otherwise, because there would be no distinction, why would even the hearing of the first word not be accepted as a producer of that [cognition], just like the eye and visible form?
This exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the eye and so forth from their producer is not established without distinction; for even that [exclusion] is considered to be their very nature (*ātman*).

The exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of entities (*bhāvānām*) from their own-nature (*svabhāvāt*) is not tenable; for, if there were exclusion from own-nature, it would follow that they are devoid of own-nature (*naiḥsvābhāvyam*).
The exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from other [things] is described as that which is produced by another producer; its lack of the nature of that producer is precisely what is accepted by us.
For it is not the case that the producer is described as such solely by its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*); rather, all those [things] arise determined by their own respective causes.
But if these [causes] are the producers of a single [effect] because they follow from a single nature, then that nature exists even in a single [cause]; so what is the use of other auxiliary causes?

[Objection: If, due to deficiency (*vaikalpyāt*), some [causes] are not producers of another [effect] because they lack specific differences (*antara-viśeṣa*), then—whether there is difference (*bheda*) or non-difference (*abheda*)—how could they be deficient?

Just as even when there is a specific difference, everything is not the cause of everything, so too, even in the absence of difference, there would be a restriction (*niyama*) regarding diversity (*nānātvasya*).

Even if there were some distinction [between them], by virtue of its own nature (*svabhāva-niyamāt*), one would be the producer; but in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), how could one single thing be both the producer and the non-producer of the same [effect]?

If it is argued that there is a distinction here as well, let it be so; for what is this distinction other than the positive concomitance? Indeed, it is not something else. Is it not the case that [the distinction] is not the causal agent?
That alone is the real entity which is indeed capable of causal efficiency; and that [entity] does not persist through succession. Therefore, that which persists does not produce an effect.
Difference and non-difference exist indeed as unconstructed (*akalpita*) modes of understanding, with reference to that very self (*ātman*), intending which this person proceeds.

For otherwise, there would be both identity through its own nature and difference through exclusion; thus, the entity itself would exist [only as distinct], and it would not persist [throughout]. Consequently, what excellence indeed has been proclaimed by the Brahmins, the Nirgranthas, and the Kāpilas regarding the conceptual construction of the diversity of activities that has been described?
When a rucaka is made by the breaking of a vardhamānaka, there is grief for the one who desires the former, and joy for the one who desires the latter.
Therefore, for one who desires gold, neutrality toward that object—which consists of three aspects—would not exist in the absence of arising, persistence, and destruction.

There is no sorrow without destruction, no happiness without arising, and no equanimity without stability; therefore, [the claim that] there is a universal eternity is also not logical for us, because arising, stability, and destruction do not have a single common substratum.
But when there is momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*), all this [following] is unconfused, provided that simultaneous mutual contradiction among [things] exists.
For how could sorrow arise for anyone regarding the destruction of a *vardhamānaka* ornament when there is no continuity (*an-anvaya*) of the gold substance?
In every respect, joy arises at the birth of the former form of the necklace; however, there is no persistence whatsoever of that very self [of the necklace].
When one of deluded intellect perceives two entities consisting of gold, then he conceives of their permanence as being identical with another entity.

If gold (*hemnaḥ*, genitive singular) were established in its nature (*rūpatve*, locative singular), then that very nature (*tat rūpam*, nominative singular) would be perceived (*dṛśyeta*, third person singular present optative passive of *dṛś*) even in the initial state (*ādi*) of the necklace (*rucaka*), and so forth, throughout all prior and subsequent states (*pūrvottarāvasthāsu*, locative plural); otherwise (*anyathā*), there would be a lack of unity (*anekatā*, nominative singular).

By virtue of its persistence (*anugama*), some Buddhists consider that gold possesses stability; even they admit that an entity (*bhāva*) can possess distinctions (*bhedavān*) according to its various states (*avasthā*).
Just as gold does not abandon its color even when in a state of transformation, so too this entity does not relinquish its substantiality throughout the [three] time periods.
Otherwise, cognition would exist without an object in relation to the past and the unborn; how could it have been stated by the Tāyin that consciousness has a dual basis?
And how is it maintained that past karma, being devoid of a sentient being, yields its fruit? Furthermore, how is the distinct knowledge of yogins regarding the past and the future possible?

Therefore, the past and future are not objects [of cognition] by way of the exclusion (*apoha*) of the nature of substance (*dravya-rūpa*), because they are included within the classification of time (*adhva-vibhāga*), just like the present.
And here, it should not be thought thus: "How can there be a distinction of time-periods (*adhvan*), since this division of the time-periods is merely conceptualized by means of activity (*kāritra*)?
For when it exists in activity, it is called 'present'; when fallen away from activity, it is 'past'; but when that [activity] has not yet been attained, it is 'future'."

The causal efficacy (*kāritva*) of phenomena (*dharma*) is the projection (*ākṣepa*) of the fruit, but it is neither that which produces (*janaka*) nor does it exist; there is no projection of past things, nor is there the possibility of causal efficacy.
They must accept this activity as either distinct from the dharma or identical to its nature; there is no other real possibility whatsoever.

If [the action] were distinct [from the entity], then just as the lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*) regarding causes, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtatva*), and so forth, would have to be understood as existing previously and subsequently, so too would it be for the activity (*kāritra*).
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of permanence due to the persistence of its intrinsic nature; for apart from this form, no characteristic of permanence exists.

The causality of that which is eternal has been previously refuted on account of contradiction with both succession and non-succession; for, if there were eternality, the state of being conditioned would clearly be without foundation. Furthermore, in describing an activity that is distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, an unavoidable contradiction with one's own tenets (*svasiddhānta*) results.
If activity were non-different from the dharma, it would follow—due to its non-separation from the dharma—that it, like the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the dharma, would be present at all times.

Consequently, this distinction of time-periods (*adhvan*) cannot be established by virtue of that [activity], for, due to the distinction [of activity], there would be either the falling away (*cyuti*), the attainment (*prāpti*), or the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) of it;
or else, because it is not distinct from the activity (*kāritra*), the dharma—just like the activity itself—would be devoid of prior and posterior states and would consist of nothing but the middle.
The activity exists, and the dharma is described as being always present; yet the activity is never other than the dharma—this is clearly the conduct of a god.
If, even in that case, the persistence [of the dharma] depends upon another activity belonging to a different time-period, then surely this same objection applies everywhere.

Furthermore, if a distinction distinct from its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is observed—just as in the case of resistance (*sapratighatva*)—and if this [distinction] does not at all assist the subject under discussion, then [your argument fails].
Resistance and so forth are not considered to be any occasional property of a persisting entity (*padārtha*), because such an entity arises only as it does;
likewise, that very existence, when not implied by its distinction from others, is expressed by the word "form" (*rūpa*). Furthermore, there is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the mind.

Now, the activity (*kāritra*) is described as being inexpressible (*avācya*) by way of the two modes—identity (*tattva*) and difference (*anyatva*)—just like the continuum (*saṃtāna*) and so forth; [if this were the case], would it not then follow that it is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*)?

Therefore, like [something] that is imagined (*kalpita*), that continuity (*santati*) is not applicable (*upayujyate*) to any effect whatsoever; because only a real entity (*vastu*) is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), its presence (*sannidhāna*)—established as being real (*tāttvika*) across the three times (*try-adhva*)—is not tenable.

That which is called "activity" (*kāritra*)—which is a power (*śakti*) whose scope consists in the projection of a fruit (*phalākṣepa*)—and which is indeed the very power of the word (*śabda*), since it is a real entity (*vastutva*), how could it be merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*)?
If that very form which is admitted as the agent of burning, cooking, and so forth, is accepted as being in a past or future state,
then how indeed can there be the occurrence or the cessation of activity for that [agent], while it exists with a single identity?
How indeed can these mutually contradictory categories be consistent with respect to this single, undifferentiated entity?

If it is assumed that this entity is not at all distinct across the time-periods (*adhvan*) because of the acceptance of a single state upon the abandonment of another, then why indeed do the states differ from the entity itself? [For] there would be no agency.
Since those [dharmas] exist precisely by virtue of being attained (*āptitaḥ*), how can their existence as effects be perceived?
How do they accept the non-difference of a thing across the time-periods (*adhvan*), given that they, while being of its nature, come into being after not having existed and then perish?

In the intermediate state, the agent exists indeed in its own nature; at that time, how could that very same nature [belong] to those two states? If these two possess agency by way of their own form, then how can there be non-agency for this [agent] again by way of another form?
If [the effect] were something other than fire and so forth, existing in a state past or future, then in this position, this fault of confusion and so on would be groundless;
for it is only that which is capable [of being produced] that arises after not having existed, and having existed, does not remain—thus, its lack of continuity is established.

That entity alone is real which is capable of action; therefore, since there is no possibility of an effect arising from those two [past and future entities], a past object would necessarily follow as being present—because it exists after having not existed—just like any other [present thing], and also because it occurs only occasionally.

If there were no cause, there would be either constant existence or non-existence, because of the lack of dependence on anything else. Furthermore, an entity (*sattva*) is said to exist as determined by its specific cause;

this is the view held by others regarding the distinctness of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*, as well as the conditioned nature (*saṃskṛtatva*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, due to their connection with birth, duration, and the rest.

In that case, [they] produce a particularity (*viśeṣa*). What is it that is called "birth" (*jāti*)? It is that which brings about its [the particularity's] production. Furthermore, that [particularity] is not distinct from the form (*rūpa*) that has not yet been born;

for an excellence (*atiśaya*) that is non-different from it cannot be produced, because [if it were already existent], it would be impossible to bring it into being, just as [it is impossible to produce] what exists previously, or like [the production of] a subsequent accomplishment (*niṣpatti*).

There is no other excellence [in it], because there is no distinction and because of its lack of connection; furthermore, since that [excellence] does not exist previously, there would be the consequence of it being a non-existent effect.

Moreover, if there were otherwise [i.e., a change in state], then while it remains, these faults—old age and so forth—which follow from the two alternatives of "otherness" and "non-otherness," would apply.
These [entities], beginning with birth (jāti), which initiate their own effects by way of their own nature, possess the capacity for restriction; and that form exists both before and after.

Since they possess the capacity for that form, why do they not then begin the action corresponding to their own [nature], especially given that its commencement occurs throughout the immeasurable time of the three periods?
Furthermore, would the entities such as the past and so forth be momentary or not? If they are the first [i.e., momentary], then that very same [momentariness] applies to them;
for that moment which is being born, which exists, and which is present—that entity which, having arisen, has perished, is the past; and that which has not yet come is the future.

Even if they were non-momentary, that established doctrine would be contradicted; for in our system, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have been demonstrated to be momentary. Even if [you argue] that existing things are subject to momentary destruction just like those currently occurring, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in this case has already been established previously.

These [things], past and future, would either be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or not; for if they possessed the capacity [for such efficiency], they would exist like other [present things] of that [same] kind.
However, being destroyed and unborn, they follow as being devoid of all powers, like a sky-lotus and so forth, due to their non-existence in the present.
The ether and all other [elements], being uncreated, are subject to the same line of questioning as you; furthermore, they do not escape the charge of inconclusiveness regarding their postulation.
For the capacity of entities to perform causal functions arises from conditions; if there were no cause, everything would be equally applicable to everything.

That which is produced by birth, fixed capacity, and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and which exists through conditions (*pratyaya*), is the sole characteristic of a present entity (*bhāva*); there is no other.
And for you, since it is unimpaired in past and future entities as well, why does that state of being present (*vartamānatva*) not follow after them? It would indeed follow.

Therefore, this effort toward association with heaven and liberation is fruitless; for here, no result whatsoever is perceived as being accomplished by such exertion. Moreover, if their capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is not admitted, then for that very reason they lack existence, just like a flower in the sky.

The reasons (hetavaḥ), which are properties (dharmāḥ) of existence (bhāva-), do not possess (na bhāginaḥ) the establishment (siddhi-) [of the probandum] when [existence] is unestablished (asiddhe); or else, they are contradictory (viruddhāḥ) because of the sublation (bādhanāt) [of the subject] by the establishment (siddheḥ) of its being present (vartamānatva-).
That form which, having existed, has ceased and is manifested as past—that, when the totality of conditions is present, is that which is to be and is future.

If [it] were attached to an existent entity (*sattve*), then "presentness" (*vartamānatvam*) would be established as nothing more than "existingness" (*vidyamānatva-mātra*); for that is indeed the definition (*lakṣaṇam*) of the present (*vartamānasya*).

The state [of being] characterized by form and so forth (*rūpāditva*) is described as past (*atīta*) through the superimposition (*adhyāropya*) of that very state—whether it has already come to be (*bhūtā*) or is yet to be (*bhāvinī*)—upon that [form] and so forth; however, it does not exist in reality (*bhāvataḥ*).

That teaching which was intended by the Seer of Reality (*tattvadarśin*), based upon the cognition of the duality [of subject and object], was taught with a specific intention (*abhisandhāya*) directed toward the mind together with its objects;
for there exists no objective support (*ālambana*) for cognitions such as those of "eternity" or "the Lord" (*īśvara*), because they are devoid of the forms (*ākāra*) of those words and names.
It is said that consciousness is so called merely by virtue of its conformity with cognition; furthermore, its non-inert nature is postulated on account of its luminosity.

The cause of the fruit, which is maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), is not admitted as past; rather, the fruit is held [to arise] from the continuum of consciousness that has been perfumed (*vāsita*). Taking that very perfuming (*vāsanā*) as the limit, that [fruit] is designated as "there is karma" by way of figurative usage (*bhaktyā*), just like the non-destruction of the root.

Thus has it been revealed by the Teacher for the sake of destroying views of eternalism and nihilism; otherwise, how could the teaching on emptiness in the Sūtras be brought to bear so that yogins may understand that very nature of the present which has entered into the state of cause and effect, either directly or through a succession?
Subsequently, they follow [those things] by means of pure worldly consciousnesses which, in reality, have no [such] objects;
nevertheless, relying upon that past or future continuum of cause and effect, the teachings concerning the past and the future proceed.
The teachings of the Tathāgata proceed effortlessly through the continuum of his omniscient wisdom, which is free from the net of conceptual construction.
If no entity whatsoever exists that persists [through time], then there would be no other world, because of the non-existence of one who goes to another world.
In the destruction of the body, intellect, sense organs, and so forth, which occurs at every moment, it is logical that there is no "other world" (*paraloka*); nor is any other [self] admitted.
Therefore, in that manner, consciousness (*jñāna*) arises or is manifested from specific elements (*bhūta-viśeṣa*), just as fermented acids, wine, and the like [arise] from those [elements].
This [notion] of the body, the sense organs, and so forth is applied (*niveśyate*) to a particular arrangement (*sanniveśa*) of earth and the other [elements]. Indeed, no other reality exists;
nor is there a causal relationship between two cognitions that are the subject of dispute, because they exist as distinct from the body, just like the cognitions of a cow and a horse.

Or rather, the cognitions (*matayaḥ*) intended [by us] are not considered to be produced by consciousness (*vijñāna*), because they possess the nature of cognition (*jñānatvāt*), just like the cognitions (*buddhayaḥ*) connected with another continuum (*anya-santāna*).

Furthermore, the mind at death (*maraṇa-cittam*) accompanied by passion (*sa-rāga*) does not effect a connection (*sandhi*) with a subsequent mind (*antara-citta*) by virtue of being a cognition of death (*maraṇa-jñāna-bhāvena*), just as that [mind] of one who is free from afflictions (*vīta-kleśasya*) [does not].
Therefore, it is logical that knowledge arises from the body itself when it is presided over by prāṇa, apāna, and so forth; this is what was stated by Kambalāśvatara.
To claim that such consciousness exists in the *kalala* and other embryonic stages is a rash assertion, for no object is perceived therein due to the absence of developed sense faculties.
It is not logical that cognition has a form other than the apprehension of the object; nevertheless, its existence is established [as real] even in cases such as fainting.
And at that time, the cognition does not persist in the form of a capacity; for indeed, the persistence of capacities is not possible due to their lack of a substratum.

Since the self is non-existent, the body alone—which serves as the substratum for knowledge—is the support for that [knowledge]; when the body has ceased at its end, what support would the functioning of knowledge have?

If another body is not perceived, how is it understood that there exists a basis for a subsequent body arising immediately after that [previous one]? How could that consciousness, having proceeded from a different body, be connected to a single continuum, like the mind of an elephant, a horse, or other such beings?
Therefore, some substratum of cognition must be accepted as a transmigrating being, without beginning or end, who is a person; otherwise, there would be the extreme of nihilism [in the thought]:
"This other world does not exist, distinct from the continuum of the elements, the cognitions, and so forth, which are the appropriated and the appropriator. This [latter view] is what is found here.

A certain state (*avasthā*) of that [stream of consciousness], which is beginningless and endless, is proclaimed as its fixed limit (*maryādā*). Just as, in this world, those attached to pleasure imagine a "next world" (*paraloka*) based merely on what is seen, so too is it spoken of by us here.

If the other world (*paraloka*), as something distinct from that [present life], is denied, then the means of proof (*sādhana*) are futile, since there is no dispute regarding its non-existence. Now, since the continuum (*saṃtati*) is not a real entity (*avastutva*), the occurrence of another state is impossible; how then can the other world be established therein as real (*tāttvika*)? Or [is it not]?

The members of the continuum (*santānin*) are not manifested by the word [“continuum”] in their totality, because they are conceived as a single entity for the sake of brevity— just like a forest and so forth— and because, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), they are considered indescribable in terms of identity, difference, and so on, just like a row [of trees] or a sky-lotus.
How could that [consciousness] attain success, being beginningless and endless, if this mind were to exist as causeless,
or as arisen from a permanent cause, or as eternally existing by itself, or as having its origin solely in the elements, or as born solely from another cognition?

The primary consciousness (*ādivijñāna*) is not logically tenable at the beginning of the womb (*garbhe*), as it would be without a cause (*ahetu*). Otherwise, its existence (*sattva*) would be merely occasional (*kādācitkatayā*). Furthermore, it is not produced by anything permanent (*nitya*), such as the mind (*manas*), time (*kāla*), space (*diś*), the Lord (*īśa*), or the self (*ātman*) and so forth; for otherwise, it would follow that it must exist eternally (*sadāsattvaprasaṅgāt*), which is contrary to fact.

[This] is a rash [claim], that consciousness is a single entity and possesses an eternal nature, while [its] differentiation is manifest through the observation of the various forms, sounds, and so forth of the minds.

Neither origination (*bhūti*) nor manifestation (*vyakti*) [of cognition] arises from the elements (*bhūta*), such as earth, fire, water, and so forth; for that would entail the simultaneous arising of all cognitions.
Although the four elements are accepted by our opponents as having a stable nature, their dependence upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) has already been refuted.
Now, if it is argued by others (*paraiḥ*) that "this is indeed momentary" (*kṣaṇikam eva*), then, such being the case, why is your own admission (*svopagamaḥ*) not contradicted (*bādhyate*)?

Let it be contradicted; [for] it is accepted (*abhyupagamyate*) that all things (*sarvabhāvaviniścitam*) are determined to be momentary. This is logical (*nyāyyam*) according to all reasonings (*sarvayuktibhyaḥ*).
If, out of partiality for your own position, you maintain a disregard for logic, then this is the ultimate consequence: that entities simply do not exist at all.

For them [the atoms], neither the state of being a whole (*avayavin*) is appropriate, nor is the state of being a form (*rūpatā*) of atoms, because of the impossibility of [the existence of] ultimate atoms; this will be explained later.
Forms external to reality appear in consciousness due to the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as in dreams and the like, and not from anything else.

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are conceptually constructed by relying upon the appearance of consciousness, which is comparable to a dream or an illusion; this [world] is not [ultimately real] at all.

It is not possible for something else to possess the status of being its cause when that [other thing] is absent; [for] a prior cognition, appearing as a manifestation of what has become [past], would have to produce the subsequent one.

If a consciousness belonging to another continuum is accepted as its cause, then what is its material cause (*upādāna*), or is it intended to be its cooperative cause? [If the former,] there would be a persistence (*anugama*) of the specific impressions (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*) derived from hearing and so forth from the parents within the offspring's continuum of cognition.
Since this phenomenon (*dharma*) established by its material cause (*upādāna*) is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) within its own continuum (*sva-santati*),

there would be no contradiction whatsoever in conceiving of another continuum (*antara-santāna*) as arising from the power of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-bala-udbhūta*) acting upon its own material cause (*sva-upādāna*).

Therefore, the initial consciousness (*ādivijñāna*) there arises from its own material causes (*upādānahetubhyaḥ*), just like [the consciousnesses] characterized by consciousnessness (*vijñānatvādivat*) in the present mind (*idānīntanacitte*).

And since the absence of a cause (*ahetutve*) is established, otherwise [if it were causeless], this would not follow as a determinate property (*niyato dharmaḥ*), because of the rejection of any other cause.

Consciousness, which is capable of perishing at every moment, [must] arise with its own appropriated object for one who possesses desire, because it is not devoid of connection [to that object], just like the preceding consciousness.
By what form does it produce a definitively determined consciousness beforehand? Why then does it not maintain that very same undivided causal capacity even afterwards?

The establishment [of the cognition] in the opponent's position is as follows: how can that knowledge [arise] from the body alone? Since the two examples [cited] are already established as possessing the property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*), the fact that the body is the cause has already been refuted previously, because [the cognition] occurs simultaneously with the mind and there is no additional [cause]. Indeed, and furthermore...
