Consciousness, determined by memory, passion, and so forth, cannot be prevented from being cultivated through the application of a virtuous mind;
for, when there is a diminution and an excellence [respectively] of preceding cognitions, there is an increase resulting from the particularity of the practice of cognition.
Because it does not apprehend anything other than its own capacity, cognition’s status as the cause of the knowledge of objects to be known does not incur the charge of being untenable.

Furthermore, the existence of a mental function (*vṛtti*) that extends across distinct bodies is not established; for what kind of function could there be for a mind that does not descend into [multiple] bodies?
If one denies [the existence of] water and so forth, there would be a support for the falling of minds; but for those that have no motion, what purpose would supports serve?

If a function (*vṛtti*) is postulated here by way of figurative construction (*parikalpyate*), [and] its persistence (*sthiti*) is [asserted] through identity (*tādātmyena*), that too is untenable; for, according to your view, cognition (*jñāna*) is not logically tenable as being of the nature of the body (*kāyātmaka*).

If there were identity [of the mind with the body] (nominative singular), why is it that the mind—consisting of passion, hatred, and so forth—is not clearly perceived by others, just as the body is perceived? Even so, it would be [perceived].

The mind (*cetas*) alone is experienced (*vedyate*) by itself (*svena*); however, the body (*deha*) is [experienced] both by oneself (*sva*) and by others (*paraiḥ*). Those two which are thus [distinguished] are differentiated (*vibhidyete*) like the belly and the base of a dancer (*naṭau*).

This reason is not established in the case of non-dual cognition, because one’s own manifestation is perceived—just like [the vision of] one suffering from cataracts and the like—to be perishing immediately upon its arising. If the mind possesses such a nature, why is its momentariness not accepted?

If its occurrence (*vṛtti*) were admitted there (*tatra*) by virtue of its arising (*sambhūti*) based upon that (*tad-āśrayeṇa*), or because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārita*) with respect to it—even so, there would be deviance (*vyabhicāritā*) regarding that which is perishable (*vinaśvare*) moment by moment (*pratikṣaṇa*). For cognition (*jñāna*) in its prior state (*prāg-avastham*) produces (*karoti*) a continuous (*nirantaram*) reconnection (*pratisandhim*) consisting of the bodily functions (*deha-vṛttam*).

If [it is argued that] there is no difference [of continuum] because of the existence of a single continuum, then let there likewise be no difference [of continuum] elsewhere as well, due to the existence of a single continuum.

How then can it be maintained that for one whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*), there is no reconnection (*asandhāna*) of consciousness from the end of one life to another? [This cannot be so], because there is no acceptance of the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the doctrines of others.
In this regard, some wise ones declare that the Jinas—who have attained nirvāṇa through the two vehicles—are established in the finality of those very vehicles.

This example (*dṛṣṭānta*) [cited] against them is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), because even when you resort to your own tenet (*siddhānta*) favored by the opponent, there is no statement of a subverting [reason]; furthermore, since there is the possibility of the existence of heterogeneous instances (*vijātīya*), the exclusion (*vyatireka*) is suspected of being doubtful (*sandigdha*), and thus there is deviation (*vyabhicāritā*).
"It is not a rash assertion" means that consciousness exists even in the *kalala* and other stages, despite the sense faculties being unarisen; why then would there be no cognition in those cases?
[Objection: This entire cognition has arisen from the power of the sense-faculties and their objects; for that [cognition] is experienced otherwise even in dreams and so forth.
Even though another form of this [cognition] is determined by its departure from the object, its existence is nevertheless established even in states such as fainting;
furthermore, since cognition does not then manifest with a form characterized by causal capacity, the establishment of cognitions is held to be by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
Why is it that [there is] no consciousness during states such as sleep and fainting? If [you say] "because," then since there is an absence of feeling, from where has that [consciousness] gone?
If your certainty regarding them proceeds in this manner—"I know the mind"—then, such being the case, the existence of a mind is established.
It might be thought: "If consciousness exists in these states, how could there not be a memory possessing its form for one who has awakened and so forth?"

That [memory] does not arise without a cause to an excessive degree, because of the impossibility of [factors such as] proficiency and so forth, like [the memory of] those born immediately after birth and the like.
If this is so, how is its existence determined? It is understood from these [reasons] due to the previously described cause.
If mind is not admitted to exist during states such as dreaming, fainting, and so forth, then either death would occur, or else mental cognition itself—
being independent because it does not depend on the eyes and other [senses]— would persist by the power of its own material cause (*upādāna*), just as in dreams and similar states.
For indeed, because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) depend upon the existence of sense faculties and their objects— even in the case of [non-existent things] such as a sky-lotus,

where there is an absence of activity regarding those two— any conceptual construction that arises concerning the past and so forth is determined to be equal [to others] by virtue of its coloring by an unreal object (*asadartha*).

Everything has been established in detail; thus, the entity that is form does not appear within conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), because it appears as the referent of words (*śabdārtha*) even during states such as deep sleep and so forth, and because there is no alteration of mental cognition (*manobuddhi*) despite bodily transformation. Therefore, this [mental cognition] has that [form] as its basis.
Even when there is a very slight disorder, such as timira and the like, affecting the eyes and other sense organs, a distorted cognition arises based upon them;
yet, even in the destruction of the body, the mental cognition remains without that [physical] support, proceeding by the power of its own material cause (*upādāna*) without contradiction.
Since our mental cognition (*manobuddhi*) alone is non-contradictory, we are not making an effort for the sake of establishing the existence of something else in another body;
nor is it possible to deny this [existence], because even when it is not perceived, there remains doubt, just as one who has weak vision might fail to perceive a very slight smoke or similar object.

[Textual variant *Baudhabhāratī*: Even though [the self] is pure (*svaccha-*), because it conforms to a different body despite being dependent [upon it], there is a specific [recollection] connected to that; thus, the prior cognition belonging to a single continuum exists like a continuous stream.
Furthermore, among those born at once, there is a desire for drinking and so forth, as well as an aversion toward injury to the breast.
All that—consisting of the drinking of blood, the breasts, and so forth—is understood as being that very self characterized by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

That [self] is possessed of attachment to names; yet no name or form has been practiced in this present life. In the absence of those [names and forms], the annihilation of that [self] would follow in another existence.

That [consciousness] is the future state resulting from the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), and familiarity (*saṃstava*) with names; because it has the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding those [objects], that conceptual construction which arises for them—born from the ripening of latent impressions, repeated practice, familiarity, and names—is what is known as the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*).
For them, [this] proceeds by the power of practice: is it memory, or are the words of eloquent speakers perfectly clear?
For these [words], this occurrence would not exist due to the confusion caused by the lack of maturation, as if by a more powerful impairment during states of derangement (*sannipāta*).
Of those great-souled ones, whose injury is very slight, their words are heard clearly, and their memory is lucid.
These [things], beginning with passion and hatred, being powerful through the application of practice, exist as they are determined by both positive and negative concomitance.
Those future beings, being devoid of any practice performed here [in this life], what cause could there be for their birth, if there were no interval between existences for us?

Arising does not occur due to the proximity of the object; even when that [object] exists, it does not arise because of the absence of its production, and because [the object] is seen to have strength both when analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) is present and when those [discernments] have ceased, as well as due to the increase of error (*viparyāsa*) regarding objects that are destroyed or not yet born.
Passion and the like arise by superimposing qualities such as beauty, ownership, stability, and so forth upon women and other objects; however, those objects do not possess such a nature.

Those residing here exist indeed as having that [object] as their support, by virtue of their capacity, because they possess a similarity to passion and so forth, just as in the case of the subsequent [cognitions] when objects are encountered;
however, those [cognitions] arising from pleasure, pain, and so on are born from the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of a similar kind.

The afflictions (*kleśāḥ*), such as attachment (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*), which are subject to analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) by those who hate [them] and are governed by improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*), do not—according to their respective powers—directly serve as causes for attachment, aversion, and so forth. Only a single affliction would exist for all [of them] in that regard, just as there is cognition (*bodha*) of that [object].
This [state]—whether through the observation of another's conduct or by hearing it from others—is subject to deviation;
for boars, deer, and the like, who have neither seen nor heard of such conduct, undergo transformation upon contact with those of similar disposition.
Qualities such as wisdom, ethical discipline, and compassion—which have not been cultivated in saṃsāra—do not arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), like intoxication and the like;
nor do they arise through the power of phlegm and so forth, like [the qualities] of a previous [life], because deviation is observed in every respect.

Therefore, that [person]—whose future states (*bhāvinaḥ*) are preceded by the practice of whatever [actions] in his first and subsequent existences—is established as such; thus, the non-existence [of the person] is refuted.

When the state of being preceded by practice in this life is the probandum (*sādhye*), there is a sublation (*bādhanam*) [of the reason]; and when the state of being the cause for another existence is intended (*iṣṭa-hetutve*), the example (*nidarśanam*) is empty of the probandum (*sādhya-śūnyam*).

Since there is no contradiction [of the reason] with respect to the probandum (*sādhye*), because the state of being a contradictory reason (*viruddhatā*) is excluded by the fact that the nature of being a reason (*hetutva*)—due to the practice (*abhyāsa*) of another existence (*anya-bhava*)—is established in exactly that same way as the probandum (*sādhyatva*) in a general sense (*sāmānyena*), there is no contradiction of the reason; nor is there any contradiction of this [reason] with that [probandum], such that it would exclude it.
If the fourfold set of elements does not exist apart from cognition, then why does this appear so clearly and distinctly?

Even if such an appearance exists for that [object], and even if your admission of its non-existence is accepted, what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could there be for you regarding the existence of the mind?
What is the nature of the external object appearing? Does it appear as having the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), or does it have the characteristic of being a composite whole (*avayavin*)?
The ultimate form of atoms is not perceived, because there is no perception of multiple partless material entities.
[Textual variant (Baudhabhāratī): (mūrttābha-)]
The ultimate atoms would appear as devoid of parts; otherwise, they could not be objects of direct perception because they do not impart their own form.
Even though they have arisen through association with you, these speakers do not, in their own nature, abandon their partless form throughout those various states.
If their form exists as something that has attained a limit of diminution (*apacaya*), how is it that they would not be formless (*amūrta*), like sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth?

If [it is argued that] there is no delusion regarding permanence because of the arising of another similar [moment], then there would be a delusion of grossness (*sthūla*) due to the unbroken perception (*graha*) of the homogeneous (*sajātīya*).
If perception itself does not produce the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa-vijñāna*) by the power of its own operation, how can those [objects] be the domain (*gocara*) of direct perception?

[Thus: "Entities are determined to be momentary by means of valid cognition; however, how are atoms understood [to exist]? If it is argued that 'white, yellow,' and so forth [are perceived],' [we reply:
the initial visual object is a form consisting of an accumulation, because of its grossness, like a mountain and so forth; this is an inference."

Coarseness (*sthūlatva*) is not established in the two [categories], namely the substratum (*dharmin*) and the whole (*avayavin*). There is no whole that is coarse, nor are atoms (*aṇu*) of such a nature; for [coarseness] is a property (*dharma*) of real entities (*vastu*).

Now, it may be argued that it exists in such a state by virtue of being spread out over space (*deśa-vitāna*); even so, there remains doubt because it appears in that form through a mistaken cognition (*bhrānta-vijñāna*).
Because of its falsity, that [cognition] is not [valid] in that way; for if its distinction [from falsity] is not established, what excellence does it possess over that [falsity]?

If it is said that there is "correspondence" (*saṃvādana*) with the effect, then that correspondence with the effect as it appears in the cognition is possible [only] otherwise, due to the restriction of the causal capacity (*sāmarthya-niyama*).

When atoms possess a dual nature, and when their form is identical [to another], that identical form is perceived; however, when their form is not identical, it is simply not perceived. In that case, why is this not logically consistent?
Because every entity possesses the nature of both the universal and the particular, atoms are of two forms, owing to their having both similar and dissimilar intrinsic natures.
In that case, that identical form which is the object (*gocara*) of sensory cognition (*akṣa-jñāna*), for that very reason, the cognition regarding atoms (*aṇu*) would have a single form.
"That form, which is dissimilar [to others], is held to be the yogin’s direct perception; thus, some of evil intellect imagine it to be confused."
If it were logical for a single entity to possess two forms at that time, then two distinct entities would result, because they would exist by way of mutually exclusive natures.

Furthermore, if there were mutual identity, the possession of two forms would be contradictory; and yet, a distinction [between them] would be perceived by the sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
How could a single form exist by its own nature as mutually contradictory? Because of [the fact of] consciousness, there is no possibility of contradictory things existing in one [place].
Thus, that which may be a single form consisting of a single aspect is not spoken by Īśvara; for it should be understood exactly as it is perceived.

That [distinction] does not exist even for the non-existent, just as in the case of the distinction [perceived] regarding a yellow conch shell; however, there is no other characteristic [of difference] than the association with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*).

Let it be that there is no [cognition] by means of a valid instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); let there be doubt. But how could those who act with discernment (*prekṣāvat*) have certainty regarding their non-existence?
That form which is conjoined, situated in a distant location, established without interval, facing a single atom, and belonging to the atom situated in the middle.
If that very [atom] is conceived as being oriented toward another atom, then an accumulation of mountains and so forth would not be possible; such being the case, it is not tenable.
If it is maintained that there is another form facing toward the intermediate atom, then, that being the case, how could the ultimate atom be a single [unit]?
In this very context, the following reflection has been made: that which is asserted by others to be an atom, devoid of parts, is not impossible, for it is not something undesired.

When they accept that the parts possess the nature of ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), then necessarily follows the consequence (*prasajyate*) of their deviation from their own thesis (*svapratijñā*), because [the argument] serves as a proof by means of an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅgasādhanatvena*). In this case, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) regarding the locus (*āśraya*); for the unity (*aikya*) is indeed refuted by the force of the connection (*yoga*) and so forth with what is accepted by the opponent (*parābhyupeta*).
Thus, in all these positions, that self is not tenable, because it is not established as a unity; nor is it possible for it to possess a manifold nature.
Therefore, for the wise, the ultimate atom is incapable of being ascertained as non-existent by its own nature, because it is empty of being either one or many, like a lotus in the sky;
since the ultimate atom is impossible [in those respects], it is not accepted by others as being composed of ultimate atoms.
Cognition does not cognize an external object—whether it be without appearance (*anirbhāsa*), with appearance (*sanirbhāsa*), or having another appearance (*anyanirbhāsa*)—in any way whatsoever.
Consciousness arises as excluded from insentient forms; this non-insentient nature is its self-cognition.

Self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) of this [cognition] is not possible because it is logically untenable for a single, partless entity to possess the state of being both an action and an agent; therefore, since it possesses the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*), self-awareness (*svavedana*) is appropriate due to its nature as consciousness (*bodharūpatva*). Consequently, how could there be awareness of another form, namely that of the object?
Form is not [perceived] by that through which another [form] would be experienced as something else in its ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), because entities are distinct.

Knowledge is logically joined with the object of cognition by virtue of its arising in the form of awareness; however, since the object has already arisen, it is not itself awareness—how then is that [object] made known?

Even though it appears as knowledge (*jñāna-nirbhāsi*), in reality (*tattvataḥ*) there is a distinction between those two; nevertheless, because the reflection possesses that same form (*tādrūpyāt*), its cognition (*vedana*) is figurative (*bhākta*).
[Textual variant quoted in *Tarkabhāṣā*, Mysore edition, p. 66, l. 20]: "The cognition of the object would be figurative (*bhāktaṃ syād arthavedanam*)."
For one by whom cognition is not desired to possess the coloring of the object's form, this same principle applies even to the perception of the object.

Intellect (*matiḥ*, feminine, nominative singular) may be (*syāt*, third person singular optative) fire (*asi-*) and so forth (*jvalana-ādayaḥ*, masculine, nominative plural), even though there is no identity (*atādrūpye*, neuter, locative singular) with the elephant (*danti-*) or the combustible object (*dāhya-ādeḥ*, masculine, genitive singular); for they (*te*, masculine, nominative plural) perform (*kurvanti*, third person plural present indicative) cutting (*cheda-*) and burning (*dāha-ādi*, neuter, accusative singular), just as that (*adaḥ*, neuter, nominative singular) [fire] and so forth do.
[Textual variant (Baudha Bhāratī): ...the causes of production (*utpatti-hetavaḥ*).
This [is] discordant, because you, though being existent, are established as causes of origination; likewise, knowledge is not a producer.

The nature of form (*rūpatva*) is established for consciousness (*vijñāna*) through its capacity for discernment (*pariccheda*), provided that such discernment of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is possible; for discernment must have the nature of cognition (*jñāna-rūpa*).
Otherwise, it must clearly be stated that consciousness is not defined as having the nature of discernment, and thus there would be no perception of the object in this manner.

[The opponent] is not subject to such a challenge; therefore, for whom is there a determination? That determination is the very nature of that [object], just as [the determination] of pleasure and so forth is the nature of continuity and so on.

The feeling (*vedanā*), which is the knower of its own form (*svarūpavedaka*), does not depend on anything else; nor is this [feeling] unknown, for this is the very nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvit*).
Knowledge of an object does not reach itself when it is veiled by ignorance; therefore, even though it possesses the quality of being luminous, it awaits something else for its own cognition.

Its nature is luminosity; it possesses both the experience [of itself] and [the experience] of the object. It is not that the experience is not of its own self, nor is it not luminous with respect to itself.
Just as, even though the eyes and other [senses] possess luminosity, a specific determination regarding form and so forth is observed, so too will it be in this case as well.
The state of being an illuminator [does not exist] in an external object, nor in itself, because of the absence of capacity; and the capacity of all entities is not subject to questioning.
Cognition (*saṃvitti*) is designated as the knowledge (*jñāna*) of the object (*artha*). When that [cognition] has come into being, what other operation (*vyāpāra*) could there be for its own self?

If the experience (*anubhava*) is the form (*rūpa*) of the object (*artha*), then that [experience] consists of cognition (*jñānātmaka*); it is logical that the nature of the experience of the object (*anubhavārthātmatva*) resides in the cognition (*jñāne*).

However, even if that [nature] were established (*prasiddhyati*) as being the very essence of the experience (*anubhavātmatve*), there would be no cognition of the object (*na vittiḥ artha-*) because of the consequence (*prasaṅgāt*) of abandoning the object already attained (*parityāga-upetārtha*).

The proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of another (*parasya*) is the basis (*nibandhana*) [for its cognition] therein; just as in the case of a cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra-vijñāna*), there is the reflection of the object (*artha-pratibimbaka*).

If, by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), because it is insentient (*jaḍa-rūpatvāt*), there is no self-experience (*anubhava-ātman*) due to the absence of the experience of consciousness (*saṃvedana-jñāna*), then likewise there would be no experience of another's object (*para-artha-anubhava*).

Experience (*anubhava*) is said to be the cognition (*jñāna*) of an object (*artha*). If that [cognition] has the nature of non-establishment (*aprasiddhi-rūpatva*), what other establishment (*prasiddhi*) could there be for it?

If, in the absence of cognition itself, there were no experience [of it], then that object would be unestablished, because its establishment is not accomplished; when, then, could it ever become established?
If that cognition is unestablished in its own nature within the arising of knowledge, yet established in the awareness of another, this is a well-spoken statement.
If that [second] experience is unestablished, then the first one lacks establishment; in that case, for another consciousness to arise, an infinite regress would result.

The transition from one object-domain (*gocara*) to another would not exist; yet it is observed to occur during such a transition between object-domains. That which is the final [moment] must be established either by itself or by something else; for if it were not established, there would be a lack of establishment for all [preceding moments], and consequently, its own non-establishment would follow.

And therefore, blindness would result for the entire world if the final cognition were established by itself; that [blindness] would certainly follow for others as well, because they too possess the nature of cognition. Otherwise, these [cognitions] would not have the nature of cognition, just like a jar or other such objects.
The eye, as the illuminator, produces consciousness with respect to form; since it is that which brings about cognition, what comparison can there be for it with the knowledge of that [object]?

Whatever cognition is invariably the cognition of something, that [cognition] is non-different from it; or else, it is not distinct from it, just as the self-nature of a cognition is [not distinct] from its blue [aspect], or as a second moon is [not distinct] from the first, so too this cognition of blue is [non-distinct] from the cognition of the blue form.

The self is not known as "other than the cognition" (para-jñāna); how, then, could there be a cognition of the form of blue upon the apprehension of a cognition of blue? If [it is argued that] there is no non-difference between those two, then all this self-cognition does not have another object as its domain, because it has the nature of being a cognition, just like the self-cognition of itself.

Primarily, it does not apprehend the object, because of its own established nature and because of its dissociation from any coloring by the form of the object; nor [does it apprehend it] figuratively. *Note: The variant *saṃvedanaṃ ca nīlasya* (the reading in the GOS edition) has been replaced by *saṃvedanasvabhāvatvāt* (the reading in the Bauddha Bharati edition).*
The proof is that for those certain people who maintain that cognition is unmarked by the forms of objects, it appears as if pure crystal.
Let consciousness, possessing similarity [to its object], be the knower of the external; even so, because that [similarity] is impossible, the status of being a knower is not tenable.

Because it is non-different from cognition (*jñāna*), multiplicity of forms (*ākāra*) would not exist; therefore, by that force, there is no persistence of the perception of an object, or else, because it is non-different from cognition, there would be non-unity [of cognition]. Otherwise, how could the oneness of these two be postulated?

If there were similarity in every respect (*sarvātmanā*), then [consciousness] would be non-cognition (*ajñāna*). However, if there is similarity only with respect to some part (*kenacid aṃśena*), then everything would be a cognizer of everything (*sarva-vedaka*).
How could cognition, which possesses a form distinct from another, be the knower of that other? Everything would be cognizable by everyone; there is no cause that acts as a restrictor.
Just as your cognition, though in reality formless, perceives a non-existent form, so too all that exists—
the unique intrinsic nature of mind and mental factors— is not primarily experienced by others in any way whatsoever.

The term "cognition" (*vedana*) would be figurative (*bhākta*), based upon the fact that it is dependent upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*)—such as its being the cause of [another] effect—and so forth; for a thing (*bhāva*) that lacks any intrinsic nature (*nīrūpya*), there is no dependence on a single causal complex, nor is there anything else [to serve as a basis]. Therefore, for this [thing], there can be no cognition whatsoever, even in a figurative sense.
Alternatively, it is designated [as such]—that is, it is known—as a non-existent form due to delusion; for it does not know [it] in its true nature, because that [cognition] is devoid of an object.
If even by you it is said that consciousness is the knower due to delusion, then such a [consciousness] is clearly pervaded by being objectless for you.
Whether it possesses form (*sākāra*) or is formless (*nirākāra*), that [consciousness] is not the knower of another; thus, no such reflection occurs regarding cognition within Buddhist consciousness.

Since passion and the like arise from something else, their existence would follow from similarity (*sārūpya*); this results in the fallacy of infinite regress (*āvṛtti*) in the view of those who maintain perception (*aupalaṃbhika*).

Like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*), the Sage (*muni*) remains unshaken even by all the winds of conceptual construction (*sarvasaṃkalpavāta*); yet he brings about the fulfillment of the aims of the world (*arthasaṃpad*).
All people call the Victor (*jina*) "all-knowing" (*sarvavid*) because of his manifestation through every effect; he knows everything without remainder (*sarvaniḥśeṣa*) effortlessly (*anābhogena*).

If [the cognition] has a nature such as white and so forth, how can that [cognition] be the experience of that [object]? And if it has a nature such as white and so forth, what is the means of valid cognition for the external object?

The arising of a blue [object] and so forth from a cause of a similar kind is established by way of its having the form of cognition and by its being consistent with it, just like [the case of] awakening.
If consistency is held to be either the attainment of an external object or the capacity for that [attainment], then that is unestablished for one who denies the external object.

If it is maintained that "conformity" (*saṃvāditva*) is desired [as the definition of validity] based on the causal capacity (*hetutā*) toward a cognition (*pratyaya*) regarding a determination (*avasāya*) of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then even this [definition] can apply to that which is without an object (*nirālamba*).

Just as there is a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of external things such as water and so forth, so too is it the case for cognitions; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatirekatā*) is doubtful.

This [inference] based on appearance is clear and common; for the form of fire and so forth is clearly not identical with that [appearance], since it appears as distinct in terms of location and because of internal causes such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), just like another mental continuum.

Even here, there is no inconstancy (*vyabhicāritva*) on account of the nature of this mind. For if it is argued that those two moons and so forth are perceived by those with impaired vision, then it is said: in this very case, the external object is [the cause]; otherwise, this appearing form would not have the nature of an external object.
Since it is manifesting in this way, it is made known by consciousness as its own form; yet the external object does not appear therein.
How, then, is it tenable that what is non-manifesting is both cognizable and mutually contradictory? Thus one knows it, or otherwise.
For this very reason, it is not difficult to establish that cognitions are self-cognizable, because one perceives the manifestation as being of the nature of consciousness itself.
Therefore, the non-erroneous cognition, while conceptualizing an object, does not conceptualize it as being otherwise than it actually is; for that reason, it necessarily preserves its own nature.

That which is the grasper (*grāhaka*) of that [object] in respect to form (*rūpa*) is distinct from the grasped (*grāhya*), because it is not cognized (*asaṃvitti*) when that [grasped object] is cognized (*saṃvitti*). Just as the grasper of taste (*rasa*) and so forth is distinct from its own grasped [object], since one who reflects upon that [grasped object] does not necessarily reflect upon the grasper of taste and so forth.
The two [factors] are distinct from one another, like taste and so forth, because they are not cognized as having a single form, like the cognition of another mental continuum;

[and] knowledge does not apprehend its own part due to its own arising, like [the apprehension of] one's own capacity; furthermore, there is the negation of the state of being an object of apprehension, for the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is devoid of duality.
The cognition of Caitra is not a cognizer of the apprehended aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*) of that [Caitra's] cognition, because it is a cognition, just like a cognition arising from another body;
since its distinctness has been established previously, there is no proof [of its being a cognizer] in the case of those at the periphery who lack knowledge of its uniform nature.

[Objection: It is said that [the cognition] is connected with this [external object] because of the awareness of an external location; [but] apart from the experience of the apprehended form, one does not remember, "I grasped some object at that time. [Reply: They do remember the arising of the apprehender, devoid of the form of the apprehended.

If there were non-difference [between the two], then there would be recollection even when the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) exists; however, this [recollection] occurs only thus [when there is difference]. Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), these reasons are thus established in the subject of the thesis (*sādhya-dharmin*).

Cognition of an object that is not established [by other means] is not established through the apprehension [of itself]; therefore, there is no cognition of the apprehended object apart from the experience of the apprehender.

Furthermore, yellow and so forth are perceived by those with impaired eyes, and the object of cognition is never found to be extracted from its aspect as the apprehender; thus is the supreme [reality].
That memory is characterized by specific external forms; it does not [apply] to all distinct forms, because of the impossibility of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) and so forth.
Otherwise, it would follow that there is no such thing as memory; nor is memory perceived as having the appearance of pure crystal.

In the two latter [reasons] (the sixth day, masculine), there is clearly an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*, feminine, nominative singular) due to cognitions such as those of a yellow conch-shell and so forth. This same direction [of argument] applies elsewhere as well in the proof (*sādhane*, neuter, locative singular).

Therefore, that which is the subject of dispute (*vivādāspadam*, neuter, nominative singular) is considered non-dual (*advayam*, neuter, nominative singular) because of its separation from the object of cognition and the agent (*vedyakartṛ-viyogāt*, masculine, ablative singular), since it is consciousness (*vijñānatvāt*, neuter, ablative singular), like a reflection (*pratibimbavat*).

In the reflection, knowledge is also held to have an objective support (*sālambana*), because one perceives one's own face and so forth when the rays of the eye are turned back. Thus [it is] in the reflection.

There is no perception of one's own face and so forth, because of the seeing of that [face] by means of facing it, and because of the perception of differences such as location and other factors, just like the meaning of another word.

Consciousness (vijñānatva) and luminosity (prakāśatva)—these two are without a basis when there is no connection with an object that lacks such appearances as [the forms of] blue and so forth; therefore, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established.

The persistence [of cognition] in the objective aspect (*viṣayagrāhyāṃśa*), which is the immediately preceding capacity (*anantarajñānaśakti*), is not accepted by us as being real (*tāttvikī*); therefore, it is established that [cognition] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The proof of the stainlessness of representation-only has been traversed by us, the wise, by way of that direction established in the *Paramārthaviniścaya*.
Others, however, whose intellects are defiled by ignorance, have declared here again: "This [representation-only] is not tenable as mere mind, because it contradicts scripture."
She stands as the authority for all, because of her being uncreated by man; for human words fall into falsehood.

(Regarding) the things to be expressed (*vācyeṣu*), it is suspected (*śaṅkyate*) that there exist (*santi*) faults (*doṣāḥ*). But for us (*naḥ*), since there is no author (*abhāvāt kartuḥ*) in the case of the Veda (*śrutau*), there is no suspicion (*na āśaṅkā*) of any fault (*doṣa-*).
An unseen agent is postulated; thus, there was at some time a relationship whose cause was previously unseen and is currently unknown...

Even if it is postulated that "it exists," [such a thing] is devoid of inference and scripture; it is not established for the sake of proving that [existence], nor does there exist anything that is uncreated [yet] created.

Being itself non-authoritative, that which is created cannot be a means of cognition for this [Veda]; furthermore, the truthfulness of the speech of Manu and others is established solely by that [same means].

How could one who is distinguished [from others] yet unconnected [to the Vedas] be a speaker of truth? Therefore, for us, there exists no scripture composed by anyone other than the author of the Veda.
If anyone were seen at present who is similar to the author of the Veda, then by means of that person as a point of comparison, there could also be a comparison [of the Veda] with its author.
If nothing whatsoever were established as cognized (*pramita*) without [the authority of] the Veda, then the Veda would be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

[Objection: Is there not something in the Veda that is not logically consistent? For, in the absence of that [inconsistency], much—such as its authority (*prāmāṇya*) and so forth—would not be established when it exists.

2095—Thus, because it is inaccessible (*agamyatvāt*) to the five [means of knowledge], that entity (*sa bhāvaḥ*) is indeed understood (*gamyate*) through its non-existence (*abhāvena*); for that reason, this entity is difficult to establish (*durlabha*), due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) to refute it.

That authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) of the Veda which is desired as the meaning consisting in the cessation of invalidity—even that is not to be established by means of proofs, because it is a non-entity (*avastutvāt*).
That proof of [the Veda's] being of human origin, which a logician might state to establish the non-human origin of the Veda, does not itself succeed;
for of the two real entities that constitute the two positions—namely, primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*)—one is unestablished, and thus the other is not established by itself.

The proof for the primacy of the cause of the world, which has been refuted, has been established by others through [the argument] that atoms are the probandum. However, regarding that [refutation], whatever proof is stated for the sake of establishing the existence of the subject (*pakṣa*), when the negation [of that subject] is properly established, [the non-existence of the subject] is established by itself.
That which is stated by others as the proof for the two extremes—the prior and the posterior—having refuted those [arguments] of ours who maintain that the meanings of the Veda are created.

Even if they were to establish that very thing which is the nature of the entity—that is, its permanence—the proof [of that permanence] would be established by itself once the two [types of] prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*) have been refuted.
The first extreme regarding the Veda is that which consists of its being of human origin; and the other extreme is its destruction—for the non-existence of that [Veda] constitutes its impermanence.
"That very [Veda] is its eternity, which is that the Veda is neither created at the beginning nor does it perish afterwards; if this is held to be so, then that too must be known."

Eternity is intended to be expressed by means of non-producedness and non-destruction; and since these two consist in the absence [of production and destruction], they do not require a proof for themselves.

He who asserts the falsity of the meaning of the Vedic statements on the basis of inference—his position is overturned by the force of the knowledge of the Vedas; and that Vedic [knowledge], being equal to perception, is more powerful and cannot be sublated in any way by inference.
Since scripture alone is established as being more powerful than that which is set aside by perception— this [scripture] is the sublater of inference—

because of the parsimony [of assumptions] regarding the authority of tradition due to its independence, and because of the absence of defects such as [the need for] an illustrative example, such [authority] does not belong to inference.
Where there may be doubt regarding an object [known] through scripture and inference, a determination must be made therein by means of scripture alone, because of its superior strength.

Even if the Veda were to make its meaning known in this manner, it cannot be said by one who speaks the truth—that it is not an authoritative means of knowledge for me—merely on the basis of [personal] aversion.
There would not be invalidity due to hatred or because it is not accepted; nor is validity conceived through pleasure and permission.
Even those who, being hostile, do not speak anything at all regarding the cause of [their own] authority—these would not be speakers of truth.

How can those who are constantly engaged in the activities of studying, memorizing, and explaining [the scriptures]—being themselves ignorant of the cause of falsity—be known by those situated at a distance?
For those who are occupied with that which they have a purpose for and are bound to it are the ones authorized to know the merits and defects pertaining thereto.

But those wicked ones, who are haters of the Veda and have been cast far outside of the Veda—how can they, being shameless, prattle on regarding the statements concerning the merits and defects of the Veda?
Furthermore, the permanence and omnipresence of sound are established by auditory recognition; who could then determine its opposite?
Therefore, oneness is well-established at all times and in all places through direct perception and recognition; that [oneness] is the sublater of this [thesis].

Even in the case of a flame and so forth, although they are momentary, recognition [occurs]; therefore, that [recognition] is not to be asserted as [proving] a permanent universal (*sāmānya*) in that regard for us.

Wherever there might be a cognition of difference in some particular aspect due to some limiting condition (*upādhi*), there no recognition occurs; rather, it is determined by the cognition of difference.

The cognitions (*buddhayaḥ*) of the individual word "cow" (*go-śabda-vyakti*), though distinct (*bhinnāḥ*) in terms of place, time, and so forth (*deśa-kālādi*), all have the same object (*samānaviṣayāḥ*); or else, they do not have various objects as their domain (*nānārthagocarāḥ*).
Because it is currently arising, this cow is, like [the previous one], manifested by the cognition of the word "cow" produced at present;
for this very word "cow" is cognized today by that cognition which was produced yesterday, by virtue of its being the object of the word "cow," just as [it was] by the previous cognition.

Both [the two cognitions] would likewise exist with respect to a single object, just like the single cognition [of "cow"]; for all cognitions of "cowness," though distinct in terms of place, time, and so forth, [would be identical].

The various cognitions of the word "cow" would be identical, because they are cognitions of the single word "cow," just like [the cognition of] a cow; or else, the word "cow" uttered today is indeed the same as that which was uttered yesterday.

Because it is something that can be understood (*gamyatvāt*), like the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) or the word "cow" (*go-śabda*), any sound whatsoever (*kaścit śabdaḥ*) uttered today (*adya uccāritaḥ śabdaḥ*)—such as "it is a cow" (*gauḥ*)—being heard today (*adya śrūyamāṇaḥ*), has been heard by me (*adya mayā śrutaḥ*).

For the very same reason stated previously, just as in the case of sound, whatever word—whether uttered yesterday or today—is stable and expressive, it possesses a long duration because it functions through the connection between the cognition and the object of cognition experienced [by the speaker]. Such a word is observed to be stable, like the common element (*sāmānyabhāga*) of smoke.
The cognizer, who depends upon the connection with knowledge, is not unstable, because he is the cause of that which is momentary, just like the light of a lamp or lightning.
Therefore, the thesis that sound is non-eternal is contradicted by all these established and firm inferences; consequently, sounds are established as being eternal.

If it is claimed that [the genus] is the means of proof for establishing the oneness of jars and so forth, and if one were to effect the establishment of the oneness of individual instances by this same method, [then the following would apply].

Likewise, it must be stated that [the word] is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the distinction between the individual (*vyakti*) and the universal (*jāti*) is well-ascertained by means of perception (*adhyakṣa*) and other [valid cognitions];

and furthermore, since the connection [of the word] is abandoned when there is artificiality (*kṛtrimatva*) in its application, and because that [connection] resides in a single individual, it is certainly not universal (*sārvatrika*).

Because of the confusion [arising] from the determination of earthiness, substantiality, existence, cowness, and so forth, even without [the perception of] abundance, the word is therefore non-artificial; it never perishes, because it is eternal due to its connection with that which is eternal, like space or an atom.
A word heard once has as its object many universals present before it; it does not, however, convey its own isolated meaning.

2137–2138. This [cognition] (*eṣaḥ*) arrives at the state of expressing the abstract property of "cowness" (*gotva*) after a long time (*cireṇa*), through many hearings (*śravaṇaiḥ*), while excluding [the properties of] "being a living being" (*prāṇitva*) and so forth, as well as "whiteness," "moving," and so on, and the individual instances (*vyaktīḥ*) such as those of the *śābaleya* (spotted cow) and others, which are based on their own respective [specific] causes (*akhaṇḍa-ādi-sva-sva-nibandhanāḥ*).
For that duration, steadily—who will destroy this? Later, by another cause, its destruction is not possible.
Just as it is understood that jars and so forth will perish through old age or by means of weapons and the like, there is no such cause for sound.
Even if there were a difference in place, time, and speakers, the phoneme *ga* and others would not possess distinctness, because the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of it therein is perfectly clear.
Even though there is a difference, the manifestation (*vyakti*) of the phoneme *ga*, being produced (*niṣpannā*), is perceived as clearly distinct from other manifestations of *ga*.

The [action of] going (*gati*) does not exist as a distinct substratum (*niṣkṛṣṭa-ādhāra*), because it cannot be determined by a cognition other than that of the [action of] going itself—just like the [action of] going imagined for something else.

Furthermore, this [action of going] is the probandum (*sādhya*), because it possesses the nature of being a letter (*varṇatva*), just like the letter *ka*, *kha*, and so forth; and because its exclusion (*vyatireka*) is not observed, what is observed cannot be a negator [of the probandum].
The self (ātman) is established as being twofold; and just as permanence and so forth are accepted for that which is conceptualized, so too should it be admitted for that which is established.
Therefore, a single cognition arises through the oneness of the phoneme, while its existence [as distinct] is due to the difference in specific cognitions [arising from] the manifesters.

For whomsoever there is a duality, for him there is a duality of cognition; but for you, since [the object] is beyond the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*), how can there be a cognition of distinctions through sounds?
Some say that when a word is perceived from the auditory organ as refined by resonance, [the cognition] arises through its connection with that [resonance].

There is indeed no apprehension of those [atoms]; rather, it is through the power of their magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth that the cognition (*buddhi*) perceives them, due to the influence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Just as those with deranged minds (*bhrānta-cetas*), by the defect of bile (*pitta-doṣa*), perceive what is sweet in the form of bitter, and what is white as yellow.
Just as those running with speed and those aboard a boat, through the delusion of their own movement, perceive mountains and other objects as moving while they themselves are stationary.
The eyes of the frog are smeared with fat; by means of the intellects of the serpents, and by the two factors of magnitude and the manifestation of minuteness, that [perception] has its locus there.

Since they perceive these [phonemes] even without the apprehension of the cause (*nimitta*), it will follow that—failing to understand this—a misconception regarding the manifested [word-meaning] (*vyaṅgya*) will arise based on what resides in the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
How can there be a contradiction between the short vowel and so forth and [their] permanence and other such qualities, since their very existence is always inherently that of the *mātrikās*?
Therefore, the pronunciation of that [syllable] lasts for one *mātrā* in duration, or two *mātrās*, or three *mātrās*; the phoneme (*varṇa*) itself is not composed of *mātrās*.

[Objection: The manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of sound (*śabda*) by means of sounds (*nāda*) is not tenable; it could [only] be due to the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sound, of the sense organ (*indriya*), or of both.
If sound is refined (*saṃskriyate*), then it would be perceived by all; for there can be no refinement in a part of that which is partless and all-pervading.
Nor could there be a restriction [of refinement] based on the difference of its substratum, since sound is without a substratum, being like space, the self (*ātman*), and so forth.

Furthermore, if space were the substratum, then since it is partless, there could be no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of it by the sound, because [the sound] pervades the whole; for as long as it is established as occupying the entirety of space, it is impossible to cognize it as refined in only one part.

(In the alternative view: because the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) and space (*ākāśa*) are all-pervading (*vibhutvāt*), there would be equality (*tulyatā*) [of distance] regarding their reaching [the object]; thus, even when sounds (*śabdānām*) are at a great distance (*dūre bhāve*), the cognition (*jñānam*) [of them] would follow as a logical consequence (*prasajyeta*).
In this way, there would be oneness of the ear for all living beings; therefore, at that time, because of that single hearing, they all would hear.

Because it is partless, the ear could not exist as a specific location of space (*ākāśa*) that has been refined by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) for the sake of establishing the two [types of sound].
The auditory faculty, once refined, would cause all sounds to be perceived; likewise, the visual faculty, when opened for a jar, would not fail to perceive a cloth.

This alone must be considered: even in the case of recollection, because the impression (*saṃskāra*) has its locus in the same place as the object (*viṣaya*), without distinction, this impression—being produced—would result in the perception of that which is situated in that location, provided there is the removal of the obstruction of the steady wind.

The two states of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are not established through the oneness of sound; furthermore, if a single state were admitted, it would either be known by all or not known at all.

The defects [of the organs] have been stated individually; they would exist even in the case of the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) of both [the organ and the object]. Therefore, in no way whatsoever is there a manifester (*vyañjaka*) with respect to the word (*śabda*).

By this [reasoning], the answer described in the *Bhāṣya*—that the distinction in hearing (*śruti-bheda*) is established for each listener due to the difference in that [refinement of the auditory organ]—is explained.

Just as a lamp and so forth are accepted as the manifesters of a jar through the assistance of the eye, so too would sound [be a manifester] through the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) of the auditory organ. (ŚV, *Śabdanityatā*, v. 42)

And there is no objection as to by what means or in what manner there is a refinement (*saṃskṛti*) regarding its production; for even in that case, the capacity (*śakti*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

Why then is it questioned whether that capacity is eternal? It is inferred from its effect (*kārya*), and in that regard, only the fact of its being produced (*bhāvitā*) is understood through the evidence of its existence (*bhāva*).

Therefore, by means of a supersensuous power (*ati-indriyayā śaktyā*), these [causes], while bestowing a supersensuous capacity (*ati-indriyām śaktim*) upon the sense organ (*indriyasya*), manifest as the causes of manifestation (*vyakti-hetavaḥ*).

For those [theorists] for whom sound is perceived by the ear without having reached it, because their non-reach (*aprāpti*) is equal in cases such as being distant or obstructed, there would be the simultaneous perception and non-perception of sounds located far and near; furthermore, there would be no sequence [of hearing], nor any distinction between intensity, dullness, and so forth.
Therefore, let this conception be examined even by a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*); there is no doubt that the internal air (*vāyu*), struck by effort (*prayatna*), moves forth.
He follows after the conjunction and disjunction of the palate and so forth; because of its possession of momentum, it necessarily persists for as long as that momentum lasts.
From the movement of its own parts, there arise for it conjunctions and disjunctions with the still air.

Having reached the ether within the ear, it restrains the power in the auditory organ; and because of the cognition of that sound, an unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*) is postulated when that [sound] exists.

Even so, for us, there is nothing whatsoever additional [to what has been said] regarding the production of power; likewise, that specific distinction might also exist because of the perception of a particularity.
Furthermore, an obstruction by a wall is possible for the wind, and even an impact upon the location of the ear [is possible] by means of that [wind] which proceeds with great force.
Because its functioning (*vṛtti*) occurs sequentially, it is the cause of the sequential intensity and mildness of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from excellence that is subject to decay;

this is not necessarily accepted by us as the auditory organ (*śrotra*) being space (*ākāśa*), nor as space (*vyoma*) being partless (*anavayava*), according to the refutations of the Jainas and the Sāṅkhyas.

That auditory organ would either be a portion of space, or it would be a distinct entity for each individual person, which is to be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on its effects.

Moreover, even if [the universal] is all-pervading and unitary, nevertheless, the embellishment (*saṃskṛti*) [of the auditory organ] occurs in the locus of the sound; it is that [embellishment] by which one perceives the word.

Furthermore, if that refinement belongs to the sense faculty, then even so, because of its location in the physical basis, the ear—which consists of the hollow cavity and is not itself refined—will not hear sound.

The embellishment (*saṃskriyā*) of the auditory organ (*śrotra*) by sound (*dhvani*) does not occur, because [the sound] does not reach the location of the ear; therefore, the restriction regarding the embellishment is established through the distinction of its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

[Objection: For the proponent of the unity of the sense-faculties (*indriya-ekatva-vādinaḥ*), might not a single sense-faculty (*indriyam*), having received its refinement (*labdha-saṃskāram*) upon one substratum (*ekasmin adhiṣṭhāne*), be capable of awakening [cognition] (*bodhakam*) in all bodies (*sarva-deheṣu*)?
The arising of consciousness is held to occur in the regions of the body of persons; therefore, because of the spatial separation from the primary [organ], the auditory faculty is impaired.
Even though our self is partless and, even while knowing, perceives [the body] in its entirety within the body alone—such a statement is not faulty.
And by this very reason [of deafness and so forth], that [object] is established as being unenjoyable and unsubjugated by another person due to their merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Just as one who has planted [a tree] does not obtain its fruit there, even while existing, because of ownership alone—so too a deaf person does not hear when others are hearing.

Furthermore, the substrata of the auditory organ and sound do not themselves possess parts, nor do they have the property of occupying a single location; thus, this [objection] does not invalidate [our position].

For the manifesting agents—the winds—possess distinct locations for their parts and a distinction of genus; therefore, by that [fact], the refinement (*saṃskāra*) remains restricted [to its respective object].
Just as that wind, though impelled for the sake of another [object], does not perform it, so too the impression (*saṃskāra*) of one phoneme, though capable, will not produce another.

Just as a phoneme (*varṇa*) is not distinct from other conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) such as those of the palate (*tālu*) and so forth, so too there is no exclusion of one sound (*dhvani*) by another sound (*antara-dhvani*) on the part of the *sāris*.

Therefore, there would be a distinction between production (*utpatti*) and manifestation (*abhivyakti*) based on the capacity [of the word] and through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding the effect; it would be the same in all cases with respect to effort (*prayatna*) and the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*).

Or else, the notion [of the word] should be understood as being produced according to the sequence of the directions [of the Vedas], for nowhere in the Veda is that which has the nature of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth ever stated.
At the times of dissolution, this [ear] is designated as "the quarters" (*diśaḥ*). That statement is like [the case of] the eye and so forth, due to its having the nature of reaching [its objects].
As it has been stated: "May his eye go to the sun"—such is the cognition regarding the nature of light; likewise, the ear has the quarters as its essence.

Space (*dik*) is indeed one (*ekā*), all-pervading (*sarva-gatā*), and established as far as the sky (*vyoma*); it is delimited (*paricchinnā*) by the ear-cavity (*randhra-karṇa*), like the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) belonging to a particular location (*deśa-ākāśa*).
Whatever reasoning there may be regarding the conceptualization of a portion of space, that is the same; however, with respect to a portion of direction, it is distinguished by scripture.
Therefore, that portion of the substance of space which is brought under control by merit and demerit, and is delimited by the cavity of the ear, is what is refined.

Furthermore, by that [cognition], there is no embellishment (*saṃskṛti*) of the object (*viṣaya*) as a whole; rather, due to the difference in capacity (*sāmarthya*), it is not apprehended by all [perceivers].
Just as this [self], while arising—even though it exists—is not perceived by all [beings] individually according to its directions, locations, and so forth.

...the word (*śabdaḥ*) is heard (*śrūyate*) by those very [persons] (*tena*) for whom its refinement (*saṃskṛtiḥ*) is produced by the sounds (*nādaiḥ*) situated nearby (*samīpa-sthaiḥ*), and not at all (*na kathañcana*) by those situated at a distance (*dūra-sthaiḥ*);

because the production (*utpatteḥ*) of the word from the sounds is refuted (*niṣiddhatvāt*), since otherwise (*anyathā*) there would be no logical possibility (*anupapatteḥ*) for the arising (*janma*) of a word characterized by a specific refinement (*viśiṣṭa-saṃskṛteḥ*) from the sounds.

In this case, the cognition (*buddhi*) which has been cultivated through that entity and which realizes its existence is like the power of hearing; for in that instance, cognition is held to be withdrawn when there is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of both [the organ and the object].

However, in the position where there is a refinement of both, that [withdrawal] is indeed useless, because the two defects [of non-perception and over-extension] would apply, whereby the sound would not be perceived by all due to the deficiency of one or the other.

Just as the sun, though single, is seen as having a manifold nature in water and other [reflecting surfaces], yet there is no actual division in it; so too, let it be understood that even the word [is thus].
He is perceived in that location because of his dependence on the manifesting sound; moreover, sounds lack the capacity to pervade the entire, uninterrupted expanse of space.

By that [person], this [sound] is perceived (*gamyate*) as having an uninterrupted form everywhere; however, because sounds occupy different locations, their hearing is obstructed in those [intervening spaces].

And because of the intervening space, it is concluded that there is a separation; furthermore, because they occupy only a small area, the cognition regarding the sound is likewise [limited], even though it is not all-pervading.
Since they come from whichever [directions] by virtue of their possessing motion and velocity, the hearer perceives the sound as if it were coming from that [very direction]. Therefore, he asks:
"By what cause are the distinct reflections perceived simultaneously and separately?"
We say: in this case, when the visual light has been projected against the current by the shimmering solar light within the water;
Just as the sun, though its form is divided in many ways, grasps its own location according to the vessel [that receives it], how then could there be multiplicity for it?
Just as even a single [sun] is perceived separately when the eye is slightly closed by a finger due to the division of the visual function, so it is for us.
But others, seeking the arising of a reflection, urge [the following]: "If that [reflection] were indeed perceived here, why is it not seen above?"
How could there be a vision below wells and the like without a reflection? How could one who is facing east, while looking at a mirror, also be facing west?
For those who do not see the sun, the eye always functions in two ways: one part upward and one downward; therein, that which is illuminated by the upward rays—

Because it does not abide straightly due to its substrate, the self does not reach the sun; though it exists as something transmitted through a succession, it perceives it by means of a downward function.
Because its upward movement is one, it is thought to be as if downward; therefore, the sun is perceived as being situated within that very space.
(Textual variant: *sūryam*)
Thus, through delusion, one perceives the face as being "in front," while actually cognizing it as presented by a function that is turned forward—that is, a function directed toward oneself.
Even when a reflection exists within a multi-situated entity, multiplicity is not found therein, precisely because it is apprehended by a uniform cognition.

This distinctness (*bhinnatva*) [established] by means of spatial differentiation (*deśabheda*) is indeed inferential (*ānumānika*); however, the cognition (*pratyaya*) that "it is this very same thing" is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), and therefore it is the sublater (*bādhaka*).
Just as a single Devadatta, even while walking through various locations in succession, is not divided [into many], so too the word is not divided.
Just as a single entity, being perceived as one, is not differentiated by difference of time again and again, so too sound is not [differentiated] by place.

Let there be no contradiction due to synonymy; let it be seen that even because of its pervasiveness, that property which is accepted by everyone for the sake of establishing what is observed [is indeed pervasive].
When the pit is large, the cognition [of it] is large; when the space is small, the cognition is small. Likewise, the cognition [of sound] is [large or small] in the absolutely uncreated [ether].

Therefore, there is such an error regarding the mental representation of sound with respect to its external adjuncts, namely grossness and subtlety; however, these two, while residing [in the ether], are not perceived as belonging to the sound itself.

The conceptualization (*kalpanā*) regarding the largeness, smallness, intensity, and dullness of cognition (*buddhi*) is always indeed sharp when [the object] such as a jar is illuminated by a great light, and it is dull when illuminated by a weak [light]. In this same way, all properties (*dharmāḥ*) such as length and so forth [belonging to] sound (*dhvani*) [are likewise conceptual].
And a word that has no connection with a perceived object does not become expressive; for if it were so, then even every entirely new word would cause its own meaning to be understood.

The connection of this impermanent thing with perception is not tenable; for if there were an establishment of its connection with cognition, its persistence over another duration of time would necessarily follow.

There could not be another [word] that serves as a communicator when a relation with one [object] is known; for when the relation with one word is known, the word "horse" does not denote the word "cow."
Now, if there were some other [cognition] that, by its own nature, were the cognizer therein where there is no causal connection, there would be no certainty as to which one it is.

In common usage (*vyavahāre*), since it is conceived (*prakalpite*) that "this is so," there may indeed be a cognition (*pratyayaḥ*) for the listeners (*śrotṛṇām*); however, it is not possible (*na... avakalpate*) for speakers (*vaktṛṇām*) in this manner.

For, without knowing (*ajñātvā*) which word (*kam śabdam*) he intends to speak (*vivakṣatu*), if he does know it (*jānāti*), he must necessarily have previously ascertained it (*avaśyam... avadhāritaḥ*).

[The word for] "light" (*tejaḥ*), because it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) as being a remainder (*śeṣatvāt*) [of the object], is indeed illuminating (*prakāśakam*) when [the object] is new (*navatve*); yet, because similarity (*sādṛśyatva*) is not perceived (*apratīteḥ*), it is also non-expressive (*avācakaḥ*) by way of that [similarity].

Of which one [among them], on account of its similarity (*sādṛśyāt*), could another be designated as the expressive word (*vācaka*)? At that time, all [words] would be equal by virtue of their connection (*saṅgatitvena*), since [the connection] has not been perceived (*adṛṣṭa-*).
If [an object] previously seen is meaningful, from where does it derive such a long duration? For it is not perceived as meaningful when it has been apprehended two or three times.
At that time, this [word] would be meaningless among other words that are not understood; thus, it alone might be meaningful for those who hear other [words], which is a source of wonder.

Furthermore, there can be no establishment of a relationship (*sambandha*) without first pronouncing a word (*śabda*). And for that which has perished after being pronounced, there is no purpose served by a relationship.

Therefore, because it has perished and lacks a relationship, the preceding [word] is useless; how then could the subsequent word, whose relationship has not been established, be understood as meaningful?

Who could perform the worldly linguistic conventions (*vyāvahārikīḥ*) regarding the utterance of sounds, their instruments, and their relations, given that there is no sequence or simultaneity anywhere? (*svabhāvatvāt kramasya yugapad vā kvacit*).

Because it is not heard previously among men who are distinct in terms of time, place, and so forth, even a single word—possessing a created relationship—is not established as being distinct from other words.

Even if there were a relation of this [person] to the narration, there could indeed be a counter-argument; for there is no possibility of a narration regarding things that are destroyed, non-existent, or present.
Of these two, which one spoken by the speaker should be said to be meaningful for the listener—namely, when he is unable to utter a word previously heard?
At that time, he does not say [it] to be meaningful; he would speak what is similar to it, for a word corresponding to the meaning is not applicable to the hearer.

Because of the absence [of the speaker], and because it possesses meaning through its apprehension, this [word] itself is not meaningful at the very time when the listener is the hearer; thus this [consequence] follows.
Therefore, let the relationship between word and meaning be accepted as eternal; however, it is not logical for it to be conventional (*sāmayika*), because that is impossible in every respect.

There is no inherent capacity (*śaktatva*) on its own part, nor is there any mutual [capacity] between the signifier and the signified; rather, the cognition of people [regarding the meaning] arises from convention, just like the contraction of the eyes [in response to a signal].

Is the convention (*samaya*) made (*kriyate*) either for every individual (*prati-martyam*), or indeed for every utterance (*prati-uccāraṇam*), or once (*sakṛt*) at the beginning (*ādau*) of the world (*jagat*) by some single person (*kenacid ekena*)?

Even the relation (*sambandha*) would either be differentiated with respect to each individual object, or it would be one; if it were one, it could not be something produced (*kṛtaka*). If it were differentiated, there would be a cognition of differentiation (*bheda-dhī*).

Because of the difference between the two cognitions of the speaker and the hearer, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is impaired; for the connection [of the word] in the mind of the speaker is one, while that of the hearer is another.
Let the speaker proceed to establish a connection with the listener; for he does not create that [connection] of the listener which was previously perceived by him.

If that which one performs (the object of *karoti*) is also a demonstrator of what is perceived (*dṛṣṭapratipādaka*), then it is the same as in the case of a jar and so forth; [it is not so] because of the non-establishment of a universal (*sāmānyaprasiddhi*).
Even if an individual is seen to possess efficacy, it cannot be produced; and as for that [individual] which is produced, its capacity for the effect has not been ascertained.

Furthermore, the capacity [of words] for utterance and so forth is established by virtue of their generic form (*ākṛti*); however, that [capacity] is not something that has a beginning, whereas your [proposed] relation (*sambandha*) is something that has a beginning.
If it is admitted that the universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal, then our own view is likewise established; however, the possibility of its having two forms (*dvirākāra*) does not exist.

The relation itself is the capacity (*śakti*), and no distinction (*bheda*) is perceived in it because it is inferable (*anumeyatva*) from its effect; that [capacity] conforms to the distinction of that [object].

Furthermore, because the existence of [multiple] capacities is untenable otherwise, when the object is established by means of a single conceptual construction, it is not admitted that there are many [constructions].

When words denoting a relation (*sambandha*), such as "cow" (*go*), are uttered at the appropriate time, some people understand the meaning through their cognition of the relation, while others do not do so in that way.
In that case, if there were no relation, no one could determine the meaning; for if it did exist, there would be universal cognition, since there would be no [restriction] by anyone.

Because it is a means of cognition (*jñāpakatvāt*), the relation (*sambandhaḥ*) requires (*apekṣate*) knowledge (*jñānam*) of its own nature (*sva-ātma-*); therefore (*tena*), even though it exists (*vidyamānaḥ*), it is not an illuminator (*prakāśakaḥ*) if it is ungrasped (*agṛhītaḥ*).

In some cases, that which exists (*vidyamāna*) is seen; there is no apprehension (*grahaṇa*) of an object (*artha*) that is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsataḥ*), nor is [its] existence (*astitva*) tenable (*upapadyate*) in relation to certain things.
Existence and non-existence, being contradictory, could not both belong to a single entity; nor is the contradiction equal even in the case of being known and being unknown.
Knowledge, which has the *puruṣa* as its substratum, is not obstructed because of the distinction between them; nor is ignorance, which resides within the *puruṣa*, prevented from persisting.

The white one, being situated near both the blind and the non-blind, is not perceived by the blind, yet it is perceived by the others; [this occurs] when that [white object] exists in relation to them.
In that case, there is no contradiction because of the difference between the capacity and incapacity of men; for here, there is no other cause for perception than the [causal] connection.

In this way, the apprehension of conventional usage is equal to that of the sense faculties; therefore, those for whom this [apprehension] exists would perceive the object, whereas others do not, just like the blind.

The relationship of all those who lack direct knowledge [of the Veda] is established through a preceding [relationship], and thus this relationship is beginningless. There is no production [of the Veda] at each individual utterance, nor is there any creation from the beginning of the cosmic cycle (*sarga*), for such a time is not admitted.
It is maintained that the entire world is never at any time otherwise than it is; nor is a "great dissolution" known as being ultimately real.
Indeed, what is called "dissolution" is simply night, because all activities are withdrawn, while "day" is so designated because of the emission of all movements.

A dissolution (*pralaya*) consisting of the destruction of regions (*deśotsāda*) and the destruction of lineages (*kulotsāda*) might occur; however, indeed, there is no proof for a dissolution whose nature is the total annihilation (*sarvoccheda*) of everything.
And no stable agent of creation and destruction, such as Īśvara or others, is logical—one who, possessing unimpaired memory, could establish this relationship.

[Objection: Since sequence is impermanent, the expressive [word] is impermanent; for it is accepted that the expressive unit is the word (*pada*), and the cognition [of meaning] is dependent upon that sequence.
Because they are omnipresent, phonemes do not inherently possess sequential functions; since sequence is an effect of impermanent sounds, it follows that [sequence] is perishable.
If this [word] were dependent upon the will (*vivakṣā*) of that person, then by virtue of that, the eternality (*nityatā*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*) would be rendered fruitless for you.
Furthermore, phonemes known [independently] apart from their sequence are not expressive; therefore, it follows that the status of being a word belongs to the sequence alone.
Only for those [phonemes] whose form would exist as something distinct from the phonemes themselves and devoid of sequence, this conceptualization of the permanence of sound would be meaningful.

The state of being a word (*padatva*) does not follow for the sequential [syllables] (*ānupūrvasya*); for us, this [sequence], which has another entity as its substratum (*vastv-antara-ādhāra*), is not observed to be illuminating (*prakāśaka*).
This alone—the mere nature of those phonemes—is not admitted to be a distinct entity; rather, it is by them that the phonemes, being perceived in this manner, constitute the means of cognition.
The sequence has no status as an effect, because it is apprehended as already established; for the speaker does not produce any sequence independently.
He desires to speak this very thing in such a way that even others [will understand] his statement; thus, for him, there is beginninglessness, just as in the case of the relationship.
Therefore, if there were no immutability, this permanence would exist for us through conventional usage; thus, the independence of persons must be refuted with effort.
Thus, [the word] will not be established even if there is non-eternality of the phonemes; for even while the phonemes exist as eternal, their sequential arising occurs through conventional usage.

Just as the construction of a jar and so forth [is possible] despite the eternality of the atoms, whereas in the absence of those [atoms], such a construction would be rootless and cannot be perceived.
The intention to speak is certainly of such a kind; thus I say in response to what has been stated by the opponent. Furthermore, there is no proof of eternality, nor is there any other mark.

Just as [the universals] of jars and so forth serve as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), so too will [the universals] of sequence (*ānupūrvya*) and the like be established by means of the universal (*jāti*). First, the universals residing in the palate and other [articulatory organs] are present in all persons; having perceived those sounds (*dhvani*) through them, the speaker emits [them].
