The various distinct universals (*jāti*) of those [phonemes] function as the causes for the manifestation of words (*śabdābhivyaktihetavaḥ*), proceeding as far as the phoneme (*yāvadvarṇam*) or as the individual manifestations (*vyaktayaḥ*) associated with them (*tadanvitāḥ*).

In that case, there would be a sequence of sounds preceded by the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and so forth; and the eternality of both [the sound and the universal] would exist solely through the universal [of the sound], just as the parts of whirling and so forth are characterized by the universal and so forth.
Thus, there is the persistence of the sequence of the universal [of the sound] which partakes in the palate and so forth, as well as the sounds and phonemes.

Precisely because individual instances (*vyakti*) are subtle (*saukṣmya*), there is the determination (*avadhāraṇa*) of their properties (*dharma*) and genus (*jāti*); furthermore, by virtue of those [properties], there is the apprehension (*graha*) of the sequence (*krama*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*), even though they are all-pervading (*vyāpitva*).

In this way, the phonemes (*varṇa*), following after all the qualities (*guṇa*) established as being eternal by means of sound (*dhvani*), would be the perceivers of the distinctions among objects (*artha*).
Furthermore, the sequential order of phonemes (*varṇa*), as well as the short, long, and protracted [vowels]—those various divisions of time—are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of sound (*dhvani*).
Time, though it is one, all-pervading, and eternal, is nevertheless understood as being divided among all entities; like color, it is manifested by something in some place.

Since that [word] is manifested within the phonemes (*varṇeṣu*), it possesses the status of being a member (*aṅgatā*) for the purpose of communication; furthermore, because it exists [therein], its own nature (*svarūpa*) remains eternal even elsewhere.
Therefore, there is no such property as being perishable even with respect to a word; by that [fact], the word is established as eternal for those who maintain the eternity of phonemes.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the property of being subordinate (*parāṅgatva*) to the subject (*dharma*) is like [the speed] of a horse and so forth; and in the case of [proving] eternity, there is a contradiction with one's own statement (*svavākya*) and so on when proving [the thesis of] the impermanence of sound. Every proposition (*pratijñā*) is uttered for the sake of the comprehension of the object to be proven (*sādhya*).

It has been established that this [word], being impermanent, does not express its own meaning; therefore, because it results in the non-eternality of the object of cognition, there is the sublation [of the thesis] by destruction.
A person, having accepted the capacity for the expression of meaning, while establishing it, contradicts his own prior admission of perishability;
furthermore, that perishability is contradicted by scripture as well, by means of those capacities for the cognition of meaning which are relied upon in every treatise.

By the aforementioned direction, there is sublation by all the world; furthermore, there is contradiction with inference through the very same previously stated reason, because non-difference of sound is determined from auditory recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Thus, its contradictory nature has already been established by perception (*pratyakṣa*) previously.

It must be stated: this sound is established as being perishable; is it composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), or is it derived from the person (*pauruṣeya*), or else is it a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇa*)?

Now, let the nature of the *ātman* [of sound] be distinct from the *nāda* (articulated sound) and the *varṇa* (phoneme), being the non-expressive *vāyu* (air). Let the *sphoṭa*, which consists of words and sentences, exist as that which effects the cessation of similarity with these others. For us, let there be impermanence (*anityatva*) in these [phonemes], while for them [the sphoṭas], let there be permanence (*nityatā*). There is no lack of distinction (*aviśeṣatva*) among them; thus, the reason (*hetutā*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to its locus (*āśraya*).
If that [position] were desired by us, then that pair would belong to you yourself; furthermore, for you, there would be the mere word "sound" while sound-ness exists.
And that [universal], being impermanent, is contradicted by everyone as being permanent; for whatever universal is postulated here by anyone is [regarded] as permanent.
If impermanence (*anityatva*) is said to be destructibility (*nāśitva*), then for us, the thesis (*pakṣa*) would be characterized by an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*).

If it is claimed that there is some way or other (*yathākathaṃcit*) of designating it as "impermanent," for that [designation] is accepted as being from the state of non-manifestation (*anabhivyakti-avasthā*) to the nature of manifestation (*vyakti-ātmatā*).

When this reason (*hetu*) is formulated here as being based solely on the nature of the sense-faculties (*indriyakatva*), an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) is now perceived by means of the universal (*jāti*) that has already been established.

Just as the reason cannot be obtained when the property (*dharmatva*) of the subject (*pakṣa*) is unestablished for the opponent (*prativādin*), so it is with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Even in that case, if the universal (*jāti*) were unestablished for the proponent (*vādinaḥ*) even with respect to the proof (*sādhana*), then as long as its lack of being a cause (*ahetutvam*) remains, it has not been refuted.

Furthermore, since the investigation (*nirūpaṇā*) regarding its sensory nature (*indriyakatva*) and so forth is clearly required, what entity could there be that is neither different from individuals (*vyaktibhyaḥ*) nor identical to them, amidst these various distinctions and non-differences?

In that regard, the non-common, unestablished, deficient in the probandum, and the lack of a similar instance (*asapakṣatā*) should be stated according to the various alternatives (*vikalpita*), depending on the proponent (*vādī*). [Textual variant, Baudha Bhāratī]: And the lack of a similar instance (*asapakṣatā*), etc.

In that case as well—where knowledge is immediately subsequent to effort and is the means for establishing [the properties of] being produced and impermanent—there exists an inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) due to the three [categories] that possess exclusion (*vyatirekin*), namely: [the three types of] cessation (*nirodha*), [specifically] through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*vyoman*). For, in the destruction of a preceding cognition, there is the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).

The prior [cessation], which is non-cognitive cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and also that [other]—these two are accepted as unconditioned (*akṛtaka*) because they are non-perishable (*anāśitva*).
They say that destruction is established as being without intrinsic nature and without cause; for from wood, through its connection with fire, there arises a continuum of embers.

Destruction, however, is inherent (*svābhāvika*), established merely as the nature of birth (*jāti-mātra-pratiṣṭhita*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and unperceived (*anupalakṣita*) due to a continuous stream of similar states (*sadṛśa-santāna-vṛtti*).
When a dissimilar cause (*vilakṣaṇa-hetu*) falls upon a stream of similar states, then it is manifested (*abhivyajyate*) as a gross destruction by means of a dissimilar effect (*vilakṣaṇa-kārya*).

Because [an entity] with a dissimilar continuum (*asantāna*) is produced (*sañjāyate*) or manifested (*abhivyajyate*) as clearly evident (*sphuṭa*), and because destruction (*nāśa*) is not being produced (*akriyamāṇa*) by that very [cause],

therefore, since it is seen to be non-contiguous (*annantarīyaka*) with effort (*prayatna*), striking (*prahāra*), a mallet (*mudgara*), and so forth, that [destruction] is a non-artificial (*akṛtaka*) cause and is thus fallacious (*vyabhicārī*).
Even though space (*ākāśa*) is eternal (*nitya*), when it is covered by earth and water, it is manifested (*vyajyate*) through digging, cutting, and so forth;

since knowledge (*jñāna*) follows immediately after effort (*prayatna*), the reason (*hetu*) [of "being perceived"] is seen to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) even in that case, as for what was stated regarding "perception" (*darśana*).

Even in the case of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there is a deficiency regarding the meaning of the scriptural statement (*śruti-artha*) in this [syllogism], as well as the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of the universal (*jāti*) as being either non-different or different from the individual (*vyakti*) which constitutes the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*pakṣa*).

Because the subject (*dharmin*) is unestablished for us (*naḥ*) in the case of difference (*anyatve*), and likewise (*api*) in the case of non-difference (*ananyatve*) with respect to others (*parān*), that entity (*tat vastu*) would be neither eternal (*nityam*) nor non-eternal (*anityam*) for me (*mama*), since there is no distinction (*aviśeṣe*).

One part of this [cognition] is called "universal" (*jāti*) and is considered eternal; the other is considered perishable. It has been established previously that a single entity possesses a variegated form.

If impermanence (*anityatā*) is thus conceptualized (*vikalpyā*) as destruction (*nāśaḥ*), then that [destruction] is a deficiency (*hīnatā*) in my proof (*sādhya*); but if it is [conceptualized] otherwise, then for you (*bhavatām*) this is the direction (*dik*) of the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) of the statement (*ukti*).

Or else, even when the relationship between word and meaning (*pada-artha-sambandha*) has been established (*sādhite*) and permanence (*nityatve*) is proven (*sidhyati*), validity (*pramāṇatvam*) is not established here with respect to the object (*artha*) of the sentence (*vākya*).

Even though the meaning is the cognition itself, it is conceived by the ritualists (*yājñika*) as being without cause (*niṣkāraṇa*), due to the linguistic convention (*samaya*) of men, just like [the technical terms] *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth.

Furthermore, because it is a composite [of sounds], this [Veda] possesses the quality of being human-composed (*pauruṣeyatā*), just like [ordinary] discourse. Moreover, there is no trustworthy person (*āpta*) here in the Veda; therefore, its lack of authority (*apramāṇatā*) is established. Furthermore, by logical necessity (*nyāyāt*), the eternity (*nityatā*) of the sentence must be rejected, because the relationship [between word and meaning] is not based on a cause (*akāraṇa*). Even if [the Veda] were eternal, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would still be possible from the very beginning, because [the relationship] is observed to be based on actual objects (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

But that [cognition] based on convention (*sāmayikī matiḥ*) is not tenable (*na yujyate*), because no connection (*sambandhaḥ*) between heaven (*svarga-*) and sacrifice (*yāga-*)—which is beyond the senses (*atīndriyaḥ*)—is ever perceived (*dṛṣṭaḥ*).

Furthermore, there is no pointlessness (*anarthakatā*) for that [Veda], since it arises from the cognition of its meaning (*tat-artha-pratyaya-udayāt*). A counter-argument (*pratisādhanam*) of this kind (*īdṛśam*) must be stated regarding the fact of being a composite (*saṅghatatvasya*).
All study of the Veda is preceded by [the study of] the teacher's recitation, because it is the recitation of the Veda [by a teacher], just like the study [of the Veda] now.
It might be so; however, even in the case of the *Bhārata*, it is sublated by *smṛti* as its author. Furthermore, whatever *smṛti* exists that is based upon the Veda, that is grounded in *arthavāda*.

The past and future times, being devoid of the activity of composing the Vedas, [are non-existent] because they are times, just like the present time which is observed [to exist]. Let it be understood that Brahmā and others are the authors of the Vedas due to reasons such as their being persons, just like the men under discussion.

Therefore, it should be understood that the Vedic word is clearly non-false with respect to its own object, because it is independent of a speaker, just like the cognition of the meaning of a word from the word itself.

The cognition is established as being produced from that [word], because it arises correctly from a permanent sentence—just like the cognition of a sentence—and this is proven by the proof of its permanence.

The cognition produced by an injunction is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is being produced by causes that are free from defects—just as [the cognition] produced by the words of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) who possesses the mark of intelligence (*buddhi-liṅga*). Likewise, [the cognition from an injunction] is [valid] because it is produced by words that are not authored by an untrustworthy person (*anāpta*), due to the absence of sublation (*bādha*) regarding distinctions such as time and place, just like the cognition arising from the words of a trustworthy person.

When the Veda stands as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even an beginningless succession (*anādi-paramparā*) of teacher and student (*ācārya-śiṣya*), though being postulated, does not result in a fault.

Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the Veda, which—like the eye—is common to all people in the world, whereas [the claim that it is] born from unrighteousness (*adharma*) is, as it were, like [the blindness of] owls in the light.
All this is the manifestation of the false pride of the twice-born; there is nothing well-spoken here by them, being like wood-boring insects amidst syllables.

Even in the absence of an agent, this [cognition] would certainly not attain the status of having a true object, due to the deficiency of its cause—the [absence of] defects that [constitute] the opposite of falsity.

In the case of human [compositions], it is suspected (*śaṅkyate*) that "there are qualities" (*guṇāḥ santi*); [but] they do not exist. Therefore, for us, futility (*ānarthakyam*) is obtained. There is no suspicion at all regarding [the existence of] qualities.
Therefore, because of the absence of truthfulness, falsity, wisdom, compassion, and so forth [in those causes], that pair does not exist; nor [does it exist] due to dependence.

Consequently, futility is established, just as in the case of sentences concerning six cakes and so on. [Objection: If the objects are perceived by yogins through the operation of the factors of action (*kāraka*).

It might be argued: "This [account], like the narrative of Puruṣa, is also [an account] of the deeds of Urvaśī and so forth; even though it does not have that as its purpose (*atādarthye*), and even in the absence of any fault, its truthfulness is not established because of the existence of another [version]. Therefore, there is yet another further consequence: the total pointlessness of the collection."
Now, if the Veda is established as being inherently free from error, then it would be considered to have true meaning and be beyond doubt.
If that were so, then that cognition would exist at all times without interruption, because of its being eternally established—just as [it is held to be] in the very moment intended.

Alternatively, all that which is produced (*janya*) is capable at that time of being the cause of a single cognition; like that [which is accepted as such], that [collection] is what is intended to be the cognition.
Therefore, due to the total destruction of the capacity for the production of knowledge, this Veda would not be eternal; or else, there might again arise a cognition regarding that capacity.

Now, even if it were to depend (*vyapekṣate*) upon explanations and so forth (*vyākhyā-ādīni*), because they exist (*sat-bhāvāt*), its cognition (*vijñānam*) would follow their sequence (*krama-*) and thus be sequential (*krami*).

But this is not so; for what kind of dependence (*vyapekṣā*) could there be for that which is already capable (*śaktasya*)? If it is already capable by virtue of its own nature (*yogāt*), what hope (*āśā*) is there here for your [doctrine of] eternality (*nityatā*)?

If [it is argued that] he was previously incapable but is made capable again by them, then this [Veda] follows as being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), because it depends on a person for its cognition.
Even though it remains [in its state], it does not produce knowledge for us until it is indeed illuminated by persons acting as lamps.

Therefore, authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) cannot be conceived as the cause of knowledge regarding the true object; for this knowledge proceeds from the explanation (*vyākhyāna*) of a person (*pums*).
Therefore, even though this authorlessness of the Veda exists, it is purposeless; for its fruit is that very knowledge which is desired and dependent upon it.
If this [cause] is always indeed capable, why does it depend on anything else? However, for you, knowledge would arise through that single, capable cause being present.
Men, being independent, while composing an exposition on the Veda according to their own liking, cannot at all be restrained by anyone.
Therefore, those who are corrupted by faults such as delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and so forth, might even provide a distorted interpretation of the *Śruti*; this is what is being apprehended.

Even for them, a single person possessing supersensuous vision (*atīndriya-dṛk*) is desired; for indeed, there is no lack of instruction regarding the knowledge of the connection between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth.
Because you do not possess a direct perceiver of supersensuous objects— for indeed,
that which perceives through eternal speech [the Veda] is itself devoid of expectation (*nirāśaṃsa*).
He never speaks for the sake of a man, but rather considers an explanation that is equal to a staff held by a blind man.
Being drawn by that [desire], he might even fall onto an evil path; therefore, it is not appropriate for the Veda to be like the light for one who possesses the eye of reality.
Even if an independent [cognition] were to possess the status of being a producer of knowledge, its validity would not be conceivable, because of the observation of [the influence of] persons.

Validity is possible because of its being the cause of the cognition of the object as it is; moreover, when this [validity] depends upon an explanation by a person, the assumption of a means of knowledge is not correct.
Thus, while the means of knowledge remains unestablished, even an assumed beginningless succession of pupil and teacher is not tenable for the sake of freedom from defect.
Since not even a single person among them is considered to possess supersensuous vision, therefore this beginningless succession of the blind is merely a conceptual construction.
Just as a blind man, being led by another blind man, certainly does not reach the right path, so too this conception of beginninglessness is fruitless.
Furthermore, [the claim] that "the wise ones, such as Tattvavida, Manu, Vyāsa, and others, do not have valid cognition regarding this [matter]"—this point was certainly not formulated by them.
Let validity arise from the mere fact of an eternal connection with a true object; however, no one at all can ascertain that supersensuous connection.
Since those objects are beyond the senses, and yoga too is beyond the senses, all these men are always by nature incapable of perceiving them directly.
That scripture does not say, "This is my connection with the meaning"; rather, the connection with the meaning is fashioned by men, and thus it differs from that which is of human origin.

Just as it is suspected that there might be falsity (*viparītatā*) in that which is of human origin, why indeed should even that which is imagined by men not be suspected? Furthermore, even though the Veda stands as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this beginningless succession (*anādi-paramparā*) of disciples and teachers has also become a blind succession (*andha-paramparā*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that a cognition (*mati*) arises regarding heaven and so forth from the word "Agnihotra" and the like, [a cognition] which is free from doubt and the like, and is as unshakable as direct perception?
How could the Veda, while composing that [work], not rely upon its own status as a valid means of knowledge? For no one knows a doubtful matter from such a statement.
Because doubt arises in this way, just as from other sentences that are contrary [to the truth], those who possess discernment do not perceive any distinction whatsoever among them.

If [these two] are joined with that which is beyond the senses, then the two certainties—existence and non-existence—are not [established]; for if there is certainty from the Vedic statement, why is it not otherwise than from other [means]?
This unshakable understanding arises among the learned śrotriyas who are helpless under the influence of faith; it is the same as that of others from another source.

For thus, an unshakable wisdom arises for the followers of the Sugata and others, because of the occurrence of suffering in the lower realms resulting from the performance of the killing of living beings.

No sublation whatsoever is perceived at present for this cognition; yet, if it were to be suspected that such [sublation] might occur at some time or place, it would be equally applicable even to the Vedic statement.
If the Veda were to reveal its own meaning by itself, independently of conventions dependent on human will, then it would be appropriate as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for in that case, it would not abandon its own meaning even when being interpreted otherwise by minds afflicted with defects such as delusion and pride.
Since it produces a cognition having that very object as its domain, but this [cognition] does not illuminate another object intended by persons.
The dependence of human desire is not different from that which is produced by a person; for its manifestation is dependent upon that [person], yet it might also be erroneous.
Furthermore, just as the natural capacity to convey meaning is accepted for that which is not of human origin, why is it not likewise suspected that there may be falsehood?

Indeed, because its truthfulness (*satyatā*) is self-evident (*svataḥ*) due to its being the cause (*hetutvāt*) of the cognition (*bodhasya*) of the object (*artha-*) as true, it is thus suspected (*śaṅkyate*) that even in the case of a false cognition (*mithyātva-*), the causality (*hetutvam*) [of the object] is self-evident (*svataḥ*).
Furthermore, if you insist upon the Veda being a means of valid cognition, then let an effort be made [to establish] its authorship, its faultlessness, and so forth.
[The treatise] has been composed by a faultless author, and it is illuminated in this world by faultless elucidators through means consisting of knowledge of the true state of things.
Even the well-ascertained true words of those endowed with wisdom, compassion, and so forth, though they are human in origin, are not the cause of knowledge that accords with reality;
for it is observed that forest fires and the like are causes even of false cognition. Thus, [human speech] is not unmade by a person.

If [it is argued that] fire, blue, and the lotus-born [lotus] are red when there is light—then fire and the like would be established as the cause of that [redness], because of their being produced [from it].

What is the cause of the falsity of cognitions regarding objects? It is their being produced by artificial means (*vaikṛtaka*). For if it were so, smoke would not indeed be a correct indicator of fire.
And likewise, even though the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), it would not be the cause of right cognition; therefore, the postulation of its [authorlessness] is entirely in vain.

Therefore, the proof for the non-human origin of the manifestor, its eternity, and the eternal connection between word and meaning, as previously described, is indeed rendered useless immediately after what was stated in detail. Even when that [proof] exists, its status as the cause of knowledge corresponding to the object is certainly not admitted.
Therefore, we have no teacher who would take offense at its rejection; for who would undertake the refutation of something that has no relevance?

In this context, the fact that the scripture (*śruti*) is the cause for knowledge that accords with reality (*yathārthajñāna*) has been established; thus, this [scripture] is not proven even in the absence of a human author (*narakaraṇa*).
Something brief is stated here by way of personal assertion (*āho-puruṣikā*), [explaining] how the destinies (*gati*) spread out for those whose vision is subtle intelligence.

The object of cognition (*prameya*) is not negated by the negation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because for them [the means of cognition], there exists no status as a pervader (*vyāpakahetutva*) therein.

Therefore, even though the agent (*kartṛ*) is inaccessible through the five [means of cognition], he is not understood through the absence [of those means] alone, just like the author of a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) and so forth whose identity remains unknown.
Or perhaps it might be inferred that they possess meaning either by virtue of being meaningful in themselves or by having distinct meanings; why then is it not likewise [inferred] from scripture?
However, the fact that [the Veda] is inaccessible to all sentient beings remains doubtful, for even this is suspected: "Perhaps someone might know [it] at some time by some means of valid cognition."
By which [means], all living beings, situated within the three worlds and unlimited by them, are clearly able to ascertain this [reality] with their entire being.

For in that case, the state of being unperceived by oneself would be deviant for you because of the mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) of another person; thus, the non-existence of that [object] is not ascertained.
Those who study [the Veda] are considered by us to be its authors; for it is not logical that they should be the manifestors of eternal things, because such manifestation is impossible.

The arising of things (*svabhāva*) is [possible] only when there is the operation (*vyāpāra*) of those [causes]; even though that [operation] exists, the apprehension (*upalabdhi*) of it would follow as having occurred previously. The Veda is determined to be capable of producing effects such as linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), because of its existence during that operation, just like a seed and so forth in relation to a sprout and so forth.

Because it possesses the nature of sequence (*krama-rūpatvāt*), like phonemes (*vyañjana-vat*), one can infer (*anumā*) that the Vedas (*vedānām*) are also of human origin (*pauruṣeyatvam*), just as in the case of dramas (*nāṭaka*), narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), and so forth. Otherwise, due to their eternality (*nityatvāt*) and pervasiveness (*vyāptitaḥ*), they would not possess the nature of sequence; moreover, there is no sequence of manifestation (*abhivyakti-kramaḥ*) when [the word] is eternal, because manifestation (*vyakti*) is impossible.

Since the validity (*pramāṇatā*) of scripture (*āgama*), analogy (*upamā*), and presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) has already been refuted, it is not logical (*na yujyate*) to introduce them [as proofs].

Furthermore, the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) of the Veda is intended as the meaning of the cessation of invalidity (*nivṛtty-aprāmāṇya*); since that too is a real entity (*vastutva*), it must be established by means of proofs (*sādhanaiḥ*).
Independence is accepted for scripture because it does not depend upon human activity; moreover, that [scripture] is a property belonging to an entity, and such an entity has that very nature.

Even though that means of proof (*sādhana*) which is stated for the purpose of establishing the existence of the subject (*pakṣabhāva-prasiddhi*) is refuted by you, its non-existence (*abhāva*) is established by itself.

Even if there is the existence of that [cause] in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there would be no certainty of its presence; however, there is no certainty [of its absence] merely from the exclusion of its presence.

Since the non-existence of objects is not established through the cessation of cognitions, by that [reasoning], even if there were [the claim] regarding these two, there would still be no proof of the thesis.

Just as the word "sound" (śabdaḥ), when stated [as a reason] in the form "because it is incorporeal" (amūrtatvāt), does not establish the perishability (vināśitvam) of sound with respect to pleasure (sukha-) and so forth, due to its deviation (vyabhicārataḥ).
Whatever proof has been stated by others for the refutation of both the prior and subsequent extremes, those arguments of the proponents of the Veda are unestablished.

If eternity is intended [to be established] by means of the two forms consisting of non-produced-ness (*akṛtatva*) and non-destruction (*avināśa*), that [eternity] is the same even in the case of the indefinable (*nirupākhya*).
Therefore, just as the eternity of a sky-lotus exists [only nominally] and is not real, so too the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda is not established even by that.

If it is argued that the negation of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "being perishable" (*vināśitva*) is not established (*na sidhyati*) when [the reason] is stated as the proof (*sādhane*), because that "permanence" (*nityatvam*) is not established; [we reply: if permanence were [defined] by those two through a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), then, by virtue of having that nature (*ātmakatvena*), those two would depend upon their own proof (*sva-sādhanam*).

Those who seek to establish that [proposition], namely the permanence of that entity which is its very nature, do not achieve their proof, because they have themselves destroyed both the prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and [the refutation].
The negation of that very means of proof—which has been set forth and is ascertained in its three aspects—can never be accomplished even by your father.
The person (puruṣa) who has been described in the Veda does not indeed perish, nor is he contradicted by inference, as has been clearly demonstrated in the discussion on selflessness (nairātmya).

Even other [reasons] of the same class (*jāti*) that have been stated and established there are sublated; for that inference (*anumā*), whose necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has already been demonstrated, is the sublater.

What deluded person would conceive of an obstruction from that [cognition], which is tied to a mere thing (*vastumātra*) that is insubstantial (*tuccha*) due to its verbal nature, or rather, from that future cognition of it?
Why is that cognition (*vijñāna*) which has arisen from a sentence regarding a supersensuous object (*ati-indriya*) not accepted by you as being equal to perception (*adhyakṣa*)?

If it is suspected (*śaṅkyate*) that there is an absence (*abhāvaḥ*) of even an example (*dṛṣṭānta-*) due to its being independent (*nirapekṣatvāt*), because [the opponent] has not seen [it] (*adṛṣṭitaḥ*), then [we reply]: sublation (*bādhā*) indeed exists for that [example] as well, on account of its having a human basis (*nara-āśrayāt*).
If this suspicion does not cease even regarding the Vedic [scripture], for its status as a cause of false cognition would then be established.
Even the word "api" (also/even), making its meaning understood, cannot be spoken by a virtuous person through mere hatred; he is no man at all.
Thus, even among those who have transcended the senses, why is every single word equally powerful or powerless? For what reason is there this attachment of yours toward only one here?

The wise speak of the reason for the lack of authority of the Veda that was just stated; therefore, they would be speakers of truth. There is nothing surprising about this, as it has been stated by those rendered dull by their constant meditation on the Veda and possessed of false attachment, who do not know the cause of its falsity.
By others, such as the Persians and other rogues, their own customs—such as marriage with one's mother and so forth—are never observed [as faulty];

however, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has already been refuted by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, because it is associated with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no certainty regarding its permanence; therefore [the opponent's position fails].
Furthermore, the cognition regarding sound is for the most part of a nature that excludes [other forms], as observed in the case of Śuka’s utterance and this [utterance] of the śārikā.

That [entity], due to the distinction of its manifesters (*vyañjaka*), we shall explain; and by this very same logic, we shall effect the refutation of manifestation (*vyakti*). Consequently, all this would become one.

Consequently, there would be nothing that is a manifester (*vyañjaka*), nor anything that is manifested (*vyaṅgya*); for in a single, undivided entity, the conceptualization of distinction (*bheda-kalpanā*) is contradictory.
Moreover, this established rule of yours—that "these words are human compositions" and "these are produced by non-divine agents"—could not be dependent upon recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Some of us, whose sequence is established by the manifestation of the sequence, are accepted as non-human (apauruṣeya) yogins with a fixed order.

[Objection: This sequence, which is a property of the manifesting [articulators] such as the palate and so forth, is a human product; its opposite might be possible because it is dependent on another, namely, upon will (*icchā*).

Furthermore, the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "fire-ness" (*tejastva*) and so forth has been refuted at length. Therefore, the universal in that case is merely something to be recognized (*pratyabhijñeya*), and not indeed eternal.

This recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) cannot possibly be established with respect to the perishable phonemes (*varṇa*), especially for those who maintain that the universal (*sāmānya*) is what is to be recognized.
Wherever there might be a cognition of distinctions such as "slow," "fast," and so forth, in that case no recognition is determined by the intellect.
However, when reasons are employed for the purpose of establishing the oneness of the word, no contradiction is established, because it is not opposed to heterogeneous [elements].
The common portion of smoke is not thus established as being permanent for me; it is merely a proof consisting of the exclusion of what is other than that, having a nature distinct from it.

When there is the occurrence of oneness (*ekatā*) for that which begins with the "go" (*ga*), the proof (*sādhana*) by means of the genus (*jāti*) is accepted as established. For indeed, the exclusion (*parāvṛtti*) of what does not possess that form (*atadrūpa*) alone is conceived as non-different (*abhinnā*) among the individuals (*vyaktīnām*). When there is the occurrence of oneness, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding difference (*bheda*), because of the determination (*viniścayāt*) of the letters (*varṇa*) through each individual application (*pratiprayogam*) by means of the sense organs (*akṣa*) and so forth.

The distinction pertaining to the mental and non-mental [cognitions] and so forth is established through direct perception; the distinction among cognitions is proven because they occur sequentially, just like sprouts and the like.

The cognitions (*buddhayaḥ*) of the individual instances (*vyakti*) of the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) are distinct according to time and place; they do not have a single object (*na eka-arthāḥ*), because there is a manifestation (*nirbhāsāt*) of different cognitions such as taste, color, and so forth.

For this will be explained later: "The manifestation of difference and so forth is determined by direct perception (*pratyakṣeṇa*)," and furthermore, [the word] is not the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of the phonemes (*varṇānām*).

All these conditions (*pratyaya*) of the word "cow" belonging to yesterday and today do not have a single object (*ekārtha*), just as in the case of cognitions produced in succession, such as those of form and taste;
otherwise, all cognitions would have a single objective support (*ekālambanatā*), which would contradict the existence of sequential [cognitions] due to the proximity of capable causes.

This has already been established previously: even when there is a distinction among word-meanings, by their very nature there is a restriction regarding the single reflective awareness of their capacity; and because of that reflective awareness of the manifold, oneness and so forth do not belong to the word. Furthermore, the world considers the multiplicity of usage to belong to a single word.
A connection with many [individuals] is possible because [the universal] is established; therefore, it is universal, for it does not reside in a single unity among the individuals.

In reality, no connection exists between the word and its object, because of their difference and because [the word] does not arise [from the object]; therefore, it is superimposed by those who are deluded.
For this entire structure of word and meaning has already been explained in detail as being corrupted by the impossibility of pervasion (*vyāpti*);

furthermore, the eternality of "cowness" (*gotva*) has been rejected, and even the relationship imagined [to exist] between space, atoms, and so forth has been cast aside; therefore, those two—the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*)—do not [hold].
Let it be understood after a long time that the state of being a cow is a verbal designation, since it is determined by deluded people as having a single form through abstraction.
Since it is momentary by its very nature, this [entity] is certainly not stable even for that long; so why is its continued existence (*sthiti*) even subsequently admitted?

Even in the case of [entities] such as a jar, there is no cause whatsoever for its destruction; this has also been pointed out. What will that [cause] be in the case of the word, when there is a subversion of recognition? The property established previously is differentiated by the distinctions of place, time, and speakers.

For, through the distinctions of ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, pañcama, and so forth, the individual manifestation of the *ga* [sound] is indeed perceived directly as something distinct and clear; this state of differentiation is consistent with the distinction of the manifestors (*vyañjaka*). Thus, there is no manifestation in eternal things, which will be explained later.

If it is not accepted that "go-ness" (*gatva*) is a real universal (*sāmānya*) distinct from the [individual] cow (*gavaya*), then the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the probandum (*sādhyatā*) in the formal argument (*prayoga*) is unavoidable. If it is argued that this is the basis for "go-ness," even though it consists of the exclusion (*apoha*) of others, such a basis is still not established (*asiddhatā*).

For what subject (*dharmī*), which has turned away from being apprehended by the phoneme *ga* due to its nature (*bhāvataḥ*) as not being the phoneme *ga*, could there be the property (*dharma*) of being indefinable by a cognition that apprehends something other [than itself]? (*bhavet*)

Every valid inference (*anumā*) depends upon (*apekṣate*) such things as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), which must be established for both [parties]; therefore, by that [reason], the example is subject to the fallacy of being unestablished with respect to the locus of the property (*dharmin*).
This entire effort of yours for the sake of establishing oneness of the agent and the goer is met there with a contradiction by perception that is difficult to ward off, as has been stated by you.
These conditions—the phonemes of yesterday and today, and so forth—do not have a single object by virtue of their sequential nature, just like cognitions of taste, form, and so on.
Therefore, this single, eternally existing phoneme is not established; for its [supposed] duality and permanence are merely imagined.

Indeed, at the very moment when the sound is perceived, the air-currents residing within the limits of the ear do not bring about the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ, nor are they perceived.
When a sound is perceived from the auditory organ through its refinement by resonance, the cognition [of it] as being in contact with that [organ] is sublated by direct perception.
A cognition that has proceeded by way of [the quality] bitterness and so forth with respect to [objects] such as sweetness would likewise be devoid of an object; so too would a cognition of sound be.

Due to the distinction [of the object], such as from liquor that has been diluted (*drutamadya*) and so forth, the word (*śabdaḥ*) does not appear as something other; and how could a cognition (*jñānam*) that lacks the form of that [object] not be without an object (*nirviṣayam*) when [the object] is of a different nature?
[One] knows that very object [as being] otherwise contradicted in the consciousness of another form; for how could that object be known?
In a cognition that is formless, that external form of yours is certainly not its own nature; thus, how can it exist as such?
Even in the view that cognition possesses an aspect (*sākārajñānapakṣe*), when cognition arises in accordance with an external appearance, the object is said to be "known" (*vidita*).
2493.—But here (in this case), knowledge does not function in accordance with the external; therefore, it is established that all consciousness is erroneous and devoid of an object.

The existence of a manifestor is not logical, especially in the case of that which is eternal; therefore, cognitions are not distinct [from one another] with respect to the sound. For, just as a lamp restricts its power to the apprehension of an object such as a jar, so too does the sound [restrict its power] in the ear for the perception of the word-sound.

If that word *prakṛti* is established as being fit for auditory perception and is perceived by the ear, why is it not perceived even when the ear is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), given the existence of its fit cause? Its perception would indeed occur at that very time when the ear is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If [it] is not capable of being perceived, how could it come into existence even later? And if it exists, having been known, another word would be capable [of denoting it].

Furthermore, even subsequently, it is not the case that knowledge alone will arise through the power of that [knowledge]; rather, its production is described as being due to the hearing of the conditioned [teachings] and so forth.
In this way, there would be an ungraspability of sound due to its lack of utility; thus, it possesses no distinction whatsoever from taste and the other [sensory objects].
Indeed, this knowledge has as its intrinsic nature the cognition of words, produced by those [factors] beginning with the hearing of refined [speech], which are devoid of expectation regarding words.
This [cognition] has the form of that which is to be known and that knowledge; just as it conforms [to its object], so too, the word "it" would be the conformity of that consciousness.
Otherwise, cognition would not be recurrent; however, that word recurs. If it were thus to be understood as "the object of knowledge," there would be a contradiction of your own position.

These two—the nature of cognition (*jñāna*) and the nature of the cognizable (*jñeya*)—are, as it were, bound together by a single chain; for there is the attainment of the second through the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the first.
Thus, even when the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is not refined (*asaṃskaraṇa*), cognition that is produced (*utpādya*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) by hearing is clearly implied (*ākṣipyate*).

If sound were not of the nature of that which is to be known (*jñeya*), just as taste and so forth are not of its nature, then auditory cognition would likewise not exist as having the nature of cognizing it.

What relation (*sambandha*) exists between cognition (*jñāna*) and the word (*śabda*), such that it is accepted? For the nature of that cognition is not identical with the word, because they are distinct.
And there can be no arising of that [cognition] from that word, because the word is not its producer; for if it were to arise from it, such [arising] would necessarily exist at all times.

Whether that cognition arises with respect to its object always or not—this being established as an exclusive alternative—the postulation of an auditory refinement (*saṃskāra*) is futile; for the occurrence of cognition itself depends solely upon a refinement that is occasional. Thus, the postulation of an auditory refinement would be appropriate only if [the cognition] were occasional.

Furthermore, that formative impression (*saṃskāra*), which is characterized by its capacity, is to be inferred from the effect, which is cognition; and that cognition must be either non-existent at all times, or else existent at all times.
How indeed could it indicate an occasional impression (*saṃskāra*) belonging to that [auditory organ]? Therefore, what has been stated following from that auditory impression is not correct.

If a power (*śakti*) is deposited (*ādhīyate*) in the auditory organ (*śrotre*), and it is non-distinct (*avyatirekiṇī*) [from that organ], then the eternity (*nityatvam*) of space (*vyomnaḥ*) or of direction (*diśaḥ*) would be lost (*hīyeta*) from birth (*janmataḥ*).

Because it is not distinct from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), due to the existence [of those phenomena], there would be permanence, just like the nature of an entity (*bhāva*); therefore, consciousness (*vijñāna*) would always be produced by that [nature].

If there were a distinction [between the two], then no connection would be established; moreover, that [ear] would not be an instrument (*akārakatva*) for the arising of cognition, because of its capacity.

Alternatively, that which is free from difference and non-difference, distinct [from them], and arising from the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ (*śrotra*), is called "unrefined" (*asaṃskṛta*).

By this very [reasoning], the refinement of the object (*viṣaya-saṃskṛti*)—whether it pertains to both [the organ and the object]—is to be refuted; therefore, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) in the case of eternal things (*nityeṣu*) is in every respect (*sarvathā*) without foundation (*nirāspadā*).
Furthermore, those [categories] such as long, short, and [various] steps, which are differentiated by depending upon manifestation— even though all of them are without a substratum—
there is nevertheless a grasping of everything due to the presence of the capacity for restriction, just as [the attraction of] iron is [effected] by a magnet.
If even there, attraction occurs through the attainment of the light of the magnet, is it not the case that this light is not visible? How is it understood—how is it known—that "it exists"?
Why? That light does not draw toward itself wood and other objects even when they have reached it, if its power is restricted;

for that [power] is equal even in the case of non-reachability, since it is understood by those standing at a distance, in the middle, and nearby, simultaneously (*akrameṇa*), following immediately upon the application of all cognitions.

Just as a form characterized by distance, proximity, and so forth is perceived indistinctly [at one time] and distinctly [at another], so too would the cognizer [be perceived] with respect to sound that is weak, intense, and so forth.

If it is asked how there can be a single object of focus for cognitions that have diverse appearances, this same objection applies equally to those who maintain that the external object is the form of the cognitions.

If [it were so], then the cognition of sound in the case of clouds and the like would not be interrupted, because it would be included within the scope of the ear, just as [the cognition of] internal objects is;

since it is the producer of cognition, the ear would be uninterrupted, just as the mind is, being an instrument that functions without reaching [its object], and not otherwise, like the skin and other [senses].

Those who say, "The mind (*manas*), even though it is an agent (*kārin*), is not logically connected (*yujyate*) when it has reached [the object], because the consciousness (*cetas*) exists at a distance merely by its momentary nature."

The proof for the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) consisting of externalness, the nature of a sense organ (*indriyatva*), and so forth, is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*) because it is excluded from heterogeneous instances due to the contradiction with other properties (*dharmavirodha*).

Furthermore, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), and so on are distinct [from the air] and precede [the action], they are not appropriate as non-distinct [properties] because the air (*vāyu*) is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).
Therefore, because there is no distinction, there is no motion for it; due to the absence of momentum, it does not continue to stand as long as its momentum lasts.

If [the auditory faculty] has reached the sky [of space] within the ear, it produces a power in the sense of hearing; why then is there no movement of that [power] toward the cognition of sound? Just as [there is no movement] from the strike of a whip, so too it is illogical for a knower [to have no awareness] of the strike of a whip occurring elsewhere. Thus, attention to the sound obstructs his sensation [of the whip].

"This" is an error [arising] from simultaneity due to rapidity, even though there is a sequential occurrence; for in this case, nothing at all [is perceived], because of the non-perception of the wind in every respect.
Or rather, just as the wind, which is beyond the senses, is described by the followers of Kaṇāda, why has [the notion of] contact with that [wind] not been established by you in the Bhāṣya?

Let it be that the wind is beyond the senses; however, there may exist a cognition of the tangible—whether hot, cold, or otherwise—which belongs to that [wind] as perceived by various yogins, just as in other cases.

Now, if it is thought that [the cognition] does not belong to him because of the disjunction from the ear-cavity, how indeed is this considered [to be so]? For [the sound] has reached the space within the ear.

Therefore, this conceptual construction, observed among the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), being devoid of any foundation, does not shine even among the learned (*vidvas*) for their satisfaction; it shines only among the Vedic scholars themselves.

Those faults previously stated against them [the Vaiśeṣikas] who assert that the sky is partless should be understood as equal even in the case of the auditory faculty being one and partless, like space.

[In the alternative view,] it is conceived that the sky (*nabhas*) pervades the one [space]; there is no division [of it], because its substratum is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and furthermore, that sky is indeed one alone.

The auditory faculty (*śrotra*), which is unitary and of the nature of space (*ākāśa*), does not exist as an unconditioned cavity (*śaṣkuli*); therefore, the restriction [of its function] is established through the distinction of the conditioning of its physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

For that reason, according to the proponent of the unity of the sense-faculties (*indriya-ekatva-vādinaḥ*), a single sense-faculty (*indriyam*)—having acquired its specific refinement (*labdha-saṃskāram*)—might be the manifester (*bodhakam*) within all bodies (*deheṣu sarveṣu*) with respect to a single substratum (*ekasmin adhiṣṭhāne*).

Let it be granted that the arising of consciousness occurs in various locations within the bodies of men; however, those [locations] do not constitute spatial distinctness for the primary ether, because of its unity.

[As stated in note 7, seventh section: "In this way, our self (*ātman*) is likewise without parts (*niṣpradeśa*); and yet, being conscious (*vidan*), it perceives (*gṛhṇāti*) [objects] in their entirety (*kārtsnyena*) within the body (*śarīre*) alone; thus, it is at fault (*duṣyati*)."
Deafness and so forth are also logically connected to this very same reason; for that [object] would be equally unenjoyable by another, since there is no distinction.

Since its original form has not been abandoned, while a particular [modification] exists and there is no arising [of another], how indeed could your auditory organ (*śrotra*)—being eternal, independent, and like space—not be unenjoyable by another? Furthermore, it would follow that the auditory organ is not brought under control by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and thus it would always be perceived by everyone at all times.

The sky (*nabhas*) can never be an object of benefit or harm (*upakārya*) by virtue of its permanence (*nityatva*) with respect to dharma and adharma; furthermore, since it lacks the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*), how could this subjugation (*vaśīkriyā*) possibly occur?
Furthermore, how could it be experienced through the power of mantras, medicines, and so forth? For, because it is eternal, that [object] does not undergo any distinction from them.

If, even though the basis is impermanent, impermanence itself is not momentary, then [the removal of] deafness and so forth would not be possible, because it lacks the nature of excellence (*atiśaya*).

Let there be an excellence (*atiśaya*) in that [space]—let it be so—but this [excellence] does not exist in space (*vyoman*), because of its lack of connection with a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), its eternity (*nityatva*), and its independence (*anapekṣaṇa*).
Therefore, in this case, deafness and so forth cannot logically be the medium [of perception], even if space possesses parts; for this [argument] is the same regarding its permanence.
Furthermore, even in that case, it is not logical for you to claim that space lacks the status of being a master (owner), if it too does not possess momentariness.

What excellence (*atiśaya*) has arisen in her (*tasyāḥ*, genitive singular feminine) subsequently (*paścāt*), because of which (*yataḥ*) she (*asau*, nominative singular masculine), being deprived (*apakṛṣṭaḥ*) of ownership (*svāmitvāt*, ablative singular neuter), would not (*na*) obtain (*āpnuyāt*, optative third person singular active) [it] again (*punar*)?

Furthermore (*ca*), since (*yadā*) no refinement (*saṃskṛtiḥ*, nominative singular feminine) is applicable (*yujyate*, passive present third person singular), thus (*evam*)—due to the impossibility (*anupapattitaḥ*, ablative singular) of refinement (*saṃskāra*) in both the auditory organ (*śrotre*, locative singular neuter) and the sound (*śabde*, locative singular masculine)—by means of the alternative (*vikalpena*) of difference (*bheda*) or non-difference (*abheda*).

If there were a distinction from the auditory organ (*śrotra*), then sound and the auditory organ would not both be refined (*saṃskṛta*); nor would there be any relationship whatsoever between the refinement and those two.
There would be a relation (*sambandha*) of that which is distinct; and in that [relation], there would indeed always be this [distinction] because the cause (*hetu*) remains present at all times.

Furthermore, in the case of [the view that it is] not different from the object, this [cognition] would be eternal, like that [object]; therefore, because it is impossible to produce [it anew], it follows that cognition is eternal.

A restriction [of the capacity] of the wind and so forth is not tenable, because of the impossibility of their connection with the object to be produced, and also because of the impossibility of [the capacity] itself.

Therefore, by the impossibility of manifestation, this cognition of sound is the result which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with its production, just like the cognition of the manifestation of a jar and so forth.

Therefore, there would be an equal distinction in capacity between production and manifestation on the one hand, and effort and the desire to speak on the other, because the effect produced by them is established everywhere through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Whatever reasoning whatsoever exists for the refutation of the "part-nature" of space, all of that should be understood by those possessed of intelligence even with respect to a [single] direction.

Furthermore, by that [cognition], there is no embellishment (*saṃskṛti*) of a single object (*viṣaya*), because of the restriction of its capacity (*śakti-niyati*); therefore, there is no embellishment of the object.
If [the object] were unfit [to be known], then this word would never be understood by anyone anywhere, because it would be of no use for the cognition thereof.
If [the word] has the capacity for the production of cognition, then this word would be understood by everyone, at all times, and in all places, because it exists as the cause of cognition.

Who—whether an opponent (*virodhin*) or an auxiliary (*sahakārin*)—is capable of destroying that [entity], which exists within itself (*ātmani*), being either by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*) potent (*śakta*) or impotent (*aśakta*)? For what purpose (*artham*) would anyone be so able?
This [cognition] is capable of producing knowledge regarding certain [objects]; therefore, while it is arising, it is not perceived by everyone.
Or rather, why indeed is it that the sound is heard by them [only] when its refinement (*saṃskṛti*) would be produced by the sounds located nearby, but not by those located at a distance?

Even in proximity, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) is postulated as the cause; and if that refinement is held to be the same even when those [sounds] are situated at a distance, then, provided that birth from sounds is understood as resulting from a specific refinement, the production of sound cannot be rejected by anyone.

That specific refinement (*saṃskṛti*) is not distinct from the word (*śabda*), because the word would then result in being unknowable (*ajñeyatā*); therefore, the word is also produced (*jāyate*) and refined (*saṃskṛta*) at one time. Furthermore, the word never (*jātu*) abandons that nature (*ātmānam*) due to its connection with impermanence (*anityatā*); thus, it should be perceived (*upalabhyeta*) at all times.

Even in the case of the two types of formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*), the statement regarding the two [types] is true insofar as there is no deficiency of either of the two previously mentioned [conditions], due to their continued persistence.

Furthermore, those phonemes (*varṇa*) which were previously manifested by manifestors (*vyañjaka*) have not perished upon the occurrence of their disappearance; therefore, they would be heard by everyone simultaneously.
If the auditory organ and the sound were both restricted to being fit for hearing only when processed [by the mind], then there would be no hearing of them by other perceivers of the phonemes.

If, on the other hand, those two conditioned [factors] are capable of producing consciousness, then surely there would also be an auditory perception (*śruti*) of those two, following upon their respective colors and persons.
(Regarding exclusion, 7th case, feminine) How is it that these other phonemes of the auditory faculty do not attain that [exclusion]? Therefore, the hope for their permanence is without foundation.
This single sun is not perceived as having a manifold nature in water and other such media, because all cognitions exist as reflections and are without external support.

Furthermore, in your view, all cognitions (*dhī*) are established as being formless (*nirākāra*); yet, an external object (*bāhya-padārtha*) is admitted (*abhyupagamyate*) to possess form (*ākāravat*).
And this reflection is perceived as being situated within water and the like, while the sun and so forth remain as they are in the sky; it does not exist [there] in that manner.
2580.—If it is asked how that appears thus through delusion, then for that very reason it is clearly not without a basis (*nirālambana*), because of its separation from the form of that object.
If his understanding were otherwise, then [the thought] "this is well-spoken" would be otherwise; however, if it were thus, everything would be a knower of all things.
If that very [cognition] were perceived as existing in such a state, then how could there be a perception of it when there is the apprehension of another form?
Even if consciousness possesses an aspect (*sākāra*), it is not logical for that [consciousness] to be the grasper (*grāhaka*) when its aspect is non-different from the object and the cognition.

Let it be understood (*avabuddhyatām*): even though [the self] exists as something present through its downward-turned activity (*ārvāñc-vṛttyā*), being offered (*arpitam*) through a traditional succession (*pāramparya*), why is it not admitted (*anumanyate*) that it possesses an upward-turned activity (*ūrdhva-vṛttim*) directed toward the very same state (*ekatve*)?

(As has been established, n. 1st s. [it is said: "If the sun were perceived (*īkṣyeta*) in such a way that it would be conceived as being exactly as it is situated, then it would be understood; not otherwise."

Thus, one who understands that which is presented by the function of the "turned-toward" (*pratyak*) through the function of being "turned-forward" (*prāñc-natā*) does not, due to delusion, perceive the face as being "this" (*iti*) [i.e., external].

That cognition of the reflection does not have one's own face and so forth as its objective support (*ālambana*), because it appears with characteristics distinct from those [of the original object], just like the cognition of taste, sound, and so forth.
In a smaller mirror, the face appears smaller; and trees and other objects are perceived as inverted and submerged in water.

The original object (*bimba*) is present facing [the mirror], whereas the reflection (*pratibimba*) is not so; furthermore, this reflection is situated within the water and other such media, while the original object remains at a distance.

Moreover, the reflection is differentiated according to the dimensions of its support (*āśraya*), such as being large or small, whereas the original object is not. Therefore, for this reason, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*).
Even if there were a distinct manifestation while the cognition of the object exists, the mind [concerning] form, sound, and so forth, would become the range of all objects.

Even though a single [reflection] is seen separately in the eye when it is slightly closed by a finger, that too is considered to be an error (*bhrānti*) devoid of an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*). However, the arising of a reflection is precluded here because two corporeal forms cannot coexist in one place due to their mutual resistance (*pratighāta*).
Even when a reflection exists, because it occurs in multiple locations and possesses distinctions such as being gross or subtle, unity does not indeed exist.
This determination which arises for men—namely, "The sun is situated above me"—is certainly erroneous.
Since all living beings see only the one maker of day simultaneously, and never a second.
Since, in this case, no second or subsequent sound is perceived—because it is not seen in the circle [of space]—therefore the sun is indeed determined to be one.
Sound, however, is not determined to be so by its oneness in any way whatsoever, whether sequentially or even simultaneously, because of the observation of its multiplicity.
When many speakers simultaneously employ a single phoneme, such as the letter *ga* and others, then a distinction [between them] is clearly perceived.
In its application, a distinction is understood not only sequentially, but also from the inferential mark (*liṅga*) due to the succession of cognitions.
The apprehension of this [object] occurs dependent upon the manifesting sound; however, its perception would be [of it] as it actually exists.
Otherwise, this apprehension would not be of that [object], because that specific form does not appear; for sound does not manifest as pervading all portions of space.
Why is it that the scripture conforms to the distinctness of location of the sound? Rather, the manifested [word] would appear by its own nature, just like a jar or other such objects.

All this that has been stated is merely a formal analysis (*prakriyā-mātra*); it does not establish the incapacity of manifestors (*vyañjakānām*), because [such incapacity] is untenable (*ayogāt*) given the nature of manifestation (*vyakti*).
"That which is [called] direct perception (pratyakṣa) is that very [cognition] already refuted previously; this [claim] that it is uncontradicted is [merely] a distinction based on location."
Someone, while moving, is distinguished from one place by virtue of its momentary perishability; otherwise, he would not possess motion.
For if his own nature were stable, because it would continue to follow the previous location, the reaching of another location would not be possible.

[It] is not conceived from the sky (the nominative singular of *nabhas*, neuter) nor from that which is indefinable (the ablative singular of *nirupākhyāt*, neuter); and likewise, there is no manifestation because it is beyond the senses (the ablative singular of *atyakṣatvāt*, neuter). That [manifestation] is held to be light (the nominative singular of *ālokaḥ*, masculine) within a hollow space (the locative singular of *khātāyām*, feminine).
Textual variant: "And because it is beyond the senses, that [manifestation] is held to be light within a hollow space in that same way."

Furthermore, even in the case of space, the manifestation of sound is not tenable; for manifestation is knowledge, and this [knowledge] would have to be eternal due to the constant presence of its cause.

Just as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is somehow conceived (*prakalpyate*) in relation to sound (*śabde*), so too there is no such error (*vibhrama*) regarding the cognition (*mati*) of another; for that [error] is merely an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) in the mind (*buddhau*) concerning words.

Therefore, it is established that long vowels and all other such [sounds] are not properties of sound; for if they were the manifesters (*vyañjaka*) of sounds, that [consequence] would follow, and that has already been refuted.

Those words of yours, which were repeatedly discussed in the past as being thus, even though their referents are absolutely distinct, are capable of a uniform reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*).

Therefore, the word does not become expressive of a relation that has been perceived with respect to its object; rather, it has been established that, in reality, this [word] is not expressive by its own function.
These [mental] cognitions are produced by words, appearing falsely as the denotable and the denoter, because universals (*jāti*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth, do not exist.
Even though there is a factual difference, speakers, through delusion, consider that word "cow" to be one and their cognitions to be identical.
Therefore, having set aside all that which was spoken by the twice-born speaker—who utters much that is incoherent—along with its distinction from sound, that [reality] remains without foundation.

For instance, there is no oneness (*ekatva*) of the hand and so forth when it is trembling, because of the difference in cognition (*buddhibheda*) due to the distinction between rapid and slow manifestation (*śīghramandavyakti*).

Furthermore, a single universal (*sāmānya*) that persists (*anugāmin*) is not perceived; rather, it is through convention (*saṅketa*) that this [conceptualization] becomes a factor for the negation of motion and so forth.

It has been stated that words do not directly cause [an object] to be understood through a connection with an external thing; rather, these [words] are indicators of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

Thus, since you are firmly convinced of this through the non-perception of [the cause] by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-anupalambha*), and because [the effect] is its result (*kāryatā*), the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*) is clearly established here by that [reason].
He by whom the relation of cause and effect has been ascertained through convention understands from words the speaker's intention, just as [one understands] a movement of the hand.
When [the speaker's] intention (*vivakṣā*) exists, this relationship—which consists of the nature of cause and effect—arises between words (*śabdānām*) and the object (*arthena*) that is present.

That which was spoken by him (the third person singular instrumental) is conventional (*sāmayika*), because it is illuminative (*dyotanāt*, fifth case singular); therefore, the connection (*sambandha*) of those [words] is called "convention" (*samaya*), though not in the primary sense (*mukhyataḥ*).

The relation (*yoga*) between cause and effect is not at all distinct from the two entities consisting of the cause and the effect; rather, those two, when thus arisen, each individually perceived by the dull-witted as having a single nature, are therefore held to be the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding time, convention, and linguistic usage.

However, a single real connection (*vāstavaḥ sambandhaḥ*) among objects (*arthānām*) is not at all tenable (*naiva yujyate*), because of their non-confusion (*asaṅkīrṇatayā*) despite their difference (*bhede*); [otherwise] there would be a state of no connection (*asambandhatā*).

Therefore, this is the established rule: both with respect to each individual person and with respect to each utterance, that which was stated by another who was ignorant of the principles of others' logic.

Convention (*samaya*) is not the primary relationship between those two [the word and the object] by virtue of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*); rather, it is the relationship that signifies [the object], and thus it would belong to that [signification] in a primary sense (*mukhyataḥ*).
Others do not acknowledge this repetition; nor is it the work of Īśvara and the like, because such a creator has been refuted at the beginning of the discussion on creation.

That relation which is distinct with respect to each [individual] due to its momentary nature, and the corresponding reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), is not contradicted by the difference [between individuals].
*Textual variant: *sambhinnaḥ* (Baudha Bhāratī edition).*
The objects of those cognitions clearly arise in succession; therefore, they say that it [the object] also possesses succession. Otherwise, there would be a lack of succession for them.

When there is a convention (*saṅketa*) regarding many [things] as a single instrument (*karaṇa*), a single simultaneous agreement (*samaya*) is not accepted as being distinct, just as a single moment of blue and so forth is not.
There is no other relation in the cognition of the speaker, nor another in that of the hearer, because that [cognition] is of a single form due to its conformity even in both [of them].
The speaker enters into a relationship with the listener and the author; he establishes that very same [relationship] which was previously perceived by him.

Therefore, since the reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa-dhī*) regarding that [object] has occurred as having a single form even with respect to differentiated things such as words and so forth, it determines (*adhyavasyati*) their oneness (*ekatva*).
Even in the case of a jar and so forth, the universal has already been refuted; no form whatsoever consisting of manifested qualities is admitted.

Nor is its capacity for holding water and so forth established by virtue of the generic form (*ākṛti*), for even those [individuals] possess eternality if they are non-different from the genus (*jāti*).

If there were a difference [between the universal and the individual], there would be the fault of [requiring] a relation; however, if it arises from that [individual], there is impermanence. Therefore, the capacity for supporting water and so forth is not logically possible on account of the form (*ākṛti*), even in the case of a jar and the like, since they are distinct [from it]; certainly, these faults apply to the capacity.

If it is held that the relation itself is the capacity (*śakti*), and there is no distinction of this capacity [from the relation], then the capacity of words for their objects would be one, because it is non-different.

If there were a difference, there would be no connection whatsoever between that [universal] and those two [particulars]. Furthermore, if it were produced from them, it would not be eternal; nor is there any other possible state for a real entity.

When words such as "cow" (*go*), which possess a connection with a narrative (*ākhyāna-sambandha*), are uttered at a particular time, some people understand the meaning through their intellect by means of that connection; however, others do not.
Since [it] has been revealed in whatever manner it exists through its connection with yours—that is, with your own connection—everyone should ascertain the meaning.
A capacity (*śakti*) alone is held by you all to be the eternal relation (*sambandha*); it is restricted to the production of the cognition of an object, or else it is not limited at all.

If [the world] were eternal (nityatve), being without limit (niravadhau), why would everyone not ascertain (avadhārayet) the meaning? Even if there were a limit, what would be the cause (hetuḥ) [for such uncertainty], if primordial matter (prakṛtiḥ) were [active] by itself (svataḥ)?

Since there was previously no grasping of the convention (*saṅketa*), and furthermore, because of the non-recollection (*asmaraṇa*) of that [convention], how could cognition (*vijñāna*) have arisen at all with respect to a single [object] existing therein?
That power is restricted to that birth and knowledge; it remains established there, and yet that power is conceived as being restricted even when known.
If power (*śakti*) is both known and unknown as distinct, its eternity (*nityatva*) is lost; but if it is one, what is the cause for this distinction (*vibhāga*) that is being described?

Furthermore, by what means (*kena abhyupāyena*) is it accepted (*iṣyate*) that there is a cognizer (*vijñātṛ*)? If [it is argued] "by presumptive testimony" (*arthāpattyā*), because this principle (*nyāyaḥ*) is established here (*yasmād iha*).
In this case, one perceives by direct perception the words, the elders, and the objects denoted; and the listener's state of comprehension is known through inference from their behavior.

He knows the power residing in the two [terms], through the impossibility of it being otherwise; by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), they perceive the relationship as established by the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is not possible to understand [the meaning] through the inherent power (*śakti*), because it is logically untenable; otherwise, there would be an unconfused comprehension from the word based on convention (*sāmayika*).
However, in the case of an eternal power, one does not depend upon anything such as convention; thus, the comprehension of the meaning from the word would occur at all times.

Just as in the case of [words] such as *śabda*, *kali*, *māri*, and so forth, which have different meanings at different times, there would be no capacity to convey another meaning from the sound (*dhvani*), because its power is restricted.

If a single power (*śakti*) is admitted as being for the purpose of illuminating various meanings, or if it were distinct [for each], then there would be a cognition of various meanings from a single word at once.

Since the manifestation of the capacity for the purpose is established as being always present, cognition would likewise always be the cause of the object; thus, it would follow that [cognition] would exist for everyone at all times.

If a capacity (*śakti*) is postulated (*parikalpyate*) in that [object] as being dependent (*sāpekṣā*) upon convention (*saṅketa*), then surely the benefactor (*upakāri*) would be expected to be depended upon (*apekṣyeta*), and that [capacity], being the beneficiary (*upakāryā*), would not be immovable (*acalā*).

Because it is based on the purpose of manifesting a convention (*saṅketa*), there arises falsity (*mithyātva*) in a person (*nara*), even though [the word] possesses the capacity (*śakti*) to produce another [meaning].
For let there be the capacity of a single sound for the illumination of various meanings; however, all [meanings] such as the *agnihotra* and so forth are not equally applicable [to every word].
Since it is possible that even the meaning of illumination is contrary to what is intended, your conception of an eternal relation between word and meaning is purposeless;
moreover, if there is dependence upon convention, why is this so-called "eternal capacity" being nourished as something causeless?
Of that [word], there is no established attendant; for indeed, no operation whatsoever is observed apart from convention (*saṅketa*) in the cognition of an object.

For this worldly practice is not seen without an agreement (*samaya*); and since the establishment of the relationship [between word and meaning] depends on that, the [infinite] succession is purposeless.
Even from mere convention (*saṃketa*) arising solely from human whim (*icchāmātra*), linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is possible; therefore, a [real] connection (*yoga*) is not established.
Otherwise, the impossibility of that linguistic usage would be suspected; furthermore, since a connection is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is not apprehended by humans.

Because [the connection] is unknown to all [people], due to its lack of established proof (*aprasiddhi*), the connection (*yoga*) with each preceding [element] is not established; thus, why is it postulated in this way?

Therefore, words such as "cow" (*go*), "horse" (*aśva*), and so forth, are certainly not [words] possessing an eternal connection (*nitya-sambandha*), because they depend upon convention (*saṅketa*), just like the word "gāvī" and others.

When the word "go" is present in its correct form, the cognition of "cow" arises from the causal efficacy of words such as "gāvī" and the like, which are produced by an incapacity [to utter the correct form] and follow that [correct form].
But how could there be such an understanding of the meaning through the influence of the original word, given that those who speak "śanaka" and so forth do not comprehend the Sanskrit [language]?
Therefore, an eternal relationship between word and meaning is not accepted; rather, it is logical that it is conventional (*sāmayika*), because such [convention] is possible in every respect.
