That dissolution which might occur—whether it be the destruction of a region, the destruction of a family, or even that which is desired by the Buddhists—is also suspected by the Brahmins and others.

In that [Veda], a supreme understanding might be conceived as having its root in the Veda itself, while all conceptualization that is contrary to it—arising from falsehood, delusion, pride, and so forth—is utterly destroyed.
The Veda might indeed have become like a mere disguise (*pratikañcukatā*); this is even suspected as long as no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) is revealed.
Furthermore, if there were a desire for it to be otherwise, the word [of the Veda] would not persist; yet that desire of men does not arise in that way, nor otherwise.

This [Veda] might be suspected (*śaṅkyeta*) as being not of the nature of the meaning of the text, but otherwise [than that], when it proceeds according to [mere] desire, the suspicion does not cease.
The sequence is not grasped by all men as established; yet they perform the sequence of words, sentences, and syllables even independently.
Otherwise, like them, there would be no Veda at all; nor would there be any composed work whatsoever, even if it were merely a composition consisting of meaningless words—thus it is destroyed.

"This indeterminacy" (eṣā)—he intends to say this very thing in that very manner, so that his statement [regarding it] by others is like that [of the relationship], and thus there is no beginninglessness (anāditā) of the relation.
(Textual variant [Baudha Bhārati]: *uktis* for *uktas*)

Such is the intention [with which] I say "I speak" regarding those things stated by another; for [this would occur] through confusion, because of the retrospective reflection on [the word] as being equivalent to the action of differentiation.

[Those things] spoken by another are not [said to be] expressed [by us], because of their difference in voice and so forth; this [sound] is not the manifestor [of the phoneme], because it is observed to have the nature of the phoneme itself.
Therefore, since the phonemes are observed to be distinct for each individual—just like jars and other objects—what sign of identity can possibly be denied when such difference is so clearly evident?

The indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of [entities] such as the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth has already been refuted by the non-existence (*asattva*) of that [usage] prior [to the production of sound], and because it is impossible for those [usages] to be associated with a universal (*jāti*) through an individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, since universals reside in the palate (*tālu*) and other [articulatory organs], the speaker does not indicate the sounds by means of them; rather, he emits (*niras*) them.

Those distinct universals (*jāti*) are not the causes of the manifestation of words; rather, they function as long as there are phonemes (*varṇa*), or as long as there are individual manifestations (*vyakti*) associated with them.

This sequential order (*ānupūrvya*) of the sounds (*dhvani*) is preceded by the sequence of conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) and disjunctions (*vibhāga*) of the palate and other articulatory organs. Furthermore, both of these possess eternality (*nityatā*) by virtue of their respective universals.

Just as the parts of [actions] such as revolving are not perceived as belonging to a genus (*jāti*), so too there is no persistence (*anuvṛtti*) of a sequence (*krama*) belonging to the palate and other [articulatory organs], nor even to the sound (*dhvani*) or the phoneme (*varṇa*).

Furthermore, although there is a determination of a genus, it does not occur because of the subtlety (*saukṣmya*) of the individual instances (*vyakti*); nor is there a perception of the sequence of phonemes by virtue of that [genus], even though [the genus] is all-pervading (*vyāpitva*).
Those phonemes, following after all the qualities of sound established as eternal, would not be cognizers of distinct meanings.

Furthermore, there are distinct universals (*jāti*) which are the causes for the manifestation of words; they function as long as the phonemes (*varṇa*) persist, or else the individual manifestations (*vyakti*) are associated with them.
Since the manifestor exists, the perception of sound is eternal; therefore, even if the sequence of phonemes possesses the nature of manifestation, a sequence of phonemes is not possible for you.

If there were a fixed status (*vyavasthiti*) of universals (*jātīnām*) characterized by forms (*rūpāṇām*) connected to individuals (*vyakti-sambaddha*), then the eternality (*nityatvam*) of those individuals (*vyaktīnām*) would also unavoidably follow (*anuṣajyate*).
If there were no fixed determination of individual instances (*vyakti*), then even for those universals (*jāti*) that are connected to forms (*rūpa*), impermanence would occur—even against your will.
Since manifestation has already been refuted previously, the phonemes, being perceived in this manner, would not be the conveyors of meaning for you.

Time, moreover, which is singular, all-pervading, and eternal, has already been refuted; furthermore, it is not manifested by anything (*kena-cit*) among all entities (*sarva-bhāveṣu*), just as color (*varṇa-vat*).

There is no status as a constituent part (*aṅgatā*) for this [word] when it is being manifested (*vyajyamānasya*) among the phonemes (*varṇeṣu*), because there is no distinction from another [manifestation], and because it exists elsewhere; therefore, it possesses no eternity (*nityatā*).
Those which are the successive orders of the phonemes—namely, short, long, and protracted—are merely adjuncts of sound; they do not constitute divisions of time.
Therefore, there exists no such eternal word-element (*pada*) for those who maintain that phonemes (*varṇa*) are impermanent; by that [fact], it is established that the word-element is impermanent.

It might [be argued]: "Even though it does not exist as a part of the dharma, just as speed and so forth [are parts] of a horse, if the individual entity (*vyakti*) were to be postulated by means of manifesting conditions (*pratyaya*)."
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) regarding the eternity of all [sounds] has been refuted; for it has been established that the nature of the cognition of meaning resides in impermanent things.
That phoneme which arises from within the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), and which is produced from that [desire], is heard immediately after it.

There is no hearing of the preceding phonemes as they arise in consciousness, because of excessive rapidity; rather, having regard for memory, that [consciousness] produces memory within itself subsequently.

The state of being produced (*janyatā*) by those [sounds] which are the causes of their own arising and apprehension, or else the state of being their cause (*hetutā*), constitutes this sequence (*ānupūrvī*) among the phonemes (*varṇa*), which has man (*puruṣa*) as its substratum (*āśraya*).

Therefore, it is quite clear that the phonemes are distinct in every word (*pratipadam*) according to their sequential order (*kramabheda*), as in the case of *dama*, *mada*, *latā*, *tāla*, and so forth.
By such a process as this, these [words] are the producers of the distinction of meaning; therefore, even the conceptualization of a *sphoṭa* here is entirely purposeless.
That which is imagined by the grammarians for the sake of understanding meaning—that is, the notion that the phonemes themselves possess that capacity—is a useless construction.

Because of the non-perception of that which is perceptible, its non-existence is determined; however, in the case of imperceptibility, this [non-perception] cannot indeed serve as a signifier, just like a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Since its existence as a cause is established by that cognition alone, its status as an indicator is accepted—just like the eye;

it would [exist] at all times, even when there is no comprehension of the convention and even when there is no hearing of the phonemes, because of the presence of its capable cause, which is the cognition of the objects.
For this entity is eternal, and it has no dependence whatsoever, nor even a manifestation through the phonemes associated with its sound-convention, because such is not observed.
They say: "The manifestation exists as cognition; cognition does not exist [as something separate]. Therefore, even the conceptualization of a manifester for this [cognition] is indeed purposeless."
When the seed has been deposited by the sound (*nāda*) and its maturation has occurred, the word (*śabda*) manifests in the intellect (*buddhi*) together with the final resonance (*dhvani*).
That which has been conceived as "this" is, even here, without a cause; for no other [word] is perceived in that [conception].

"Let it be produced" (*janyatām*), "or let it be manifested" (*vyajyatām*) by means of future sounds (*dhvanibhiḥ*); for those who maintain that the *sphoṭa* [is eternal], its sequential order (*kramaḥ*) is contradicted (*viruddhyate*).

In that which is partless, two individual manifestations (*vyakti*) of a universal (*jāti*) cannot logically be joined through a sequence, because there is an absence of any external, single form; for those two would necessarily exist [simultaneously] in every respect.

If [the sphoṭa] possesses parts, just as phonemes (*varṇa*) are the expressers [of meaning] through a sequence, why are the parts of the sphoṭa not likewise imagined, even though they are unperceived?
They employ other phonemes (*varṇa*) more intensely for the sake of the accomplishment of meaning when the universal (*jāti*) has been manifested by a single sound (*dhvani*) once.
Since that [nature] of his is of such a kind—rendered difficult to discern—it is manifested even further by other phonemes possessing identical powers.

[Objection: In that case, whether it be that very [entity] or another single entity, when it is repeated again and again, its manifestation does not recur, because there is no distinction [between the instances].

Moreover, its manifestation in the form of the impressions of objects and sense-faculties within the mind—which bears the appearance of those [objects and faculties]—must be negated, just like [the manifestation of] color-forms.
Therefore, that cognition which is the final among all the letters and which occurs prior to the cognitions of the sequence is the cause of the cognition of the meaning.
When the final phoneme is cognized, a recollection of all the phonemes arises simultaneously, produced by the impressions of all [the preceding ones].
This mental cognition that arises from a synthesis [of all objects] is accepted by all proponents, even when all objects are already known in their sequential order.

If it were not admitted that, with respect to things perceived in succession, that cognition of a collection (*samuccaya-jñāna*) whose nature consists of a hundred or more [letters] would never arise;
for if, even so, there were a cognition of the letters by means of the ear and the mind following the prior sequence, then subsequently there would be a simultaneous recollection (*smaraṇa*).

Therefore, because the phonemes (*varṇa*) have ascended to the comprehension of that meaning (*tadarthāvabodhana*), they are not far [from it]; thus, the cognition (*mati*) is designated by worldly people as "derived from the word" (*śabda*).
All this is logically consistent with consciousness possessing an aspect; for otherwise, how could those [objects] that have perished appear in memory?

Now, if the phonemes (*varṇas*), which were previously known as manifest entities (*vyaktayas*), are remembered even while remaining in a state of concealment (*tirobhūta*), then it would follow by implication that they possess a clear appearance (*spaṣṭābhā*).

Stability [of that cognition] has already been refuted; therefore, in the case of its stability, recollection would arise at the time [of the subsequent cognition] due to the single cause consisting of the experience of the color-cognition.

However, we do not at all prevent the identity of the cognition (*ekamatitva*) [with the object], on the grounds that "the cow" is the cognition and that there is oneness of the word with the apprehended object and with its single referent.

That [word] might exist in the sound of a cow due to its rapidity and because there is little difference between it and the sounds of Devadatta and others; thus, the distinction [between them] is clearly perceived.

This cognition arising from the object is [the means of knowledge], because it arises immediately after the cognition of that [object]; for it is just like the cognition of fire from smoke and so forth.

A cognition (*dhīḥ*) that arises immediately after a sound possessing a distinct phoneme (*varṇa*)—which is not different from the appearance (*ābha*) of the object (*artha*) and the word (*śabda*)—is not found (*na vidyate*). Therefore, there is no other word (*śabdaḥ*) that exists as a signifier (*vācakaḥ*).

Consequently, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are everywhere determined (*viniścitau*) to be the two factors (*aṅgam*) for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). For it is by means of that [determination] that pervasion (*vyāptiḥ*) is ascertained (*niścitā*) here.
When the capacity to denote meaning has been established, and recognition and inference have been refuted as proofs for the eternality of the phonemes (*varṇa*), which are [in fact] non-eternal;
The objection raised out of ignorance regarding the contradictions in one's own statements and so forth—all of these exist in your own position concerning the eternal [word], because of that.
Thus, speech, being existent and eternal, is not logical as an indicator [of things], because it lacks connection with sequence and so forth, and because it is not perceived at all times.

That which is called the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the locus (*āśraya*) by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the distinction of the subject (*dharmin*) is due to ignorance of the definition of inference; for the status of being a subject (*dharmitva*) belongs only to that which appears [to consciousness].
That object which appears in cognition is well-known even to children and the like; therefore, it is stated that such an object alone possesses the status of being the subject (*dharmin*).
In this very context, this dispute has arisen among the proponents; however, there is no dispute for anyone regarding a distinction created by mere whim.
Therefore, when [the object] is indicated as being without distinction, the conceptualization of a specific [quality] contradicts the very operation of every inference.

The cognition thus produced by the injunction is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is being generated by causes that are devoid of defects such as error and the like; so it is conceived (*vikalpyate*).

If this position—that cognition is produced by an eternal injunction that is eternally connected to an eternal object—is maintained, then the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) follows with respect to the opponent. Furthermore, regarding its eternity: is it identity with that [previous state], or difference from it? If there is the cessation of that previous state, what indeed is intended to be established as remaining constant?

When this reason (*hetu*) is formulated as "being exclusively perceptible" (*kevala-aundriyakatva*), no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is perceived through the universal (*jāti*), which has already been refuted.
The cause appearing as sensory cognition would be sensory; for that has been established [to be so] regarding eternal things, and thus causality does not exist in the eternal.

This well-known fact—that such a thing is the cause of all [cognitions] of this kind—would otherwise be the same as this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) everywhere, even in the case of smoke and so forth, and in the case of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and the like; for us, it would not be established that these possess the capacity to initiate a cognition immediately following an effort, nor would it belong to anything merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
Note: Read *siddhā na* instead of *na siddhā*.

The two cessations (*nirodhau*) are not accepted as having the nature of destruction (*nāśa-ātmake*), because analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodhaḥ*) is that which is disjunction (*visaṃyogaḥ*) from the contaminated (*sāsravaiḥ*) factors, taken individually (*pṛthak-pṛthak*).
Another [kind of] cessation is the absolute obstruction of arising through non-analytical [cessation]; therefore, those who pride themselves on their own false tenets float about.

The two—sound and destruction—are not invariably concomitant with effort, because they lack that intrinsic nature; [this is] due to the basis of knowledge such as a heap of potsherds, light, and so forth.
The duality of form belonging to a single intrinsic nature of an object has been refuted; therefore, it is not tenable that there exists within a jar a permanent part designated as "universal."

Impermanence alone is intended [as the probandum]; since the state of remaining as it is (*tādavasthya*) is what is to be negated by way of being the probandum, a lamp and so forth are clearly the illustrative examples (*udāharaṇa*) in that case.
Furthermore, the perishability of flames and the like at every moment is not unestablished; in that case, the light constituent parts go to another location quickly.
A mass of condensed brilliance remains in that place where it exists; as long as it moves upward, so long is it understood to be a flame.
That which moves away from it, even though it possesses its own nature of light, is not perceived because of its subtlety when it moves beyond it.
The preceding [parts] do not proceed because they are obstructed by the subsequent parts in the path; just as the preceding ones release [their hold], so do the subsequent ones proceed.

There is no possibility of the occurrence of these [powers] during the transition [into fire], nor in grass and such; therefore, this is merely a product of imagination (*kalpanā-mātra*), because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated.
Furthermore, if there were an unimpeded conjunction of the powers residing in grass, cotton, and so forth, this consequence—that burning would occur—would not cease, just as in the previous case.
Otherwise, what kind of eternal nature could that [nature] have when the distinction between the capable and the incapable intrinsic nature is established among those [things]?
The eternality of the relation has already been refuted; therefore, by the principle that [the relation] is without cause, the eternality of the sentence is not tenable.
Of which sentence is the eternity of the self—consisting merely of the sequence of phonemes—or of that which is distinct from it, accepted?
Of phonemes that are devoid of sequence, no expressive power is found; therefore, such as they are, they do not constitute a sentence, nor is any sequence found among them.

Because these [entities] are all-pervasive (*vyāpti*) and eternal (*nityatva*), neither sequence (*krama*) in terms of time (*kāla*) nor space (*deśa*)—such as that of letters (*lipi*), fruits (*phala*), flowers (*puṣpa*), and so forth—is logically possible (*upapadyate*).
Furthermore, if their sequence were inherent (*svābhāvika*), it would necessarily exist; however, this cannot be the case, because it contradicts the established nature of sequence.
The phonemes beginning with *repha* and others, though situated at the end, do not indeed arise for yogins from another sequence of air; they are described as being eternal through their oneness.

Otherwise, the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) stated by you as the proof (*sādhana*) for [the soul's] permanence (*nityatva*) and unity (*ekatva*) would be fallacious (*vyabhicārin*), because it occurs even when there is difference (*bheda*).
The sequence [of phonemes] is not the sentence, because it excludes the manifestation [of meaning]; therefore, eternality does not logically follow from its being a sentence.
Just as words such as *vṛddhi* and others are understood to have meanings created by [human] will, so too are words such as *svarga* and *yāga* considered to be [of the same nature].

In the case of [works] such as the *Utpādya*—namely, dramas (*nāṭaka*), narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), and the like—the relationship between word and meaning is not intended to be real, eternal, or permanent;
even there, the eternality of the capacity (*śakti*) exists only through the force of the author's injunction (*niyoga*), which gives rise to the illusion of eternality regarding that capacity.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no external object there? Where, then, is the manifestation (*vyakti*) imagined (*prakalpyate*) with respect to the referent (*arthe*)? If it is argued that [it exists] in the reflection (*pratibimba*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then the same may be suspected (*śaṅkyate*) regarding the Veda (*vede*) as well.
Who can resort to a power that is connected with objects beyond the senses? Therefore, even in the Veda, an injunction dependent on a person cannot be postulated.
There is no understanding [of it] from the elders; for they themselves are established as being ignorant. However, comprehension arises from an exposition based on a person.
[Objection: Is this objection not equally applicable even to the case of a scripture that is a product? For [trust] does not arise therein either through faith or through doubt regarding the meaning.

When an object is present and pure, [it is known] through perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*); however, it is not so in the case of Vedic speech (*śabda*), because that [Vedic word] is self-evident (*svayaṃ-pratyaya*).
N.B.: Read *na tvevam* instead of *na hyevam* or *nanvevam*.
Thus, this [point] described by others here is irrelevant, since they have failed to consider the Dharma that is equal to the Veda in its production of meaning through discourse.

If one were to abandon the beginninglessness of the relationship between word and meaning, there would be no other cause for that beginningless relationship; therefore, no beginning of the relationship exists in the Veda.

Furthermore, an inference [based on] the absence of a creator of the relationship is impossible because it lacks a means [of proof]; however, an inference [based on] the non-explanation [of the relationship] is contradicted by what is actually perceived.
Furthermore, the means [of proof] being observed again and again among the elders—[namely], "it is thus"—is not established in relation to comprehension.

If this entire [Veda] were to be considered as such, provided that its meaning regarding the Vedas were established as non-contradictory even by the elders; otherwise, there would be a loss [of validity].

No counter-proof whatsoever is possible for the reason consisting of "being a composite" (*saṅghātatva*) and so forth, because it is pervaded by the established [conclusion] that [all things] are included within everything.
Thus, the phonemes (*varṇāḥ*), which possess meaning, have distinct referents, and are designated as being associated with specific sequences, are declared to be aggregates of words and sentences.
The possession of a meaningful, distinct, and logical sense in sequence is negated in the case of [the Veda's] being authorless; therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) remains unimpaired.

However, there is no such certainty regarding the pervasion in the case of the "recitation of the Veda" (*vedādhyayana*). Consequently, in this proof (*sādhana*), the negative concomitance (*vyatirekitva*) is clearly doubtful.
When certainty regarding a person is established, yet there is an incapacity for such an effect in that kind of sequence, then this pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot at all be ascertained here.
There could indeed be certainty regarding all phenomena when there is the direct perception of every person; this [certainty] is possible for an omniscient one.

It is clearly conceivable that the Veda possesses the character of being human-authored (*pauruṣeyatā*), because it contains false statements regarding desire, ritual action, injury to living beings, and untruth; likewise, qualities such as difficulty of pronunciation, lack of accentuation, obscurity, and unpleasantness to the ear—which are characteristics of the Veda—are indeed observed even in the words of atheists (*nāstika*) and others.

Whatever [is observed] as real—such as the disappearance of poison and so forth—is seen even in the recitation of mantras like that of Vainateya; yet, nothing whatsoever produced by human effort, even that which is Buddhist, can be inferred by this method, because [it is merely] speech.
Because it has the nature of form (*rūpatva*), that which is manifested from it is its own; and there also arises a memory (*smṛti*) of the agent, which is based upon the object (*arthanibandhana*).

If this is not accepted by the opponents (*paraiḥ*) in the case of an equal logical principle (*nyāye tulye*), why is it not considered so? Or let there be no desire for the opponent’s position; nevertheless, it is suspected to be so on the basis of that same logic.

"And (ca) men (puruṣāḥ), being for the most part (prāyeṇa) speakers of falsehood (anṛta-vādinaḥ) at all times (sarvadā eva), just as there is no confidence (na viśrambhaḥ) in them today (adyatve), so too [there is none] regarding the recounting (kīrtane) of past (atīta) events (artha)."
By this aforementioned reasoning, no author whatsoever is established anywhere in any treatise, even while one is speaking of one's own composition.
Therefore, let this hope for [the truth of] non-human [authoritative scriptures] be abandoned; for in those [scriptures], the meanings are presented in a manner contrary to the meaning of the Veda.

Moreover, in this way, beginninglessness (*anāditā*) would be established; however, it would not have a non-human basis (*anarāśraya*), or else, since it is uncreated (*akṛtakatve*), something else (*anya*) might also be uncreated.

For instance, the linguistic conventions (*vyavahārāḥ*) of the Pārasīkas and others have a foreign basis (*parāśrayāḥ*), and the doctrines (*siddhāntaḥ*) of the nihilists (*nāstikānām*) are based on external mental formations (*bhāvikaḥ saṃskāraparaḥ*).

Even if such a state of being without an author were established, what benefit would there be for you? For this entire effort of yours is directed toward proving [the Vedas'] lack of falsehood (*avaitathya*), their temporality (*kālatva*), their being produced by a person (*puruṣatva*), and so forth; yet [these arguments] are of doubtful validity (*vyatirekitā*) because, as in previous cases, the incapacity of men (*narāṇām aśakteḥ*) to produce [such works] has not been demonstrated.

Since manifestation (*vyakti*) has been refuted, let the speaker (*vaktṛ*) be understood as the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, in both types of formal argument (*prayoga*), the example (*nidarśana*) stated is empty of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Because [the Veda] depends upon human instruction and because it establishes what is produced, the independence of the speaker regarding its own meaning does not exist in either the subject (*dharmin*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Furthermore, if the sentence were eternal, since it would lack the quality of being produced, the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the [reason] would be clearly perceived even in the case of both the subject and the example.
Thus, as long as the authorlessness of the Vedic injunction remains undetermined, there is a defect—namely, the fallacy of being "doubtful" or "unestablished"—in the latter reasons as well;
and once the destruction of momentariness has been proven, the Veda is clearly sublated. Therefore, how can there be any conviction in that [authorlessness]?

The person (puruṣa) mentioned in the Veda (śruti) is not destroyed (na śīryate); no sublation (bādhā) of him has been stated (uditā) previously; thus, his lack of proof (asiddhatā) is very clear (su-vyaktā).
He for whom there is direct perception of another time, place, person, or like the *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of the hand—by him, this absence of sublation (*abādha*) is determined therein.
Therefore, when the meaning of the form remains unperceived by men, there is an attachment—just as among the Persians—to their own custom regarding that which exists in darkness.
And thus, these people, unaware of that meaning, engage in the defilement of harming living beings and so forth, due to the outflow of evil.

Therefore, the validity (*pramāṇatā*) of injunctions (*codanānām*) with respect to dharma (*dharmam*) is not established, because it cannot be determined (*anavadhāraṇāt*) either intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or by others who are dull-witted (*mandebhyaḥ*).

Therefore, let it be accepted that the person who composes the Veda is one who dwells within darkness, from whom light and knowledge have been cast out, and who provides instruction regarding objects that are [otherwise] obscure.
And thus, when the human origin of the Vedas has been established, their intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is also refuted without effort.
What meaning is intended by you for this statement? Let it be understood that the validity of all means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

The power (*śakti*) residing in the cognizer, the object of cognition (*meyādi*), and so forth, is indeed their inherent (*svābhāvikī*) power; for a power that does not exist by itself (*svataḥ*) cannot be produced by another.
Independence alone is the sole basis for validity; if dependence were resorted to, that [validity] itself would be destroyed.

Who, as a proponent of logic (*nyāya-vādī*), would assert (*adhyavasyati*) a thesis (*pakṣam*) that destroys (*haram*) the very root (*mūla-*) by which even the means (*upāyaḥ*) for its establishment (*siddhi-*) perishes (*vinaśyati*) through his own statement (*uktyā*)?
Validity is not established anywhere as being dependent on something else; and since there is no fixed cause, who will establish the probandum?
If it is argued that such is the case, then surely the non-distinctive potency of all word-meanings has already been demonstrated previously.

Power (*śakti*) is said to be its own nature (*svarūpa*), which is capable of the desired effect. In the absence of that [nature], because it would lack the essence of being an entity (*bhāva-ātmatā*), that entity (*bhāva*) would not be an agent (*kāraka*).
How can such a power of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which is impermanent, yet arises from its own causes and strength—be asserted by you to be intrinsic (*svābhāvikī*)?

In the case of inherence (*svābhāvikī*), there would necessarily be either eternality or causelessness of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of their identity (*tādātmya*) with it; thus, both eternality and causelessness [would follow].

If there were no cause, then [an entity] would either always exist or never exist, because it would not depend on anything else; therefore, it is logical that an effect is dependent upon that [cause], and not that it occurs only occasionally.

The nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is observed to be occasional; it is indeed an effect. Therefore, for you, their capacity (*śakti*) is logical [only as something produced], not as inherent (*svābhāvikī*).

The intrinsic nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) attains manifestation (*vyakti*) through manifestors (*vyañjaka*); and that [nature], being dependent on other conditions (*pratyaya*), initiates an effect (*kārya*).
Since [the individual] depends on other causes [that are] distinct [from it], therefore, for those things that are assisted by it, there would be a constant perception of that [individual].
Let there be distinctness, or even the nature of both; nevertheless, that cognition itself would be eternal, for it is conjoined with an eternal power.
Otherwise, it could not be eternal, because of its lack of uniformity; for it might at one time be connected with the cognition of that [object], and not at another.

Now, the capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from their own causes; however, once they have been produced from their own causes, no further capacity can be imparted to them by others.
There is no dispute for us on this point; for who could possibly attribute a capacity to a partless entity that arises subsequently from its own cause?
That form which is subsequently attributed by others—that alone is the interval of existence; thus, its self is not taught.

The distinctness of things is stated [to exist] upon the accomplishment of contradictory properties; since that [distinctness] does not exist when they are unaccomplished, it exists even in the case of potentiality.
Since all things have been established as being subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), nothing whatsoever has the capacity to produce any further effect within them.
They have no abiding beyond [this], by which they might obtain power from within a causal condition for some result whatsoever.
These wise followers of the Sugata say here: even this much [of a self] which exists in some way within cognition cannot be understood by itself.
Who indeed is the master capable of determining from the mere nature of experience alone the capacity [of that experience] to cognize an object as it actually exists,

such that this very nature of experience would exist even in a vision of a mass of hair and the like, which, though appearing clearly with distinct forms, is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*)?

Therefore, it is cognition (*jñāna*)—whether it be that which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) or something else—that is required for ascertainment (*niścaya*), but not for the production (*ādhāna*) of this [ascertainment], just like poison and so forth. For, from the observation of the similarity between that [poison] and another [substance], there is an absence of the immediate occurrence of the result (*phalānantaratā*), and because of this [absence], there is no certain determination of its nature (*etadātman-viniścaya*).

Identity (*tādātmyam*) is also understood (*gamyate*) through the arising of its effects, such as fainting, perspiration, delirium, and so forth; thus, when there is knowledge of that capacity (*tac-chakti-jñāne*), certainty (*niścayaḥ*) [is attained].

Furthermore, the validity (*prāmāṇyam*) [of perception] is undisputed (*avivādam*); the definition (*lakṣaṇam*) of capacity must be determined (*niśceyam*) by another means of valid cognition (*antara-pramāṇa-*)—for it has been stated by you (*tvayā*) in this very way (*iti evam*).

Thus, since all capacities (*śakti*) of all things (*bhāva*) are the means of proof (*sādhana*) for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), how is it that what is established by presumptive testimony is not established from something else (*parataḥ*)?

Thus, since validity (*prāmāṇya*) is partless in nature and is produced from its own causes, there is no destruction [of it]; nor is another means of knowledge (*antara-pramā*) required for its ascertainment (*niścaya*), because that [ascertainment] does not depend on anything else. However, for the sake of the realization (*pratipatti*) of its own nature (*tad-svabhāva*), it does depend on [another means of knowledge].

Furthermore, in this way, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would also follow as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*). For its occurrence (*sambhava*) from itself (*svataḥ*) [would imply] that it could arise from anything whatsoever;
indeed, independence (*anapekṣatva*) alone is the sole ground for invalidity. All such [objections] can be stated here as well.
Just as the capacity for non-discrepancy is to be determined from another source, so too is the capacity for correspondence; therefore, in every respect, the two are equal.
(Note: read *niśceyam* for *niścayam*).

Under these circumstances, what excellence (*atiśaya*) of validity (*prāmāṇya*) is observed through its contrast (*viparyaya*), by virtue of which that [validity] alone is held to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*), whereas invalidity (*aprāmāṇatā*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*)?

Nevertheless, because this validity [of cognitions] is described as being due to the means of valid cognition themselves, it is accepted that there is an intrinsic operation of those [cognitions] toward their own effects once they have arisen.
It is maintained that there is a dependence on a cause for the existence of entities; however, once they have acquired their own nature, they proceed spontaneously toward their respective effects.

Therefore, cognitions have dependence (*vyapekṣā*) upon their own causes (*sva-hetuṣu*) merely for their arising (*utpatti-mātre*); however, they do not [depend on them] for the production (*janmani*) of their own certainty regarding qualities (*sva-guṇeṣu*).

For when the production of the determination of validity (*viniściteḥ prāmāṇya-artha*) occurs, those [cognitions], being independent (*svatantrāṇām*) and indifferent (*nirapekṣāṇām*) toward their own causes, function (*vṛttiḥ*) just like jars and other such objects.
At its production, a jar depends (*apekṣate*) upon a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, and so forth; however, for its fetching of water, it has no dependence (*apekṣā*) on those [same things].

For indeed, at the end [of its utility], that very self-validity (*svataḥ-pramāṇatva*) necessarily follows as contingent upon another (*parādhīna*), which results in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If you desire that the fundamental validity [of cognition] should have its proof established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then we would not obtain a firm position for you in this regard.
Just as the first cognition requires corroboration with that [second], so too must that [first] cognition be sought through corroboration by another.
If the validity of something were held to be intrinsic, for what reason would there be such hostility toward the first [case]?
Likewise, if validity were dependent upon perception and so forth, and if those qualities never exist without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [then how could it be intrinsic?]
Furthermore, even for one who desires that [cognition] to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its status as such depends upon another determining quality (*guṇa*).

Just as it was in the first case, so it would be in other cases; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, we would not obtain a stable determination (*vyavasthā*) anywhere.

If it is not accepted that knowledge possesses validity dependent upon excellences (*guṇa*), then even the initial cognition of an object would not require excellence as a means of valid cognition (*pramā*).

Therefore, even if one were to go far, that intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) which must necessarily be admitted somewhere is better established right there at the outset. Or else, by what superior power of corroboration (*saṃvāda-vijñāna*) or excellence (*guṇa-bala*) is the dependence of the first [cognition] upon that [subsequent one] established?

Therefore, validity is established as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in all cases; it is that which is normally the rule (*autsargika*), and it is set aside (*apohyate*) by two [factors]: sublation (*bādha*) and knowledge of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇa-duṣṭatva-jñāna*).

Furthermore, since this [invalidation] depends on another [means of valid cognition], there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*); for this [invalidation] is dependent upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-adhīna*), and that [means of valid cognition] is itself established intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
Just as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established by another means of valid cognition, so too invalidity (*apramāṇatva*) is not established by that which is itself invalid.

For when there is a basis of the same kind (*sajātīya*), no firm foundation is possible; however, it is firmly established through a different kind (*vijātīya*), because it has a different cause (*hetu*).

The subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) is, for its part, the definitive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) of the object's difference [from others], because it possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*) independently [of anything else]; it sublates (*apohate*) the preceding cognition (*pūrva-jñāna*).
Furthermore, even in that case, there might be an expectation of an exception in some instances where there is a suspicion arising from what has preceded; yet even that is removed by a small amount.

If a sublater (*bādhaka*) has arisen for one who is searching for another [sublater], then the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) belongs to the middle [cognition] precisely by virtue of the sublation of the preceding one. On the other hand, if a correct search is made with appropriate effort and no sublater is found, it is because of the absence of a root-sublater (*mūla-bādhaka*).

Therefore, because it is free from contradiction, that very stronger [cognition] sublates the first one; by that [sublation], its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is indeed set aside. Thus, the triad consisting of the cognition, the examiner, and the object is not bypassed. Consequently, since there is no sublation of what has not arisen, a further sublater is not to be suspected.
He who, out of delusion, might imagine even an unarisen sublater, he would go to destruction in all worldly transactions characterized by doubt.
And likewise, O Kaunteya, Vāsudeva has censured this state of being characterized by doubt; for there is neither this world nor the next for one whose self is possessed of doubt.

Therefore, in whatever measure an exception (*apavāda*) is conceived (*sambhāvyate*) within that very cognition (*mate*), when that much alone has been sought and no such [exception] has arisen within its own nature (*ātmani*).
The cognizers, reflecting further upon that very object, should not remain with their desires; this might even be so at some time.

Those distinctions of place, time, person, and state which are established merely through conventional usage and must be taken into account by an inquirer due to sublation—because they are situated at a distance, when there is no correct perception, there may arise some suspicion regarding them; in that case, [the remedy] is simply going near.
The limit [consisting of] time, persons, and circumstances does not exist in other cases; however, dependence is found there, as in the case of the cognition of a mirage and the like.
(Textual variant: *tasmin*)

Thus, that which is the ascertainment (*nirṇaya*)—the limit (*avadhi*) for the removal of doubt (*saṃśaya*) regarding cows, horses, and so forth, arising from delusion (*bhrānti*) in deep darkness—is the manifestation of light (*bhavanaprakāśī*) therein.

For indeed, when there is error (*anyathātva*) concerning the moon, confusion regarding the directions, colors, accents, the Vedas, and so on, the definitive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) arises from questioning another person (*antarapuruṣa*).

Because there is an absence of that [cognition] when the object is being known—[an object] which is difficult to discern due to the senses being impaired by passion, hatred, pride, insanity, hunger, thirst, and so forth, and which is [thereby] perceived erroneously.
In a legal proceeding concerning a debt or similar matter between two disputing parties, there shall be one statement from the defendant and two statements from the plaintiff.
For fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), no further statement is recorded; rather, the master, the witness, and the members of the court shall deliver the verdict.
In this manner, such a transformation of the triad of cognitions is accepted everywhere; for this very reason, even the "threefold truth" (*tri-satyatā*) of the gods is proclaimed.

If validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) even for both [validity and invalidity]. Therefore, since validity and invalidity are established according to their respective application,
that statement which is determined to be either eternal or composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) is not contradicted in the slightest.
We, who are the teachers of knowledge and fellow students, by warding off destruction, are capable there of protecting such [works].
Therefore, the statement is neither corrupted by the prohibited defects, nor—since there is an absence of an agent—are those defects without a substratum.

In that regard, two things have been observed from what was stated: that which consists of the absence of faults and the presence of qualities, just as validity exists; it has been declared that [validity] does not [arise] from qualities.
Therefore, because the speaker possesses excellence, faults are excluded; and that sentence is established as valid by itself, being characterized by the absence of defects.
If the absence of defects in the words of a trustworthy person is understood from their qualities, then that very same [infinite regress] would follow for one who pursues the possession of qualities.
This fault does not apply to knowledge; at that time, qualities are certainly not required to be perceived, nor are they beneficial there by virtue of being known.
By that alone, all of us are capable of turning away from faults; while those faults exist, knowledge regarding an object characterized by human defects does not arise.
Because it is being cognized by defects, its validity is not sublated; that which is established as unsublated remains self-evident even in this case.

In the case of that which is of human origin, it is suspected (*śaṅkyate*) that "there exist defects" (*santi doṣāḥ*); however, in the Veda, because there is no author (*abhāvāt kartuḥ*), there is indeed no suspicion for us (*nāsty eva na āśaṅkā*).

Therefore, that which is said to be the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda because of its independence (*anapekṣatva*), is established all the more easily (*sutarām*) as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) even in the case of [a text] composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*).

By that very fact, namely the non-concordance with other means of valid cognition at all times regarding the subject matter of this Veda, its status as a means of valid cognition is established; otherwise, it would be a mere restatement.

Concomitance (*saṅgati*) is certainly not the cause for the validity (*pramāṇatva*) of another [cognition] as well; for among things that have the same object (*tulyārtha*), validity belongs to only one through conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, where there might be a determination by subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), surely even there that object has not been clearly ascertained by the preceding one.
Validity would not exist with respect to an object that has already perished; furthermore, auditory cognition would be invalid, as it lacks connection with the eyes and other [senses].

If the validity of this [Veda] is established through its connection with knowledge other than auditory perception, then since it is also connected with another cognition produced by that [same cause], there exists a single cognition of both; it is not produced by a different means. Therefore, a correspondence based on a cause other than [the Veda] itself is not desired.

Just as in the case of perception, the cause—namely, the conjunction dependent on another consciousness and a single sense organ—is stated, so too let it be declared that [this cause] is established even in the Veda.
When [the fact] is being obtained by a single sentence alone regarding time, place, person, and so forth, no further cause for the correspondence of the meaning need be sought.
Therefore, that firm cognition which has arisen and does not contradict other cognitions regarding place and so forth is undoubtedly a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The validity (*pramāṇatā*) of words and so forth is not to be established by inference (*anumānena*), lest it [validity] also be established by inference for perception (*pratyakṣasya*) as well, without distinction.

If the validity (*pramāṇatva*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established (*sādhyate*) by another [means of valid cognition], then for that [second one] as well, because it must be established, there follows an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to its being established by yet another.

If the validity of the means of proof were to exist without being established by another, then that [validity] would indeed be established; likewise, the objects to be proven would also [be established] from that.
[Objection: Perception and the other [means of knowledge] are not apprehended as being "thus" [i.e., as valid]; and if they are not apprehended in this way, worldly practice cannot be accounted for.

Because it was apprehended previously, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established in its own form; and with respect to its own object, being independent once the object has been cognized, it is measured (*mīyate*) by others.
Just as all objects are perceived by the sense organs, such as the eye and others, even though they themselves are unknown, so too are those [objects] by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In this case, being known (*jñāyamānatva*) is not required (*na upayujyate*) for validity (*prāmāṇye*); rather, even the experience (*anubhava*) of the object (*viṣaya*) is obtained (*labhyate*) from this very [cognition] when it is unknown (*ajñātāt*).
A valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [which is] again established as invalid (*apramāṇa*) with respect to its own object—its falsity would not be apprehended without another valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Otherwise, the alteration of the object is not apprehended by what precedes it, just as its state of being so [is not]; therefore, even here, there is cognition of an alteration, or else [it occurs] when the cause is defective.
To that extent, falsity is apprehended; it is not caused by anything else. This very state of arising is measured as "this is a valid means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, even where falsity is demonstrated to others, there too this pair must be stated; however, it is not the similarity [of the subject] with the mother.
Those who are unwise, relying on a mere semblance of similarity with invalid cognition, falsely establish the falsity of all valid cognitions.
(Note: read *ye* for *yat*).

The construction of such a proof for them is indeed produced for the destruction of their own self, even with respect to another, by means of a reflection; and because it is refuted by that [reflection], a proof that is not as it truly is is not capable of subverting an injunction, since [the injunction] possesses the status of a general authority (*autsargika-pramāṇatva*).
To this it is replied: But surely, this systematic arrangement of those entities is held to have a basis; their stability is thus maintained.
(Note: read *bhāvānām* instead of *jñānānām* or *jñātānām*).

[The existence] of things such as the self (*ātman*) is accepted (*iṣyate*) upon their acquisition (*lābhe*); for those things that have acquired their own nature (*labdhātmanām*), there is simply (*eva*) a dependence (*apekṣitā*) on causes (*kāraṇa*) for their own activity (*pravṛttiḥ*) toward their own effects (*svakāryeṣu*).

As for that knowledge which you also maintain to be unstable, occurring immediately after the birth of a non-existent thing that has subsequently acquired its own nature—what kind of activity could it possibly possess?
The operation of causes is observed to be distinct from their arising; thus it is intended [to be said] that this may not be the case even with respect to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That [cognition] does not exist even for a moment, nor does it arise as something that is non-valid (*apramā*), by which it might subsequently be employed in the apprehension of an object, just like the sense organs and so forth.
If, moreover, knowledge is admitted to be non-momentary and eternal, this is a contradiction of what has been accepted; thus there is a sublation by means of reasoning.

Since every established thing (*vastu*) has been demonstrated in detail to be subject to momentary destruction (*bhaṅga*), and since that which is eternal is not produced (*na janyate*), what need is there for a cause (*kāraṇa*) for it?
Therefore, it is possible to say that [valid cognition] does not exist by itself; subsequently, it does not function toward its own effects because of its lack of form, just like a sky-lotus.

Let it be that cognition is indeed free from apprehension (*nirākāṅkṣa*) and proceeds spontaneously (*svataḥ*) for the sake of determining its own validity (*svaprāmāṇya-viniścayāya*). Why, then, [should there be] doubt and the like?
Because the certainty regarding validity is intrinsic (*bhāvika*) therein; when that [certainty] alone has arisen, doubt and error have no footing (*anāspadau*) in it.
Because of the existence of the superimposition of certainty upon the two minds, when there is a distinction between the sublater and the object of sublation, every certainty occurs.
And therefore, for the sake of establishing that cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is valid, an argument arising from a reason devoid of defects is useless.
If it is maintained that [intrinsic validity] is the remover of objections, even so, that is not the case because such a suspicion is impossible.
That suspicion exists only as long as the certainty has not arisen; once that certainty has occurred, how indeed could there be this [suspicion] regarding its lack of validity?

The effort made for the sake of excluding that [other possibility] would indeed attain its purposeful significance; for one who has ascertained identity with the post does not suspect it to be otherwise.

When a firm conviction (*niścayaḥ*) arises regarding a certain form (*yat-rūpa*) in a particular object (*yatra vastuni*), because it is the removal of that very doubt (*śaṅkāyāḥ*) and its opposite (*viparyaya-viparyaya*), it follows from that alone—just as the existence (*astitā*) of fire (*pāvaka*) and so forth is understood from signs such as smoke (*dhūma*) and so forth—that the non-existence (*nāstitā*) of that [opposite] is established (*upapadyate*); thus, the exclusion (*vyavacchedaḥ*) [of the opposite] occurs from that very [conviction].

Thus, let it be accepted that the exclusion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) itself is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Therefore, for the sake of removing invalidity, a means of proof (*sādhana*) is not appropriate.

If, however, there were a suspicion of the two types of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), then there would be no certainty regarding validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*), because that which was made an object by cognitions (*pratyaya*) produced through error—
namely, doubt (*saṃdeha*) and misconception (*viparyāsa*)— would, at that time, lack certainty regarding its nature, just like [the cognition of] a post (*sthāṇu*).

Just as a post, fire, an invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), and so forth, are determined by others through cognitions arising from [the presence of] a crow, smoke, defects, and causes; and since that which has become the object of doubt and error must be understood [as such], the certainty regarding its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

Your position is that where there is the direct hearing (*śruti*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) in a sentence, there alone is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of another [object], while elsewhere it is only its own nature (*svātmā*) that is understood.

The cognition "this is [the case] here" produced by an injunction (*codanā*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). There is no application of the negative particle (*nañ*), and therefore there is no exclusion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
Furthermore, if the validity of all means of valid knowledge were determined to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then for what reason would there be a difference of opinion among the various proponents?

Some [people] say that the restriction (*niyama*) is "from itself alone" (*svata eva*), while others maintain that there is no restriction (*aniyama*), [asserting that] something may be "from itself" (*svataḥ*) and also "from another" (*anyataḥ*).
Since the dispute arises from error, and that [error] is sublated by certainty, therefore the disputants, ascertaining the reality, would not engage in dispute.

If the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established through itself (*svataḥ*), then no one would ever be subject to contradiction (*visaṃvāda*), since [contradiction] occurs when there is a functioning based on what is not a valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). However, through the understanding that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), no one would be deceived; nor would anyone be mistaken.

But surely, that which has arisen without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇataḥ*) encounters contradiction; for its ascertainment (*niścayaḥ*) is held to be dependent upon another, namely, a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*).
That which has proceeded from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not incur contradiction (*visaṃvāda*), and we maintain that its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is indeed intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

This is because [the validity] is not due to a lack of awareness of the speaker’s intention (*abhiprāya*); for in this determination (*viniścaya*), this [intrinsic nature] belongs to the validity of all means of valid cognition.

Where there is no certainty regarding intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is understood by force of the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) in that case, through the absence of dependence on the cognition of the object being otherwise (*arthānyathātva*), due to the ascertainment of the causes arising from defects (*doṣa*). Therefore, immediately after its production, [invalidity is established].
Therefore, the validity [of cognition] is not logically consistent with error; for this very reason, nothing at all would proceed from a non-discrepant cognition of that [object].
Furthermore, no time for action exists apart from the time of the arising of the jar and so forth, because of their momentariness; thus, the illustrative example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For those who do not depend on others, such as potters and the like, subsequent to [the production of the object], there is no need for dependence on a potter or similar agents; rather, because they depend on their own material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth, the operation [of the means of knowledge] occurs by itself (*svataḥ*).

Furthermore, since it does not depend on another, there is no resulting infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). Therefore, the certainty of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) exists in the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

[Objection: What excellence (*atiśaya*) does it possess over its preceding [cognition], such that it is not accepted as being like the previous cognition? It is said that "conformity with the object" (*saṃvāda-vastu*) is designated as its "validity" (*prāmāṇya*); and yet, there is no characteristic of it other than the cognition of the appearance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Note: Read *arthakriyābhāsajñānāt* for *arthakriyābhyāsajñānāt*.

And the cognition (*jñāna*), which has the appearance (*avabhāsa*) of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), is clearly experienced (*saṃvedyate*) and ascertained (*niścīyate*) by the mind (*cetas*) that arises from the mere reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) of that [appearance].

Therefore, because its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is correctly ascertained by itself (*svataḥ*), no subsequent cognition (*uttara-pratyaya*) regarding the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-prāpti*) is required;

and even when that state of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-bhāva*) is manifested in the first cognition (*prathama-pratyaya*), the ascertainment of its validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*) arises from this very reason.

In the first case, regarding an object that is a non-entity (*avastu*), the second characteristic—namely, correspondence with a real entity (*vastu*)—would apply; however, for that reason, it cannot occur because such a cause is impossible.
(Note: Read *tasya*, not *yasya*, before *hetoḥ*.)
In the case of [objects] such as a flame, a cluster of flowers, or an *aśoka* tree, a cognition (*vijñāna*) that manifests (*nirbhāsi*) burning or cooking is never produced (*na jāyate*).

If it were produced, it would follow (*prasajyate*) that it is not of a different kind (*vijātīya*) from fire (*vibhāvasu*), because its characteristic is merely the capacity (*yogyatā-mātra*) for that effect (*tat-kārya*).

Therefore, as long as a cognition possessing the appearance of an object does not produce purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), so long is there a suspicion regarding the first [cognition] due to the cause of error (*bhrānti*).
The cause for this is the non-perception of the fruit immediately following the error, the perception of similarity, and the lack of acuity of the cognition, and so forth;
however, when a consciousness in which the effect appears has arisen, this [cause] does not exist, because there is the direct apprehension of the action bound to the object.

Even when the first fruit has not yet been attained, a distinction [of the cognition] from the knowledge of that which is not its object is perceived through the practice-endowed state (*vṛtti*). However, in the absence of the perception of such a distinction, there is no ascertainment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) without the suspicion of a heterogeneous object appearing as the effect [of the cognition].

Even in that case, its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇyam*) cannot be determined (*viniścetum*) while it exists; rather, it is cognized (*pratīyate*) solely from a subsequent cognition (*uttara-jñānāt*) regarding the initial action (*ādya-kriyā*).
Therefore, the first cognition requires confirmation by that [subsequent one]; likewise, a confirmation is not to be sought again by means of another confirmation.

The validity (*pramāṇatā*) of that [cognition] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), because of the non-existence of error (*bhrānti*) as the cause; for when there is the presence of such [intrinsic validity], error is impossible.
(N.B.: read *tathābhāve* rather than *tadābhāve*.)

[Objection: "If the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that cognition (*vijñāna*) is not yet ascertained, how could a discerning person (*prekṣāvān*) engage in it? For he has not yet attained what is desired. [Response: It is said: That wise man (*vicakṣaṇa*) indeed acts out of doubt (*saṃśaya*) alone; and thus, no loss of wisdom (*vaicakṣaṇya-kṣati*) follows for him.

Since the means for determining that validity (*tat-prāmāṇya*) consists in the ascertainment (*viniścaya*) [of it] through doubt (*saṃśaya*) regarding the activity (*vṛtti*), and since that [ascertainment] also exists when there is doubt—
if, upon activity accompanied by doubt, I were to obtain the result (*phala-prāpti*), then in that very case, the ascertainment of its validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*) would be known.
And since it is not otherwise, this inquiry is indeed logical here. Why does it proceed with respect to the means? For there is no other way;
for without the means, no one attains the goal. And even though [the means] has been undertaken, one does not abandon the state of being a discerning person.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a cognition appearing as [an object] capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) exists even in a dream? And yet, that [cognition] lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*), for that same reason as the first [case].
For indeed, all that state is erroneous and lacks any external basis; in those states, there is no correspondence with an external object.
Since they have their own cognized nature and are non-distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), even the distinction between the two states is clearly perceived.

It may be thought: "If [the validity] were determined extrinsically (*parataḥ*), then for that [validity], the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) would follow; surely this is not contradictory."

The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that [cognition] (*tasya*) is said (*gīyate*) to depend (*apekṣam*) upon the apprehension (*avagateḥ*) of the object (*vastu*) to be grasped (*grāhya*) by it; thus, its establishment (*vyavasthitiḥ*) as an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is not contradicted (*na virudhyate*). In this way, the distinction (*bheda*) between the state of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) and the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*)—based on their mutual dependence (*apekṣā*)—is like [the distinction between] the nature of a cause (*kāraṇatā*) and an effect (*kārya*), and so forth.

Thus it is established that in the determination of validity (*prāmāṇya-viniścaya*), there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because of the cessation of further expectation (*parākāṅkṣā-nivṛtti*) once the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) has arisen;
for even when a cognition has arisen, it is not ascertained (*avadhāryate*) until its purity (*śuddhatva*) regarding the cause is apprehended from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even the wise say that there is no infinite regress here, by which that purity is recognized through a non-dependent, concordant cognition.

Because [the cognition] is seen to have the same effect as a [verbal] report regarding a proximate object, its purity is understood with ease; for even when the object is remote, the cognition that arises is valid because it is produced by that very [same cause], just like this [cognition] which has a proximate object as its domain.

Just as, when a conch shell is present before one, through the attainment of the action to be accomplished—namely, whiteness—it is understood that the cognition is not produced by eyes affected by jaundice;
so too, when the purity of the cause has been thus perceived, whatever cognition of a yellow form might then arise regarding a conch shell made of gold.

The certainty of its validity (*prāmāṇya-niścayaḥ*) arises from the production of a pure cause, just as in the case of that cognition (*mateḥ*) which has the form of a white conch-shell (*ākāra-sita-kambau*), once the action to be accomplished (*niṣpādita-kriye*) has been performed.

Furthermore, the author of the *Bhāṣya* also stated this (*uktavān idam*) because of the absence of impairment by hunger and so forth (*anupaghāta-kṣud-ādi-vacanāt*). Therefore, the charge of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is raised here (*iha*) on account of delusion (*mohāt*).
The first [cognition] is not apprehended through doubt regarding its being produced by a defective cause; therefore, that cognition is considered to possess superior purity.

If the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of cognition is established as the general rule (*autsargika*) everywhere, then it is sublated by two cognitions—namely, the cognition of the cause of purity (*śuddhi-hetu-viniścaya*) and the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-jñāna*)—which function with respect to the object (*arthe*) and the purposeful action (*arthakriye*), and which are themselves uncontradicted (*akṛta-vṛtti*). Thus, that [self-validity] becomes inexpressible (*avācyā*).

Validity [is] attained due to the absence of sublation, the cognition [of a defect], and the state of being defective; and thus, for you, the ascertainment of validity would arise from something else.

Thus, this non-existence, which is the very essence of that [non-perception], is called "valid cognition" (*pramā*) in your view; however, in my view, it is called "inference" (*anumāna*) based on non-perception (*anupalambha*).
By this very same reasoning (*upapatti*), even invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) might be [established] intrinsically (*svataḥ*), since such a principle (*nyāya*) can be stated (*śakyate vaktum*).

Therefore, non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇyatva*), which is established as the general rule (*autsargika*) everywhere, is set aside (*apodyate*) by the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*) caused by defects (*duṣṭatva*).

Likewise, the non-authoritativeness of a cognition (*buddhi*) that has attained [its status] through its very nature of being a consciousness (*bodha*) is set aside by a cognition that accords with the object (*yathārthajñāna*), which arises from causes characterized by excellence (*guṇotthahetu*).

If validity depends on something else, there will indeed be an infinite regress; for this [validity] is dependent upon a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and that [means of knowledge] is itself not established intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
For you say: "Validity [is established] from the absence of a sublater; yet the absence of a sublater is also accepted as being designated as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

Its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is also stated [to be established] through the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*). Since that [absence] is perceived in every such case, there is no fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) whereby validity would be established independently of a sublater cognition; therefore, this [sublater cognition] does not at all negate the preceding cognition.

Moreover, if validity is accepted [only] in some cases on the grounds that there is no sublater (*bādhaka*), then what is the cause for this aversion toward the first [cognition] if it were likewise [valid]?

And if this subsequent cognition (*pratyaya*) sublates the preceding cognition because it is independent (*anapekṣa*) due to its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatvāt*), why would there be any suspicion regarding this [first cognition]?

It is suspected that here there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) independent of its being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*). For such a suspicion does not arise even with respect to the position (*pakṣa*) of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), because of the certainty [of it] by its own force (*sva-rasena*). Why, then, is an effort made for the sake of establishing the existence of a subverting factor?

In that case where there is no certainty regarding [the object of] pride by its own inherent force (*svarasena*), even a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is ascertained effortlessly through the force of implication (*sāmarthyāt*).

Therefore, why is it said that "the triad of cognitions exists here for the investigator"? Since [certainty] is established by itself (*svataḥ*) with respect to even a single [cognition], there is no room for [the other two].
Even if doubt arises from uncertainty regarding non-perception—since non-perception is not invariably concomitant with the absence of sublation.

(Being [the case], as in II C., n. 7th s. (from what, n. 5th s. (by you, 3rd s. (was made, m. 1st s. (satisfaction, m. 1st s. (in the triad, n. 7th s.); for even (*hi*) (*api*) (when there is non-perception, f. 7th s.), just as (*vat*) (in the case of) the prior (*pūrva-*) (sublation, f. 1st s.), (sublation) (*bādhā*) (might be suspected, *śaṅkyeta*, passive of *śaṅk*, *atra*).
As long as there is no correspondence with the effect, so long does the suspicion of sublation not cease; thus, the restriction regarding that triad is fruitless.
Furthermore, because of this, a sublater may again be suspected through a pretext; [therefore] the true nature of the object never remains established.
Knowledge that has arisen regarding a conch shell, appearing as yellow and devoid of any subverting cognition, does not indeed become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for as long as one lives.
A subverting [cognition] would not arise because of the absence of a cause for its purity, or due to some other cause; therefore, doubt does not cease.

Wherever this suspicion arises from delusion (*moha*), it is indeed accompanied by a cause; however, in the case of [perception] that is pure and consistent with reality, no suspicion would occur for one of sound intellect.
He is not born with doubt regarding the self in all worldly transactions, for his intellect is free from doubt upon seeing purity and consistency.
If anyone here, even one who is dull-witted, should entertain a doubt regarding this, I consider him to be possessed of a doubting nature, which is censured by the Unborn One.

When validity (*prāmāṇya*) is postulated as being determined (*niścaye*), there is clearly a dependence (*apekṣā*) upon differences of place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), person (*nara*), and state (*avasthā*). Therefore, the ascertainment (*niścitiḥ*) of validity must come from something else (*anyasmāt*)—namely, from the absence of sublation (*bādhā-abhāvāt*) when place, time, and so forth are well-ascertained (*su-niścitau*). Thus, the determination of validity arises from within the preceding cognition (*prāñce jñāne*) itself by means of the instrument of knowledge (*antaraḥ pramāṇa-*).

That legal proceeding concerning debts and so forth which possesses the threefold statement—that is its nature—and it should not be cited as an example in the context of the establishment of valid cognition (*pramā*).
In that matter, having reflected, the plaintiff and the defendant clearly obtain the ability to perform a subtle investigation regarding that matter.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established by way of the persistence of the object (*vastu*), but not through verbal quibble (*chala*). Therefore, worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is declared to be similar to that of ordinary people.

Even for the gods, the state of having three truths (*tri-satya-tā*) is itself the cause of certainty; for when there is an absence of certainty, that [certainty] arises from the first [truth], and even subsequently it is [derived] from the others.
By which [word], this [word], the two subsequent words, and that [word] belonging to it—since there is no cognition of the first [word], what distinction is there between those other two?

Therefore, by the aforementioned reasoning, there is an infinite regress in your position as well; thus, validity and the state of being a means of valid cognition are established according to their respective applications.

The statement that [the Veda] is eternal has already been refuted by us at length; furthermore, according to your own view, there exists no authoritative person (*āpta*) who has destroyed all defects.
Of what kind will that authoritative person be, who possesses an unexhausted accumulation of obscurations, such that his word might even be suspected of being otherwise?
Even when an authoritative person has arisen, by whom can that flood of qualities be known, such that there might be a definitive ascertainment of a statement composed by an authority?

Even if one who perceives that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya-dṛk*) were to behold his (*tadīya*) perfection of qualities (*guṇa-sampad*), what purpose (*kiṃ prayojanam*) would there be even for him (*tasya*) by means of the speech (*vacasā*) composed (*praṇītena*) by such a trustworthy person (*āpta*)?

He himself attains the meaning without expectation of [anything else] from the statement; however, another person, due to a lack of knowledge of the authoritative source (*āpta*), does not understand the meaning from that.
In the theory that validity is intrinsic, since the ascertainment [of validity] arises from its own nature, how could there be any purpose for the prevention of its arising and destruction?

The sentence (*vākya*) is not corrupted by faults (*doṣa*), since those [faults] have been refuted by excellences (*guṇa*); however, because of the lack of certainty regarding excellences, it is not possible to determine it with absolute certainty.
The fact that a sentence has no author was already refuted previously; therefore, in the absence of an author, there can be no faults that would otherwise lack a basis.
Just as it has been stated that validity arises from excellences (*guṇa*), so too, when excellences are not fully known, the absence of defects (*doṣa*) is not perceived.

It is not logical that a statement characterized by the absence of defects should be valid by itself; for the absence of defects is not a defining characteristic [of validity] due to its being unperceived.

If people do not recognize [the absence of defects], then the statement "this person is a staff-bearer" is not perceived as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by that [absence of defects] which is intrinsic (*svataḥ*); thus, [your position] is refuted.

The absence of defects is the defining characteristic of a sentence, which is of a determinate nature; because of the absence of valid cognition [of such defects], the establishment of valid cognition is therefore extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

When those [faults] exist, knowledge arises with respect to an object characterized by human faults; however, when there is an absence of faults, how indeed could cognition arise in the absence of faults?

The faults—hatred, delusion, and so forth—are sublated by compassion, wisdom, and the like. For if there were no certainty regarding compassion and the rest, how could their non-existence be established? However, at that time, the virtues do not function [merely] by being known through their mere existence; rather, they are benefactors with respect to the object of cognition when the faults are absent.
If this were so, there would be no doubt; likewise, the distorted cognition is held by the authoritative [person] to be such that "faults exist in him" or "they do not exist at all."
If, for you, doubt and error regarding that [object] exist here as long as it is not understood— [that is,] "this is the substratum of the collection of qualities"— then,

even if there is certainty regarding its own validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), and even if there is ignorance of or absence of defects, there would likewise be no lack of doubt regarding that speaker, just as in the previous case.
If the non-existence of the defect is not known, how can the non-existence of the two [types of] invalidity be cognized, by means of which there might be a determination of validity?
Furthermore, even if the non-existence of the two types of invalidity is not cognized, validity is understood intrinsically (*svataḥ*); thus, as before, there is no disagreement.

Is its statement a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it not a means of valid cognition? Furthermore, is that very [statement] itself not a means of valid cognition, because the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all [cognitions] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*)?
Therefore, by necessity, the cognition [of validity] must be accepted as residing in three things: the absence of defects, the absence of non-validity, and the presence of excellences.
Since these are thus conceptualized, how could that [cognition] be invalid? For how could it be invalid while serving as a factor for the ascertainment of the object as it truly is?
