How can its ascertainment regarding validity be understood through that cognition—given that the attainment of validity occurs extrinsically (*parataḥ*)? For that [cognition] is itself the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā-ātmatā*).
Since there is no subverting cognition (*pratyaya-bādhaka*), is that [cognition] valid (*pramā*) or not? Furthermore, every fault (*doṣa*) [previously mentioned] recurs here once again.

The validity (*pramāṇatā*) of the subject under discussion is either [established] extrinsically (*parataḥ*) or [intrinsically]; how could that which is non-valid (*apramāṇa*) be considered the cause (*hetutva*) of a cognition that accords with reality (*yathārtha-jñāna*)? By whom is its validity even understood? Since there is an absence of a subverting cognition (*pratyaya-bādhaka*), it follows that an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭā*) results.

Therefore, due to the non-existence of excellences (*guṇa*), there is the non-existence of defects (*doṣa*); from that non-existence, the non-reality of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) follows. Consequently, the general rule (*utsarga*) remains unrefuted.
If validity were thus ascertained everywhere, then here too that same group of faults previously mentioned would follow, and an infinite regress would result.

If this [statement], "The existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramā*) is the negation of defects in the absence [of the object]," were to be postulated (*kalpyeta*), then only that [negation] would be possible; there would certainly be no establishment (*siddhi*) [of the means of valid cognition].
That [non-existence] is not established by means of perception, because [perception] is absent; nor is it logical [to establish it] through non-perception, due to the fault of infinite regress.
Non-existence is understood through non-perception [of existence], but the non-existence of that perception itself must be understood by another [means]; thus, there is an infinite regress.

If that [cognition] were of the nature of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of another through the observation of what is distinct from it, then there would be the fault of non-existence (*abhāva-dosa*). Furthermore, it would follow (*prasajyate*) that the nature of the cognition is of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*), and that the cognition is the very form (*svarūpa*) of the intended valid means of knowledge (*pramā*). Moreover, the cognition would be the negation (*vyatireki*) of the two types of invalidity (*apramā*).
Alternatively, since the pair of non-cognitions is not known independently, how can you have the certainty that the remainder is of the nature of valid cognition?

If [it is argued that] there would indeed be a certainty (*niścaya*) through the non-occurrence of [the effect] otherwise (*anyathā-anupapattyā*), whether by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or by inference (*anumāna*), or even from some other source—then it would likewise follow from that other source.
Therefore, by that very same reasoning, non-authoritativeness follows for you even intrinsically (*svataḥ*), since this can be clearly stated in that regard.

Therefore, the non-existence of qualities [is established] by virtue of the non-existence of those defects; thus, the absence of the form of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [in them] remains unrefuted by that [reasoning]. Consequently, the general rule (*utsarga*) stands uncontradicted.

Since this entity, which is produced by the general rule (*utsarga*) consisting merely of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣāmātra*), can be clearly expressed even when it lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), like [the word] "measure" (*mānavat*).

For, because the cognition of the intellect (*buddhi*) has the nature of awareness (*bodhātmakatvena*), its status as non-valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*) is set aside by a cognition that accords with the object (*yathārthajñāna*) arising from the excellence of the cause (*guṇotthahetujñānāt*).

And non-authoritativeness is not set aside by excellences (*guṇa*), because [the excellences] are not being cognized; and that [non-authoritativeness], being unrefuted, is established as being inherent (*svataḥ*).

In the case of human compositions, it is suspected (*śaṅkyate*) that there exist (*santi*) defects (*doṣāḥ*); however, because the author (*kartuḥ*) of the Veda (*vede*) is established (*siddhatvāt*), we (*naḥ*) have no suspicion (*āśaṅkā*) of defects (*doṣa-*) therein.

Therefore, that which is stated—that the Veda possesses authority because it is independent—is established; for even that [Veda] depends upon an author, provided that either a corroborating cognition or the purity of its cause is not ascertained. In that case, due to the arising of doubt, there is no authoritative status for the Veda.
Even for another [means of knowledge], such a connection (*saṅgati*) is indeed postulated (*kalpyate*) as the cause, because the ascertainment has that as its basis (*nibandhana*).

When its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is already established, its certainty is produced by this [subsequent cognition]; however, a previously non-existent validity is not generated for it by this [subsequent cognition].

When the object has perished, the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) would indeed exist [only] once it has arisen; yet that [status] exists even when [the object] is not ascertained, and there is also certainty [of it] through a sequence of what has arisen.

If cognition possesses purity as its cause and so forth, then there is certainty; and if purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is directly obtained—characterized by burning and so forth—or if there is a habitual engagement that is independent of the arising of a result, yet in the absence of all means, there is no definitive ascertainment of it as a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, even though validity exists in that [cognition], it is not ascertained; being imagined as non-existent, it is thus designated.
Thus, there is no inconsistency at all with the auditory cognition and the visual [cognition] and so forth, for color, sound, and the rest exist dependent upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Due to their mutual non-distinction through a continuous series, they are the cause of one another; thus, that [connection] exists very clearly as a relation between them.

Even in the case of cognitions of smoke, transformations, fuel, and so forth, there might be a cognition of the ear [as a valid means of knowledge] due to its connection with another cognition of that [object];

however, this cognition produced by a different means is ascertained by that [other cognition], and therefore a correspondence (*saṃvāda*) brought about by a cause distinct from the [initial] cognition is desired.
In this way, the cause [of perception] is the conjunction [of the soul] with a cognition dependent on various sense organs; however, this [conjunction] is not observed to be postulated in the Veda.

For instance, the first cognition produced from water arises as something born of the sense organ, appearing as the supreme [cognition] based upon drinking, bathing, and so forth, [and] dependent upon the tongue and the body.

Furthermore, agreement regarding the meaning with a single sentence cannot be obtained in all cases—such as time, place, persons, and so forth—due to the arising of doubt. [Otherwise,] heaven would result from the *agnihotra* sacrifice; for it is heard thus: "Indeed, the mere verbal determination devoid of [actual] limbs is like the croaking of frogs."
Even among Brahmins, a difference of opinion regarding heaven and so forth is observed; therefore, agreement on the meaning [of the Vedas] is not found among men and others.

The firmness [of certainty] regarding a cognition produced by an injunction (*codanā*) has already been set aside; for, in that case, the existence of the object to be grasped is doubtful due to its similarity with other things. Moreover, how could that [cognition] be ascertained by Brahmins who do not perceive everything? A cognition produced by an injunction that is consistent with all [other means of knowledge] is what is required.

The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of perception (*pratyakṣa*), although [already] stated, is also ascertained by means of inference (*anumāna*); for that [inference] is produced from a pure cause, just like other [cognitions].

This valid cognition (*pramā*) of everything is not to be established from within [the system of] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it has already been established that there is no error (*bhrānti*) regarding the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
When inference arises from a mark (*liṅga*) that is non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to its effect (*kārya*), there is no error whatsoever;
rather, any potential error arising from various causes of delusion is removed by another [means], since in that case there is no certainty [without it].

An object that is manifest does not become established by way of being manifested from what is unmanifest; therefore, let it be accepted that cognition is like a cognition [of something] other than perception.

However, because they are themselves insentient in nature (*jaḍarūpatvāt*), objects are not apprehended in this manner by the sense organs such as the eye (*cakṣurādibhir indriyaiḥ*); rather, it is their status as causes (*hetutā*) with respect to cognition (*jñāne*).

The state of being known (*jñāyamānatva*) is employed (*upayujyate*) for [establishing] validity (*prāmāṇye*), because an experience (*anubhava*) that is unknown (*ajñāta*) with respect to its object (*viṣaya*) is simply not obtained (*na labhyate*). However, even in this case of grasping consciousness (*saṃvid-grahaṇe*), there would be no certain determination (*viniścaya*) regarding its being such [as it appears], because of the presence (*sadbhāvāt*) of causes of error (*bhrānti-kāraṇa*).

At that time, the entity is not at all determined as being the object itself by this perception, because of its similarity [to it], the possibility of the superimposition of another [concept] upon it, and [the presence of] error.
Just as knowledge arising from repeated practice is understood to be valid by itself, so too some false knowledge is established as invalid by itself.

Even if it is stated that there is no infinite regress (*anavasthiti*) regarding the cognition of sublation (*bādha-jñāna*) which is the cause of the defectiveness [of the previous cognition], its falsity (*mithyātva*) cannot be grasped by that much alone.

First of all, this is not cognized as "this is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) while it remains in that very state of its own arising, because the self-cognition (*saṃvit*) of its nature is not admitted.

Nor is it cognized without a [subsequent] cognition, because at that time [the subsequent cognition] is not present, since that [means of valid cognition] exists unmanifestly, or else because it would entail an undesirable consequence.

Even if it were stated in the Veda that there is a subverting means of knowledge consisting of inference, therefore, because of the exclusion (*apoha*) of the self (*ātman*) and so forth as previously described, that [inference] is not logically tenable as a means of knowledge.
Since [the truth] is established, the state of being caused by a defective human source is to be suspected; or else, an inherent capacity—just like that of fire—might exist in false cognitions.
Therefore, it is suspected that knowledge arising from a defective cause, as well as that which possesses a suspect defect, does not differ from what is observed to have a defect.

Therefore, intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is not tenable for the Veda; by that very fact, let it be admitted that [the Veda] possesses the status of being composed (*kṛtākhyātatva*) by one who is ascertained to be free from defects.
Indeed, to whatever extent the speakers are possessed of passion, hatred, and so forth, to that same extent they protect their own recitation all the more.

Of what [is it weak]? What [is weak]? What [is] weak? Who [is he]? Or from what [cause]? Which [is] the first section? Who [is he]? Who would cause the weakening of the accent? Who would split a word in the middle of a non-word?
Thus, for one who indeed has [enemies] intent on seeking out his vulnerabilities, how indeed could he not recite the Veda without fault, being full of reverence?
If those men who study [the Veda] were pure and indifferent [to their duty], they would not thus proclaim the Veda as having been destroyed by others.

Then, after a long period of time, the Veda might become neglected and destroyed; yet another [Veda], having assumed a mere semblance [of it], would appear. However, that which has been protected at all times by those who restrain passion, hatred, and the like, and which destroys [the corruption of] the Veda, will not abandon its own true nature.
It is maintained that the entire world has never at any time been otherwise [than it is now]; nor is there such a thing as a "great dissolution" known to exist in an ultimate sense.

This is not so; for if it were thus, there would be an equality of status with the reading [of the scriptures]. However, the realization of the reality of those [scriptural] meanings occurs without the perception of supersensuous objects.
And all those people for whom both place and time, in their entirety, exist clearly manifest in the mind of the observer, like a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of the hand.
He is capable of understanding even the identity of the recitation; otherwise, however, how could there be a lack of consensus due to differences in place, time, person, and condition?
"‘[The world] is not authoritative here’—thus [thinking], the world is always of such a nature; even the non-existence of Saṃvarta is not logical merely on the basis of non-perception."

On the other hand, the Veda brings about the ascertainment of its own validity intrinsically (*svataḥ*) with respect to its own form and its own meaning; therefore, [the occurrence of] delusion and so forth is not possible.
Therefore, since [the self] remains without a basis for ignorance, doubt, or error, even some twice-born person would not require instruction.
Furthermore, even the destruction of the root is not possible; or rather, what kind of destruction could there be of that which is eternal and superior to the diamond?

Is it not the case that this manifestation is indeed a change [in state]? That [change] has been refuted in the case of eternal things; therefore, the wise perform protection for this [manifestation], which is fruitless.

Therefore, let it be accepted that there exists a creator who is a seer beyond the senses, whose internal darkness has been dispelled, who knows the objects and the divisions of the Vedas; for, since the validity of all means of knowledge is not established intrinsically, one does not strive to prove the existence of a being who possesses knowledge of supersensuous objects.

Since the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) of the Veda is established even as depending upon a person, therefore, when that person possesses knowledge of objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya-arthajñatva*), [the Veda's authority is secured].
Otherwise, if there were a person who was subject to ignorance, doubt, and error, this [cognition] would not possess validity, just like any other [cognition].
By whomsoever the connection between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth has been stated—having known that, one who possesses clear knowledge of supersensible matters must be accepted even by others.
If only that [consciousness] is employed here, by whom can the person—who knows everything else—be prevented from possessing the quality of omniscience?
The word "all" (*sarva*) is everywhere accepted as being dependent on the context (*prakṛta*); therefore, when there exists a knower of all that is under discussion, what is lost for us?
Since some effect is impossible in the case of the object, it is postulated (*kalpyate*) in the case of the word as well; therefore, let him who knows all words be called "omniscient" by name.
Even so, as in the case of oil, water, ghee, and the like, let it be that the Omniscient One exists; by that [fact], he is not precluded by anything.
Or, if the world has the nature of both existence and non-existence, why is the person who is omniscient with respect to that [world] not accepted in brief?
Thus, even by relying on the state of being omniscient through a brief summary of the knowable as being objects of cognition, who is capable of refuting him?

Those by whom all word-meanings (*padārtha*)—as many as there are in their entirety—have been ascertained, they are all knowers of the treatises; thus, even they are omniscient by virtue of that knowledge.
Who indeed would not accept him as omniscient in a condensed sense—he who possesses discernment regarding the six objects of knowledge by means of the six instruments of valid cognition?

But he who conceptually constructs (*kalpayati*) the seer (*darśinam*) of all objects (*sarva-artha*) by means of specific distinctions (*viśeṣeṇa*), [doing so] directly (*sākṣāt*) through perception (*pratyakṣa*), for him that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is both futile (*mudhā*) and false (*mithyā*).

Who is capable of knowing all the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) of a single body, as many as there are, or all the hairs on the head and body? An investigation (*parīkṣā*) into the detailed manifestation of every single part being undertaken as a means of knowledge (*jñānasādhana*) is as useless (*anarthaka*) as the examination of a crow’s teeth (*kākadantaparīkṣā*).

Just as he knows all things to be fruitless, so too his claim to have direct perception of everything is fruitless; for it is established that one who possesses mere knowledge of the properties of virtue and non-virtue can determine what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected according to the scriptures composed by him.

In this regard, while [the capacity for] knowledge exists in its subtle distinctions regarding the entire world, people are afflicted out of place by their agitation over [doctrinal] texts and debates;

because they exclude all means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest from all cognizers, they will incur both merit and demerit, and [their position] will be understood solely through scripture.
Since the position of the Mīmāṃsakas is established by this much alone, that effort made toward the refutation of the Omniscient One is like killing one who is already dead.
Even if the knowledge of dharmas exists, it is destroyed because its root has been severed; those who call [such people] "omniscient" have merely performed the threshing of chaff.

But for one who [holds that] taste and so forth are directly perceived through their own manifestation, they would follow as being impure; since they are self-cognized, who indeed could imagine such a thing?
The speech of the Buddha and others is not seen to provide knowledge of the Vedas, the Upavedas, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), and so forth; how then could he be omniscient? It would be in vain.
If it is accepted that a meaning not bound within one's own books is understood by all poets through their own poetic compositions, then they would all be omniscient.
When all those who teach possess contradictory reasons for their doctrines and are equal in every respect, which single one among them can indeed be determined as the authority?
If the Sugata is omniscient, what is the authority [for this]? And if Kapila is [omniscient], then how can there be a difference between the views of these two, since both are omniscient?
In one respect, such as in mathematics and so forth, no distinction is perceived among all beings, including the Jinas, Buddhas, and others, regarding their truthfulness.

By whatever reason (*yena hetunā*) omniscience (*sarvajñatvam*) is established (*prasādhyate*) for one person (*ekasya*) merely through the pleasure (*prītimātreṇa*) in his own position (*svapakṣa*), that same [reason] applies (*upatiṣṭhate*) to another (*anyasyāpi*) as well.
Those very refutations which the Śākyas, in their agitation, utter when debating the proof of the Omniscient Jina, those same ones the Jainas employ.

In that case, how can a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) be reached (*kriyate*) by means of various proofs (*sādhana*) and refutations (*dūṣaṇa*) that are unstable (*anavasthita*), swallowed up (*grasta*) by the rising (*udaya*) of those very [refutations], and which are like reflections (*pratibimba*)?

Thus, when all the proponents of omniscience (*sarvajña-kalpa*) have been mutually destroyed (*nihata*) and all but a few remain (*śeṣīkṛta*), will the proponent of the Veda (*veda-vādī*) destroy them?
Just as a certain herb, when touched by the tips of a mongoose's teeth, destroys all the poison of a serpent, even when administered by those playing with it.
Thus, any worldly or Vedic reasoning whatsoever that is a destroyer of the poison of the knowledge of the Śākyas and others is [the remedy] for the mouth of the proponent of the Veda.
Who indeed will now conceive that [self], for whom the reasons characterized by being knowable, being an object of cognition, being a real entity, existence, and so forth, are capable of refuting it?
He who is conceived as omniscient must surely perceive all tastes and so forth by means of a single sense organ alone.
Whatever kind of object the perception of the world [is], by whatever kinds of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even at another time it was so seen; likewise it is seen now.

Even those men who are seen to possess excellence through their powers of wisdom, intelligence, and strength—[excellence] which exists by virtue of only slight degrees of difference—are not [seen] on account of [their possessing] supersensuous faculties.
Even a wise man, though he may be capable of perceiving subtle objects, does not surpass his own kind without overstepping its limits.

An excellence (*atiśaya*) of the person (*puruṣa*) is observed (*dṛṣṭa*) through perceptions (*upalabdhibhiḥ*) regarding sounds (*śabdeṣu*) that are accessible to the ear (*śrotra-gamyeṣu*), [namely] by means of [perceiving what is] distant (*dūra*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*). However, this is not due to the perception (*upalambhanāt*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Furthermore, through the eye (*cakṣuṣā*), an illumination (*prakāśanam*) of distant and subtle forms (*rūpa*) is produced (*kriyate*) by way of reaching [the object] (*prāptyā*); but there is no seeing (*darśanam*) of sound (*śabda*) and so forth.

Thus, a great excellence is observed in the investigations of the treatises; however, by that alone, knowledge of other treatises is not obtained. Having learned grammar, the intellect is drawn far toward correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*), but it is not [sufficient] for the determination of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the lunar days (*tithi*), or eclipses (*grahaṇa*).
Even an eminent astrologer, though he knows the eclipses of the moon, the sun, and so forth, is not capable of knowing the correctness (*sādhutva*) of words such as *bhavati*.
Likewise, even one who possesses superior knowledge of the Vedas, the Itihāsas, and so forth, is not able to perceive heaven, the deities, or the unseen merit (*apūrva*).
He who, having cast off [the body], travels through the interior of the sky, though capable of traversing ten cubits, is not able to go even a single *yojana*, despite hundreds of practices.

Therefore, even by those who have attained extraordinary cognitions that reach very far, it is possible to know only something slightly more [than ordinary knowledge], but never that which is beyond the senses.
That which proceeds directly before one standing in a single room would have its power [to act] there; indeed, it does not [have power] within another room.

And those objects (*arthāḥ*) which are separated by great distances of space, mountains, and oceans, or those which are [separated] by intervening regions (*varṣa*) and islands (*dvīpa*)—who, being present here, could see them? (*kaḥ paśyet tān*) [No one.]
Of Nala and Ṛtuparṇa, who were known for their knowledge of hearts, horses, and dice, as they were traveling together in a chariot, this speech was spoken by Ṛtuparṇa.
No one knows everything; nothing is established as omniscient. There is no finality of knowledge in any single person whatsoever.
Moreover, perception has not been observed to possess even the slightest capacity regarding the future, nor does inference and the like arise without signs (*liṅga*) and so forth.
Therefore, there exists no direct perceiver of objects that transcend the senses; rather, he alone sees who sees by means of the eternal Word.
He who, being unable to tolerate this, thinks even that the cognition of the Buddha and others regarding supersensible objects [is derived] from a human-authored scripture other than [the Veda].

The lack of authority of that statement belongs to it because of its similarity to that [other statement]; therefore, the untrustworthiness of the person must also be stated by means of the very same reasons previously mentioned.

However, that beginninglessness which is asserted for the sentences composed by an author—being based on two types of non-valid cognition—is not a means of establishing the validity of the sentences of Śauddhodani, because it is dependent; and likewise, because Śauddhodani himself did not perceive the Dharma.

Even if such individuals (*pudgala*) are postulated as being beginningless (*anāditā*), because they lack the status of an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa-pada-sthāt*), they do not surpass that [Veda] (*na atiricyate*). Therefore, by those who act like Mīmāṃsakas, it is asserted that there is a commonality (*sāmānya*) between the Buddhas and the students of the Veda (*vedādhyāyin*) regarding their beginninglessness (*an-āditva*).

Because they possess the specific quality of ignorance (*ajñānaviśeṣatvāt*), they do not attain equality (*tulyatām*) regarding validity (*pramāṇatva*) and invalidity (*apramāṇatve*); for in this way, these two would indeed be beginningless (*anādinī*).
Those qualities, means of valid cognition, and defects of ours—which are beginningless and resemble those [of others]—do not all attain equality merely by virtue of being beginningless.

For example, gold that exists as it is, which is a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), is beginningless and endless; yet even so, what is that [gold] [to us] by means of that [beginninglessness]? It is nothing.

To those who prattle that there is omniscience and the eternity of the Veda—both of which are [merely] equal [to other claims]—first of all, no omniscient being is perceived by us and others at present; nor does there exist any single part [of scripture] or a logical mark (*liṅga*) which might lead one to infer [such a being].
And there is no scriptural injunction (*āgama-vidhi*) that makes known an eternal omniscient being; and how could he be established by means of something artificial and untrue?
If the Omniscient One is understood by others solely through His word, how can the establishment of those two—which are mutually dependent—be conceived?
Since [the statement] "He is omniscient" has been spoken as true, how could both his existence and that [statement] be established without a proven foundation?
Understanding [him] to be omniscient on account of his well-composed speech—which is not [the speech] of one who is not omniscient—why do they not know [this] from their own words?
For the sake of [their] accomplishment, many omniscient ones must be postulated; yet even among those omniscient ones, he who is himself not omniscient does not perceive the omniscient one.
For even by those cognizers who possess that same time, it is not possible to know—by means of empty consciousness, the object of knowledge, and the knowledge thereof—that "this one is omniscient."

He would not be omniscient if he were not himself understood by that [person] to whom those words are addressed; for in the absence of knowledge of the source, those words possess no authority, just like the words of another.
Even if he were to verify all the objects known by his disciples, he would not be omniscient because of the exclusion of objects known by others;
nor is there any possibility of verifying all that is knowable known by all men throughout the three times and situated in the three worlds, nor is there any meeting with them.

Even one who possesses knowledge (*jña*) is not able to cause even a few men to wander (*bhramayituṃ śaknoti*), by means of which they—whose minds are already deluded regarding devotion (*bhrāntabhakticetas*)—might grasp him as being omniscient (*sarvajña*).
Some deceivers are capable of predicting the objects thought of by others while they remain within their grasp; yet they are devoid of knowledge regarding the Dharma and other such matters.
Likewise, some who are skilled in illusions, sorcery, and the like, delude ignorant people by means of which they appear to them as omniscient.
He who is celebrated in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as the beginning of Brahman, who is all-knowing, and whose knowledge and dispassion are unimpeded.

He too must indeed be described as being figurative (*gauṇatvena*), like the *arthavāda* mantras; or else, non-obstruction (*apratighatā*) is said to be [the result] from the knowledge (*jñānāt*) of the Dharma and so forth under discussion.
His knowledge, moreover, is unimpeded with respect to the four subjects—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—and it does not have all objects as its domain.

It is not said that [it] possesses the state of having all things as its range merely on account of its non-obstructiveness; for that [mind] becomes non-obstructive because it does not encounter resistance even with respect to its own objects.
This [knowledge], which has as its object the Dharma and so forth that bestows the fruit, exists; however, there is no purpose whatsoever for all trees and other such things being known.

As long as there is knowledge of the appropriate means (*aupayika-jñāna*), and that knowledge is not obstructed (*jñāna-pratihanyate*), by virtue of that it receives the designation "unobstructed" (*apratigha*).
*Textual variant (Baudhabhāratī):* *etat* in place of *jñāna-*.

Alternatively, that very knowledge which has been set in motion within the self through the practice of meditation—by virtue of the non-obstruction of that very knowledge—it is called "non-obstructiveness."
Even he who is heard of as Śaṅkara, the ten-fold immutable one—his knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—even he is possessed of knowledge through the consciousness of the Self.
That alone is knowledge which is the perception of the pure self, and that which pertains to the impure cause is called ignorance.
Moreover, O Brahmin, since Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara possess bodies composed of the Veda—which is my own omniscient knowledge—are they not all omniscient? What then of a mere human being?

Where are mortals, and where are the Buddhas and others? And where is the triad of supreme deities, by which [they] might have such a view as "we too are omniscient," out of rivalry with them? Even they are deluded.
Furthermore, the mention of the three Vedas and so forth in the eternal Veda and the eternal scripture does not contradict the eternity of the Vedas, because of that [scripture’s] own eternity.

We [the Buddhists] are not contradicted by those who possess eternal qualities and eternal actions, because of the possibility of their [the Vedas'] being expressive of the eternal Veda; however, since the Buddha and others are non-eternal, they cannot be understood as the source of scripture (*āgama*); and even if the eternity of scripture were accepted, the postulation of an omniscient being would be futile.

The understanding of Dharma is superior to the knowledge of an omniscient one who has been made known by the Veda; for from that [Vedic] Dharma, which is obscured, there arises a knowledge of Dharma and so forth that is unobscured. Thus, being accessible through scripture (*āgama*) is not obtained for an omniscient being.
Textual variant: (Baudha Bhāratī) -dharmādijñānam eva for (GOS) -dharmavijñānam eva.
If someone similar to the omniscient one were seen at present, then the existence of the omniscient one could be understood by the force of analogy (*upamā*).

Having seen that all men of the present time are not omniscient, the conclusion reached by means of analogy—that there is a similarity with those who are not omniscient—is indeed the domain of the teaching of the Buddha and others regarding dharma, adharma, and so forth; otherwise, it would not be tenable that he is omniscient, if he were not [so].

Even though perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of knowledge] have been refuted, he who establishes the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) through the very fact of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*)—

or rather, that proof (*sādhana*) which has been set forth here for the Omniscient One— is called "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), because it is seen elsewhere [to be preceded by] prior knowledge (*jñāna*).
Whatever instruction there may be, all of it is preceded by knowledge; just as the instruction regarding the *abhayā* and other medicinal herbs is of such a nature.
This instruction regarding dharma and adharma has been composed; therefore, it is inferred that this [instruction] possesses the quality of being preceded by his [the author's] own knowledge.

Because it is established (*upapannatvāt*), this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is not tenable in any other way; therefore, this remains as an inference (*anumā*). It is not correct [to claim otherwise], for the teaching of the Buddha and others is possible even through delusion arising from dreams and the like, or from the Veda heard erroneously.
First, for those who are ignorant of the Veda, it is impossible that the instruction which was composed by them arose from the Veda alone; rather, it proceeded solely from delusion.
In the world, the teaching of corrupt instructors proceeds either from delusion (*vyāmoha*)—which does not rely on that [reality]—or for the purpose of deluding their disciples.
If he were the root source of the Veda, then he would surely provide instruction to the proponents of the Veda just as Manu and the others do.
Since, however, that instruction is known to have been composed by fools for Śūdras, it is therefore corrupt and merely conventional, like a fraudulent ritual act.

Manu and the others who are established as preeminent among those who know the three Vedas—their compositions, which rely upon those who know the three Vedas, are utterances originating from the Veda.
Neither the composition of a text nor the transmission of those [Vedic passages] is possible without having seen them oneself or without having shown the Vedic sentences to the students.
If there exists some person who is omniscient, such that a means of proof (*sādhana*) is employed [to establish it], then that very omniscience is deficient in its thesis (*pratijñā*).
That object which is intended to be established is not expressed by this [statement]; however, there is no purpose whatsoever in establishing that which is [already] stated.

By that much alone, the common attainment of omniscience is obtained; that is called "omniscience. If the scripture belonging to him is established as true, then as long as the Buddha is not proven to be omniscient, how can his word be false? For where could truthfulness be established if there were no omniscient being whatsoever?

If there were truthfulness of speech regarding one [person] who is omniscient and another [person] who is not, then, in the case of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there would be a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitā*).

Everything whatsoever that is perceptible to someone in this world exists by virtue of its being an object, such as the nature of a thing of cognition, the knowable, or [qualities] like curd, color, taste, and so forth.

If [the term] "mere" (*mātra*) were not specified after "knowledge" (*jñāna*), a deficiency (*nyūnatva*) regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) would follow; for he who is intended as "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) has not been established in this manner.
If there were some other [person] distinct from the Buddha who had attained omniscience, where would that knowledge be of use regarding the authority (*pramāṇatva*) of the Buddha’s word?
Having reached the tenth stage through the complete destruction of all passion and the like, he perceives everything by means of a knowledge equal to pure crystal.

Having entered into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), maintaining a concentration (*dhāraṇā*) directed toward all objects, and likewise pervaded by all things (*artha*), he is certainly not capable of providing instruction.
If one were to teach something like a speaker of generalities, that would be the singing of one who knows only a single part; it is not the speech of an omniscient one.
When he has entered that meditative absorption and remains therein, teachings issue forth at will—even from walls and other such objects—just like [the light of] a wish-fulfilling gem.
By means of them, those men know all the matters they have desired to know; and they quickly attain, according to their destiny, all that is beneficial.
Thus, that which is being proclaimed shines forth among those who have faith; but as for us, we who lack faith seek out logical arguments.
For those [words] that have issued from a wall, there could be no status as being taught by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), nor could there be any confidence in them; so by whom were these proclaimed?
Could these be the sublime teachings of the Buddha, or could they be instructions taught by deceitful Brahmins playing with distant echoes?
Or rather, since [they are] merely insignificant beings such as unseen piśācas and the like, wise men should not place their trust in them.
Thus, omniscience is without foundation for men by virtue of their independence; and how can this be conceived: that he is once again considered a seer of all?
Whether knowing simultaneously, or in succession, or all at once by virtue of a single nature, or according to what is predominant, the omniscient one is held to exist through his power.
Nowhere has it been observed that there is a single cognition of mutually contradictory intrinsic natures, such as the pure and the impure, or that destinies are distinct.
Who could possibly be able to understand, even in the course of hundreds of years, the infinite reality—past, present, and future?
He who perceives everything through his own undivided nature does not perceive the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*bhāva*).

Is it that even by that omniscient one, the awakened one (*boddhā*), the entity (*vastu*) in its general form (*sāmānya-rūpa*) is not understood (*na avagamyate*) through another form (*anya-rūpeṇa*) by means of awakening (*bodhena*)?
That single-aspected cognition might be either correct or even false; if it were correct, there would be a contradiction with what is perceived. Thus, it follows that everything is non-dual.

Then, your statements regarding the dharma and adharma of the omniscient disciple would not exist, because his own nature would not be ascertained. However, if there were a difference in form, [and yet he were] false, the omniscient one would become deluded; at that time, his word would not be trustworthy, being like the speech of a madman and the like.

If he is accepted as omniscient—he who knows everything, including every action along with its cause, by means of supramundane, innate knowledge born of meditative concentration—then [he is omniscient].
There is no means of valid cognition—whether perception, inference, or verbal testimony—that establishes its existence; such [a thing] does not exist.
How can there be inference—either simultaneously or in succession—without an effect? Even if there were capacity, or even if there were capacity, everything [would follow];
and yet all the *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field) are capable of understanding everything, but because they lack the means (*upāya*), they do not perceive it in its entirety.

Thus, when it is established that there is no omniscient person whatsoever— since a single individual who has attained uncommon means and possesses knowledge distinct from all other men is devoid of any proof— then at that time, human speech is the cause for the realization of Dharma.
Thus say the Mīmāṃsakas: "The independent Vedic revelation has been established at length, and the human authorship of the Vedas has been refuted."
Therefore, there exists a direct perceiver of supersensuous objects; however, no one perceives [them] through eternal speech, because such a thing is impossible.
For an eternal word cannot possess the capacity for knowledge—whether regarding its own object, by itself, from another, or even through non-succession or succession—without contradiction.

Since heaven, sacrifice, and so forth have been revealed by you even after knowing them for yourself, you possess such an authorship of the Veda as one who perceives supersensuous objects, or one who knows the purpose of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the person (*puruṣa*), or indeed one who knows all dharmas; for if he were not accepted, there would be no authority (*prāmāṇya*) for the Veda otherwise.
By that very admission [of yours] which is obtained through the cognition of dharmas by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), this negation which you have formulated at length is sublated.
Furthermore, it has been said: "Who is capable of knowing how many those hairs and body-hairs are, which have been produced without cause by one who is ignorant?"

Since there might be some entity (*kaścana*) that is a complete object (*akhila-vastu*) illuminated by a lamp of stainless and unshakable knowledge (*jñāna*), this does not constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*) here;

for even by the mere non-perception (*adṛṣṭi-mātra*), there is no ascertainment (*viniścaya*) of its non-existence (*asattā*), because of the impossibility of [non-perception] being a reason (*hetu*) or a pervader (*vyāpakatā*) with respect to entities (*vastuṣu*).

In the case of non-existence (*abhāve*), the cessation (*nivṛttiḥ*) of the pervader (*vyāpaka-*) is logically connected (*yujyate*) with that which possesses a cause (*hetumat-*) and with the two things that are pervaded (*vyāptayoḥ*), because they arise from a single existence (*ekabhāvataḥ*).

Otherwise, in the absence of fire (*kṛśānu-*) and a tree (*pādapa-*), there would be the cessation of smoke (*dhūma-*) and mango trees (*āmra-*) and so forth; [if this were not the case], it would follow (*prasajyate*) that these are without a cause (*ahetutā*) and that they possess distinct natures (*nānātva*).

If [you maintain that] there is the ascertainment of your own apprehension regarding all objects through some cognition characterized by the states of being a cause or a pervader, then you yourself would be established as an omniscient knower of all things without effort; and therefore, why do you harbor such hatred toward yourself as an omniscient one, [despite this] arising from your own [position]?
Therefore, this omniscient one of yours is not established as being perceptible; for if he were indeed perceptible in that manner, omniscience would exist effortlessly.
How can that visible object be perceived by you, for whom knowledge has as its domain all objects, if it were not also yours?
Therefore, this distinction—that the non-perception of the self-natures of the causes of pervasion is established for the Omniscient One—does not hold, because they are by nature invisible.

This threefold non-perception (*adṛṣṭi*) proceeds in nine forms (*rūpā*) according to its application (*prayogataḥ*): through the distinctions of non-cognition (*abhedāgati*), cognition (*gati*), and the cognition of that which is contradictory to it (*tadviruddhādigati*).

When the incapacity (*śaktivaikalya*) of this [non-perception], which consists of these various divisions (*mūlaprabhedarūpā*), has been established with respect to the Omniscient One (*sarvavidam*), then another [form of non-perception] is set aside without effort (*ayatnataḥ*).
Causality, the state of being pervaded and the pervader, and contrariety—these, along with that very nature which possesses its qualifiers, are established provided that [the object] is perceptible.
The omniscient one is not visible to you; furthermore, these non-perceptions are not capable of negating him; and there is no other factor for his negation.
If the omniscient one is negated merely by [his] non-perception, then there would also be for you a negation of [your own] marriage with your mother and so forth.

If the existence of the son, who is designated as an effect, is perceived through his vision because of that [vision] being its cause, then surely that effect is observed even in the absence of that [vision].
If its non-existence is not apprehended through the perception of something else, then how, according to you, is the perception of that other thing—which has it as its object—established?
Is this not [the case] through instruction? Why then is this not likewise seen in the case of the Omniscient One? Furthermore, why is this other [argument] stated here by yourself?
Generally, men are always speakers of untruth; just as there is no confidence in them today, so too there is none in their recounting of past events.

Or [the word] "was" (*abhūt*) is an augmentless aorist; or rather, how can there be for you any certainty regarding the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of this [scripture], since an omniscient being (*sarvajñ*) is not perceived by anyone?
For in this way there would be the certainty: "Because [you] see all beings as yourself, you have become an omniscient one"—thus it is described.

Even if there is non-perception [of such a being], doubt remains, just as in the case of [the existence of] living beings (*sattva*); for some suspect that those who are omniscient (*sarvavidaḥ*) do indeed know [all things]. Furthermore, it is suspected that he, being self-luminous (*ātma-jyotis*), perceives himself by means of himself; therefore, his non-perception of all things remains unestablished.
For indeed, by means of sound, all living beings are considered to be all [beings]; and since he is not excluded from all [beings], non-perception is thus uncertain.
By way of avoidance, what single obstacle could there possibly be here? For indeed, one's own passion and so forth do not cease through others, because of their lack of full knowledge.
Moreover, some who are of limited vision will attain [this] through inference; for indeed, certain thoughts of some people are somewhat skillful.
For indeed, the proof for [the properties] such as momentariness, the Veda, the earth, and so forth, has been stated by us very clearly before; yet it was not perceived by the dull-witted.

Thus, because of doubt, the non-existence of this [object] of cognition is not ascertained; for indeed, those who are free from doubt perceive non-existence even in the absence of inference. Therefore, there is no certain determination of non-existence, just as there is no certainty regarding the existence of fire and so forth when the effects such as smoke have not yet begun.

[Objection: When an object has been perceived at some time, doubt is appropriate, as in the case of a post; for this [post] partakes of both aspects, since both a post and a man have been seen at some time—thus doubt is appropriate. But the Omniscient One is not seen in that manner.

"Indeed, O wise one, by this very same method, the non-existence of the marriage of one's mother and so forth is described by us as being free from doubt; yet, in this matter, there is still a doubt regarding the absence of valid cognition (*pramā*), the presence [of it], and the cessation of things due to the absence of means of valid cognition."

In the case of the deficiency of the eyes and so forth, there is no valid cognition even when the object exists, because those [causes] lack the completeness of the object, just as in the case of a jar and the like.

Therefore, since there is the observation of the non-apprehension of the solitary [omniscient being] in both ways, let there be, rather, doubt regarding the existence of that omniscient one; this is better.

Even though it exists, it would not be perceived directly by the dull-witted, like [the self-nature of] conceptual construction or other [entities]; nor would it be a producer of effects, like fire, iron balls, or embers.

When that effect is invisible—just like [the effect] born of passion (*rāga*) or other conceptual constructions (*kalpa*)—then its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with respect to a visible effect is not perceived by him.
Since the knower of all objects is always invisible to those whose intellects are dull, therefore its existence will not attain proof through inference.

It has been stated that [the absence of] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this object (*vastu*) is neither a non-reason (*ahetu*) nor a non-pervader (*avyāpaka*); furthermore, even when this [means of valid cognition] is absent, the existence [of the object] is observed, and thus doubt (*saṃśaya*) arises.
Therefore, there exists no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the existence of an omniscient being; rather, a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for him will be stated in detail.
The wise followers of the Sugata exert effort toward the accomplishment of the complete understanding of all objects— even if it were fruitless—
because one directly perceives that the person who knows the attainment of heaven and liberation is not only recognized as such, but is indeed known to be omniscient.
Furthermore, when there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) and a clear proof (*sādhana*) exists, why do those of dull intellect (*jaḍabuddhi*) disagree regarding the omniscient one (*sarvajña*)?

But when there is no proof (*sādhana*), and when there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*) that is definitely ascertained (*aviniścita*), there might indeed be doubt (*saṃśaya*) in that case; but what is the basis (*nibandhana*) for this certainty (*niścaya*) regarding them?

This restriction—that it is the injunction alone and not anything else that is joined to the cognition of "past" and so forth—is indeed [correct], for when another [object] is determined to be non-existent.

That measure (*māna*) has been proclaimed for the sake of establishing the knowledge of the *pradhāna*, the *puruṣa*, the objects of the *puruṣa*, and all objects; furthermore, another [measure] will be stated both before and after this.

Therefore, the world is afflicted in vain by its zeal for books and doctrines, which are connected to all cognizers through perception and other means, and which do not preclude the fact that merit and demerit are accessible to one who knows how to establish the subtle distinctions of all things in the universe; [for such merit and demerit] cannot be understood through scripture alone.

Even in the case of the Mīmāṃsaka, since [the reason] is unestablished by this much alone, that effort which has been made by others once again to refute the omniscient one was due to extreme stupidity.
Because the Dharma exists as something known, unimpaired, and being its root, they call those men omniscient; by them, wisdom has been revealed.
If impure tastes and so forth were perceived due to the connection with the sense organ of taste (*rasanendriya*), then blame would belong to that [organ] alone.

Even those who are censured are perceived (*vedyante*) within the conventional reality (*saṃvṛttau*), though they are not actually reached by the mind (*cetasā*) or by the mental faculty (*mānasena*) that has arisen from the cultivation of true objects (*udbhūtabhāvanābhūtārtha*).

Furthermore, since the word of the Protector (*tāyinaḥ*) is seen to be expressive of the meaning of what was proclaimed in the Vedas and other scriptures, for that very reason he is omniscient (*sarvavit*).

It is possible that there exists an uncommon status [of the Veda], for [the Buddha] declares that the false [teachings concerning] the Self and so forth, which were studied in the Veda, are the errors of all non-Buddhist outsiders.
Selflessness, clearly stated by him for the benefit of those to be trained, is the peerless gateway to the auspicious and the terror of those with wrong views.

That which is unfamiliar to worldly beings, known to be the remover of all misfortunes, and for those endowed with the practice of that [knowledge] and so forth, it is the supreme mine of the jewels of virtue.

If poets (*kavayaḥ*) know such (*īdṛk*) the supreme (*paramam*) reality (*tattvam*), being knowers of the principles of *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, and *artha*, and being omniscient (*sarvajñāḥ*), who (*kaḥ*) would not honor them (*na manyate*)?
This kind of knowledge of selflessness does not exist at all in Vardhamāna and the others; for all the non-Buddhist teachers have perished through their [false] view of a self.

How indeed could those by whom much that is improper—such as the refutation of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syād-vāda*) and [the doctrine of] non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), which is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge—has been stated, be omniscient (*sarvajña*)?

How can it be possible for those who stumble regarding this object—which is directly perceived and well-established in the case of the Vāhīkas and others—to have a clear comprehension of that which is beyond the senses?

Thus, non-omniscience is clearly understood through the following consequence: because of the manifestation of false knowledge, just as another person is perceived as deluded when [he says] "it is a man" regarding a post; and by all these investigations, the establishment of the reason is to be known.

Because of the knowledge of the reality (*tattva*) of all objects (*padārtha*) in their entirety, he is omniscient (*sarvavit*); therefore, the exclusion (*vyatirekitā*) [of the reason] from the subject (*sambodhyā*) is not doubtful (*sandigdha*).
(Textual variant [Baudha Bhāratī]: *saṃvedyā*)

If the speech of these [Buddhas] regarding the "syādvāda" and so forth were intended figuratively, then what is the true nature (*rūpa*) of all things that is asserted by them as real (*tāttvika*)—namely, [their] selflessness (*anātmatva*), momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), and so on? If this is so, [it follows that] those who see everything perceive directly (*sākṣāt*) the true nature of all things in their entirety.
May you all be united in harmony; for you have not spoken anything that is mutually contradictory, whether in its literal meaning or its intended sense.
And because of their direct cognition of the reality that has been established and which pervades all things, the Sugatas are all-seeing.
In such a knowledge, their state of being a Sugata is not differentiated (*na bhidyate*), because of the possession of excellent knowledge; this much is its defining characteristic.

Although an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) is possible, he has been established in a general sense (*sāmānyena*) because of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with that definition (*tallakṣaṇa*). Thus, the Sugata alone is established as such.

Even if some particular (*viśeṣa*) omniscient being were not specified—one who knows the entire world (*jagat*) exactly as it is, in its true form (*yathāvad rūpataḥ*), such as its selflessness (*anātman*) and so forth—[the general proof remains valid].
When selflessness has been directly realized, no fault can maintain its existence, because it is contradictory to that realization—just as darkness cannot remain in a brightly burning lamp.

Furthermore, due to the specific excellence of direct realization, the fault along with its latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) does not exist; therefore, liberation from all obscurations, omniscience, is established.

Since this [teaching] was taught by the Sugata at the very beginning through the proclamation of selflessness (*nairātmya*), for that reason the Tathāgata stands at the head of all the founders of other schools (*tīrthakṛt*).

For that yogin who possesses the vision of reality consistent with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvādittattvadarśanayogin*), there is no equality of cause (*atulyahetutā*) with others who teach contradictory matters (*viruddhārthopadeśinām*).

Valid knowledge (*pramā*) is beyond the scope (*agocarā*) of those whose words are confused by contradiction (*bādhākulavacaḥ*); for the capacity of direct perception (*atyakṣavijñānaśakti*) is far removed from them.
Even that which expresses the means conducive to the goal of man, when it concerns an object perceived by the senses, is slightly uncontradicted by the two means of valid cognition.

Just as a jewel that is stainless, purified by washing, and which—when being examined—does not undergo any alteration through heating, cutting, or rubbing on a touchstone; so too is the arising of the Tathāgata’s word, which conforms to the destruction of all the darkness of evil doctrines and which has not been attained by those with many impurities.
Then those possessed of intelligence said: "We [acknowledge] the Sugata alone as the omniscient one, the knower of the primary purpose of man; and him alone as the excellent physician."

Therefore, by this [reasoning], the Sugata alone is the omniscient one, and not Kapila; this [truth] has been clearly stated immediately following [the previous argument], yet it was not perceived by the deluded.
Even from what was stated immediately before, a distinction is perceived [as being maintained] from the false teachers such as Bhaṅga, Smara, Ṛṣabha, and others;
for what dull-witted person would consider one who knows merely the *mātṛkā* to be a knower of the reality of all meanings, on the basis of a knowledge equal to that of one who has finished eating?
That [reason] by which omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is established for one [person] does not apply to another thing, because that reason is absent in it.
Those refutations which the Śākyas, free from agitation, utter in the teaching of the Omniscient Jina—against these, the naked ascetics (Digambaras) are powerless.

That reality which has been established by the Buddhist school through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on a proven logical connection (*pratibandha*) is not established in that same way in other systems.
Let it be done; there is no need for a definitive conclusion reached through various means of proof and refutations that are established as distinct or swallowed up by the reflection of arising.

However, there exists no contradiction whatsoever—whether directly or otherwise—between omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the state of knowing all aspects of the knowable (*sarvākārajñeyatā*), and so forth.

[The properties of] knowability and so forth are established through their distinction from unknowability and so forth; however, that [knowability], which is characterized by being established, and omniscience itself have never occurred anywhere previously as a complete cause, and subsequently they cease when there is the possibility of existence and so forth.

In the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) and the lack of self-cognition (*asva-vitti*), [cognition] is not born (*na jāyate*); for it is born (*jāyate*). Thus, prior to its operation (*pravṛtti*), this omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) would be established (*prasiddhā*).

In a formulation that is not contradictory, what is joined [with it] does not exclude anything else; otherwise, because of the existence of its own form, the absence of taste would also be understood.

In this regard, concerning the speakerhood that has been implied by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), whoever conceives of a certainty regarding its exclusion (*vyatireka*), and who likewise conceives of speakerhood existing when there is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— for an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpataḥ*)— indeed, a real entity (*vastu*) is not apprehended by a cognition (*jñāna*) permeated by verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).

In this regard as well, those who imagine that the omniscient one possesses the status of a speaker by virtue of conforming to discursive thought (*vitarka*) do not accept him as omniscient; for while such speech might occur through the presence of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), it does not exist in his non-conceptual state (*avikalpa*).
In the seventh moment, speakerhood (*vaktṛtva*) is not established (*prasiddhyati*);

and likewise, it is not tenable (*na yujyate*) that he possesses the quality of being composed by one who is not omniscient (*asarvajña*), because of the inclusion (*samākṣepāt*) of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Therefore, there would be consistency (*saṃvādana*).

Just as someone, having experienced [something], later speaks [of it], there is non-discrepancy [between that speech and the object] because it arises from the experience of that object. Therefore, at the time of omniscience, the non-establishment of this [omniscient person] as a cause is [the point]; however, at the time of his activity and discourse, [his existence] is established as proven.

Even in the case of the exclusion (*apākaraṇa*) of all objects (*samasta-vastu*) through cognition (*vijñāna*), the consequence (*prasajyate*) follows that the state of having a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdha-vyatirekitva*) remains exactly as it was (*tad-avastha*).

Even when [cognition] is accepted as a valid reason (*hetutva*) by virtue of its capacity (*sāmarthya*) for verbal expression (*vyāhāra-vṛtti*), the fault of having a doubtful negative concomitance persists (*anuvarttate*).

Even in the Protector, who is free from conceptual construction, the teaching proceeds by virtue of the power of the accumulation [of merit and wisdom], through the connection with the revolution of the wheel.
Those wise ones who say this [in response], for them it is not established; however, speakerhood—that which is determined and accepted by the world—is indeed established.

In that case, because of such a reason (*hetu*), there would be a doubtful exclusion (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*). Indeed, in this view, since [the reason] is untenable (*anupapattika*), by what could its unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) be said?

If "speakership" (*vaktṛtva*) is considered as an independent (*svatantra*) means of proof (*sādhana*), then there is an unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddhi*); or else, there is unestablishedness due to doubt (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*).
Because there is doubt regarding this meaning, its non-establishment remains constant; therefore, you must state such a proof by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*).

In that regard, the dharma is revealed (*prakāśyate*) by means of the mere authority of scripture (*āgamamātreṇa*); however, it is not the ultimate indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the establishment (*siddhi*) of its actual existence (*tadbhāva*).

Thus, for whomsoever the reasons—namely, being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), existence (*sattā*), being a real entity (*vastu*), and so forth—are incapable of refuting [the opponent], who will not postulate him?

Likewise, there is no reasoning whatsoever, whether worldly or Vedic, residing in the mouth of a proponent of the Veda, that can remove the knowledge of the Śākyas, which is like the poison of a fierce serpent.
Even a dull-witted twice-born man of very little strength, when bitten by snakes, is unable even to draw a breath, let alone to ward off the poison.
Even a sound argument, when situated at the mouth of a Vedic proponent, is as unfortunate as a necklace placed upon the feet.
Even the non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*) of smoke from fire cannot be stated by him, because in his view, smoke exists elsewhere as well;
since a thing possesses a single nature (*eka-svarūpatva*), it exists even in the ocean despite the presence of fire—so what basis for exclusion (*vyatireka*) could there be?

Or else, why should there not be a representation (*vijñapti*) of form as its effect? Or even in that case, let there be a real (*tāttvika*) distinction of substance (*vastu-bheda*) characterized by difference within the self-nature (*ātman-bhāva*).
A single mental cognition, which is omniscient, arisen from the practice of reality, and connected with all things, is conceived.
But visual consciousness and the other [sensory cognitions] do not arise from that; why then is it said [in the passive voice]: "He perceives all tastes and so forth with the eye"?

Mental cognition (*mānasa-jñāna*), which consists of the nature of the experience of form and so forth, is established; moreover, there is no dispute even among others regarding this much of a matter.

Therefore, memory (*smṛti*) having as its object (*gocarā*) form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth, is described (*varṇyate*) even in a dream (*svapne*); [for] mental cognition (*mānasaṃ jñānaṃ*) has as its nature (*ātmakaṃ*) the experience (*anubhava*) of all objects (*sarvārtha*).

Furthermore, if the Omniscient One is conceived as having an object determined by the mind, why would he perceive tastes and so forth with the eye? It is because [the object] is unrestricted. Why, then, does he perceive tastes and the like through the visual faculty?
This fault might indeed occur in the postulation of that [object] by means of visual perception alone; however, he himself knows the taste and so forth by means of the mental consciousness.

Even where an excellence (*atiśaya*) is observed in the perception (*dṛṣṭi*) of subtle, distant, and other such objects, that [excellence] would exist by not overstepping its own object (*svārtha*), and not by way of the function (*vṛtti*) of the ear with respect to form (*rūpa*).

Therefore, such undesirable [consequences] as these, which have been stated by others, do not apply to us, because the excellence [of the cognition] is held to reside in the mental [cognition] itself, without transgressing its own object.
Whatever kind of perception of an object is observed by people at present through such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it remains the same even at another time.
All knowledge would be pure; some excellence might even be possible in the fruit, provided it has as its scope objects that are entirely real.

The *āmalaka* fruits (feminine, nominative plural) were seen (feminine, nominative plural) in the desert (masculine, locative singular) as having small fruits (a bahuvrīhi compound); thus, all of them (feminine, nominative plural) have that very same form (feminine, nominative plural) even elsewhere (adverbial).

There is also this scriptural passage (*śruti*): "The serpents hear with their eyes. Therefore, the powers of the actions of sentient beings (*sattva*) are indeed diverse, as are the objects to be accomplished.
It is fitting for him to speak thus, for whom every single entity situated within the three paths appears as having its specific capacity determined.
Whatever kind of perception of whatever kind of object may exist for people at present through various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it was likewise so in other times as well;
yet even now, the capacity of people to know [it all] cannot be ascertained by you, who are merely a living being, because of the lack of certainty regarding universal capacity.

Alas, there is no proof through inference of the omniscience of all beings in their knowledge of every power, because of the possibility of its being otherwise [due to] the possession of super-sensory cognition; yet, even so, the state of being a yogi—characterized by qualities such as wisdom—is perceived in men by virtue of their mastery of spells (*vidyā*) and the like.
There exists a science known as divination (*īkṣaṇika*) and so forth, which, when well-cultivated, brings about the thorough knowledge of another's mind in this very life.
They know and they speak of an entity that is past, present, and future, which has not been inferred, heard, or seen in this life.
Men, possessed [by them], [utter] here what is manifest, accompanied by discourse, according to their power, [concerning] the various mantras of the lords of nāgas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and so forth.

[One might argue: "Let it be that [the word] 'seen' (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth [is used] in the sense of 'let it not be' (*mā bhūt*), an aorist without the augment; nevertheless, there exists no subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, its non-existence is not established."
The person who possesses supersensuous vision must necessarily be admitted by you in the manner already stated, which has been established through the Veda.
Therefore, a wise man should be capable of perceiving subtle matters; even while transcending his own kind, he may surpass other men.
Just as the capacity of the auditory organ and others is distinguished by specificities such as the perception of [their] own objects, distance, and connection, so too would it be for the mind;
for indeed, form situated at a great distance is seen by vultures, and likewise, that which is concealed by death and the like is seen by those possessing accomplished collyrium and other such means.
In this way, there would be a specific perception of gods and so forth—of subtle, obstructed, and other such [objects]—in accordance with their respective births.
Due to the excellence of the practice of yoga, the mental state of yogins may likewise possess knowledge that is of a preeminent nature; thus, there is no sublation here.

If it is argued that an excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced in cognition (*jñāna*) due to a deficiency in the application of movement (*gati-yoga*), this is indeed incorrect; for in the absence of a cause (*hetv-abhāvāt*), there can be no effect (*phala*).
Cognition does not arise from something else, nor is it obtained merely by that [movement]; likewise, an excellence cannot exist when there is a deficiency in each successive subsequent cause.

The existence of an omniscient being is not asserted on the basis of a single portion of cognition, by which [cognition] there might arise direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) of heaven and so forth from the Veda and other sources.

However, from the observation of the increase of wisdom, compassion, and so forth, through the repeated practice of those [qualities], another excellence is perceived as arising from that very [practice] as it increases.

Furthermore, the arising of these [qualities] from the mind as a quality—just like [the attainment of] the ultimate limit—is due to the awakening of ruthlessness toward all objects, resulting from great practice.
Wisdom, defined by its characteristic as the comprehension of the meaning of objects, remains incomplete even when one single [object] is not fully known.

Furthermore, those [mental states] of ours which are activities (*pravṛtti*) that possess the nature of ultimate growth— being of the same kind as the preceding seeds— and which, like rice and so forth, are characterized by excellence through refinement (*saṃskāra*), such as compassion, intelligence, and the like, possess the aforementioned properties when they have reached full development, namely, omniscience (*sarvadarśitā*).

And for those phenomena (*dharmāḥ*) which consist of diminution (*apacaya*), when in the presence of their counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), an absolute diminution (*atyantāpacayaḥ*) is possible—just as in the case of stains on gold and the like—and likewise these [phenomena] such as the afflictions (*kleśa*), the false (*anṛta*), and the knowable (*jñeya*), which possess the characteristics as they have been taught.

If it is possible that the stains of those aforementioned phenomena might arise again even when their intellects have abandoned them, then indeed there would be no skillful antidote for their absolute uprooting.
In some cases, an absolute diminution [of darkness] is perceived—due to its connection with the reality of vision—as if it were being traversed; this applies both to external and internal darkness.
When that [obstruction] has been diminished, his great, unimpeded knowledge would proceed independently throughout the entire circle of all that is knowable.

Those things which, being stable by nature, have been placed even with some difficulty upon a firm substratum, do not require further effort for their continued existence, provided there is no subverting cause.

These—namely, excellence through the differentiation of the ultimate limit of cultivation, as well as purity, gold-like intellect, compassion, and so forth—possessing the aforementioned qualities, [attain] luminosity, which is omniscience, when they reach their ultimate state.

Nor is there any deviation here [in our argument] due to jumping (*laṅghana*) and the heating of water (*udaka-tāpa*), for jumping does not arise from that [heating] alone, but rather from strength (*bala*) and effort (*yatna*).

Or else, even jumping may reach its ultimate limit (*paryanta-kāṣṭhā*) through its own causes, owing to the excellence (*viśeṣa*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), strength (*bala*), speed (*gati*), and so forth.
There is a power called "mind-swiftness" (*manojavā*), which is likewise heard of as supreme; by means of it, the Lord travels even to a great distance merely by thinking of it.
The non-existence of that [object] is not established merely by its non-perception; nor is it possible for another to state any subverting argument here.
A young swan of a king, though unable to go out from the house, reaches even the further shore of the ocean through the power of practice.

Just as his movement [is such] due to the distinction of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) consisting of practice based on a substratum (*āśraya*), why is it not possible that a similar [movement], even one superior, could arise from that very same [substratum]?
In this state, a bodhisattva is not able to attain such a state; however, a sage would be able [to do so] when he has attained a distinguished meditative absorption.
If, having leaped, he were to go through an interval of ten cubits in the sky, such a power of movement would belong to him for that reason.
Of water (being carried away), there occurs the destruction of its heat; therefore, due to the instability of the substratum, what could have excellence in what?

The continuum of mind (*citta-santati*), which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the mental qualities (*mānasānāṃ guṇānām*), does not cease under any circumstances due to its connection with a supporting basis (*ādhāra-vṛtti-yogataḥ*).
As long as the flood of qualities continues to flow toward it, for that long it becomes increasingly more luminous (*prabhāsvaratarā*).
This mind, which possesses a self, is by its very nature luminous regarding the reality of vision; it is indeed stable, whereas the impurities are considered to be adventitious.

If the mind were to arise as something essentially consisting of the cognition of another self, then the cognition of the object would not be possible, because [the mind] would be unestablished due to the absence of perception.

Therefore, the mind possesses self-nature (*ātmatva*) because it is self-cognizing (*sva-saṃvedana-prakāśana*). This self-awareness (*sva-saṃvitti*) exists in the form of being non-superimposed (*anāropita-rūpa*).

Therefore, when the path has become habitual to the mind, there is indeed no overcoming by passion, hatred, and the like; for they were previously weak, and because the path—which destroys all defects—has become second nature, there is no loss without effort, nor is there effort due to the perception of its qualities.
Therefore, the Jina—the essence of stainless and unshakable virtues, whose nature is free from the defects that cause instability—is understood to be omniscient.

Furthermore, whatever things are clearly conceptualized (*vibhāvyante*), those very things appear quite vividly (*parisphuṭam*) upon the perfection of cultivation (*bhāvanā-pariniṣpattau*), just like objects of desire (*kāma-viṣayāḥ*) and so forth.
All phenomena are cultivated by great beings over a long period of time in manifold ways, in their true form as empty, selfless, and so forth.

The reality of emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, regarding form, has been established by that [means]. Because it arises from the cultivation of a real object, it is considered a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it appears clearly; it is a valid means of cognition because of its correspondence with the entity, just like the appearance of blue and so forth which arises based on the eye and other [faculties].
Even the simultaneous clear manifestation of all dharmas is possible within a single cognition; therefore, let it be understood in this way.
Just as in the case of a woman, one's own son, or a thief, when they are being clearly visualized, such a cultivation is not difficult to achieve, provided there is the mere inclination of the will.

All phenomena (*sarva-dharmāḥ*) are clearly manifest (*spaṣṭa-prakāśanāḥ*) due to the causes of cultivation (*bhāvanā-hetubhyaḥ*) consisting of the excellence (*utkarṣa*) of a single-pointed mental state (*eka-buddhi-niṣṭha*), just as in the case of [the perception of] objects (*vastu*), sentient beings (*sattva*), and so forth, such as [the cognition of] the pleasant (*priya*) and so on.

In this way, for whomsoever reasons characterized by substantiality (*vastutva*), existence (*sattva*), origination (*utpāda*), and so forth, are capable of establishing certainty, who will not establish him?
Herein, the Omniscient One is established as one whose circle of a single moment of knowledge encompasses all that is to be known—both human and divine—and who is the crest-jewel of men.
Those [qualities], beginning with dharma, are known by someone even without verbal testimony, because they are taught as being true in their very nature, like the purity of gold and so forth.

Since the human origin of the Vedas is established, the proof [for their authority] is not established; for the teaching of that which is unknown cannot be accidental. Indeed, there exists no capacity in seals (*mudrā*), mandalas, mantras, and the like—which is capable of effecting the removal of liberation, piśācas, ḍākinīs, poison, and so forth—[if they were merely accidental].
If stainless consciousness were directly perceived through a cognition distinct from hearing and inference, how could it have been spoken of by the Sage, Tārkṣya, and others?
Moreover, his knowledge is not derived from inference, because no prior perception of it has occurred, and because a logical mark (*liṅga*) connected to it is impossible to perceive.
Nor [is it] heard from another [source], because the same line of questioning applies; and such a form, which is non-contradictory, has been cultivated, not by chance.
This very teaching is not a conceptual construction based on another cause; for when [the function] has been performed by another cause, that [name] is suspected [to be applied].
