Just as there is a chance occurrence of a tree’s standing still for one who is approaching a river with a turbulent current and thirst, so too is the stability of the mind.
And this which has been spoken is not for the foolish whose minds are distracted; for this is a proven means for the fruit, possessing a fixed sequence.
He who is that supreme reality which shines forth as the true object—unheard and un-inferred—is of such a nature as to be the communicator of direct perceptual knowledge.

Just as water and other such things perceived through direct perception are established by another person—namely, the Supreme Sage—who, out of his own firm conviction, has declared them; for he possesses the capacity to know that which is unheard, inferred, beyond the senses, characterized by ritual procedures, seals, mandalas, and so forth, and unknown to others.

Therefore, by means of superior cognitions (*atiśaya-jñānaiḥ*) acting as lamps (*varttibhiḥ*), through power and skillful means (*bala-upāyaiḥ*), it is possible (*śakyate*) to know everything (*sarvaḥ*) that is additional (*adhikaḥ*) and beyond the senses (*atīndriyaḥ*).

Just as for one who stands within a single room (*eka-apavaraka-sthasya*), that which is perceptible (*pratyakṣam*) and functions (*pravarttate*) therein might have the capacity (*śaktiḥ*) [to perceive it], but certainly not (*na eva*) with respect to what is inside another room (*apavarka-antare*).

This is appropriate for you to determine (*niścetum*) when there is an experience (*anubhave*) possessing the capacity (*sāmarthya*) for all sentient beings (*sarva-sattva*). Otherwise (*anyathā*), what would be the basis (*nibandhana*) for determining the effect (*kārye*)—given the absence of capacity in another nature (*anya-ātman*)—by means of examples (*udāharaṇena*) such as "being human" (*puruṣatva*) and so forth? [In that case,] an over-extension (*atiprasajyate*) would follow.
For if your dullness (*jāḍya*) were thus established even by your own example, then all wise men (*sūri*) would become dull-witted (*jaḍabuddhi*).
That "there is no finality (*pariniṣṭhā*) of knowledge (*jñāna*) in any person (*puruṣa*)"—this too is merely a statement (*vāṅmātra*) uttered without reason (*ahetuka*).
Alternatively, the statement thus proclaimed by Ṛtuparṇa was made with reference to sentient beings who are dull-witted and whose own intellects are unpurified.
The proof for the existence of the Omniscient One has been stated in detail, and the refutation of that [proof] by others has already been rejected.
Alternatively, even if its occurrence in that means [of proof] has not been stated, by the mere fact of the absence of a subverting [reason], its occurrence is understood.

For when no subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is perceived and a proving factor (*sādhaka*) is manifested, doubt (*saṃśaya*) arises by which that [doubt] reaches the state of being considered probable (*sambhāvanā*).
When that [Veda] is being considered as possible, this restriction—that dharma is characterized by the Veda alone as an independent authority—is established.

The capacity of perception (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to an object of cognition (*vijñeya*) that is future (*anāgata*) would likewise exist; that has been stated in the examination of the three times (*traikālya-parīkṣaṇa*).
Or rather, by the power of yoga, the mental [cognition] of yogins may become clearly manifest, resembling that which is real, unborn, and free from the desire for signs and scriptures.
Because consciousness has as its object the manifestation of its own self, and because it is clearly manifested, that [consciousness] is held to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, there exists indeed a perceiver of objects beyond the senses directly; because an eternal word does not exist, no one perceives [them] by means of it.
The wise have said that the cognition of the Sage regarding supersensuous objects is derived from inference based on what was previously stated, and not from any other scripture composed by him.

Furthermore, beginninglessness (*anāditā*) is not stated as the reason for establishing the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of artificial sentences (*kṛtrima-vākyānām*); because that [beginninglessness] exists even in the case of invalid [cognitions] (*apramāṇe*).
For instance, there is no validity (*mānatā*) even for the words of nihilists (*nāstika*) and others, despite their being beginningless.

The beginninglessness of the speaker—which is said (*ucyate*) by us (*asmābhiḥ*) for the sake of establishing (*siddhyai*) the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of unauthored sentences (*akṛtrima-vākyānām*)—is indeed refuted (*niṣidhyate*) by us out of rivalry (*spardhayā*).
The speakers are equal to the authors, and the authority of the Vedas arises from the production of the meaning through the narration of that which was composed by them.

Therefore, because the Vedic sentences are dependent [on others], there is no validity even for the speakers themselves who do not personally perceive dharma; indeed, that [validity] does not exist at all.

Even for such speakers, if beginninglessness (*anāditā*) is postulated (*kalpyamānā*), it does not differ from that of the nihilist (*nāstika*) and others, because of the persistence of the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of their words.

Therefore, since there is no distinction (*viśeṣatvāt*) regarding what is unknown, everything falls into equality (*tulyatām*). In this case, both validity (*mānatva*) and invalidity (*apramāṇatva*) would be beginningless (*anādinī*).
Or rather, there is this very distinction: that [the Sage] has himself seen the Dharma and, being composed of compassion, has spoken it; whereas [there is no such thing] regarding his words.

That dharma is said by all the wise to be such, because from it— performed according to the prescribed rules of its specific mantras, yoga, and so forth— there arises both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*),
as well as visible results (*dṛṣṭadharma*) such as wisdom, health, and sovereign power.

From the vision of the selflessness of all phenomena as they have been revealed, there is the turning away from that [vision]. From the arising of the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*) proceeds, characterized by the aspects of "I" and "mine. Through such conceit (*māna*), every affliction (*kleśa*) proceeds.
That illustration of selflessness, which is the adversary of the perception of a sentient being, ceases once it has become habitual through repeated practice.
The heap of afflictions, which has that [self-grasping] as its root, is abandoned through the absence of its cause; when that [cause] is no longer present, existence is not born again.
This is proclaimed as liberation, the absolute deliverance; therefore, the vision of selflessness is the sole, peerless gateway to peace.

Even for all the non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthya*), liberation (*mukti*) is desired through the cessation of the *ahaṃkāra*; yet, as long as there exists a self (*ātman*) as a sentient being (*sattva*), the *ahaṃkāra* does not cease.

This is because its capable cause remains present, and because the object [of that cause] has not been refuted. However, if that [object] were refuted, it would follow by necessity that there is a cognitive inversion (*viparyāsa*).
Thus, it is not at all fitting for me to think, "If indeed I exist by necessity, or if I am false"—for one who knows reality thus attains nirvāṇa.
Therefore, even if there exists, in other [non-Buddhist] systems, a slight attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) by way of the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions,
there is not even the slightest attainment of liberation (*apavarga*), because the roots of existence— the afflictions (*kleśa*)— have not been uprooted due to the persistence of [wrong] views.
Furthermore, those ten wholesome paths of action which were proclaimed by the Protector and embraced by right view become exceedingly powerful.
Enveloped by views regarding sentient beings due to attachment, we are impure because of our misconceptions; therefore, the pure fruit does not arise from them.
Thus, when one does not see for oneself that which is taught by the Sage, the seventh [teacher] of reality, who—possessing a healthy intellect—would proclaim the Dharma?
And the wise do not assert that omniscience belongs to the Protector (*tāyin*) or that there is any permanence of the Veda, because such permanence is impossible in both cases.

The sublation of that [omniscience] has been stated due to the contradiction between succession and non-succession; therefore, it is not in any way logical for the effect, such as cognition and so forth, to exist. Furthermore, since an omniscient being is not perceived at present, this refutation has been stated by you and by all others.
Your non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is solitary and subject to deviation; however, the absence of perception of all other [things] is doubtful. Thus, it is not a means of proof (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that "it existed" is not possible—just as [the past] cannot be negated—and even regarding the past, its negation is improper because such negation is impossible.
It might be thought: that path which is past is empty of the All-Seeing One because it is time, just as the present time is perceived.

This proof is not tenable because it is characterized by exclusion (*vyatirekitvāt*) and is doubtful; therefore, this present time is not ascertained to be empty [of a creator], nor is the past time so ascertained at present due to the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī-hetu-abhāvāt*). However, by what means could it not be possible that [a creator existed] in the past, just as in the case of Rāma and others?

Having established that [qualities] such as wisdom (*prajñā*) possess the status of being the subject (*dharmitva*), the logical mark (*liṅga*) has been stated; therefore, neither is a logical mark perceived, nor is existence (*sattā*) proven.
(Note: Read the fourth quarter as *na nāto dṛśyate liṅgam*.)
We do not establish that the omniscient one [exists] by means of scripture; for when the previously mentioned mark exists, who indeed would say [it exists] on the basis of scripture?
But if you accept that the Veda possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then why is the omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) of the Blessed One not understood by the deluded?
For, within the branches of the [Vedic] tradition, the name of the Supreme Sage, the Omniscient One, is clearly recited by learned Brahmins as the cause [of his existence].

Thus, he who, having manifested himself in a dream as a six-tusked, pure white elephant, was born as a Bodhisattva—an ocean of virtues, renowned as "The Omniscient One," whose very self is compassion, and who has attained the state.

The father of all the world, pure and immortal, does not admit that this internal space within the branches is contained within the Veda; therefore, there is no reason for you to harbor hatred toward him.

Those well-known properties beginning with accent (*svara*) and so forth, which are to arise from the Veda, are capable of being produced even here, because there is the mere possibility of human will.

[Objection: But surely the eternal scripture cannot be understood in this way here, if it is eternal; [if] there were an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) by others regarding that [eternal scripture], then there would be non-eternality.
Since the scripture's eternity is established, the postulation of that [eternity] is futile; for people will understand that very dharma from it.

Indeed, even in this well-known Veda, there is no eternality whatsoever [of the words], because their fruit consists of cognitions that arise immediately after an effort and proceed in a sequential order.
But if the acceptance of the authority of this well-known [Veda] is admitted, then for you, authority would also follow for other branches, because they too possess the nature of being Veda.
Alternatively, that which is to be made known must certainly be established through reasoning as being unauthoritative; otherwise, its lack of mention in the Veda would remain doubtful.
Let the Veda possess eternity; however, in that case, how could there be its dependence upon others, since it would be non-eternal due to its connection with perishable objects?

If this is so, how is it that clarified butter (*ājya*), wild rice (*nīvāra*), gold-crested [peacocks] (*cāmīkarajaṭa*), and so forth, which are impermanent (*anitya*), are said (*ucyante*) by that existent (*satā*) eternal self (*nityātmanā*)?

Even there, [if it is argued that] the universal (*jāti*) is eternal, surely that too has been refuted; moreover, when words denote only that [universal], there would be no cognition (*mati*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth.

Even in the case of his speech, its eternity is not lost; or rather, let there be the form [of the word] even in the Omniscient One, for by that [form], the eternity of the other [the Veda] is established.

If the Vedas possess independence regarding their meaning, there can be no certainty of that meaning from the Veda itself (*svataḥ*), nor from another (*parasmāt*), because [the speaker] is helpless under the influence of delusion and other such defects.

(The word) "that" (is the third person singular pronoun); "valid cognition" (is the nominative singular feminine); "in this regard" (is the adverb); "thus" (is the particle); "this is the meaning" (is the masculine nominative singular); [derived] from "the scripture" (the feminine genitive singular); "thus" (is the particle); "one desiring heaven" (masculine nominative singular) "should offer the agnihotra sacrifice" (second person singular optative of the root *hu* with the prefix *pra-*, i.e., *juhuyāt*); "not" (is the negative particle); "in this manner" (is the adverb); [refers to] "the Victor" (masculine nominative singular), "the Omniscient One" (masculine nominative singular).
Thus, the Omniscient One is clearly understood through his teaching (*upadeśataḥ*), because of his thorough knowledge of the primary matters of heaven and liberation.
In what way is the knowledge of the number of grains of sand in the ocean of use to us? What is the point of our being aware of his knowledge other than that [knowledge]?

Even this rule must indeed be stated as being figurative (*gauṇatvena*), like an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) or a mantra; for [the rule] would otherwise be established only when the Omniscient One has been refuted.

Since the previously mentioned sublation (*bādhaka*) does not apply (*ayoge*), and since [the capacity] has been established in detail (*savistaram*), the restriction (*niyama*) regarding the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense is doubtful (*sandigdha*), because the primary (*mukhya*) meaning is also possible (*sambhavāt*).

If non-obstruction (*apratighatā*) consisting merely of cognition (*jñānamātra*) is described as being fruitful (*saphalā*) with respect to objects such as *dharma* and so forth, then clearly the world (*jagat*) has been conquered by the Buddhas (*buddhaiḥ*).

Because it has been established previously that their knowledge regarding worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), along with these [qualities], is non-obstructive (*apratigha*), extremely clear (*atisphuṭa*), and unique (*ā-vaṇika*).
That consciousness which has been set in motion within the self through the practice of meditation—its non-obstructed nature has also already been established previously for them.
This very knowledge is that vision of the pure self which arises from the realization of the mere nature of the mind, free from adventitious stains;
it was previously established by the Fully Awakened Ones as the intellect whose form consists of the knower and the unknowable, and which is empty of the two-fold affliction.
By him, the perfected ones, the great-minded, the wise, who have not been accustomed to saṃsāra, whose teachings will come to possess sovereignty—[those teachings] which shine even today.
In a mind that is luminous by nature, yet stained and non-dual in its aspect—who, being undeluded regarding the dual aspect, could conceive of it otherwise? (Who could form a contrary notion?)

In the awakening to the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya-dvaya*), the faults such as passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) that arise from conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpa*) regarding women and so forth are exhausted without effort (*aprayatnataḥ*).
This is that supreme reality which the speaker of truth proclaimed, and which bestows all prosperity, being beyond the reach of Keśava and others.

The self (*ātman*) is known by others as being stable, resembling pure crystal; yet that [notion] is their misconception (*viparyāsa*), because of the refutation of a permanent self (*nitya-ātman*). If consciousness (*vijñāna*) were the grasper of itself by itself, then it would follow that consciousness perceives its entire self simultaneously.
If it were not born from that [cause], or if it were admitted to be eternal, then it would not have as its object another mind or a person;

for this alone is the knowledge of that [object], and not that which is the perception of a pure self, because of the detailed proof established regarding the deficiency of the characteristics of the apprehended.
If the nature of cognition (*jñāna-rūpatva*) is admitted even for itself, there would still be no apprehension [of it] due to the existence of a difference between the seen and the seeing.

If that cognition is held to have a self-luminous nature (*svayaṃprakāśa-rūpatva*), then self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is attained, and cognition (*mati*) is [established as being] perceptible (*pratyakṣā*).

There exists no connection whatsoever between Brahman and the others on the one hand and the Veda on the other, because of their difference, because of [Brahman's] eternity, and because of the impossibility of its dependence on anything else. Furthermore, it is therefore illogical that Brahman and the others possess the nature of being embodied by the Veda, nor that the Veda consists of all knowledge and meaning, since these remain undetermined.

The Omniscient One, the Perfectly Awakened One, has been established by His own independent power; yet He is not conceived as being like Brahmā and others, because [He lacks] a body [composed of] the Vedas.

Because they exist outside of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the state of being mortal is not admitted by us for the Buddhas who possess the five destinies as their very nature; rather, that [state] is considered to be an emanation (*nirmāṇa*).
There, in the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha, which is devoid of impure dwellings, the perfectly awakened ones awaken; however, it is the emanation that awakens here.
How, then, is mortality determined by you independently, without the mediation of his own admission? For such is the state of affairs.
Nor is it accepted by us that you are omniscient out of a desire for rivalry with them; for who would conceive a rivalry between those who are true and sky-flowers?
It has been established that eternal things, by virtue of their separation from all power, are devoid of form; therefore, the Three-Eyed One and others are not accepted as being supreme by us.
Furthermore, their knowledge is erroneous because of [their] perception of a self and so forth; however, that of the Buddhas is non-erroneous, as has been established in detail.
There is no rivalry with them in reality, because there is a vast difference; for what man of sound vision would seek to rival those afflicted by cataracts?

Furthermore, the eternality of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth, as well as of the Vedas, has been cast aside; therefore, we do not accept an eternal scripture (*āgama*). Nor do we accept the establishment of the existence of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) by means of analogy (*upamāna*), because of the lack of authority (*apramāṇatā*) regarding that [analogy] which has been stated; and thus, its existence is not established from that source.
Existence being established, similarity is understood; and this proof under discussion is for the sake of [establishing] the existence of the omniscient one.

Therefore, there is no establishment [of the omniscient being] by means of analogy; consequently, the negation [of such a being] is fruitless. However, if all men have been seen by you to be non-omniscient, then [the negation is indeed possible].

[Your] omniscience (*sarva-vittā*) would exist (*syāt*) solely (*eva*) because of [your] seeing (*īkṣaṇāt*) what is obstructed (*vyavahita*), distant (*dūra*), and because of [your] power (*śakteḥ*) regarding knowledge (*jñāna*) in relation to another continuum (*santāna*).

While [a person] stands before one, how could there be a certain determination regarding him that "this man is not omniscient"? For you are a knower of things beyond the senses (*atīndriya-vid*) in such a state.

If, upon seeing a non-omniscient person who is [regarded as] certain [to be such], one were to conclude that all [others] are non-omniscient—because of the certainty regarding [him] as being like the unborn [Brahmā] and so forth—then [if this is] accepted, there would be no certainty regarding the property [of omniscience] because of the sublation of what is seen. Indeed, even when the doubt regarding sublation has been stated, it does not differ from the sublation of what is seen.
Who else, other than a dull-witted person, would out of delusion conceive such a faultless statement concerning the Buddhas—established as it is regarding the path to heaven and liberation?
Even though delusion was produced by him, those who perceive it attain from that very source worldly prosperity as well as supreme peace from the defects of the mind.
This instruction of the Buddhas alone is not rooted in the Veda; for that [Veda] is proclaimed to be flawless, whereas in the Śruti it is possessed of flaws.
Such an instruction is not for the sake of their own accomplishment; rather, this entire undertaking was made for the sake of others.
Therefore, those whose nature is compassion have said that this state belongs to all who are initiated through their kinship with the world, which is based on the establishment of its welfare.
For those who have been brought under the sway of greed, fear, hatred, envy, and so forth, the teaching for them—being pitiless by nature—might be merely partial;
however, those who are dependent upon compassion, who clearly demonstrate reality, and who are free from all suspicion of fault, have everywhere performed the teaching.
Just as a person may become corrupted by faults such as ignorance and the like, even so does the compassion of the Protectors arise toward them.
They certainly do not desire a relationship such as marriage or bringing a bride; rather, they must provide assistance, and for that reason, this song of the virtuous was sung.
O wise ones, [those who are] seers regard with equanimity a perfected brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even a dog-cooker;
for what pride can there be in birth when it is prohibited in hundreds of ways? And since that [birth] is unestablished, how can it be considered a distinction based on some other excellence?

Moreover, all those of a different species (*vijātayaḥ*) here would, without distinction, become the supports (*ādhārāḥ*) for qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*), provided they have destroyed all impurities (*prakṣīṇāśeṣakalmaṣāḥ*) and rely upon that; otherwise, they do not achieve excellence (*vaiśiṣṭyam*), just like the twice-born (*dvijajāti*) and the hunter (*lubdhaka*).

The practices that are well-known, such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others, are indeed conventional (*sāṃvṛta*); for they are like those [practices] belonging to others, even though they occur among artificial [beings].
A long time has passed, and the extreme fickleness of women is such that even for one who exists [among them], it is not possible to ascertain his status as a Brahmin.
There exists no one who is a knower of supersensuous objects; moreover, even the eternal Veda has not declared your lineage's purity.

Therefore, even Manu and the others, being twice-born themselves yet ignorant of these [twice-born ones], would not have imparted this instruction to the twice-born, due to their uncertainty regarding that matter.

I suspect that Manu and others, being dull-witted in their study of the Vedas, were unable to provide a rational justification for some point regarding the Veda; perceiving themselves to be incompetent, those brahmins gave instruction to other brahmins alone.
The Purāṇa, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs, and medical science—these four established authorities must not be refuted by means of logical arguments.
I consider this mere intimidation to have been given by them to the dull-witted; therefore, how indeed could the status of being an authority exist anywhere other than as a matter of words?

Furthermore, by those great-souled ones who have clearly ascertained the logical consistency (*yuktārthatva*) of their own utterances (*ukti*) and their own capacity (*sāmarthya*) for making [the truth] understood.
Free from all fear, we roar the lion’s roar, O you who bring about the exhaustion and intoxication of the wicked heretics, like rutting elephants.
O monks, my word is to be accepted by the wise after they have examined it—not out of mere respect—just as gold [is tested] by heating, cutting, and rubbing on a touchstone.
Those Brahmins who are ultimate—because they have cast off evil and have practiced the stainless selflessness—are indeed [those] within the teaching of the Sage.
By him alone is the ascetic proclaimed as such by the ascetics and likewise by the brahmins; for the fourfold doctrines of others are empty.
Thus, the proof has been established: that there exists some person who is omniscient and so forth, yet this is not faulty due to the deficiency of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

"For indeed, the wise followers of the Sugata exert effort toward the accomplishment of the complete comprehension of all objects, even though [such effort] is fruitless at the outset; yet, even in this case, it is proclaimed that [the teaching] concerning one portion of what is known would not be the speech of an omniscient one, because of the prior statement [to the contrary] based on the connection with the knowledge of all."
Just as one of limited vision, having experienced desired objects and so forth, and having projected them into the mind, subsequently speaks of the bases of that experience.
That statement is not his birthright; that knowledge of that object might exist for him in such a way, but the word "omniscient" is distinguished by the distinction of its cause.

[The state of being] its cause has passed away; for him, consciousness is the sign of all things. However, since there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding any object whatsoever, what kind of intention (*vivakṣā*) could he possibly have? Indeed, because his conduct has been abandoned, no conceptual construction occurs for him.
For such a thought is not afflicted; it does not exist because of the destruction of his obscurations. But who can prevent that which is favorable to the welfare of the world and is wholesome?
He does not settle upon the meaningfulness of that conceptual construction; for he knows it to be without objective basis, since he is equal to a magician.
Just as a certain magician knows that the mind has a determined range of objects—such as horses and so forth—which are actually devoid of objective reality, he does not become deluded by them.

This [statement], beginning with "by the twice-born" (*dvijātinā*), shines when it is being proclaimed (*kīrtyamānam*) to those who have faith (*śraddadhāneṣu*); however, this has not been stated in accordance with the subject matter at hand (*anurūpeṇārthaprakṛtasya*).
And what is under discussion here is this: thus, being uncomprehending of all objects, he is not capable of providing instruction; and regarding that, those of great intelligence have said: "ah."
If he were not capable of providing instruction, what would happen then? Therefore, you should say that there would be no scripture (*āgama*).
Regarding this, they say: "It might be so if that [person] were seen by you as speaking thus; but if this undesirable consequence is urged by means of a *prasaṅga*-proof," [then it is not so].
If speakerhood were not admitted, there would be no acceptance of scripture; but if that [scripture] composed by him is accepted, let his speakerhood be admitted.

If such a principle is well-known among proponents of logic (*nyāyavādins*), and if [the property] is considered by others to be established through a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*) based merely on faith, [then...]

In the case of [the scripture's] being well-known, there would be a self-reliant proof based on reasoning; moreover, that scripture is accepted by the opponent as having been composed by him [the Buddha]. Such is it.
The teachings on the accumulations issue forth at will from that person—even from walls and the like—just as from a *cintāmaṇi*.

Therefore, by virtue of his sovereign power (*ādhipatya*), he is designated as the "author" (*praṇetā*) of it; yet his status as a speaker (*vaktṛtva*) does not follow, for it is not accompanied by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, we, being faithless (*aśraddadhānāḥ*), [say] that this which has been spoken is thus; for we, who do not know the meaning of the *prasaṅga*, seek logical arguments (*yuktīḥ*).

And why is there no status of being taught by an authoritative person (*āptopadiṣṭatā*) for those [sounds] emerging from walls and so forth, when their occurrence is due to the state of being under the influence of that [authoritative person]?
(Variant: *kuṭya-*)

How could those [speeches], which are devoid of confused talk, violence, and other such contemptible matters, be uttered by those whose nature is playfulness, such as *piśācas* and the like? For the teaching of confused talk, violence, and other such contemptible matters—the activity of those whose nature is playfulness, such as *piśācas* and the like—is not found among them.

That [cognition] which is consistent with the two means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its entire object-domain, and for which not even the slightest sublation (*bādhā*) is observed by those two means of valid knowledge, is considered [to be valid].

That which is free from contradiction between earlier and later parts, even regarding matters entirely beyond perception, which serves as the motivator for all persons in the arising of virtues such as compassion,

which possesses all aspects, which is endowed with true activity, which establishes what is beneficial both in this world and the next, and which brings about various forms of prosperity for those who are fortunate— [that is the scripture].
If that [statement] which expresses the antidote to the entire mass of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and which shatters the gates, doors, and fortresses of the city of *nirvāṇa*,
were the speech of those whose nature is playfulness, or of *rākṣasa*s, then let them alone be the perfectly awakened ones (*saṃbuddha*s), because of their abiding in all those characteristics.

When another name is applied to an entity that possesses a distinct nature, that [nature] does not cease; however, one who applies an improper designation to a distinguished object would be censured by the virtuous.

Those unrefined actions characterized by sexual misconduct, false speech, violence toward living beings, and so forth, which have been manifested by a certain word—that word is suspected (*śaṅkyate*) to have been composed by *bhujaṅgas*, *piśācas*, and the like; for such [speech] is likely (*sambhāvyate*) from those who delight in such activities.

A single cognition is indeed observed to perceive simultaneously multiple mutually contradictory natures, such as the pure, the impure, and so forth; for these are not contradictory to consciousness by virtue of having characteristics that exist through mutual exclusion, nor do they contradict one another because they cannot coexist in a single [cognition]. If they were contradictory, it would have to be possible for them to exist within that same [cognition].

Note: Read *asahasthānāt* for *asahasthānam*. (The state of being illuminated, nominative singular; *eka-* [single]; *jñāna-* [cognition]; *tu* [but]; *na* [not]; *virodhitā*, feminine nominative singular; *teṣu*, masculine locative plural; *sakṛt-* [simultaneously]; *īkṣaṇāt*, neuter ablative singular; *cakṣuṣā*, neuter instrumental singular; *śuci-* [pure]; *aśuci-* [impure]; *ahi-* [snake]; *śikhin-* [peacock]; *ādeḥ*, masculine genitive singular. There is no contradiction among those [objects], because they are perceived simultaneously by the eye, as in the case of the pure and the impure, the snake and the peacock, and so forth.

That sensation which exists in the distinction of pleasure, pain, and so forth, does not exist simultaneously; it should be understood as such because of the non-proximity [of all objects] due to the absence of a cause.
It is not contradicted, since distinctions such as blue, yellow, striking, and so forth—which are mutually exclusive—are perceived simultaneously through their spatial differentiation.
The Omniscient One has been established as one whose circle of cognition in a single moment pervades all objects of knowledge; therefore, a sequential process is resorted to.
Whatever he desires to know, he knows that very thing by necessity; for such is his power, since he has abandoned all conduct.
He proceeds either simultaneously or sequentially, according to his own will; for a being who has attained knowledge is indeed a master.
(Note: The phrase *sakṣaṇair hy ādibhiḥ* was not translated as its meaning was not understood.)
Or rather, he knows all that is to be known by nature, through sixteen moments of mind in succession; therefore, he is "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*).
In such a consciousness of the Lord, there occurs [cognition] gradually; not even a mere fraction (*lava*) is required, so what need is there to mention a limit of a hundred years?
He who perceives all that is his own with an undivided state of being, he indeed perceives the essential natures of all things.

That which is called "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtta*) from things possessing a self (*sātmaka*), non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), and so forth—that very thing is the particular characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*); it is what is here termed the "universal" (*sāmānya*), because it serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for tranquility (*śama*) and imaginative construction (*utprekṣā*).

That consciousness which is the grasper is that which is to be realized by the lords of yogins through the manifestation of the power of cultivation; it has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
That universal which is imagined by others as being inexpressible in terms of identity, difference, and so forth, is not grasped by this mind of the yogin.

That mental consciousness of the lord of yogins is non-conceptual and non-erroneous; however, with respect to the apprehension of that [object], it is subject to the consequence of being "clung to" as being permeated by conceptual construction and delusion.

That which is proclaimed as the universal (*sāmānya*)—which has the nature of conceptual construction, is inexpressible, and consists of the form of eternal persistence—that is devoid of any real form (*nīrūpa*).
He is designated as "omniscient" who knows everything—every action together with its cause—by means of supramundane, innate knowledge born of meditative concentration.

Existence (*sattā*, feminine nominative singular) exists before that (*tasya*, masculine genitive singular) by means of inference (*anumānena*, neuter instrumental singular); that (*tat*, neuter nominative singular) is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇam*, neuter nominative singular) regarding its (*asya*, masculine genitive singular) existence (*sat-bhāve*, masculine locative singular)—such is the case.
Whether simultaneously or in succession, when he imparts instruction from the effect that has been manifested, he possesses the capacity for that as well.
This teaching—immaculate, characterized by the selflessness of phenomena, thoroughly practiced, established by all the scriptures, and uncontradicted by all means of valid cognition—belongs to him.

That which is beyond the range of Keśava and others— beings who wander through saṃsāra and are unaccustomed to such knowledge— and which is worshipped with exceeding devotion by the wise with their heads,
is the cause of the destruction of the host of enemies and evils, and the means for the attainment of various prosperities and final liberation.
He who has obtained uncommon means, who is distinct from all men without exception, he alone is the omniscient Lord; this [statement] is supported by valid means of knowledge.
And thus, when someone indeed arises as omniscient, then human speech is the cause for the realization of Dharma and so forth;
however, reflection on [his] being formless and so forth is not applicable to the omniscient one, for just as your knowledge pertains to some particular object, so too does the supreme [knowledge].
